(2) **§15.2's two expiry rules are row CHECKs** — `sessions_expiry_absolute` (`expires_at <= created_at + SESSION_MAX_AGE_MS`, "no later than 30 days after creation") and `sessions_expiry_inactivity` (`expires_at <= last_seen_at + SESSION_INACTIVITY_TIMEOUT_MS`, "expire after 7 days of inactivity"), the durations exported (`30 × 86_400_000`, `7 × 86_400_000`) with the shipped literals drift-pinned in the spec. `expires_at` carries the **effective** expiry the session layer maintains — the tighter of the two bounds, refreshed together with `last_seen_at` (task 155) — so one column plus the expiry index answers validation and §11.3's cleanup completely while `created_at`/`last_seen_at` keep both rules independently auditable; at-bound values pass (`<=`). `last_seen_at` is NOT NULL initialized to creation: the login that mints a session is its first sighting, so the inactivity window runs from a real timestamp from birth and the inactivity CHECK needs no NULL escape. No lower-bound ordering CHECKs — the D-032/D-034 clock-skew leniency, and §15.2 states upper bounds only; an already-expired row is inert, never lost history a rejected write would have preserved. (3) **Not account-bound** — §15.1's service has one user; sessions are service state, not account history, so the §11.2 cascading-deletion policy for purged account history does not reach this table: no `account_id`, no foreign key, and purging every account leaves rows untouched (pinned by test, foreign keys on). (4) **Index** — `sessions_expiry (expires_at)` is §11.2's "sessions by expiry", named the D-034 way; the primary-key autoindex serves the token-hash lookup; no query orders sessions any other way, so no other index. (5) **`meta` is exactly key/value** — `key TEXT PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL` with `meta_key_nonempty`, `value TEXT NOT NULL`, no further columns (the D-032 exact-set rule) and deliberately no shape CHECK on `value`: §11.2 states none, and a JSON or charset contract would freeze a writer convention into the on-disk schema (changeable only by successor migration) and could reject states the service produces — the D-039 identical-states rule. Task 091's cleanup metadata lands as rows it defines; the repository (088) types them.

**Reasons.** The done-condition demanded a structural, test-verified no-raw-token guarantee, and the accounts D-032 precedent (exact column pin + credential-fragment rejection) transfers directly — strengthened here by the hex-shape CHECK, which the accounts table never needed because it stores no token-derived value at all. Encoding §15.2's two expiry bounds as CHECKs follows the D-034 rule of encoding exactly what the spec states as a property of the record: a session row claiming validity beyond either bound is a spec violation no honest writer can produce, and the bounds are durations added to a stored timestamp — computed, not independently wall-clock-read — so the clock-skew argument that rejected `ended_at >= started_at` does not apply to the upper bounds (it does keep lower-bound ordering CHECKs out). The single effective-expiry column over separate absolute/sliding columns was chosen because cleanup (§11.3 "delete expired sessions") and validation both reduce to one comparison against one column, the index list stays minimal, and both underlying rules remain recoverable from the stored `created_at`/`last_seen_at`; a two-column design would double the writer's coherence duties for zero additional guarantee. The 43-character base64url demonstration in the test suite pins that the raw token's expected wire form is unrepresentable, closing the loop between §15.2's cookie text and the schema; the lowercase-hex wire form is the one no schema can exclude, which is why this decision records the non-hex precondition for task 154 instead of claiming the shape CHECK's totality. `meta` stays shape-free for the same minimal-contract reason D-032 kept `plan_name` at absent-or-non-blank: nothing in the spec constrains values, so nothing in the schema does.

**Consequences.** `MIGRATIONS` carries seven entries; a fresh database migrates to schema version 7 at startup, `schemaVersionStatus` reports `up-to-date` at version 7 after the run, and the schema-6→7 forward test §11.4 requires lives in `test/integration/sessions-meta.spec.ts`. Task 081–086 canonical-set pins in `accounts.spec.ts`, `collection-runs.spec.ts`, `snapshots.spec.ts`, `metric-values.spec.ts`, `quota-events.spec.ts`, and `raw-responses.spec.ts` were updated to the grown set (D-031's planned growth, recorded here as those tests' deliberate fixture changes). Tasks 154/155 build session minting, refresh, and revocation on this shape — minting the cookie in a non-hex wire form (base64url; a 64-lowercase-hex cookie would be shape-identical to the digest this table keys on, the D-056 precondition), storing only the digest, computing `expires_at` as the tighter bound (the CHECKs reject anything looser), supplying all timestamps from the injected clock (D-021), and hashing with `digest('hex')`; task 091 deletes expired sessions through the `sessions_expiry` range scan and stores its cleanup bookkeeping as `meta` rows; task 088's repository owns typed reads/writes for both tables. The table, column, constraint, and index names (including `sessions_expiry`), the hex-shape and expiry-bound CHECKs, and the exported duration constants are on-disk contract: renaming any of them, widening a bound, or changing a duration requires a successor decision (and a successor migration for already-migrated databases). Raw `DatabaseSync` test handles default to `foreign_keys=OFF` (D-034's pinned note) — the not-account-bound test sets the pragma explicitly.

## D-057 — Finite derivations only: Z.ai metric derivations (and the windowSeconds scaling) fire only when their arithmetic is a finite number; the property suite is the standing proof (spec §8.4)

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§8.4](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#84-normalized-snapshot-and-metric-model), [§17.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#171-required-test-coverage) · **Tasks:** [101](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-010, D-047, D-053

**Decision.** Task 101 audited every §8.4 derivation path in `mapping.ts` and confirmed the two structural rules by reading — percentages never feed an absolute field (the done-condition), and derivations never chain (D-053.4: `percentUsed = 100·used/limit` reads only _supplied_ `used`/`limit`). One behavior gap found and closed: (1) **A derivation fires only when its arithmetic yields a finite number.** IEEE-754 overflow turns finite inputs into `Infinity`/`NaN` — `MAX_VALUE − (−MAX_VALUE)`, `MAX_VALUE + MAX_VALUE`, `100 · MAX_VALUE / MIN_VALUE`, `number × 3600` at extremes — and the pre-101 code emitted such results as metric values, which `findNormalizedMetricProblems` rejects as non-finite: the emitted snapshot broke the very invariants D-053 guarantees it always satisfies. Now the field stays absent and unlisted, the supplied values survive, and the metric stays valid — §8.4's "only when the required original fields support it" read as: source values whose operation overflows do not support the derivation. Result-finiteness subsumes task 100 review's P1-1 zero-allowance guard (`0/0` NaN and `x/0` ±Infinity are non-finite), so zero-allowance behavior is unchanged. `percentRemaining = 100 − percentUsed` stays unguarded: subtracting a finite percentage from 100 cannot overflow (the true sum sits far below the rounding threshold). (2) **The proof is property-based and standing**: `test/unit/zai-coding-plan-mapping.property.spec.ts` proves the done-condition over every recognized identity × arbitrary finite percentage (no absolute fields, `unit: PERCENT` except the fixed-`REQUESTS` monthly quota, verbatim `percentUsed`, `percentRemaining = 100 − percentUsed`, `derivedFields` exactly `['percentRemaining']`), and a generated field-subset oracle — exact triples (identity holds by construction: oracle and mapping evaluate the same float operation), provably violated triples, arbitrary field presence, IEEE-754 extremes always in play via constants — asserts per entry each field's presence/absence and exact value, the validity branch and its `invalidReason`, unit discipline, the `windowSeconds` rule, `derivedFields` listing exactly the computed fields (D-010 closed set, no duplicates), no-chaining, the percent-sum identity, finiteness of every emitted number, and a clean `findProviderSnapshotProblems`. Reverting the finiteness guard fails four property tests and four example tests — the proof has killing power, not just coverage. (3) **Deliberate non-changes**: the supplied-triple identity check keeps exact float equality (`used + remaining !== limit`) per D-047.1's documented rule — rejecting a rounding-inconsistent triple as an invalid metric is the safe direction, no epsilon introduced — and `DerivedMetricField` stays the D-010 closed set (no enum extension, no migration).

**Reasons.** The audit's job was to make the done-condition genuinely verified rather than asserted; the gap it found is exactly the failure class task 100's review flagged (zero-allowance NaN) but patched only for quotients — addition/subtraction/multiplication overflow is the same mode on the other three derivation paths and the window scaling. Skipping rather than invalidating is the right response: the supplied values are finite and self-consistent, so dropping them would lose real measurements (spec §2.5), while emitting a non-finite value breaks every downstream consumer of the §8.4 model. Property tests were chosen over more examples because the firing conditions are arithmetic predicates over a continuous input space the examples can only sample; the oracle is written from the rules (declarative, per-field) rather than mirroring `buildMetric`'s branches, and the `FC_SEED` convention (test/helpers/property.ts) keeps failures reproducible.

**Consequences.** A payload whose values are extreme enough to overflow their sum/difference/quotient now maps to a metric without the derived member (nothing listed — nothing was derived); plausible Z.ai scales (integer credits/requests) are unaffected. The finiteness guard, the exact-equality triple identity, and the property suite are contract: relaxing any requires a successor decision. Downstream consumers (task 105's classifier, 088's storage) receive §8.4-invariant-clean metrics as before; no storage or API change — the D-010 closed derived set is untouched, so no migration.

## D-058 — The repository facade: synchronous typed methods, writer-supplied time, internal FK carriers, and the SQL-text gate (spec §8.1, §11; task 088)

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§8.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#81-provider-interface), [§11](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#11-persistence-schema-retention-and-migrations), [§3](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#3-technology-and-packaging) · **Tasks:** [088](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-009, D-021, D-027, D-032, D-034, D-036, D-039, D-046, D-051, D-056

**Decision.** `src/storage/repository.ts` implements `QuotaRepository` — the §8.1 core-service name, already pinned by D-009 as the storage layer's public facade — as `createQuotaRepository({ database })` over the already-migrated canonical schema, with these pinned interpretations: (1) **Every method is synchronous.** The driver is `node:sqlite`'s `DatabaseSync` (D-002); an async facade would only add promise allocation around calls that cannot await anything, and the one async seam in the storage layer (Umzug's storage contract, D-027) exists because the library demands it, not because I/O happens. (2) **No clock.** All timestamps are explicit writer arguments (insert inputs, `archiveAccount(id, archivedAt)`, `touchSession(hash, {lastSeenAt, expiresAt})`, `delete…Before(cutoff)`) — the D-021 injectable clock belongs to the services that own write timing, and the repository cannot become a hidden time source the D-032/D-034/D-036/D-056 no-SQL-time rule missed. (3) **The named CHECK constraints are the write gate.** Tasks 081–087 built the schema so every domain invariant is a named SQL constraint; the repository re-validates nothing and wraps nothing — constraint failures propagate with their self-explanatory names (`CHECK constraint failed: metric_values_invalid_clean`), and the only value mapping is what SQL cannot express: `is_valid` 0/1 ⇄ boolean and the `derived_fields` bitmask ⇄ `DerivedMetricField[]` (D-039's explicit repository assignment; a duplicated field name OR-collapses instead of shifting the mask, since the no-duplicates rule is §8.4 boundary validation). (4) **FK carriers are internal.** `insertSnapshot` writes the CHECK-bound `'success'` carrier and `insertRawResponse` the `'parse_error'` carrier (the D-036/D-051 technique); callers cannot express the linkage wrong, and the composite FKs make an error-cycle snapshot or a success-run raw payload structurally unreachable through the facade. (5) **`withTransaction(work)` is the §11.1 atomicity seam task 089 composes** — `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` … `COMMIT` on the repository's connection, best-effort `ROLLBACK` that never masks the callback's error before rethrowing it (the D-016/D-030 cleanup precedent), and a loud nesting refusal (D-027's no-nested-`BEGIN` rule); the `BEGIN` sits inside the guard's try/finally so a BEGIN that itself fails (SQLITE_BUSY past the §11.1 budget, stale transaction residue) resets the re-entrancy flag instead of latching it — a latched flag would refuse every later transaction on a healthy connection (review finding). Plain inserts stay single statements, so multi-record atomicity is always an explicit wrap. (6) **Retention deletes return counts** (`deleteCollectionRunsBefore` and siblings) so task 091's cleanup can report what it removed; account purge is `deleteAccount` (the cascade does the §8.2 history purge), `archiveAccount` updates only an `active` row so re-archiving cannot rewrite the lifecycle timestamp, and `deleteRawResponsesByRunIds` is the identity-delete primitive task 103's 20-per-account cap composes with the newest-first listing (a global time cutoff cannot express a per-account cap; review finding). (7) **Optional query filters assemble SQL from constant fragments with values always bound**, the prepared statement cached under the SQL text itself as key — a collision-proof cache key, since the fragment set is finite. (8) **The done-condition is enforced, not just true today:** `test/unit/storage-sql-gate.spec.ts` fails `make check` on any statement-shaped string literal outside `src/storage/` (uppercase-keyword match — the house SQL style — with terminators on the ambiguous transaction words, proven non-vacuous by positive-control fixtures), complementing the layout test's `node:sqlite` import gate; the per-table integration specs and `test/helpers` remain sanctioned direct-SQL users as storage-module tests. Scan scope is `src/` only: `ui/` copy is English prose a code gate must never parse ("select your plan from the list").

**Reasons.** The done-condition ("application services do not issue ad hoc SQL outside the storage module") could be met by nothing more than today's grep-clean tree, but a boundary that only convention holds is the exact failure mode D-009 rejected for import direction; the SQL-text gate is the same mechanical-contract idea at one layer's distance — services still cannot construct a `DatabaseSync`, but a received handle plus a string literal is the residual hole, and the gate closes it. Synchronous methods and no clock follow the same explicitness principle from opposite sides: the driver makes awaiting impossible, and D-021's time discipline makes hidden time undesirable — both would be facade theater adding seams without guarantees. Re-validation was rejected because the schema already is the validation (D-032's named-CHECK diagnosability rationale); a TypeScript-level pre-check would duplicate every rule and drift, while constraint names are pinned by the per-table specs. Carrier internalization and count-returning deletes are consumer-driven: 089's transaction, 090's archive/purge split, 091's retention + meta bookkeeping, 103's newest-first bounded raw queries, 110's per-cycle run rows, 142's latest-success/last-error lookups, and 154/155's session lookup/refresh/revocation each compose from the surface without extending it — the API was designed by walking those tasks' done-conditions, not by abstract completeness.

**Consequences.** Services, the composition root, and the CLI consume `QuotaRepository` (typed records over the §8.4 vocabulary; no snake_case row or `DatabaseSync` handle crosses the boundary); adding storage behavior means extending this facade or adding a sibling storage module, never issuing SQL elsewhere — a violation fails `make check` in any layer. `test/integration/repository.spec.ts` pins the surface against the canonical schema (round-trips per table, structural rejections — non-success snapshots, non-parse raw payloads, denormalization drift, duplicate keys — transaction commit/rollback/nesting including the §11.1 no-partial-snapshot case, bitmask round-trips, and the series-index query plan). Residual untestable branch (D-028 convention): `withTransaction`'s ROLLBACK-fails catch arm is unreachable without a broken connection. Changing the method surface is additive for consumers; renaming a record field or a method is a breaking change for the consuming tasks and must note this decision. The SQL-text gate may false-positive on future prose that quotes an uppercase SQL keyword at a literal's start — the remedy is rewording the string (the gate message names the file), never widening the pattern silently.

## D-059 — Retry/backoff as a services-side cycle wrapper: eligibility delegated to D-048's classifier, additive bounded jitter, a total result object

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§7.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#72-retry-and-error-behavior), [§17.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#171-required-test-coverage) · **Tasks:** [106](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-009, D-020, D-042, D-048, D-053

**Decision.** `src/services/polling-retry.ts` implements §7.2's first table row as `runCycleWithRetries(attempt, options)`, a wrapper around one **collection-cycle attempt** (the polling service's single `fetchSnapshot` call, task 109's wiring). Pinned interpretations: (1) **Placement is services, not the transport** — retry eligibility is `classifyTransportError(error).retryable` (D-048's `RETRYABLE_OUTCOMES`: network failure, timeout, 5xx — and nothing else), so the loop must live where that import is legal; `providers:core` may not import services (D-009, mechanically enforced), and a transport-level loop would force a divergent eligibility twin. D-042's own contract already defines retries as a downstream consumer of the taxonomy, and D-048 hands 106 the `retryable` flag as data. (2) **The retried unit is the cycle, not the HTTP request** — §7.2 says "within the current cycle" and stores one run record with the total attempt count; per-request retry inside the adapter would spend up to 14 s + jitter of delays on D-053's fail-soft endpoints 2/3 (whose failure never fails a cycle) and make that count ambiguous. Non-`TransportError` failures (adapter parse errors, wiring bugs) are never retried; the classifier's fail-fast `TypeError` on a malformed `http-status` construction propagates. (3) **The schedule and its jitter bound** — `RETRY_BASE_DELAYS_MS = [2 s, 4 s, 8 s]` (at most three retries, `MAX_CYCLE_ATTEMPTS = 4`), each delay plus a uniform integer jitter of 0–500 ms (`RETRY_JITTER_MAX_MS`, `retryDelayMs` pure and exported). §7.2 mandates jitter without a magnitude: additive jitter keeps every delay at or above the spec's own figure (never below the base), the 500 ms cap keeps the schedule recognizable (worst single wait 8.5 s, worst total 15.5 s against 14 s of bases) while still decorrelating accounts sharing a schedule; `random()` must return a finite number in [0, 1) — a roll outside that range would break the bound, so it fails fast rather than being clamped. (4) **A total result object** — `{ ok, value | error, attempts }` never throws for provider failures, carrying the attempt count §11.2's `collection_runs.attempts` persists (task 110); only programming mistakes throw, so one account's failed cycle cannot take down the polling loop (§7.2's "a failure for one account/provider must not stop other accounts" is 109's isolation, which this totality makes trivial). (5) **Abort semantics** — the caller's §8.1 signal interrupts the backoff wait (an abortable real timer that keeps the event loop alive: mid-backoff is in-flight collection work, reached at shutdown through the signal and the D-020 drain, not through process liveness); a mid-wait or pre-wait abort ends the cycle with `TransportAbortError` (105's `'cancelled'`), reporting the attempts actually made. The per-attempt §7.2 timeout stays with the transport (D-042): a timed-out attempt is simply one more retryable failure, and the loop adds no deadline of its own. (6) **Seams** — `random` and `sleep` are injectable, and the seam inputs are validated fail-fast at entry (`attempt`/`random`/`sleep` as functions, `signal` as an `AbortSignal` duck): a programming mistake must throw, never silently become a failed cycle — the delay computation sits outside the backoff guard so a bad roll propagates like the classifier's `TypeError`, and a backoff rejection becomes a result only when it is the abort signal's own `TransportAbortError` (any other rejection is a broken seam and propagates; review P3). The fake-timer unit suite drives the default sleep itself, while integration tests stub the wait (delay bounds are unit-proven) to pin eligibility and counts against real sockets. `withFakeTimers` (test/helpers/isolation.ts) gained `advanceMsAsync` and an opt-out of `shouldAdvanceTime` — exact-boundary timer assertions are flaky under time drift, which §17.3 forbids.

**Reasons.** The no-divergence requirement decides the placement on its own: eligibility already exists as data one import away, and duplicating it in `providers:core` would be the second §7.2 retry table, drifting exactly when a future transport kind or status class changes. Cycle granularity matches both the spec's wording and the run-record contract, and avoids taxing soft-failure endpoints with waits that can never change the outcome. The jitter bound is the tightest reading of "2, 4, and 8 seconds plus jitter": the schedule's numbers stay recognizable in logs and tests, and the bound is exact in both directions (never under the base, never more than 500 ms over). The worst total backoff (15.5 s) exceeds the 10 s drain window (§5.6, D-020) — harmless by construction, because shutdown reaches a mid-backoff wait through the abort signal rather than by waiting it out; the bound exists to keep the schedule a bounded, known quantity, not to fit the drain. A result object beats a thrown wrapper because §11.1 stores one row per cycle regardless of outcome — the count must survive failure, and wrapping the error would pollute the D-042 taxonomy 105 consumes.

**Consequences.** Task 109 wraps each account's cycle closure in `runCycleWithRetries(fn, { signal })`, classifies the final outcome with 105 from `result.ok`/`result.error`, and hands `result.attempts` to 110's run writer; 107 (Retry-After scheduling) and 108 (401/403 suspension) consume the unchanged passthrough errors — the 429's raw header still travels on the `TransportStatusError`. The exported schedule constants, the jitter bound and distribution, the result shape, and the abort behavior are contract: changing any requires a successor decision. Fake-timer tests are the standing proof of the done-condition: four attempts exactly, delays at the millisecond boundaries (1 999/2 000; 2 249/2 250; 2 499/2 500), a 14 000 ms total at zero jitter and 15 500 ms at maximum jitter, zero scheduled timers for 429/401/403/parse/abort failures, and attempt counts 1–4 reported per outcome.

## D-060 — The atomic cycle write: a sibling storage module composing the facade, writer-supplied identity, the classified cycle as the input contract (spec §11.1; task 089)

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§11.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#111-database-settings), [§7.4](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#74-sanitized-raw-responses), [§12.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#121-quota-reset-events), [§17.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#171-required-test-coverage) · **Tasks:** [089](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-021, D-036, D-039, D-046, D-048, D-051, D-058

**Decision.** `src/storage/collection-cycles.ts` implements §11.1's sentence — "Store a run record for every collection cycle, successful or unsuccessful. Write the snapshot, its metric rows, and associated events in one transaction" — as `persistCollectionCycle(repository, cycle): number`: one synchronous function composing the repository facade's public inserts inside its `withTransaction` seam (D-058.5) and returning the assigned run id. Pinned interpretations: (1) **A sibling storage module, not a facade method** — D-058's growth rule offered both; the sibling composes the surface D-058 explicitly designed for this task ("089's transaction … composes from the surface without extending it"), keeps the classified-cycle vocabulary (the services-facing hand-off task 110 drives) out of the per-table facade contract, and — decisively — leaves every internal call on a public method, so failure injection at each insert position works through a delegating proxy in tests; a facade method would call its sibling closures directly and resist position-targeted injection. (2) **The writer supplies every identity field**: `CycleMetricInput`/`CycleEventInput`/`CycleRawResponseInput` are `Omit` of the facade row types minus `accountId`/`runId`/`collectedAt`, and the function injects the cycle's account, the database-assigned run id, and the snapshot's `collected_at` into each row — D-039's denormalization pinning and D-046's account pinning are unrepresentable in the input shape (the composite FKs remain the structural backstop), and `eventAt` stays writer-supplied because §12.1 makes it deliberately its own value. (3) **The input is a classified cycle** — a discriminated union on `outcome` in D-048's vocabulary: the success branch carries `snapshot { collectedAt, planName?, metrics, events }` and cannot express `errorMessage`/`retryAfterSeconds` (so `collection_runs_success_clean` is unviolable by construction); a parse-failure branch carries the optional §7.4 sanitized payload — the only outcome §7.4 sanctions, made unexpressible for the other five by the same union; the other five failure outcomes carry only run evidence. Either snapshot array may be empty: §11.1 stores a snapshot for every successful collection, and the §8.4 boundary admits zero-metric snapshots. Task 110 hands a classified cycle to this seam; detection (117/118) and scheduling stay outside. (4) **No pre-validation, no error wrapping** — the named CHECK constraints remain the write gate (D-058.3); any throw inside the transaction — SQL constraint, UNIQUE collision, or driver error — rolls the whole cycle back and propagates unchanged (D-058.5's rethrow discipline). (5) **The done-condition is verified at every insert position** (§17.1 failure injection): `test/integration/collection-cycles.spec.ts` injects a SQL-level rejection at the run insert (unknown-account FK), the snapshot insert (blank `plan_name` → `snapshots_plan_nonempty`), the first metric (a valid-but-empty row → `metric_values_valid_has_value`), a later metric (a mid-batch duplicate key → the `UNIQUE (run_id, metric_key)`), a later event after the snapshot and an earlier event landed (blank evidence reason → `quota_events_details_reason`), and the raw payload (a 65 537-byte body → `raw_responses_body_size`), each asserting zero residue across runs/snapshots/events/raw-responses; a driver-level throw through a delegating proxy (the `withTransaction` callback's repository proxied too) proves a non-SQL exception rolls back identically; and the connection stays usable after each rollback. The success paths pin the row set each outcome class produces: a run row for all six failure outcomes and never a snapshot (D-036 keeps that structural as well), the complete success cycle with identities linked, and the §7.4 payload beside its parse-error run.

**Reasons.** The placement question (facade method vs. sibling) was the task's one structural decision, and D-058's own reasons section had already answered it in spirit: the facade was designed by walking consumers' done-conditions so this orchestration "composes from the surface without extending it" — a method would re-open the facade for what its surface already expresses, and would break the test technique the done-condition demands (data-driven SQL faults cover every position either way, but only public-method composition lets a proxy place a _non-SQL_ throw at an exact insert position deterministically). Identity injection extends D-058.4's "callers cannot express the linkage wrong" one step further than the facade already did: `insertMetricValues` still accepts caller-supplied identity (the facade is a general per-table surface), but a cycle's rows reach the database only through this seam, where the identity fields do not exist to be gotten wrong — unrepresentable beats rejected-loudly, the schema's composite FKs become the backstop rather than the first line. The union on `outcome` follows D-048's classification seams (the caller already knows the class before persisting), and folding the §7.4 payload into the parse-failure branch — though the task sentence names only run/snapshot/metric/event — completes the cycle as one classified hand-off: 099's `SnapshotParseError` already carries `sanitizedPayload` for exactly this storage, and leaving it out would force task 110 to open a second transaction for the same cycle, re-deriving this module's atomicity pattern per outcome. No pre-validation repeats D-058.3 verbatim — the schema is the validation, and a TypeScript-level pre-check would duplicate every named CHECK and drift.

**Consequences.** The repository facade is untouched; task 110 drives every polling cycle through `persistCollectionCycle` and owns the classification and attempt accounting that produce the input; 117/118's detectors produce the events array as data before the call. A cycle's writes are one transaction by construction — no caller can produce a partial snapshot through this seam, and `test/integration/repository.spec.ts`'s transaction tests (the seam) plus `collection-cycles.spec.ts` (the composition) pin both layers. The input type names (`CollectionCycleWrite` and its three branches, `CycleMetricInput`, `CycleEventInput`, `CycleRawResponseInput`, `SuccessfulCycleSnapshot`) and the function name are the task-110 API: changing them is a breaking change for that consumer and requires a successor decision; the `Omit`-based row inputs track the facade row types automatically, so a facade field change flows in without an edit here. The `'cancelled'` pseudo-outcome (D-048) remains outside the persisted enum and outside this union — how a cancelled cycle is recorded or skipped stays task 110's call, unreachable through this writer.

## D-061 — Account lifecycle as a sibling storage module: disambiguated retirement outcomes, a reporting self-verifying purge, and the status-independent explicit action (spec §8.2, §11.2; task 090)

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§8.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#82-accounts), [§11.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#112-required-logical-tables) · **Tasks:** [090](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-032, D-056, D-058, D-060

**Decision.** `src/storage/account-lifecycle.ts` implements §8.2's sentence — "Deleting an account archives it while retaining history; purging history requires a separate explicit action with confirmation" — as two operations composed over the repository facade, one per path: `retireAccount(repository, { accountId, archivedAt })` for the default retirement and `purgeAccount(repository, accountId)` for the explicit action, with `test/integration/account-lifecycle.spec.ts` pinning them as the done-condition demands — distinct suites, archive ≠ purge. Pinned interpretations: (1) **A sibling storage module, not facade methods** — D-058's growth rule, and its reasons section had already listed "090's archive/purge split" among the consumers that "compose from the surface without extending it"; the lifecycle-outcome vocabulary (an API-facing union, the task-159 hand-off) stays out of the per-table facade contract exactly as D-060 kept the classified cycle out of it, and no new SQL exists — the module calls only public facade methods. (2) **Retirement disambiguates the primitive's boolean** — the facade's `archiveAccount` returns one boolean for "unknown account" and "already archived" alike; `retireAccount` adds the follow-up `getAccount` read and returns `unknown` / `archived` / `already-archived`, the §13 API's 404-versus-idempotent-success distinction, with `already-archived` deliberately a success (the D-058 archive-once semantic — the original timestamp is immutable, re-retirement a no-op). (3) **Purge works regardless of account status** — §8.2's "separate explicit action" states no archive-first requirement, so an already-archived account purges identically (decided against a mandatory two-step dance the spec does not carry; pinned by test). (4) **The purge reports what it removed** — `PurgedHistoryCounts` (one count per §11.2 account-history table) is captured synchronously before `deleteAccount`: the single DELETE statement is atomic alone (D-058), nothing can interleave between the reads and the write on one synchronous connection, so no transaction wrapping is added and the counts describe exactly the rows the cascade removes; the `metric_values` count rides the captured run ids because that table has no account-level facade read — every metric row carries one. (5) **The purge self-verifies its post-condition** — §11.2's "use cascading deletion consistently for purged account history" enforced at runtime: after the delete, a residue sweep through the facade reads (the four account-level lists plus `getMetricValuesForRun` over the captured run ids) throws a loud error naming every surviving table class if anything remains. The defense targets the foreign-keys-off connection class — raw `node:sqlite` handles default the pragma off (D-056's pinned note) — where the account row deletes cleanly while every history row orphans silently, unreachable by any account query; the destructive path is where that wiring bug must not pass silently. (6) **Retirement verifies nothing at runtime** — archiving is an UPDATE on the account row and cannot endanger history; "archive keeps history" is the tests' pin, not redundant reads (the same no-theater rule D-058 applied to re-validation). (7) **Reactivation is out of scope** — §8.2 names no archived-to-active transition and the facade has no primitive for it; the config-sync tasks extend the surface when they need one, per D-058's additive-growth rule.

**Reasons.** The placement question answered itself the same way it did for D-060: D-058 designed the facade by walking this task's done-condition and named the archive/purge split as composing without extension, so a facade re-opening would need a reason stronger than preference — and none exists, since the two primitives plus the read surface express everything. The module's added value over the primitives is exactly what the boolean-returning facade cannot express: the API needs unknown-vs-already-archived as data (task 159 maps them to 404 and idempotent success), and the confirmation flow around §8.2's "explicit action" needs the evidence of what was removed — a report the counts provide without a second query surface. The residue sweep is the one runtime check in the module because it is the one check that can actually fire in production: FK enforcement is a connection pragma, not a schema property, and a connection opened without task 079's pragma block would pass every insert (FK checks off) and then orphan an account's entire history on delete — the failure mode is silent precisely where silence is worst. Counts-before-delete rather than after is forced (deleted rows cannot be counted), and the synchronous single-connection execution makes them exact without a transaction; wrapping one atomic statement plus its evidence reads in `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` would be ceremony D-058 already declined for plain inserts. Status-independent purge follows the spec's own shape — §8.2 separates the default (archive) from the explicit action (purge) without sequencing them, and §13's `?purgeHistory=true` carries no archive precondition.

**Consequences.** The repository facade is untouched; task 159's `DELETE /api/accounts/:id` (archive) and `?purgeHistory=true` (this purge) and the configuration sync (accounts removed from configuration get retired, history retained by default) consume `retireAccount`/`purgeAccount` as their storage seam. The outcome union names (`AccountRetirementOutcome`, `AccountPurgeOutcome`, `PurgedHistoryCounts`, `RetireAccountInput`) and the two function names are the consumer API: changing them is a breaking change and requires a successor decision. The residue sweep's error message is contract for diagnostics only (it names the account id and the surviving table classes, never a filesystem path). Sessions and meta surviving a purge is now pinned at the lifecycle-operation level as well as D-056's schema level; cross-account isolation and the archive-keeps-every-history-row guarantee are pinned by the distinct suites. A future reactivation primitive (config re-adding an archived account) lands as a facade method or a third operation with its own decision — `retireAccount`'s already-archived branch intentionally does not guess it.

## D-062 — `Retry-After` as a services-side pure decision: RFC 9110 parsing, zero-floor, one-hour ceiling, the 429-only gate inside the entry point

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§7.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#72-retry-and-error-behavior) · **Tasks:** [107](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-021, D-034, D-042, D-048, D-059

**Decision.** `src/services/polling-retry-after.ts` implements the second half of §7.2's HTTP 429 row ("Respect `Retry-After` up to one hour and do not poll before that time") — the first half, no within-cycle retry, is already D-059's. Pinned interpretations: (1) **Placement and the single entry point** — a pure sibling of `polling-retry.ts`/`polling-outcomes.ts` (the layout's 093–111 slot, `src/services/polling*`); `deferNextPoll(classified, nowEpochMs)` is the one function task 109 schedules through, so the eligibility rule cannot be re-derived at a call site: §7.2 sanctions honoring `Retry-After` only for a 429, which task 105 already carries as `retryAfterEligible` (D-048), so any other outcome — including a 503 whose transport error retained the raw header — returns `'ineligible'` and gets D-059's within-cycle retries instead of a next-poll deferral. The low-level `parseRetryAfter(raw, nowEpochMs)` beneath it is exported for the seam's own testability; time is an argument on every path (D-021), never a clock read. (2) **The decision vocabulary** — `{ deferred: true, seconds, capped, notBeforeEpochMs }` or `{ deferred: false, reason: 'ineligible' | 'absent' | 'malformed' }`; `seconds` is always an integer in `[0, 3600]` (`RETRY_AFTER_MAX_SECONDS`, the same bound D-034's `collection_runs_retry_after_range` CHECK enforces) and `notBeforeEpochMs = nowEpochMs + seconds · 1000` — one source of truth for the persisted value (task 110 stores `deferred ? seconds : null`) and the scheduler's gate (task 109). (3) **Parsing per RFC 9110 (§10.1.3, §5.6.7)** — the value is stripped of optional HTTP whitespace (exactly SP/HTAB/CR/LF, the byte set the fetch header reader strips; wider Unicode whitespace such as NBSP is not OWS and is reported malformed — a review finding), then either `delay-seconds` (`1*DIGIT`, matched as ASCII `[0-9]+` so signs, decimals, exponents, and non-ASCII digit forms cannot pass) or an `HTTP-date` parsed with Luxon's `DateTime.fromHTTP(value, { zone: 'utc' })` — the dependency `clock.ts` already uses; empirically verified on the pinned runtime (Node 22.13.0, luxon 3.7.2) to accept IMF-fixdate and both legacy obs-date forms (RFC 850, asctime) and reject the near-misses (impossible day, lowercase `gmt`, weekday contradicting the date, non-GMT zone, missing day-name, five-digit year). Anything else is `'malformed'`. For the RFC 850 two-digit-year form, §5.6.7's **sliding 50-year rule** ("a timestamp that appears to be more than 50 years in the future" is the most recent past year with the same last two digits) is applied over Luxon's accepted instant, because Luxon itself uses a fixed 1950/2050 pivot (the review's P2, verified on the pinned runtime): the two legal readings sit exactly 100 years apart, so the RFC reading is the one not more than 50 years ahead of `nowEpochMs`. One corner stays with Luxon by design: a weekday name written for the RFC-correct century may fail Luxon's day-name cross-check against its own pivot reading and be reported malformed — no deferral, the fail-safe direction. (4) **The three done-condition failure modes are decisions, not crashes** — malformed ⇒ no deferral (the account keeps its normal interval and the run row stores `NULL`: a broken header must not wedge the account, produce `NaN`, or wait forever); past (an HTTP-date already elapsed — still a _valid_ parse) ⇒ clamped to `seconds: 0`, the boundary value D-034's CHECK anticipated, so the record stays truthful while the schedule is unchanged; excessive (any value over one hour, including syntactically valid digit strings whose magnitude overflows IEEE-754 to `Infinity`) ⇒ capped at 3600 with `capped: true` — the cap deliberately overrides the provider, "up to one hour" being the spec's own bound on how long a 429 may silence an account. (5) **Date quantization rounds up** — whole seconds are the shared unit of the persisted value and the defer, and `ceil(deltaMs / 1000)` is the only direction "do not poll before that time" permits: a date 400 ms ahead defers a full second; a 3 599.4 s-away date defers exactly 3600 (uncapped), a 3 600.4 s-away one hits 3601 and is capped. Exactly `3600` delta-seconds is honored at face value (`capped: false`) — the cap is a ceiling, not a reduction, of values within it.

**Reasons.** D-059's boundary note reserved exactly this seam ("the 429's raw header still travels on the `TransportStatusError`"), and D-048 had already moved the header's eligibility question into data — so the module's only structural choices were placement and vocabulary. Placement next to the classifier follows D-059's own reasoning (`providers:core` cannot import services, and the transport must stay policy-free); the eligibility gate lives _inside_ the entry point because a 503-with-header is a real, reachable input (the transport retains `retry-after` on any non-2xx observation) whose wrong handling — deferring the next poll of an outcome §7.2 routes to within-cycle retries — no call site should be able to express. Zero-flooring the past case rather than reporting `'malformed'` keeps the run record honest (the provider _did_ answer; its indicated time had simply elapsed) and was anticipated by D-034 admitting `retry_after_seconds = 0`; Infinity-magnitude digit strings are classified excessive, not malformed, because they satisfy the RFC grammar and the distinction is what `capped` exists to record. Luxon over a hand-rolled regex: `fromHTTP` already encodes the three-format acceptance set with its near-miss rejections verified on the pinned runtime, and importing it adds no dependency — the same package `src/util/clock.ts` uses; the acceptance set is pinned as this module's own table-driven contract, so a Luxon behavior change fails `make check` rather than silently drifting. `src/util/clock.ts` is deliberately untouched: HTTP-date is provider header data at a trust boundary, not machine time, and D-021's discipline is satisfied by the injected `nowEpochMs`; if a second consumer ever needs HTTP-date parsing, the helper graduates to `util` via a successor decision.

**Consequences.** Task 109 gates each account's next poll on `notBeforeEpochMs` (falling back to the configured interval on every non-deferred reason) and task 110 persists `seconds`/`NULL` — neither re-derives parsing, capping, or eligibility. The exported names (`parseRetryAfter`, `deferNextPoll`, `RetryAfterDefer`, `RetryAfterIgnoreReason`, `RETRY_AFTER_MAX_SECONDS`, `RETRY_AFTER_MAX_MS`) and the decision shape are contract: changing any requires a successor decision. The unit spec (`test/unit/polling-retry-after.spec.ts`) is the standing proof of the done-condition — table-driven over both RFC forms and all three failure modes, the exact one-hour boundary on both sides, OWS variants, the sliding 50-year rule in both directions (a '68 date read as 2068 → capped; a '99 date kept in 1999 → clamped to zero), the eligibility matrix through real `classify*` outputs, and the D-059 interplay (a 429 escaping `runCycleWithRetries` after one attempt carrying its header into the parser) — with 100% line/branch coverage of the module; no timers or network are involved, `now` being data. Auth-suspension cadence (task 108) and the scheduler itself (task 109) are untouched: a 401/403 with a `Retry-After` header classifies `'ineligible'` here and 108's 60-minute verification cadence governs.

## D-063 — Retention cleanup as a sibling module over the facade, a separate maintenance primitive, and §11.3 policy validated at the storage boundary (spec §11.3, §7.4, §15.2; task 091)

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§11.3](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#113-retention-and-cleanup), [§7.4](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#74-sanitized-raw-responses), [§15.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#152-passwords-and-sessions), [§5.6](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#56-process-lifecycle-backups-and-upgrades) · **Tasks:** [091](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-021, D-030, D-036, D-046, D-051, D-056, D-058, D-060, D-061

**Decision.** `src/storage/retention-cleanup.ts` implements §11.3's cleanup sentence as `runRetentionCleanup({ repository, database }, { now, retentionDays }): RetentionCleanupReport`, with `src/storage/maintenance.ts` alongside it exporting the post-cleanup step as `runStorageMaintenance(database)`. Pinned interpretations: (1) **A sibling storage module plus a separate maintenance primitive, not facade methods** — D-058's growth rule, and its reasons section had listed "091's retention + meta bookkeeping" among the consumers that compose the surface without extension. The maintenance call is deliberately its own module rather than part of the cleanup: it takes the raw `DatabaseSync` (a checkpoint is a statement about the database file, not about any table, and the facade rightly never hands a connection back), §5.6's shutdown wiring ("close the database, and checkpoint WAL") needs exactly the same call, and folding it into the cleanup would force the shutdown path to run deletes' plumbing to reach a checkpoint. (2) **`now` and `retentionDays` are writer-supplied; the cutoffs are computed inside** (D-021/D-058) — the future scheduler owns the clock (startup, then daily) and hands the loaded configuration's `app.historyRetentionDays`; the module reads no clock, which is what makes an identical repeated call the same cleanup over the same rows — the done-condition's repeat-safety by construction. (3) **§11.3's 7–3650 bounds are validated here, before any delete runs** — an integer-range check on a query parameter is policy no schema CHECK can express, so this is not a replay of D-058's no-pre-validation rule (which concerns row data the named CHECKs gate); the config layer keeps validating its own copy, and a direct caller with a rejected window (6, 3651, 180.5, NaN) gets a loud error with the rows untouched. (4) **The run is the retention unit** — `deleteCollectionRunsBefore` is the history delete and the schema's cascades take each expired run's snapshot, metric values, snapshot-linked events, and raw payload; snapshots and metric rows get no separate cutoff calls because a snapshot cannot outlive its run, and the report's run count covers the cascade (counting those children separately would mean O(history) reads on every cleanup at §11.3's ~52,000-snapshots-per-account scale, for numbers the run count already implies). Events and raw payloads do get their own deletes because their time columns are genuinely their own: §12.1's `event_at` can predate its run and run-free events (§11.2) have no run to cascade from; §7.4's raw window is 30 days, not the history window. (5) **Raw payloads follow §7.4's fixed 30-day window (`RAW_RESPONSE_MAX_AGE_DAYS`)** — the time-based half of "no more than 20 responses per account and no more than 30 days"; the per-account 20-record cap is task 103's (`listRawResponses` newest-first + `deleteRawResponsesByRunIds`), so this module never counts records, it only expires age — the explicit boundary with 103's scope. (6) **Sessions follow §15.2 at `now`, not the history window** — the D-056 CHECKs already cap `expires_at` at 7 days of inactivity and 30 days of life; cleanup deletes `expires_at < now`, whatever the retention window. (7) **Deletes and markers commit as one `withTransaction` unit** — the last-run markers (`retention:last-run` = the run's `now`, `retention:applied-days` = the window applied, both §11.2 meta rows via the facade upsert) must never claim a half-done cleanup; an injected marker-write failure rolls every delete back and the next (startup/daily) run redoes the whole cleanup. (8) **Maintenance runs after the commit, unconditionally, in §11.3's own order** — "Then checkpoint WAL…", also when the deletes removed nothing: `wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)` whose `{busy, log, checkpointed}` row is reported as data (`busy` — another connection's read snapshot, e.g. `doctor` — is an outcome, not an error; the next cleanup checkpoints again), then `incremental_vacuum` executed unconditionally with the database's `auto_vacuum` mode in the report: the §11.1 pragma set configures no `auto_vacuum`, so the service's own databases are `NONE` where the pragma is a documented no-op (verified on the pinned runtime), and "where supported/configured" is expressed by running the call and reporting the mode — real work only on an operator-configured `INCREMENTAL` file. (9) **§11.3's "do not delete" protections are by construction, and the reduce-retention warning is a recorded hook** — the operation touches no `accounts` row (active or archived: expired history of archived accounts still goes, retention being a history rule), no configuration, no connection setting, and no `meta` key except its own two markers; the config/UI layer reads `retention:applied-days` and warns when a newly configured window is smaller — the records between the two windows are exactly what the next cleanup deletes. The warning surface itself is not built here.

**Reasons.** The placement followed the sibling precedent for the third time running (D-060's cycle write, D-061's lifecycle, now the cleanup): D-058 designed the facade by walking this task and named it as composing without extension, and the cleanup-report vocabulary plus §11.3 policy constants would widen the per-table contract for no consumer's benefit. The one genuinely new structural question was the maintenance call's home. Making it a facade method would leak a `DatabaseSync`-shaped concern into a row-typed surface; burying it inside the cleanup would couple §5.6's shutdown checkpoint to deletes that shutdown does not want; a separate `maintenance.ts` answers both and keeps each module one spec-file-sized concern. Validation-in-module was decided against the tempting "the config layer already validates it" argument because the module is the boundary every caller shares — the CLI, tests, and the future scheduler all reach §11.3 policy here, and a range check on an explicit argument is the same fail-fast D-058 applied to what SQL cannot express. The transaction choice reverses D-061's no-transaction purge on its own criterion: there the single DELETE was atomic alone and reads could not interleave, while here five statements plus two marker writes are one logical batch whose markers are bookkeeping about the others — the marker that lies about a half-done cleanup is precisely the state §11.3's daily cadence must never see. Cascade-only counting (no per-child reads) is the §11.3 scale sentence's direct consequence, and the history-query-usability half of that sentence stays where D-058 already pinned it — the query-plan-proven series and account/time indexes — rather than re-tested per task. The unconditional vacuum follows SQLite's own semantics instead of a mode gate: the call is free on `NONE`, useful on `INCREMENTAL`, and a readback-gated skip would duplicate the database's own decision and drift if the mode could change under us.

**Consequences.** The repository facade is untouched; the server-lifecycle tasks wire `runRetentionCleanup` at startup and once a day (computing `now` from the injectable clock and reading the configured window — the call is the operation, never the schedule), §5.6's shutdown reuses `runStorageMaintenance` for its checkpoint, task 103 layers the 20-per-account cap over the same 30-day constant, and the config/UI warning tasks read `retention:applied-days` as their hook. The exported names (`runRetentionCleanup`, `runStorageMaintenance`, `RetentionCleanupReport`, `RetentionRemovedCounts`, `StorageMaintenanceResult`, `WalCheckpointOutcome`, `AutoVacuumMode`, `MIN_RETENTION_DAYS`, `MAX_RETENTION_DAYS`, `RAW_RESPONSE_MAX_AGE_DAYS`, `RETENTION_LAST_RUN_KEY`, `RETENTION_APPLIED_DAYS_KEY`) and the two meta keys' names/values are the consumer contract: changing any requires a successor decision (the marker values are epoch-ms and day-count strings, §11.1's vocabulary). The done-condition — startup and daily cleanup safe to repeat — is pinned by `test/integration/retention-cleanup.spec.ts` (identical second run removes nothing; a later `now` only the newly expired; an earlier `now` a no-op; injected marker failure rolls all deletes back) and `test/integration/maintenance.spec.ts` (the TRUNCATE checkpoint observable as a zero-byte `-wal` file on the production connection, the `auto_vacuum` mode mapping, the `busy` outcome under a second connection's stale read snapshot). Foreign-keys-off residue (D-061's purge sweep) is deliberately not re-defended here: retention runs on the service's own `openStorageConnection` handle whose foreign-key pragma is fail-fast-verified at open (D-030), the raw-handle exposure class the purge sweep targets cannot schedule cleanups. The WAL-observable tests bind to TRUNCATE mode's zero-byte file; a future mode change (e.g. PASSIVE for concurrency) is a successor decision with those tests as its migration checklist. One recorded scale observation (review, task 091): the cleanup's account-unbounded deletes cannot use the account-led §11.2 indexes (only `sessions_expiry` serves its delete), so each cleanup full-scans the history tables — tens of milliseconds daily at §11.3 scale, and the natural trigger for `started_at`/`event_at`-led indexes in a future schema task if multi-account × 3650-day deployments appear.

## D-064 — Auth-rejection suspension as a pure state machine: admission-rearmed cadence, monotone armed instant, and an admission floor that survives release (spec §7.2, §7.3)

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§7.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#72-retry-and-error-behavior), [§7.3](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#73-account-status-precedence) · **Tasks:** [108](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-021, D-048, D-059, D-062

**Decision.** `src/services/polling-suspension.ts` (the 093–111 placement row's `src/services/polling*` home) implements the §7.2 401/403 row's pause sentence — "pause normal polling for that account until the key changes or a manual test is requested. Perform a verification attempt once every 60 minutes" — as a pure state machine with time as an argument on every entry point (D-021). Pinned interpretations: (1) **The state is a value the caller holds** — `{ suspended: false, admissionFloorEpochMs }` or `{ suspended: true, keyIdentity, suspendedAtEpochMs, nextVerificationAtEpochMs }`, frozen by the module; the scheduler (109) owns storing it, the run writer (110) persists each probe cycle, and the status derivation (111) consumes the `Auth rejected` contribution D-048 already attaches to the outcome (§7.3 rank 1 — the highest-precedence status, which is why the pause gates polling rather than merely labeling it). Key-change detection is an input event, not a filesystem read: `applyKeyIdentity(state, identity, now)` compares the caller's opaque key identity (a generation counter or hash — key material never reaches the module) against the episode's and releases on inequality; a manual-test request (`applyManualTestRequest`) releases unconditionally. Both are idempotent, so the caller may report the current identity on every configuration observation without risking a missed or duplicated release. (2) **`applyCycleOutcome` is the outcome seam** over D-048's classification: `auth_error` enters suspension from a not-suspended state (entry arms the first probe a full window ahead — the rejected cycle itself was this window's attempt); a further `auth_error` under the same key re-arms to the rejection time + 60 min ("a failed verification keeps the suspension and re-arms the 60-minute timer"); `auth_error` under a _different_ key — normally unreachable, because a key change releases first — begins a fresh episode that still cannot open the gate before the armed instant the old episode left; `success` releases; **every other outcome is a pinned no-op**: an inconclusive probe (network, timeout, 5xx, 429, parse — and `'cancelled'`, which is caller lifecycle) neither releases the suspension nor moves the timer, because it proves nothing about the key and the admission-anchored schedule already paces attempts at least 60 minutes apart. (3) **`admitVerification` is the gate and the cadence enforcement in one**: granted iff suspended and `now >= nextVerificationAtEpochMs` (the boundary admits — exactly 60 minutes is not too early), and a granted admission **re-arms the armed instant to `now + 60 min` at admission time**, so an outcome that is never recorded cannot re-open the gate early (self-healing) and two admissions are at least 60 minutes apart by construction. (4) **The armed instant is monotone and survives release**: every re-arm takes the maximum (a regressed clock reading changes nothing — fail-safe), a different key's fresh episode respects the old armed instant, and `release` carries the armed instant forward as `admissionFloorEpochMs` on the not-suspended state, so even a clock that jumps backwards across a release cannot pull the next automatic attempt closer than 60 minutes to the last one. Under a forward-moving clock the floor is inert (any event's `now + 60 min` already lies above it), so no legitimate flow — manual test, key replacement, re-suspension — is delayed by it.

**Reasons.** The done-condition — "no rapid retry loop is possible" — demanded a mechanism whose safety is structural rather than a caller convention, because 109 owns the loop: admission-re-arming makes the spacing between automatic attempts a property of the state itself (admission requires passing the armed instant and immediately moves it a full window ahead), and the monotone-max plus admission-floor rules extend that guarantee to the two ways a naive design leaks attempts — duplicate/regressed rejections pulling the arm earlier, and episode changes (release + re-entry) forgetting the last arm entirely. Re-arming at admission rather than only at outcome recording was chosen because the outcome path has a real failure mode (a lost or late-recorded outcome) whose worst case under outcome-only re-arming is two admissions in the same millisecond; under admission re-arming it is a slightly later probe, the fail-safe direction. The no-op pin for non-auth outcomes follows §7.3's own precedence: `Auth rejected` outranks everything, so an inconclusive probe must not silently downgrade the account to `Unreachable`/`Format changed` handling, and re-arming on it would only slow recovery without adding safety (the admission arm already covers the window). Manual-test release is deliberately unconditional and un-paced: the spec names it a release condition, so each manual attempt is one operator-initiated action whose 401/403 immediately re-enters suspension with a fresh window — a scripted hammer of manual tests is operator behavior the spec explicitly permits, not an automatic loop. D-062's boundary note reserved exactly this seam ("a 401/403 with a `Retry-After` header classifies `'ineligible'` here and 108's 60-minute verification cadence governs"), and `deferNextPoll` is untouched: the 429 deferral and the auth suspension are different mechanisms with different release conditions (provider-indicated time vs. key change/manual test/probe success).

**Consequences.** Task 109 gates each account's normal polling on `!state.suspended`, schedules verification wake-ups through `isVerificationDue`, requests attempts through `admitVerification`, and feeds every classified cycle outcome (probe, manual, or normal) through `applyCycleOutcome`; task 111 derives `Auth rejected` from the outcome contribution plus suspension state rather than re-deciding entry. The exported names (`AUTH_SUSPENSION_VERIFICATION_INTERVAL_MS`, `INITIAL_SUSPENSION_STATE`, `applyCycleOutcome`, `applyKeyIdentity`, `applyManualTestRequest`, `admitVerification`, `isVerificationDue`, `isSuspended`, the state and result types) are contract: changing any requires a successor decision. The interval is fixed at 60 minutes by §7.2 — no configuration may raise or lower it (a successor decision would need spec grounds). The unit spec is the table-driven pin of every boundary (entry, re-arm at/exactly-at/before the boundary, the 59:59 rejection, failed-verification re-arm, key change and manual test mid-window, lost outcome, cross-release regression, fail-fast validation), and `test/unit/polling-suspension.property.spec.ts` is the standing proof of the done-condition: over generated adversarial sequences — every admission followed by an auth rejection, releases, key changes, lost outcomes, and regressed clock readings — no two admissions are ever closer than the cadence, the episode invariant (`next >= suspendedAt + 60 min`) holds after every transition, and admission agrees with the armed instant at every probe time; a directed release-and-regress property admits at the armed instant each round, releases through both release events, and records the release attempt's rejection _below_ the admission it follows — the exact attack the admission floor exists to block — asserting per round that the gate stays shut for the rest of the window (vacuity tripwires guarantee the generated walks actually produce admissions; the suite was verified non-vacuous by mutation: removing the admission re-arm, the monotone guard, or the admission floor each fails it). Persisting suspension across restarts (so a suspension survives a process cycle) is deliberately not this module's concern: the state is a value; a future task that persists it must round-trip the frozen fields exactly, and the admission floor rule makes any restored-but-stale state fail safe.

## D-065 — Migration backups as a separate `VACUUM INTO` primitive plus a startup orchestrator, refusal before any write, and retention by parsed name order (spec §5.6, §11.4; task 092)

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§5.6](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#56-process-lifecycle-backups-and-upgrades), [§11.4](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#114-migrations-and-backup-behavior), [§6.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#61-paths), [§11.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#111-database-settings) · **Tasks:** [092](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-021, D-027, D-030, D-031, D-058, D-063

**Decision.** Task 092 lands as two sibling modules. `src/storage/backups.ts` exports the automatic-backup primitive — `automaticBackupsDir(dataDir)` (`<data>/backups/`, the `databaseFilePath` resolve convention), `listAutomaticBackups(backupDir)` (oldest first), and `createAutomaticBackup({ database, backupDir, now }) → { backup, evicted }` — and `src/storage/startup-migrations.ts` exports the §11.4 operation the server startup wiring will call: `runStartupMigrations({ database, dataDir, migrations, clock? }) → { status, applied, backup? }` plus `NewerSchemaError`. Pinned interpretations: (1) **A separate backup module, not a maintenance annex** — D-063 placed the checkpoint/vacuum in `maintenance.ts` because they tend the live file after cleanup; a backup is a different concern (a standalone copy written _before_ a risky change, retained _after_ it), and §5.6's shutdown path needs maintenance without ever wanting backups, so `backups.ts` is its own module taking the raw `DatabaseSync` (D-058: the facade never hands a connection back). The orchestration is a second sibling, not `migrations.ts` growth: D-027's harness stays the apply-and-record engine, and the ordering policy around it (check → refuse-or-skip → back up → apply) is §11.4's, composed over the harness exactly as D-060/D-061/D-063 composed theirs over the facade. (2) **Refusal before any write, and the runner is constructed only after the check** — `schemaVersionStatus` is read-only (never creates the journal table), but D-027's _runner construction_ does create it, so `runStartupMigrations` refuses (`NewerSchemaError`, carrying `supportedVersion`/`appliedVersion`/`newerThanSupported`, message naming both versions, the newer entries, and §5.6's `npm update -g quotameter` + restart remedy) before any backup, migration, or runner exists. The refused database is byte-identical (main-file bytes compared by test) — §11.4's "leave the database unchanged" read at full strength, not merely transactionally. (3) **`'up-to-date'` returns without touching anything** — §5.6 guards _migrations_ and none are pending, so no backup and not even the journal-table write; pinned by test (empty set on a fresh database leaves no `schema_migrations` table). (4) **Backup iff `'behind'` and the database holds a pre-migration state** — the carve-out is emptiness, not the journal's version number alone: a fresh install (no journal rows and no tables beyond it — what this application itself produces) has nothing to protect (`VACUUM INTO` of an empty file protects nothing and costs a directory plus a file copy), while a journal-less database _with_ tables (a foreign file at the data path, or a lost `schema_migrations`) **is** backed up — the pending migrations are about to transform or collide with that content, exactly when an operator wants the image (review finding). In practice `appliedVersion > 0` covers every database this application wrote; the emptiness probe (`hasNonJournalTables`, a read-only `sqlite_master` query) closes the foreign/journal-lost corner. An up-to-date database has no migration to guard. A migration failure after the backup leaves both the image and D-027's rolled-back database intact for the next startup; a _backup_ failure propagates before any migration runs, keeping the database at its current schema. (5) **Naming and collision grammar: `backup-<epoch-ms>[-<seq>].sqlite`** — SQLite's `VACUUM INTO` refuses an existing output file (verified on the pinned runtime), so the same clock reading twice (a fixed test clock; two startups inside one millisecond) appends `-1`, `-2`, … instead of failing startup; the filename binds as a parameter (`VACUUM INTO ?`), never interpolated into the SQL literal — a data-directory path may contain quotes. (6) **Retention orders by the parsed `(timestampMs, seq)`, evicts only after the new backup exists, never the new backup itself, and only ever automatic names** — the grammar (`parseAutomaticBackupName`: prefix/suffix anchoring plus a digits-only check per number) is the retention scope, honoring §11.4's "automatic backups": operator files with names outside the grammar are invisible to listing and eviction (pinned by test). Lexicographic ordering was rejected explicitly: `'-'` (0x2D) sorts before `'.'` (0x2E), so a name sort inverts `backup-T` against `backup-T-1` and would evict the wrong generation (and inverts across digit widths, `backup-999` vs `backup-1000` — pinned by test); parsed numeric order with the unsuffixed name as sequence 0 keeps same-instant generations in creation order and survives any future name-width change. Eviction runs after the new image is complete on disk so a creation failure (full disk) costs no existing generation, and the just-created backup is exempt from its own pass (review finding, reproduced before the fix): ordering is by the name-parsed timestamp, so a clock reading _earlier_ than the retained window (an NTP step-back — a shape `src/util/clock.ts` acknowledges — or a same-instant revisit after the unsuffixed name was evicted) would sort the fresh image oldest and delete it, migrating with zero pre-migration backups exactly when the safety net matters. The window keeps three total — the new backup plus the newest two others — converging back to the three-newest rule on subsequent runs; fs errors propagate unwrapped (D-058 style). (7) **The image is the live database's committed state** — verified on the pinned runtime: `VACUUM INTO` includes committed-but-uncheckpointed WAL frames, emits a standalone `journal_mode=delete` database with no `-wal` sidecar, passes `PRAGMA integrity_check`, and refuses to run inside a transaction — the last point making the orchestrator's backup-before-runner ordering structural, not stylistic. (8) **Sync `node:fs` and a single-level, EEXIST-tolerant `mkdirSync` of the backups subdirectory** — the layer is synchronous (`DatabaseSync`, the `statSync` precedent in the integration suites); the backups directory is this operation's own artifact under the same auto-create carve-out §11.1 grants the database file. Deliberately _not_ `recursive` (review finding on the draft's own comment): a missing data directory is an operator problem that fails loudly with `ENOENT` instead of being silently re-created at the umask default — the D-030 "no directory creation" posture; task 074's lock path owns the data directory and its `0700` mode. `now` is writer-supplied (D-021) and validated (non-negative integer) before the filesystem is touched — a fractional or negative timestamp would mint a name outside the grammar, invisible to retention.

**Reasons.** The task context explicitly delegated placement, citing D-063's separate-concerns precedent; following it produced the two-module split (a primitive the wiring, `doctor`, or an operator tool can call alone, and an orchestrator that is pure ordering policy). The refusal-strength question the task raised — byte-identical versus transactionally unchanged — resolved to byte-identical because the check-and-throw path performs no statement that writes (the only writes on any path are the backup, the runner's journal-table creation, and the migrations themselves, all sequenced after the check), and the test compares the main file's exact bytes; the journal-mode sidecar question does not arise because the refusal runs on the caller's already-open connection. The schema-0-no-backup call follows §5.6's own wording ("before any _schema migration_ [of existing state] create a backup") read against what a backup is for: there is nothing to roll back to worth keeping when the pre-state is an empty file, and the §11.4 forward-test requirement is unaffected — every release still migrates forward from the previous supported schema, now through the startup seam. The same-instant grammar was driven by the fixed test clocks D-021 mandates: an API whose startup fails because two backups asked for one millisecond is an API that punishes determinism, and the seq suffix costs nothing in the common case. Parsed ordering over lexicographic was found the hard way — the first draft of the test's own directory listing sorted names lexicographically and inverted the expected eviction order, which is precisely the bug class retention must not have.

**Consequences.** `src/storage/migrations.ts` is untouched except its header pointer; the canonical migration set stays closed at version 7 and the server startup wiring (later tasks) calls `runStartupMigrations` on task 079's open connection, mapping `NewerSchemaError` to the refuse-to-start exit (the error class carries everything the message needs, so wiring formats rather than re-reads). The backup directory name (`backups`), the file grammar `backup-<epoch-ms>[-<seq>].sqlite`, `AUTOMATIC_BACKUP_RETAINED_COUNT = 3`, and the exported names (`createAutomaticBackup`, `listAutomaticBackups`, `automaticBackupsDir`, `AutomaticBackup`, `AutomaticBackupResult`, `runStartupMigrations`, `NewerSchemaError`, `StartupMigrationsResult`) are consumer and on-disk contract: changing any requires a successor decision. `test/integration/startup-migrations.spec.ts` pins the done-condition — fresh schema-0 migrates the full canonical set without a backup; a journal-less but non-empty database _is_ backed up; a 6→7 forward run takes exactly one backup that opens independently with the pre-migration schema and data; an up-to-date re-run takes none; five same-instant upgrade rounds keep exactly three automatic backups with the oldest evicted and a foreign file untouched; the newer-schema refusal leaves the main file byte-identical with no backup directory; a failing migration preserves the backup and the rolled-back pre-migration state, and the corrected re-run completes. The review round added four pins to the same suite: a clock step-back (and a same-instant unsuffixed-name revisit) never evicts the backup its own pass just created, retention ordering survives a digit-width boundary (999→1000), committed-but-uncheckpointed WAL content lands in the standalone image (on a §11.1 WAL connection, sidecar proven non-empty first), and the in-transaction refusal writes no file. One deliberate scope note: `doctor`-style listing of backups reads `listAutomaticBackups`; no backup _restore_ path exists in v1 (§5.6 names none — an operator restores by file copy), and building one is a successor decision if a future spec revision asks for it.

## D-066 — The polling scheduler: sequential dispatch behind a hang threshold, monotonic dues with wall-expressed gates, and the attempt/settle account seam

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§7.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#71-polling), [§7.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#72-retry-and-error-behavior), [§5.6](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#56-process-lifecycle-backups-and-upgrades), [§17.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#171-required-test-coverage) · **Tasks:** [109](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-020, D-021, D-048, D-059, D-062, D-064

**Decision.** `src/services/polling-scheduler.ts` implements §7.1's collection loop as one dispatch loop over per-account state, composing the landed seams without re-deriving any of their policies. Pinned interpretations: (1) **The account seam is a closure pair** — `attempt(signal)` is the raw cycle attempt (the single `fetchSnapshot` call; D-059's wrapper around it is the scheduler's, with the scheduler's `random`/`sleep` seams passed through so one injection point drives both jitters), and `settleCycle(result)` is task 110's seam: it receives the retried result (value/error plus the §11.2 `attempts` count) and returns the D-048 classification the scheduler gates on. The scheduler never classifies, persists, or imports storage/adapters — the one reading it needs (suspension transitions, `Retry-After` deferral, next schedule) is exactly the seam's return value. (2) **Sequential means single-start dispatch with a hang threshold** — the loop starts at most one cycle while none is in flight, so accounts are non-concurrent and per-account overlap is structural (an account with a live flight is never dispatchable, single-threaded start decisions make a second concurrent cycle for the same account unrepresentable). A flight unsettled after `cycleHangThresholdMs` (default 255 500 ms = §7.2's own worst legitimate cycle: four attempts at the 60 s request-timeout ceiling plus D-059's 15.5 s worst backoff; injectable) is declared hung: it is skipped for dispatch — its account still cannot start another cycle — and other accounts proceed around it. Strict sequential below the threshold, per-account serialization always, global concurrency above one only for declared-hung flights; a hung flight that eventually settles is post-processed normally and its account resumes. (3) **Intervals are monotonic; gates are wall-clock** — next-poll dues are `clock.monotonicMs()` values (`now + interval + jitter`), honoring §7.1's monotonic-interval sentence; the wall clock is read only where other decisions are expressed in epoch form (D-062's `notBeforeEpochMs`, D-064's armed instants), by sampling the remaining wall delta and waiting it on the same monotonic sleeper, re-checking after every wake so wall/mono disagreement can only delay, never duplicate. Every wake is sliced to `MAX_WAKE_MS` (one hour, §7.2's own longest gate horizon): Node clamps oversized `setTimeout` delays to 1 ms, so an un-sliced multi-week wait — a gate computed from a wall regressed by an RTC reset or VM restore — would busy-spin instead of sleeping, and slicing also bounds the detection latency of a wall correction to one slice. The deferral gate applies to every dispatch, manual tests included ("do not poll before that time" is unconditional); each completed cycle's own `deferNextPoll` decision replaces the previous gate. (4) **Release semantics** — a release caused outside a cycle (key change via `setAccounts`, `requestManualTest`) owes the account one attempt: a `pendingManualTest` flag consumed at dispatch, so the owed attempt survives an in-flight cycle (whose settle rescheduling would overwrite a due timestamp) and a concurrent interval change, dispatches through the loop (sequential/overlap rules hold), bypasses the suspension gate (D-064: the manual attempt runs "unconstrained by this machine"), and still respects the `Retry-After` gate; a manual test of a healthy account is just a cycle, run now. A release caused by a cycle's own success (a successful probe) schedules the next normal poll a full interval out, since the probe just collected. While suspended, the 60-minute D-064 cadence governs (the boundary predicate is the machine's own `isVerificationDue`, never a hand-rolled twin) and `nextPoll` stays stale until release. (5) **Mid-run changes** — `setAccounts` diffs by id: added accounts get an immediate first poll (mirroring startup), removed accounts drop their state (an in-flight cycle settles in the background, its outcome discarded by an entry-identity check; removals never abort — `stop()` is the only aborter), a kept account's changed `keyIdentity` is fed to `applyKeyIdentity` (the idempotent observation D-064 recommends).
