A key change **mid-flight** additionally discards the in-flight cycle's outcome as stale: the flight snapshots the account wiring at dispatch (one cycle never mixes keys — old closures on retries, new identity on the verdict), and an old key's 401 must never suspend a brand-new key that was never tried; task 110's seam has still recorded the run (history is per-account), only the engine's gates ignore it. `setIntervalMs` validates §7.1's 60–3600 s range (mirrored from the config contract, drift-tested against `AppConfigSchema`) and re-anchors every not-suspended account to `now + newInterval + jitter` — never leaving a stale long wait, never firing earlier than one new interval. (6) **§7.2 isolation is containment, not propagation** — provider failures arrive as `CycleRetryResult` values; a throwing `settleCycle` (or any programming mistake inside a flight, e.g. a fail-fast random roll) is caught, and the account reschedules on the plain interval; diagnostics for contained failures ride the future server logger wiring. A flight's promise never rejects (cleanup runs before the third-party tracker call, so a throwing `done()` cannot brick the account's dispatch), and the wake path propagates a sleep rejection other than the documented `TransportAbortError` abort — broken seams fail loudly, per D-059's convention. (7) **`stop()` is prompt, and a dead engine is observable** — stop scheduling, abort every live flight, resolve when the loop has exited; cycle tasks are detached from the loop precisely so a hung closure cannot delay teardown, and the optional structural `inFlight` tracker (D-020's `InFlightTracker` shape as a local type — `services` may not import `src/server/`) lets the composition root's graceful drain wait for aborted cycles' actual settlement. A wiring-level loop failure (a non-finite clock reading, a broken sleep seam) is retained: `running` turns false so the composition root sees the engine died, and `stop()` re-surfaces the error.

**Reasons.** §7.1's two sentences leave one genuinely open question — what "poll accounts sequentially" means when a cycle hangs — and the done-condition ("fake-timer/concurrency tests pass", §17.1's "no overlap per account") forced an explicit choice: bounded-wait degenerates into sequential-with-skip with extra latency once the bound expires, so the threshold form was taken directly, with the bound anchored in the spec's own worst-case arithmetic rather than an arbitrary number (a cycle beyond 255.5 s is either hung or configured past §7.2's envelope — either way other accounts must not starve). The two-seam account closure reconciles D-059's "the retried unit is the single fetchSnapshot call" with the task-110 hand-off: retry eligibility needs the thrown `TransportError` (so the raw attempt must reach `runCycleWithRetries` unwrapped), while parse-outcome classification is adapter-island knowledge the scheduler cannot import — the seam returns the classification and the scheduler's gates consume it as data, exactly the D-048 pattern. Monotonic dues with wall-delta waits keep §7.1's letter without duplicating D-062/D-064 in monotonic form (their states are epoch-valued contracts shared with persistence); re-checking gates after every wake makes clock drift fail safe. The settle-containment rule follows D-059's broken-sleep precedent (a throwing consumer seam must not kill the engine) extended to §7.2's account-isolation sentence; prompt `stop()` follows D-020's placement note that the drain — not the scheduler — owns the bounded wait.

**Consequences.** Task 110 builds each account's `attempt`/`settleCycle` (classify + persist, returning the classification) and the composition root registers the scheduler as the polling `LifecycleComponent` with the shared in-flight tracker; task 111 consumes suspension state alongside D-048 contributions. The exported names (`createPollingScheduler`, `PollingScheduler`, `PollingAccount`, `PollingSchedulerOptions`, `PollingSleep`, `PollingInFlightTracker`, `pollingDelayMs`, `MIN_POLLING_INTERVAL_MS`, `MAX_POLLING_INTERVAL_MS`, `POLLING_JITTER_FRACTION`, `MAX_WAKE_MS`, `DEFAULT_CYCLE_HANG_THRESHOLD_MS`) and the jitter quantization (additive uniform integer 0…10% of the interval, both ends included — the D-059 shape, so a delay is never below the configured interval) are contract: changing any requires a successor decision. `test/unit/polling-scheduler.spec.ts` is the standing proof of the done-condition: immediate first polls in account order, exactly-one-at-a-time dispatch (global in-flight 1 in normal operation), inter-poll gaps pinned at the 0%/10% jitter boundaries and across varied rolls, per-account entry count staying 1 while another account's closure hangs past many intervals (overlap structurally impossible), the strict-sequential hold below the threshold, Retry-After gating at `notBeforeEpochMs` with the one-hour cap and manual-test respect, the hourly probe cadence with key-change/manual-test/probe-success releases, settle-failure containment, mid-run add/remove/interval changes, and prompt aborting `stop` with zero pending timers — plus the review-round regression pins: the mid-flight key-change discard, the owed manual attempt behind an in-flight cycle, loop-death observability (`running` false, `stop()` rethrowing), a 40-day wall regression during a deferral (sliced waits, no spin, exact gate resumption), the loud broken-sleep death, and a throwing tracker `done()` not bricking dispatch. `withFakeTimers` gained an additive `now` option (pinning the fake epoch to 0) so absolute-timestamp assertions are exact.

## D-067 — The §7.4 per-account cap at the write moment, and the raw-payload access gate confining the surface to storage plus one CLI diagnostic file (spec §7.4, §5.5; task 103)

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§7.4](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#74-sanitized-raw-responses), [§5.5](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#55-doctor), [§11.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#111-database-settings), [§17.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#171-required-test-coverage) · **Tasks:** [103](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-041, D-044, D-051, D-058, D-060, D-063

**Decision.** Task 103 lands as three pieces. (1) **The cap is a sibling storage module enforcing at the write moment.** `src/storage/raw-response-retention.ts` exports `RAW_RESPONSE_MAX_PER_ACCOUNT = 20` (fixed §7.4 policy, not configuration — the count twin of D-063's `RAW_RESPONSE_MAX_AGE_DAYS`) and `enforceRawResponseCap(repository, accountId) → { retained, evicted }`, composing exactly the two D-058 primitives designed for it — `listRawResponses` (newest first, the facade's deterministic `captured_at DESC, run_id DESC` order) and `deleteRawResponsesByRunIds`. `persistCollectionCycle` calls it inside the cycle's own transaction (§11.1) whenever it stores a §7.4 payload, so after any committed parse-failure cycle the account holds at most 20 payloads — continuously true, not eventually true; the eviction pairing is atomic with the write (an injected eviction failure rolls the whole cycle back, run row included, pinned by test). A daily-pass placement was rejected: §7.1's 60 s polling floor allows ~1 400 parse failures/day, so a cleanup-cadence cap would retain hundreds of rows between passes; a read-time cap was rejected as cosmetic — the rows would still be retained. `retention-cleanup.ts` is untouched: D-063's recorded boundary (time-based expiry = 091, per-account cap = 103, "that module never counts records") stands. One pass repairs any overshoot (the listing is unbounded on purpose — facade-seeded states, a future cap-lowering successor, are cut to the newest 20 by a single call; a pathological overshoot beyond SQLite's ~32 766-statement-variable ceiling fails the eviction statement loudly with nothing partially deleted — accepted and documented rather than chunked, since the sanctioned write path evicts at most one row per cycle), and eviction deletes payloads only: the dropped runs' `collection_runs` rows survive, because §7.4 caps the payload, not the §11.1 history unit. (2) **The diagnostic read path is one CLI file.** `src/cli/raw-diagnostics.ts` exports `readRawDiagnostics(repository, accountId)` — the bounded `listRawResponses(accountId, { limit: 20 })` call, so even a pathological state never floods a terminal — and `renderRawDiagnostics(records)` — header per record (run id, `toUtcIso` captured instant, explicit `no HTTP status`/`unknown content type` words for absent evidence) with the body verbatim and indented (D-041 pinned "doctor --raw renders it as text"; pretty-printing is a display concern). The `doctor` dispatch row now declares the §5.5 surface — `--raw <account>` as a string option with its description — while its handler stays the D-044 stub: the option is the spec-fixed surface, the checks are task 145's, and 145's handler composes these two functions. (3) **CLI-only exposure is enforced by a gate, not by today's absence of an HTTP API.** `test/unit/raw-response-gate.spec.ts` (the D-058 SQL-gate pattern) fails `make check` on any `src/**` or `ui/**` file outside `src/storage/**` and `src/cli/**` that references the raw-payload surface — detected as `/(?<!sanitize)[Rr]awResponse|[Rr]awDiagnostics|raw-diagnostics/`, covering every camelCase identifier the stored payloads travel through (facade methods, record/input types, the cycle field) **and the diagnostic module's own API and import path** (a route importing `readRawDiagnostics` would receive the full payload list without ever naming a facade identifier — review finding P3-1), while exempting the provider-side sanitizer `sanitizeRawResponse` (D-041 — the write-side purification that _makes_ payloads safe, never a read of the stored table). The CLI allowlist is the layer, not the one file, deliberately: §7.4's prohibition is HTTP and the web UI — exactly the layers denied — and task 145 must be free to wire the doctor handler wherever the dispatch table needs it; within the CLI, the doctor `--raw` path is the recorded consumer. Direct SQL over `raw_responses` stays the existing gates' territory (`node:sqlite` import gate + uppercase-literal SQL gate) with their documented non-security-boundary caveat; the exposure guarantee is this gate **plus** the layout table (which keeps `server`/`ui` from importing `cli` at all), each layer catching what the other cannot see.

**Reasons.** The task delegated three choices and the spec text decided each. _When the cap runs:_ "retain no more than 20 responses per account" is a statement about the retained set, and the write moment is the only enforcement point that keeps it true without a window — every sanctioned parse-failure write goes through the D-060 seam, so embedding the cap there is structural (task 110 cannot bypass it), and the eviction is one bounded listing plus at most one small identity delete per write. _Where the cap lives:_ the D-060/D-061/D-063 sibling pattern for the fourth time — D-058's reasons section had already named `listRawResponses` + `deleteRawResponsesByRunIds` "the 103 per-account-cap primitive", and the cap vocabulary would widen the per-table facade contract for no consumer's benefit. _How "never over HTTP or in the web UI" is made forward-enforceable:_ there is no HTTP API yet, so the honest form is a mechanical tripwire in the established gate style — Stage 12's `src/server/api/**` routes and `ui/**` components fail `make check` on their first reference to the surface instead of shipping an unsanctioned route; the identifier-stem detector (not the table name) is the precise subject because the typed facade is the only payload path the existing gates cannot see, and the sanitizer exemption is by name because D-041 deliberately placed that function in `src/providers/` — flagging it would make the gate wrong on day one.

**Consequences.** Task 110 persists every cycle through `persistCollectionCycle` and needs no cap wiring of its own; task 145's `doctor` handler reads `--raw`'s value and calls `readRawDiagnostics` + `renderRawDiagnostics` through the `CliOutput` seam. The exported names (`RAW_RESPONSE_MAX_PER_ACCOUNT`, `enforceRawResponseCap`, `RawResponseCapResult`, `readRawDiagnostics`, `renderRawDiagnostics`), the renderer's line format, and the gate's allowlist (`src/storage/**` and `src/cli/**`, with the identifier pattern) are contract: changing any requires a successor decision — widening the gate's allowlist especially (a third sanctioned layer is a deliberate exposure decision, the D-058 no-silent-widening rule). `test/integration/raw-response-retention.spec.ts` pins the done-condition (after every write ≤ 20; the 21st evicts exactly the oldest, its run surviving; the boundary at exactly 20; cross-account independence; the same-instant `run_id` tiebreak; an out-of-order arrival older than everything retained evicting itself; the eviction-couple atomicity; overshoot repair; the blank-account fail-fast), `test/integration/cli-raw-diagnostics.spec.ts` pins the bounded account-scoped read against a real database, and `test/unit/cli-raw-diagnostics.spec.ts` pins the render text and the `doctor --raw` dispatch surface. The 30-day half of §7.4 remains D-063's, unchanged.

## D-068 — Rolling ranges as a util sibling: the §14.4 closed vocabulary, pure-duration closed intervals, and subprocess-proven `TZ` invariance (spec §10, §13, §14.4; task 116)

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§10](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#10-time-and-time-zones), [§13](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#13-http-api), [§14.4](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#144-history-charts) · **Tasks:** [116](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-013, D-021

**Decision.** `src/util/rolling-ranges.ts` implements §10's "last N hours/days" sentence — "a rolling interval ending now; compute and pass explicit `from`/`to` bounds to the server; filter history server-side" — with these pinned interpretations: (1) **The vocabulary is §14.4's five ranges, read through §13.** §13's endpoint table carries only explicit `from`/`to` values and names no ranges; the spec's sole normative list of rolling ranges is §14.4's "24 hours, 3 days, 7 days (default), 14 days, and 30 days". The module models exactly that closed set — `RollingRangeId = '24h' | '3d' | '7d' | '14d' | '30d'` in ascending-duration order (`ROLLING_RANGE_IDS`), with `DEFAULT_ROLLING_RANGE = '7d'` and exact millisecond durations (`rollingRangeDurationMs`; `HOUR_MS`/`DAY_MS` exported) — nothing speculative; a future range is a code change plus a changelog entry. (2) **Placement is a `util` sibling of `clock.ts`, not a `clock.ts` extension and not `src/services/`.** The computation is pure duration arithmetic on the `EpochMs` type — no zone, no `Clock` object (`now` is an argument, the D-021 discipline; the module imports only `type { EpochMs }` from `./clock`, same layer): `clock.ts`'s charter is zones/ISO/formatting, and the services layer (which the package-layout map's coarse 112–127 row names for its _service_ files) is task 109's concurrent territory — a dependency-free §10 time helper is the `util` row's charter, so the placement keeps parallel file sets disjoint by construction. (3) **Bounds are pure duration, closed at both ends.** `rollingRangeBounds(range, now)` returns a frozen `{ from: now − duration, to: now }` — exact UTC ms arithmetic with no calendar or DST wall-clock component, so a 24 h range across a spring-forward transition is still exactly 86 400 000 ms of absolute time. The spec is silent on `from`/`to` inclusivity; the pin is a **closed interval `[from, to]`** — the newest snapshot sits at/near `to` and must be included, and a point exactly N units old is inside "last N hours/days" — made executable by `rollingRangeContains(bounds, epochMs)` so the Stage 12 server-side filter (`collected_at >= from AND collected_at <= to`) has a canonical, machine-pinned definition instead of a comment. (4) **Loud failure and float honesty.** An unknown range id throws with the valid ids listed (the D-013 registry error discipline); a non-finite `now` throws (the `clock.ts` `requireFinite` pattern). For finite `now` the subtraction itself cannot overflow — the largest duration (2 592 000 000 ms) is far below the float spacing at `Number.MAX_VALUE`, so at `now = ±MAX_VALUE` the result is absorbed (`from === now`): documented float-exact behavior, pinned by test, not an error; zero-length ranges are impossible in the vocabulary (§14.4's minimum is 24 h). (5) **The done-condition is proven in real processes.** `TZ` is read by `Intl`/libc once at process start, so in-process `process.env.TZ` mutation proves nothing; `test/integration/rolling-ranges-tz.spec.ts` therefore spawns the real module through `test/helpers/rollingRangeRunner.ts` (the jiti child pattern of `singleInstanceRunner.ts`, task 074) under `TZ` = UTC, Europe/Berlin, America/New_York, Asia/Kolkata (half-hour), Asia/Kathmandu (quarter-hour), Pacific/Kiritimati (+14), and with no `TZ` at all — all sharing one pinned injected `now` — and asserts the bounds JSON is byte-identical across every child while their `Intl`-resolved zones genuinely differ (each child echoes its resolved zone; the suite requires ≥ 4 distinct zones and a concrete UTC-vs-Kiritimati difference, so a spawn bug that left every child in one zone fails loudly instead of passing vacuously; exact resolved-name matching was deliberately rejected — this ICU canonicalizes `Asia/Kolkata` to its CLDR alias `Asia/Calcutta`, the D-014 item 8 behavior).

**Reasons.** (1) §13's `from`/`to` parameters are the wire contract, but the _ranges_ the product supports are a UI-facing closed list; §14.4 is the only place the spec enumerates them, and inventing an id vocabulary beyond those five would violate the task's closed-set instruction in both directions. (2) The util layer is the one place both later consumers can import without new dependency edges: the Stage 12 API layer (serializing bounds with `toUtcIso` for `/api/history`, `/api/events`, `/api/peak-hours`) sits above `util`, and the §14.4 history view's range selector conceptually owns the same vocabulary; extending `clock.ts` would blur its zone-and-clock charter for arithmetic that needs neither. (3) §10 says "interval ending now" — an interval is naturally closed at its endpoints for filtering, and half-open bounds would exclude a snapshot taken in the same millisecond as `to = now`, the freshest point a monitoring chart must show; the executable predicate prevents the documented pin and the Stage 12 SQL from drifting apart silently. (4) IEEE-754 subtraction of a small constant from a finite double can never reach ±Infinity here (the result magnitude is within `|now| + duration`, which rounds back inside the finite range at every magnitude), so an overflow guard would be dead code against a tested invariant — the honest alternative is pinning the absorption edge in tests and documenting it. (5) The §10 requirement is "works consistently under any `TZ` environment setting"; a module that reads no environment is invariant by construction, but the task's done-condition demands boundary tests that _pass with several `TZ` values_ — only a subprocess with `TZ` fixed before startup exercises the real failure surface.

**Consequences.** Stage 12's history/events/peak-hours routes serialize these bounds with `toUtcIso` (§13's ISO 8601 UTC `Z` requirement) and filter with the closed-interval comparison; the §14.4 view's default range is `DEFAULT_ROLLING_RANGE`, and retention-aware disabling compares `rollingRangeDurationMs` with the configured retention window (§14.4's "disable ranges that exceed the configured retention period" stays with the consumer that holds the config). The exported names (`ROLLING_RANGE_IDS`, `DEFAULT_ROLLING_RANGE`, `HOUR_MS`, `DAY_MS`, `RollingRangeId`, `RollingRangeBounds`, `rollingRangeDurationMs`, `rollingRangeBounds`, `rollingRangeContains`), the id spellings, the exact durations, and the closed-interval semantics are contract: changing any requires a successor decision. `test/unit/rolling-ranges.spec.ts` pins the exact-boundary table (modern instant, epoch 0, negative epoch, leap-day fractional, US DST spring-forward), the vocabulary order and default, the error contract, the frozen result, the float-edge absorption, and the inclusivity pins; the integration suite above pins the done-condition. Task 126's fuller time-zone regression matrix may extend the runner's zone list, not the module.

## D-069 — The cycle recorder: the settle seam filled with classify-then-persist, cancellation unpersisted, and a one-file §7.4 write-side gate widening (spec §7.2, §11.1; task 110)

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§7.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#72-retry-and-error-behavior), [§11.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#111-database-settings) · **Tasks:** [110](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-013, D-021, D-034, D-036, D-039, D-048, D-058, D-059, D-060, D-062, D-066, D-067

**Decision.** `src/services/polling-persist.ts` implements the run writer D-066 reserved for this task: `createCycleRecorder(options)` produces one account's closure pair — `attempt(signal)` stamps the cycle's wall-clock start (§7.1's "store actual wall-clock collection timestamps": `collection_runs.started_at` is a real reading at the fetch, not a settle-time reconstruction) and makes the single raw `fetchSnapshot` call D-059's wrapper needs unwrapped; `settleCycle(result)` classifies with task 105, maps into D-060's `CollectionCycleWrite`, calls `persistCollectionCycle`, and returns the classification the engine gates on — nothing here re-decides retry, deferral, suspension, or the raw cap. Pinned interpretations: (1) **A cancelled cycle is deliberately unpersisted** — the record-or-skip call D-048 left to this task: a `stop()` abort is service lifecycle, not a provider outcome, and §12.2's timeline already separates "failed collection cycles" (non-success run rows) from "periods with no collection-run records" (the service was stopped) — a shutdown abort belongs to the second class; the classification is returned (the engine consumes it), the database untouched. (2) **An error outside both taxonomies throws** — a non-`TransportError` rejection without the adapter parse-failure shape is a programming mistake; fabricating one of the seven provider outcomes for it would lie in the audit trail, so it fails fast (`TypeError`) and is contained by the engine's §7.2 isolation (D-059's broken-seam precedent); a settle without a recorded attempt (or a second settle for one cycle) throws the same way. (3) **A provider-level success that fails §8.4 validation is a `parse_error` run without a snapshot** — D-066 types the settled value `unknown`, so the seam must narrow it (`findProviderSnapshotProblems` plus a `providerId` cross-check against the collecting adapter); an invalid value still leaves §11.1's run-row-per-cycle true, the account surfaces `Format changed`, and no snapshot can exist (D-036 keeps that structural in SQL as well). (4) **The §7.4 payload hand-off is consumed structurally** — services may not import `providers:adapter` (the layout's island rule), so an adapter parse failure is recognized by field shape (`reason` a non-blank string, `sanitizedPayload` a string, `httpStatus` absent or an integer in 100–599) mirroring the Z.ai `SnapshotParseError`, whose real class the unit spec narrows against; `captured_at` is the settle reading (a parse failure is un-retried, so it is milliseconds from the response's arrival), `content_type` stores `NULL` (the error carries none). (5) **`retry_after_seconds` is D-062's decision at the settle reading** — `deferNextPoll(classified, endedAt)`: `seconds` when deferred, `NULL` otherwise (ineligible, absent, or malformed headers store nothing; a past HTTP-date stores the truthful `0`); the engine re-derives its gate from a marginally later wall reading — both come from the same header under the same one-hour cap, the stored value being evidence, not the gate. (6) **Timestamps are readings, never computed** (§7.1, D-021): `started_at` at the cycle's **first** attempt (D-059's wrapper invokes the attempt closure up to four times per cycle — the stamp is taken once and kept, so a retried cycle's run row spans all its attempts; review P1), `ended_at` (and the deferral decision and `captured_at`) at the settle, `collected_at` the adapter's own §8.4 stamp; durations stay monotonic in the engine; the per-cycle timing cell is one variable per recorder — safe because D-066's per-account serialization is structural — cleared at settle. (7) **`intervalSeconds` is read at settle** — §11.2's "interval in effect" at the cycle, a closure the composition root wires to the live configuration so a §6.4 runtime change lands from the next cycle on. (8) **`events` travel empty for now** — §12.1 detection (tasks 117/118) arrives as data before D-060's writer is called; this recorder is where the detector plugs in, so the success write already carries the (empty) array through the same transaction. (9) **The D-067 gate allowlist gains exactly one file** — `src/services/polling-persist.ts`, the successor decision D-067's no-silent-widening rule exists to force: the recorder is the write-side composer of D-060's parse-failure branch (D-067's own consequences sentence — "task 110 persists every cycle through `persistCollectionCycle`" — requires naming the classified-cycle field to hand the §7.4 payload over), composes no read of the stored table, and the entry sanctions one file, never the services layer; the read-path confinement (storage plus `doctor --raw`) is unchanged.

**Reasons.** The one question D-048 explicitly deferred — whether a cancelled cycle is recorded — was decided from §12.2's own vocabulary: the timeline treats missing run records as "the service was stopped", which is exactly what a shutdown abort is; storing it would require one of the seven provider outcomes (SQLite's CHECK rejects `'cancelled'`, pinned by 105's integration spec) and would paint every clean shutdown as a provider failure on the error timeline. The invalid-success branch follows the same evidence rule as the done-condition's first half: a cycle that failed classification must not produce a snapshot, but §11.1's run-row-per-cycle has no exception for "the adapter lied" — the `parse_error` run row keeps the history truthful while D-036's composite FK keeps the absent snapshot structural. The structural §7.4 narrowing was forced by the layout (services → `providers:adapter` is forbidden, mechanically enforced): moving the field-shape contract into `providers:core` would edit task 070's landed registry for one consumer, and duck-typing an explicitly pinned public field set is the same boundary D-042/D-048 already draw between the transport's data and its consumers. The gate widening over identifier avoidance: computed-key construction or a storage-side naming proxy would evade a mechanical gate rather than satisfy it — the gate exists to force exactly this decision to be recorded, and D-069 records it.

**Consequences.** The composition root builds each `PollingAccount` as `{ accountId, keyIdentity, …createCycleRecorder({ account, provider, repository, clock, intervalSeconds }) }`, and the account-sync wiring must land the account row before the scheduler starts (a run insert for an unknown account fails its foreign key loudly, contained per §7.2 isolation); tasks 117/118 extend the success write's `events` array through this seam. Two recorded gaps (review round): a success run row stores `http_status = NULL` because §8.4's `ProviderSnapshot` carries no status — 105's "retained whenever a response arrived" has nothing to retain on this path, and populating it would be a §8.4-surface successor decision, not this seam's; and a `settleCycle` whose storage write fails is silently contained by the engine (no diagnostics channel yet) — the already-recorded D-066 deferral to the server's logger wiring is the fix, and a miswired `intervalSeconds` seam (a seconds/milliseconds unit mismatch) surfaces only through that channel today, the `collection_runs_interval_range` CHECK refusing each write deterministically (D-060's no-pre-validation rule deliberately keeps this seam from duplicating the range a third time). The exported names (`createCycleRecorder`, `CycleRecorder`, `CycleRecorderOptions`) and the D-067 gate's one-file entry are contract: changing either requires a successor decision. The done-condition's two halves are pinned end-to-end through the settle path against a real migrated database: `test/integration/polling-persist.spec.ts` proves (a) every failure class — network, timeout, 5xx, 401, 429, an adapter parse failure with its payload, a transport-level parse failure, and a provider-level success failing §8.4 — writes exactly one run row and no snapshot, metric, or event rows, and (b) after a success followed by failures, `getLatestSnapshot`/`getMetricSeries`/`getLatestCollectionRun(…, 'success')` still return the last valid values with their collection time, never zeroed (§7.2's "missing data must never be represented as zero"); `test/unit/polling-persist.spec.ts` pins the row mapping (label dropped per D-039, optional fields nulled, identities writer-supplied), the attempt-count pass-through (1 and 4 through the real wrapper), the `retry_after_seconds` evidence matrix (37 / capped 3600 / past 0 / absent NULL / malformed NULL / ineligible 503 NULL), the cancelled-unpersisted pin, both fail-fast branches, the settle-time interval read, and the factory validation.

## D-070 — Account status derivation as a pure evidence function: the suspension-or-latest-rejection rank 1, a first-attempt `Stale` anchor, and `Collecting` as the no-data window state (spec §7.3, §14.6; task 111)

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§7.3](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#73-account-status-precedence), [§14.6](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#146-statuses-and-authentication-screens), [§13](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#13-http-api), [§7.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#72-retry-and-error-behavior) · **Tasks:** [111](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-021, D-034, D-048, D-058, D-060, D-064, D-066, D-069

**Decision.** `src/services/polling-status.ts` implements §7.3's account status precedence as one pure function, `deriveAccountStatus(input, nowEpochMs)`, plus `readPollingRunEvidence(repository, accountId)` — the storage seam assembling the evidence from exactly the three D-058 lookups its reasons section designed for this consumer (`getLatestCollectionRun`, `getLatestSnapshot`, and `listCollectionRuns` with `limit: 1`, whose ascending order selects the account's _oldest_ run). The input model is `{ enabled, configured, suspension, runs, intervalSeconds }` — configuration flags the caller resolves, the D-064 suspension state the scheduler holds, the frozen run evidence, and the §7.1 interval validated against `polling-scheduler`'s exported millisecond bounds (one source of truth); time is an argument (D-021). Pinned interpretations: (1) **Rank 1 is the disjunction D-064 reserved for this task** — `Auth rejected` when the suspension is active _or_ the latest run is an `auth_error`. The suspension arm keeps rank 1 over an inconclusive verification probe (network/timeout/5xx/429/parse while suspended: D-064 neither releases nor re-arms, and the probe proved nothing about the key, so §7.3's rank order must not downgrade the display to `Unreachable`/`Format changed`); the run arm covers the windows where the in-memory machine has not caught up with storage — a restart (suspension state is process memory and starts fresh) and the moment after a key-change or manual-test release (D-066 makes the next poll immediately due, so the window is one cycle). (2) **`Collecting` is the no-data window state**: an account with no successful collection yet, within three configured intervals of its _first attempt_ (or with no runs at all — §7.1's immediate first poll due or in flight). The live-activity reading ("a cycle is in flight right now") is rejected: the precedence list is ordered by evidence (failure class, then data age), an in-flight indicator would drag scheduler activity state into a status view, and it leaves no state for an idle account without data — while the no-data reading completes §7.3's partition with no gap and no overlap. (3) **The `Stale` anchor is the latest success, or the first attempt when none exists** — "no successful collection for more than three configured collection intervals" measures how long the lack has lasted, from when it began; the boundary follows the spec's own words (`Fresh` at an age of at most three intervals, "no older than"; `Stale` strictly past them, "more than"), and a wall reading behind the last success (a regressed clock, D-021) yields a negative age and stays `Fresh` — fail-safe in the not-alarming direction. (4) **Ranks 2–3 read the latest cycle's class only**, through D-048's `STATUS_CONTRIBUTION_BY_OUTCOME` consumed as data: §7.3 attaches no recency qualifier to `Unreachable` ("latest cycle failed due to network issue, timeout, or 5xx"), older failures of a higher rank do not survive a newer failure of a lower one, and `rate_limited`/`success` contribute nothing and fall through to the age states — exactly 105's delegation note. (5) **`Disabled` precedes `Not configured`, both ahead of the ranked list** — the operator's enablement is the outermost switch, so a disabled account shows `Disabled` whether or not its key is resolved; `configured` means a usable secret is _resolved_ (`apiKey` set, or `apiKeyEnv` naming a variable the process provides, §6.3) — the config contract's exactly-one-source invariant makes "neither declared" a configuration error, so the reachable `Not configured` account is the unresolved-`apiKeyEnv` one, resolved by the caller from live configuration. (6) **`lastSuccessAt` is the latest snapshot's §8.4 `collectedAt`** — the data's own collection stamp; D-060 commits snapshot and success run atomically, so run-stamp and snapshot-stamp reads cannot disagree, and the snapshot read is what stays honest when later failed runs arrive. The wire vocabulary is kebab-case machine tokens (`ACCOUNT_STATUSES`, ranked order then the two separate states) with `ACCOUNT_STATUS_LABELS` carrying the exact §7.3/§14.6 English spellings for §5.2's CLI; the UI maps tokens through its i18n catalog.

**Reasons.** Placement followed the package-layout map's 093–111 row (`src/services/polling*`) over the task hint's "e.g. account-status" filename: the map is what makes parallel task file sets disjoint by construction, and the module _is_ the polling pipeline's status view (the task hint's own "e.g." conceded the choice). A pure function over an explicit evidence object — rather than a repository-coupled or scheduler-coupled service — is forced by the consumer set: §13's `/api/status`, §5.2's `quotameter status`, and §14.3's overview each hold different pieces (repository, CLI process, config) and none of them should re-derive precedence; the derivation is also the one place the "every state and transition" done-condition is exhaustively testable, which needs `now` as data (D-021). The rank-1 disjunction is the interpretation D-064's consequences text announced ("task 111 derives `Auth rejected` from the outcome contribution plus suspension state rather than re-deciding entry") — either input alone loses a real state: suspension alone drops the restart window (the machine is memory, the runs are durable), the run alone downgrades a suspended account on its first inconclusive probe. The `Collecting`/`Stale` anchor pair comes from taking §7.3's list as a _total_ partition: `Fresh` needs a latest success, `Stale` needs a measurable lack — an account with attempts but no success has neither a success age nor an infinite one, and the only duration the spec's sentence can denote for it is time-since-collection-began; anchoring instead at the _latest_ attempt would report a 429-hampered account as eternally `Collecting`, and anchoring at account creation would paint a brand-new account `Stale` during its first cycle. Consuming 105's table (and 108's state, and 058's reads) rather than re-deriving is the no-divergence rule every sibling pinned: a future outcome class or release condition must change exactly one module.

**Consequences.** Task 142 (`quotameter status`), the §13 `/api/status` route, and the §14.3 overview consume `deriveAccountStatus` with `readPollingRunEvidence` plus their own `enabled`/`configured` resolution and the scheduler's per-account suspension state (a status view outside the process passes `INITIAL_SUSPENSION_STATE` — the `auth_error`-run arm keeps that display truthful for the first post-restart cycle); the composition root's account-sync wiring owns nothing new. The exported names (`ACCOUNT_STATUSES`, `ACCOUNT_STATUS_LABELS`, `STATUS_FRESHNESS_INTERVALS`, `PollingRunEvidence`, `AccountStatusInput`, `AccountStatus`, `readPollingRunEvidence`, `deriveAccountStatus`) and the token spellings are contract: changing any requires a successor decision; the eight tokens are the §13 wire values and the labels are §5.2's display strings. The done-condition — every state and transition has tests — is met threefold: `test/unit/polling-status.spec.ts` pins each of the eight statuses from defining evidence, both boundary sides on both anchors, every precedence overlap, and an event-driven transition matrix (disable/lose-key from every state, each failure arrival, recovery, both suspension releases plus probe success, restart with a lost suspension, aging past the window); `test/unit/polling-status.property.spec.ts` proves totality, the dominance of `Disabled`/`Not configured`/an active suspension, biconditional agreement with D-048's contributions and the three-interval arithmetic, freshness downward-closed in the clock reading, and time-shift invariance; `test/integration/polling-status.spec.ts` derives end-to-end from real rows — one run of each of the seven outcomes through its §7.3 status, the snapshot-stamp last success, the oldest-run anchor under out-of-order insertion, and per-account isolation.

## D-071 — Peak-schedule §9.2 validation confirmed landed at 061/064; non-finite numbers named distinctly in type errors; the matrix suite as the task-113 deliverable (spec §9.2)

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§9.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#92-configuration-and-validation), [§6.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#62-configuration-contract) · **Tasks:** [113](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-014, D-015, D-018, D-043

**Decision.** Task 113's audit of the §9.2 peak-schedule validation produced three pinned interpretations. (1) **The rule set already landed with the configuration contract and its runtime composition** — D-014's structural schemas (closed `days` enum with `minItems: 1`/`uniqueItems`, anchored `HH:mm` patterns with `24:00` admitted only as an end, `exclusiveMinimum: 0` multipliers) plus its `findConfigProblems` invariants (IANA zone, `start < end` — which is also what makes a cross-midnight window unrepresentable — duplicate window ids, same-day overlap including containment), composed by D-018's `parseConfig`; D-043's record ("schema validation rules landed with 061/067") is confirmed by the executed matrix, and the task adds no rule, schema keyword, or validation module. (2) **Non-finite numbers are rejected as _type_ violations by both engines — verified empirically on the pinned runtime (Node 22.13.0)**: TypeBox `Value.Check` and the Ajv 2020-12 compilation both fail `Infinity`/`-Infinity`/`NaN` against `type: number` (JSON numbers are finite; strict `JSON.parse` yields `Infinity` for an out-of-range literal such as `1e400`, the hand-edit route into a file-shaped value), so §9.2's "multipliers must be positive numbers" needs no new finiteness keyword — every numeric setting (port, polling interval, retention, provider timeout, both multipliers) already excludes non-finite values. (3) **The one repair is to D-018's type-error vocabulary**: `jsonTypeName` maps non-finite numbers to `a non-finite number`, because the previous rendering contradicted itself (`multiplier: expected a number, got a number` — a wording task 067's env test had even pinned for its digit-string route into `server.port`); the message stays value-free per §15.4 (a type-level fact, not an echo). The task's done-condition is delivered as the dedicated matrix suite `test/unit/peak-hours-validation.spec.ts`: every invalid §9.2 dimension pinned to its exact field-level problem through `parseConfig` — the pipeline startup and reload actually run — every boundary pinned accepted, plus an overlap property test (flagged exactly when two generated windows share a day and their minute-intervals intersect, `24:00` as 1440 in the oracle).

**Reasons.** Reading "positive numbers" against JSON's data model settles the finiteness question: JSON numbers are finite, and both validators already enforce that at the type keyword — duplicating a finiteness check (a `maximum: MAX_VALUE` hack in the schema, or an invariant in `findConfigProblems`) would add unreadable vocabulary for a case nothing can bypass, while the actual defect was the _message_, not the gate. Consolidating the matrix in a dedicated suite rather than scattering additions across the per-task specs keeps the §9.2 proof owned by one file: `config.spec.ts` pins the contract's shapes, `config-load.spec.ts` the loader's message vocabulary, `config-validation.spec.ts` the 073 submission seam — none of them had the cross-cutting §9.2 dimensions complete (`offPeakMultiplier` bounds, non-finite values, `24:00` endpoint semantics through the real pipeline, and the overlap property were the open cells).

**Consequences.** Message wording is contract (D-018 pins it by tests): the affected task-067 expectation was updated in the same commit, and any future consumer matching type-error text for non-finite inputs must expect `got a non-finite number` (none existed in-tree). The published JSON Schema document is unchanged — finiteness is `number`-type semantics, already implied, and D-015's committed artifact stays byte-identical. Any future numeric configuration setting inherits both the finiteness gate and the truthful naming automatically. Task 114 (interval calculation) consumes the schedule this matrix guards; the suite is the executable form of task 113's done-condition.

## D-072 — Success returns verify the exchange signals: a `done` body is not by itself a completed exchange, while delivered observations stay observations (spec §7.2; task U-007)

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§7.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#72-retry-and-error-behavior), [§7.3](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#73-account-status-precedence), [§8.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#81-provider-interface) · **Tasks:** [U-007](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-042, D-048, D-059, D-069

**Decision.** `providerFetch` consults D-042's signal-state classification authority on the **success returns**, not only the rejection paths: the read loop verifies deadline and caller signal state at the `done` resolution (before anything is declared delivered), and the bodiless-2xx return verifies the same before returning an empty body. A `done` resolution is not proof the exchange completed — CI run 41162981449 (matrix job `test (22.13.0)`, `test/integration/transport.spec.ts` "times out while reading a slow body") demonstrated that under a rare abort-vs-read race on a loaded 2-core runner, undici closes an aborted body stream as `done` instead of rejecting, so a deadline-exceeded exchange resolved as `{ status: 200, … }`, possibly truncated — which task 105's mapping would have recorded as a parse failure (`Format changed`) instead of the §7.2 timeout (`Unreachable`) it was. Pinned interpretations: (1) **One classifier, three call sites** — `classifyAbortedExchange(deadline, callerSignal, timeoutMs)` is the single signal-state authority (deadline first, caller second, `undefined` while both are quiet); `mapExchangeFailure` composes it ahead of the network taxonomy exactly as before, and a `throwIfExchangeAborted` guard runs at both success returns, so the both-fired deadline-wins precedence exists in exactly one place (it was documented but unpinned by any test before; the done-path both-fired case is now pinned). (2) **The benign corner resolves to timeout honestly**: a body that genuinely completed in the same window where the deadline fired still classifies as `TransportTimeoutError` — a fired `AbortSignal.timeout` means the full §7.2 budget was consumed, which is the definition of the timeout row; determinism (the signal state) beats reconstructing whether the last byte raced the timer. (3) **Delivered observations are never overridden**: the non-2xx (`TransportStatusError`), wrong-content-type (`TransportContentTypeError`), and over-cap (`TransportResponseTooLargeError`) paths keep their classifications even when the deadline or caller signal fired before the check — an arrived status is a complete, actionable observation, §7.2 assigns 429 and 401/403 rows distinct downstream behavior (deferral, auth suspension) that must not collapse into the retryable timeout row on a timer race, and none of those paths resolves an incomplete exchange as success, so the hole does not exist there. (4) **One check per success path is sufficient** because everything between each guard and its `return` is synchronous (merge/decode; the object literal) — no event-loop turn, so no timer can change the answer in between; a code comment pins the invariant for future editors.

**Reasons.** D-042's own sentence — "signal state is the classification authority, not the rejection shape" — was enforced only where a rejection existed to map; the CI failure showed the authority must also decide exchanges that _appear_ to succeed, because the runtime's stream teardown can express an abort as a clean close. The classification choice on the benign corner follows from the same authority: the alternative (trusting `done` when the body's length is unknown to the transport — JSON bodies carry no expected length to compare against) would reintroduce the hole for exactly the truncated case that motivated the fix. The observation-paths decision comes from §7.2's table structure: its rows are distinguished by evidence (status class, header, payload defect), and discarding arrived evidence because a timer raced it would make the classification depend on scheduling rather than on the exchange's facts; the status paths also consume nothing as success, so no completeness claim is being smuggled through them.

**Consequences.** Adapters (098, 099) and the downstream seam (105/106/107) change nothing — a transport timeout now surfaces as the `timeout` kind instead of a spurious parse failure, which is what those tasks always assumed they were consuming. The success-return verification and the observation-paths non-override are contract for any D-042 successor (a new return path must verify; a new observation class must not be overridden by signal state): changing either requires a successor decision. The lost race is pinned deterministically socket-free in `test/unit/transport.spec.ts` through the injected `fetchImpl` (a fetch double that resolves its `Response` only after the composed signal aborted — the shape undici produces when the abort loses to a delivered reply): done-resolving bodies (empty and truncated) and bodiless 2xx responses map to `TransportTimeoutError`/`TransportAbortError`, a clean completion still succeeds, the both-fired case keeps the deadline winning, and the observation paths keep their classes after the deadline fired; the real-socket suites (unit-shape pins and `test/integration/transport.spec.ts` slow-body) are unchanged and stay the honest-runtime guards.

## D-073 — Peak-hours intervals as a pure zone-driven timeline: half-open UTC intervals with an off-peak complement, and an injectable local-instant seam whose Luxon default leaves §9.3's DST policy single-sited in task 115 (spec §9.3, §10; task 114)

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§9.3](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#93-schedule-calculation-and-display), [§9.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#92-configuration-and-validation), [§10](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#10-time-and-time-zones), [§13](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#13-http-api) · **Tasks:** [114](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-014, D-018, D-021, D-068

**Decision.** `src/services/peak-hours-intervals.ts` implements `PeakHoursService`'s calculation half as a pure function, `calculatePeakHoursIntervals(schedule, range, resolveLocalInstant?)` — a validated `PeakHoursConfig` plus an explicit query range in, a timeline out; no storage, HTTP, CLI, or clock reading (the range endpoints are arguments, the D-068 discipline). Pinned interpretations: (1) **Output contract** — a `PeakHoursTimeline` `{ timezone, offPeakMultiplier, intervals }` whose intervals are a discriminated union (`peak` carrying `windowId`/`name`/`multiplier`, `off-peak` carrying `offPeakMultiplier`), each with exact UTC epoch-millisecond boundaries and both boundaries' local times in the schedule zone as `yyyy-MM-ddTHH:mm`. §13's endpoint row promises "UTC peak/off-peak intervals", so the timeline **partitions** the whole range — off-peak intervals are the complement of the peak occurrences — and §14's highlighting consumes a partition, not a sparse list. All intervals and the range are **half-open** `[start, end)`/`[from, to)`: minute-granular wall-clock windows are mirrorable without double coverage at shared edges, `24:00` ends, and clip boundaries; §9.3 is silent on inclusivity and the future route serializes whatever this pins. Local times are the **emitted (possibly clipped) boundaries** read in the zone — the truthful rendering of "local time in the schedule time zone" for a clipped interval, and the day is part of the string because off-peak stretches span days. (2) **Iteration and clipping** — the calculator walks the local calendar days of the schedule zone from one guard day before the range's first local day through its last, because a window ending at `24:00` can reach into the range only through that day's midnight. The walk is **count-bounded and anchored**: each day is one `firstLocalDay.plus({days: offset})` from the range's first local midnight, and the loop runs a fixed day count — never a cursor-stepping instant comparison, which silently drops the range's last local day in zones whose spring-forward gap starts at midnight (America/Havana, Africa/Cairo, America/Santiago), where a stepped cursor keeps the shifted 01:00 wall clock forever after (review finding, fixed with `America/Havana` regressions; task 115's §17.1 matrix should include a midnight-transition zone for the same reason). Same-day disjointness comes from the landed §9.2 validation, cross-day adjacency from the seam's monotonicity contract, so peaks are disjoint by construction and the complement needs no defensive clamping. A window that resolves to `end <= start` (collapsed entirely into a DST gap) is dropped and its wall-clock span stays off-peak — the only policy-neutral reading. `from === to` returns an empty timeline rather than an error; non-finite or inverted ranges throw; spans over `MAX_QUERY_SPAN_DAYS` (3660 — §11.3 retention's 3650-day ceiling plus headroom, measured on the query's own local days, guard day excluded) throw **before** the day loop, converting a potential multi-billion-day walk into a loud refusal while the §13 route keeps owning retention truncation. (3) **The seam** — every local wall-clock → instant conversion goes through an injectable `LocalInstantResolver` `(LocalScheduleTime{year, month, day, minutesSinceMidnight: 0–1440}, TimeZone) => EpochMs`; `1440` is the `24:00` end, resolved by the default to the following local day's midnight. The seam's documented contract is **weak monotonicity in local reading order** (a lexicographically earlier local reading never resolves to a later instant) — the property that keeps validated-disjoint windows disjoint as instants; any §9.3-faithful policy satisfies it. The default `resolveLocalInstantLuxon` follows Luxon's documented resolution, verified empirically on the pinned runtime (Luxon 3.7.2): a nonexistent local time lands shifted forward by the gap, an ambiguous one takes the first occurrence, `plus({days:1})` preserves wall clock — behavior that matches §9.3's words; the §17.1 transition matrix that **pins** the policy, per D-021, stays task 115's, which can pin the default by test or replace it at the seam without touching this algorithm. The default re-runs the IANA gate and validates its inputs (integer minutes, real calendar date, Luxon range), throwing English errors instead of returning `NaN`. (4) **Defaults** — omitted multipliers resolve through `CONFIG_DEFAULTS.peakHours` (`1.0` for both window and off-peak, D-014 item 6), one source of truth; zone validation is `resolveTimeZone` at this module's boundary (D-021's once-per-entry-point gate), and the §9.2 structural/invariant rules are never re-stated — the input is the validated contract's type.

**Reasons.** A partition is the only shape that makes both §13 consumers (route, chart) correct without client-side arithmetic — "the browser must not calculate windows independently" (§9.3) — and half-open bounds are the only choice under which a `24:00` end, touching windows, and range clipping compose without overlap or gap verdicts depending on inclusivity accidents. The guard day removes the one real boundary hazard (midnight-ending windows) at the cost of one filtered iteration. The span cap is deliberately a sanity bound, not policy: nothing in §9.3 limits ranges, but an unbounded local-day loop over full-range epochs would hang, and the loud refusal names the bound. The seam exists because D-021 deliberately left wall-clock → instant conversion out of `clock.ts` pending task 115; delegating to Luxon's documented behavior gives 114 a default that already matches §9.3 (probe-verified) without 114 legislating policy, and keeps 115's matrix — or its replacement resolver — authoritative in exactly one place. Property tests restrict generation to fixed-offset zones on purpose: there the epoch → local oracle (`zonedParts`, the D-021-unambiguous direction) agrees exactly with the local → epoch walk, while DST zones are 115's territory.

**Consequences.** The Stage 12 `/api/peak-hours` route serializes the timeline (epoch milliseconds → ISO 8601 `Z` via `toUtcIso` at its boundary) and owns retention truncation; the §14 UI renders the local-time strings verbatim. Task 115 pins or replaces `resolveLocalInstantLuxon`; changing the partition/half-open contract or the `PeakHoursTimeline` shape requires a successor decision. The module's scoped coverage is 100% statements/branches/functions/lines (§17.3's peak-hours target), and its suite is `TZ`-invariant by pinned-literal epochs (verified under four zones), extending D-068's invariance discipline without a subprocess suite because the module reads no machine zone by construction.

## D-074 — Conservative §12.1 reset detection: rolling-window value evidence inadmissible, monotonic-rounding tolerances, and the reason vocabulary the event writer stores (spec §12.1; task 117)

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§12.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#121-quota-reset-events), [§8.4](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#84-normalized-snapshot-and-metric-model) · **Tasks:** [117](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-010, D-021, D-046, D-047, D-048, D-058, D-060, D-069

**Decision.** `src/services/events-detection.ts` implements §12.1 as a pure service — points in, events out; no storage, no clock (every timestamp is data on the points, D-021). Pinned interpretations: (1) **Two entry points, one comparison core.** `detectResetEvent(previous, current)` compares one new valid point against the previous valid point of the same **account and metric** series (§12.1's words; at most one event per comparison — §12.1's "either condition" is disjunctive evidence, not two events); `detectSeriesResetEvents(points)` folds a flat interleaved list across accounts and metrics, each (account, metric) pair its own series, skipping invalid points entirely (neither compared nor made the comparison base — §12.1's "invalid points do not participate"), processing each series in input order (chronology is the caller's contract: both producers — history reads and snapshot arrival — are chronological, so disorder costs a missed event, never a false one). (2) **Tolerances.** `ABSOLUTE_TOLERANCE = 0` for `used`/`remaining` and `PERCENT_TOLERANCE = 1` percentage point for `percentUsed`/`percentRemaining`: every monotonic quantization (floor, ceil, nearest — the only roundings a provider applies) preserves ordering, so an apparent absolute decrease always implies a real one and there is no absolute rounding noise to allow for, while the provider's percentages are integers (D-047) whose one-point move is the documented noise class ("integer rounding makes 1-vs-0.1% expected noise") — a percentage signal fires only beyond one point. (3) **Condition 1 is judged jointly across every field pair both points carry.** The reset hypothesis predicts a direction per field — usage (`used`, `percentUsed`) falls, remaining (`remaining`, `percentRemaining`) rises — and the condition fires when at least one carried pair moves beyond its tolerance in the predicted direction **and no carried pair moves beyond its tolerance against the prediction**, whatever signal the contradicting field belongs to: within one signal, `percentUsed` rising against a falling `used` is provider inconsistency; across signals, `remaining` (or `percentRemaining`) falling against a falling `used` is a limit re-statement — under D-047's checked `used + remaining = limit` arithmetic, both sides of a coherent re-statement move together, which is the plan-change case, not a replenishment — and either kind of counterevidence makes the pair ambiguous. Which predicted movements were observed becomes the reason's `usage_decreased`/`remaining_increased` codes. Absent pairs do not participate; a `NaN` compares false everywhere (§8.4-invariant inputs are the contract; the boundary check and the storage columns already exclude non-finite values, so finiteness is not re-checked — the D-057 rule against defensively unreachable branches). (4) **Condition 2 reads "has passed" at the new snapshot** (`previous.resetsAt <= current.collectedAt`) **and "later" strictly** (`current.resetsAt > previous.resetsAt`); equal, earlier, missing, or not-yet-passed declarations do not fire. (5) **Event time:** the previous `resetsAt` when it lies strictly between the snapshots (`previous.collectedAt < resetsAt <= current.collectedAt`, `eventTimeSource: 'previous_resets_at'`), else the new collection time (`'current_collected_at'` — covering absent declarations and stale ones that had already passed before the previous snapshot). (6) **The conservative approach is admissibility, not magnitude.** For `ROLLING_WINDOW` metrics condition 1 is inadmissible on its own: a replenishing window can shed any amount between two samples — down to a full drop when a burst exits the window — so no value threshold is unambiguous, and requiring corroboration by condition 2 collapses to condition 2 anyway; only the declaration condition records rolling-window events, with `rolling_window_conservative` appended to the reason so the exception is visible in the stored evidence (D-046's "any conservative-approach exception"). Fixed-period quotas (`DAILY`, `WEEKLY`, `MONTHLY`, `OTHER`) do not replenish: both conditions fire independently. (7) **Ambiguity suppressions versus fail-fast** (the D-048 rule): data ambiguity records nothing — an out-of-order pair (`previous.collectedAt > current.collectedAt`), and a series redefinition between the points (`limitType` or `unit` changed; values are not comparable across accounting regimes) — while caller-contract violations throw `TypeError`: an invalid point reaching the pair comparison, or two points of different accounts or metric keys (the fold cannot express the latter two; the pair API guards both). (8) **The reason vocabulary is the stored contract**: `usage_decreased`, `remaining_increased`, `resets_at_advanced` (exported as `RESET_SIGNAL_CODES`) joined by `'+'` in canonical order, plus `rolling_window_conservative` on rolling events — D-046 deliberately made `$.reason` a free non-empty string and reserved its vocabulary to the detector; this is that vocabulary. (9) **The output is the D-046 writer contract verbatim and structurally identical to `CycleEventInput`** (`Omit<NewQuotaEvent, 'accountId' | 'runId'>`): `ResetEvent` carries exactly its four fields — `metricKey`, `eventType: 'RESET'`, `eventAt`, and `details` (`reason`, `previous`, `current` in the camelCase point vocabulary carrying only the fields the compared points carried — `runId` passed through when known — plus `tolerance` and `eventTimeSource`, the sole home of the event-time source; a top-level duplicate was rejected in review as a silent-drop-and-drift risk) — so task 118 plugs the detector into polling-persist's success write (D-069's empty `events` array) with no conversion, and the `quota_events` CHECKs accept the serialized evidence as-is.

**Reasons.** The done-condition — "ambiguous rolling-window transitions do not generate reset events" — forces the detector's central choice, and the spec's own sentence settles it: §12.1 says rolling quotas "can replenish gradually", so a value decrease on a rolling metric has a benign explanation by construction; magnitude thresholds (fire only on near-total drops) fail because a burst entering the window one poll before its exit produces exactly a total drop with no reset — no threshold separates the classes, and corroboration-by-declaration reduces to the declaration firing on its own. The tolerance split follows from what "allowed rounding tolerance" can mean per field class: absolutes are monotone under every rounding a provider applies (an apparent decrease is provably real), while D-047's verified integer percentages carry a one-point noise floor the house record itself names. The contradiction veto extends the same conservatism to within-condition evidence, and review made it joint rather than per-signal: §8.4 permits a metric to carry both absolutes and percentages, and a genuine reset moves every carried field the predicted way — so any beyond-tolerance movement against the prediction contradicts the hypothesis whatever field made it; the verified false-positive class is the plan change (under D-047's checked `used + remaining = limit` arithmetic, a coherent re-statement moves both sides of the identity together, so a falling `remaining` against a falling `used` is a smaller allowance, not a replenishment), and a per-signal contradiction check would have minted a `RESET` row for exactly that case. The suppression/fail-fast split copies D-048's distinction between data-dependent ambiguity (silence) and wiring bugs (loud `TypeError`): an invalid point or a foreign account/metric key reaching a pairwise comparison is a caller defect the next layer would otherwise silently mis-file — and keying the fold on the account as well as the metric makes the multi-account conflation unrepresentable instead of merely documented. Reusing the D-046 vocabulary and the `CycleEventInput` shape keeps the on-disk contract single-sourced: the repository serializes what the detector produced, and no naming layer can drift between them.

**Consequences.** Task 118 maps `ResetEvent[]` into the success write's `events` array unchanged and supplies `accountId`/`runId`; task 124 extends `test/unit/events-detection.property.spec.ts` (the done-condition property — arbitrary rolling value transitions without declaration evidence never fire — is standing and must survive any generator growth). The exported names (`detectResetEvent`, `detectSeriesResetEvents`, `ResetPointInput`, `ResetEvent`, `ResetEventEvidence`, `ResetPointEvidence`, `ResetEventTimeSource`, `ABSOLUTE_TOLERANCE`, `PERCENT_TOLERANCE`, `RESET_SIGNAL_CODES`, `ROLLING_WINDOW_NOTE`) and the reason strings are contract: the codes land in persisted `details.reason` rows, so changing any of them requires a successor decision (a UI or API consumer matching stored reasons would otherwise break silently). A future §12.1 event type or a provider whose rolling window declares resets differently gets a successor decision; relaxing the rolling-window rule (value-only firing) is precisely the false-positive class this decision exists to prevent.

## D-075 — Gap detection as a pure series function: the jitter-expanded strict three-interval threshold and the earlier-point interval anchor (spec §12.2; task 119)

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§12.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#122-collection-gaps-and-errors), [§7.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#71-polling), [§8.4](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#84-normalized-snapshot-and-metric-model) · **Tasks:** [119](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-010, D-021, D-066, D-069, D-070

**Decision.** `src/services/history-gaps.ts` implements §12.2's collection-gap rule as one pure function, `detectCollectionGaps(points, intervalSource)`: successful metric points plus the effective interval source in, `CollectionGap` records out — no storage, no clock (D-021), no error indicators (task 120's separate inputs), no chart semantics. Four interpretations are pinned. (1) **"Exceeds" is strict and the threshold is jitter-expanded.** §7.1 schedules each poll at the configured interval _plus_ an additive jitter of up to 10% of it — `pollingDelayMs`'s exact shape (D-066) — so three fully-stretched polls legitimately span 3 × 1.1 intervals; the effective interval is `effectivePollingIntervalMs(seconds)` = seconds × 1100 ms (exact integer arithmetic; the 100 ms/s allowance derives from `POLLING_JITTER_FRACTION`, imported from the scheduler as the one source of truth per D-070's precedent, and a property test pins integrality across the whole §7.1 range so a future non-integral fraction forces the arithmetic to be revisited), the threshold is `gapThresholdMs(seconds)` = 3 × that, and a gap requires elapsed strictly greater — an elapsed of exactly three raw intervals (900 s at the 300 s default) or exactly three effective intervals (990 s) is not a gap, 990 001 ms is. The strict boundary reads the spec's own verb, the same line D-070 drew for §7.3's `Fresh`/`Stale` pair ("no older than" vs "more than"). (2) **"The `interval_s` in effect at the relevant collection time" resolves at each adjacent pair's earlier point, _widened to the span's most permissive cadence when an interval change lands between the two points_.** Elapsed is measured from the earlier point and the polls that should have followed it were scheduled under the interval then in effect — a singular, causal anchor matching the spec's singular phrasing, and the rule for every pair whose span contains no change. A pair whose span _does_ contain a change is judged by the largest interval the span ever ran under (its start cadence, its end cadence, and every change inside the span): D-066's `setIntervalMs` re-anchors a pending poll to `now + newInterval + jitter`, so after a runtime grow the first post-change point legitimately arrives up to 1.1 × (old + new) after the last pre-change one — under the bare earlier-point anchor every grow beyond 2× (60 s → 300 s is one §6.4 edit away) would deterministically mint a false gap on a healthy series (a review finding against this task's first draft), and how many polls should have arrived during a re-anchored span is ambiguous evidence that resolves fail-safe, §12.1's own "do not create an event when evidence is ambiguous" spirit. The interval arrives as a constant or an explicit timeline of `IntervalChange`s (a constant is exactly a one-entry timeline; a change timestamp applies inclusively — a point at the change instant resolves the new interval, and a change at a pair's start edge is not "inside" its span; unsorted timelines are sorted; duplicate change times are ambiguous history and fail fast; every point must fall inside the timeline's coverage, or the call fails loudly rather than silently skipping pairs). A per-delay chained walk that re-resolves the interval at each _would-be_ poll was rejected for the same reason in both drafts: the spec names one interval per gap, and the walk would encode scheduler internals (re-anchor timing, suspension and `Retry-After` gates) into a history view §12.2 keeps consumption-side; the span widening keeps the singular anchor and repairs exactly the ambiguity class, at the price of under-detecting a real outage that happens to straddle a change — the conservative direction. (3) **Successful points only, edges only between observed points.** The caller supplies adjacent-successful-snapshot points (§12.2's own words; invalid metrics and failed cycles are excluded before detection — task 120 derives the separate error indicators), and no gap is invented before a series' first or after its last point: silence with no records is §12.2's stopped-service class, not a gap. (4) **Series partitioning is structural and the output deterministic.** Points partition by `(accountId, metricKey)` through nested maps (no composite-string keys — an id containing a joiner must never alias two series), each series is compared chronologically regardless of input order (stable sort; equal timestamps are a zero elapsed time, never a gap), and the result order is fixed: accounts in first-appearance order, metrics likewise within an account, gaps chronologically within a series. Validation is fail-fast with caller-addressed messages: §7.1's 60–3600 s range checked against the scheduler's own bounds (a seconds/milliseconds wiring mistake fails at the call, not as a nine-fold-off threshold), finite timestamps, non-blank ids, non-empty unique timelines, full coverage.

**Reasons.** §12.2 states the rule in one sentence with three open questions — the boundary comparison, jitter's effect on "three intervals", and which interval a pair is judged by when configuration changed — and §17.1's events-coverage line demands exactly the cells this pins ("three-interval gap threshold, and interval changes"). The jitter expansion is forced by the landed scheduler: its delays are additive (`interval + jitter(0..10%)`), so the largest legitimate three-poll silence is 3 × 1.1 × interval, and a raw 3× threshold would paint every fully-jittered cadence as an outage — the fail-safe direction (a false gap breaks the chart line; §12.1's sibling rule says not to create events on ambiguous evidence) also agrees. The earlier-point anchor is the only singular choice that is causal rather than coincidental: the later point's interval describes the schedule _after_ the silence, which says nothing about the polls that failed to arrive during it. The span widening is forced by D-066's landed re-anchor (`polling-scheduler.ts` `setIntervalMs` → `now + newInterval + jitter`): the change-caused silence is not an outage at all, and 1.1 × (old + new) > 3.3 × old exactly when a grow exceeds 2× — reachable by one runtime settings edit, and it would reach the chart line break and `GET /api/events` the moment tasks 120/125 consume these records. The pure-function shape follows D-070's evidence-function precedent: the `/api/events` route, the history consumers, and downsampling each hold different repository/config context and none should re-derive the threshold; exact-integer millisecond arithmetic exists because epoch timestamps are integers in practice and a float-noise threshold at the strict boundary (300 000 × 1.1 = 330 000.00000000006) would make the pinned boundary tests depend on representation error.

**Consequences.** The exported names (`GAP_THRESHOLD_INTERVALS`, `effectivePollingIntervalMs`, `gapThresholdMs`, `SuccessfulMetricPoint`, `IntervalChange`, `PollingIntervalSource`, `CollectionGap`, `detectCollectionGaps`) are contract; changing any requires a successor decision. Task 120 (error indicators) and the §13 `GET /api/events` route consume the gap records as data; downsampling (task 125) consumes `gapThresholdMs` and the gap edges for its "preserve gap boundaries" rule; task 124 extends `test/unit/history-gaps.property.spec.ts` (scheduler-producible cadences never gap, one stretched delta is exactly one correctly-placed gap, the boundary is exact at every §7.1 interval, a scheduler-producible runtime grow or shrink never gaps the straddling pair, and arbitrary multi-series input agrees with an independent oracle independent of input order), while `test/unit/history-gaps.spec.ts` pins both boundary sides at both thresholds, mid-series interval changes in both directions, straddling pairs in both directions — including the D-066-re-anchor grow scenario (390 000 ms straddle stays healthy) and a straddling silence that exceeds even the widened cadence — timeline edges, interleaved multi-account/multi-series input, unsorted input, duplicate timestamps, and the validation table. This wave's file-set discipline kept `src/services/README.md` untouched — the module's header documentation carries the consumer contract until the next sequential docs pass. A real outage that happens to straddle an interval change is under-detected by design (the widened threshold); a deployment needing per-poll chained resolution must bring a successor decision with the scheduler-resolution evidence.

## D-077 — Last-valid queries as a facade read: per-metric recency, the snapshot-pinned collection time, and absence instead of zero (spec §7.2, §11.2; task 122)

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§7.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#72-retry-and-error-behavior), [§11.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#112-required-logical-tables) · **Tasks:** [122](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-010, D-036, D-039, D-058, D-069, D-070

**Decision.** `QuotaRepository.getLatestValidMetricValues(accountId)` (in `src/storage/repository.ts`) answers §7.2's "retain and display the latest valid values and their collection time after an error" as one facade read: for each `metric_key` of the account, the most recent `metric_values` row with `is_valid = 1`, returned `metric_key`-ascending as full `MetricValueRecord`s — generalizing D-069's narrow settle-seam proof (task 110 showed failed runs keep the last success queryable; it never exercised per-metric invalidity, because a failed cycle writes no metric rows at all). Pinned interpretations: (1) **Recency is per metric, not per snapshot.** §8.4's "validity is per metric" plus the task's done-condition ("invalid metric rows do not erase last valid measurements") make each metric key independently keep its own newest valid row — a later invalid row for one metric neither erases that metric's last valid value nor delays the valid siblings of the same snapshot, so the returned rows may come from different snapshots. Whole-snapshot semantics (the latest snapshot's rows, invalid ones blanked) is rejected: it is exactly the erasure the done-condition forbids, and no existing facade read can express the per-metric answer — `getLatestSnapshot` returns only the newest header, `getMetricSeries` needs a key the caller cannot enumerate without scanning every run. (2) **The collection time is the metric row's denormalized `collected_at`**, structurally pinned to the snapshot's §8.4 stamp by the D-039 composite FK — the time of the collection that produced the value, not the run's `started_at`/`ended_at` (D-070's `lastSuccessAt` precedent for which clock a "latest valid" answer reads). (3) **Ordering is `collected_at DESC, run_id DESC`**: `collected_at` is not unique across snapshots, and the later-inserted run (the strictly increasing rowid snapshots are keyed by, D-036) is the more recent collection — the same deterministic-tiebreak rationale as the quota_events rowid order. (4) **Failed runs are invisible by structure, not by filter**: a failed cycle owns no snapshot and therefore no metric rows (D-036's composite FK), so the query needs no run-outcome term — parse failures, network failures, and auth rejections all change nothing because they contribute no rows. (5) **Invalid rows never surface**: the `is_valid = 1` filter is §7.2's "missing data must never be represented as zero" as SQL — an invalid row (NULL numerics per D-010) can neither win the recency window nor be returned, and an account with no valid rows (only invalid data, no runs, or an unknown account) yields an empty array — absence, never a synthetic row. (6) **One window-function statement**, `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY metric_key ORDER BY collected_at DESC, run_id DESC) = 1`, served by the §11.2 `metric_values_series_access (account_id, metric_key, collected_at)` index (proven via `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN`); the SQLite window-function support floor (≥ 3.25) is far below the pinned 3.47.2 runtime.

**Reasons.** Placement follows D-058's own taxonomy: this is a single-table read returning one existing record type — the `getLatestSnapshot` kind — so it is a facade method, not a sibling storage module (D-060/D-061 own multi-method compositions with policy) and not a `src/services/history-last-valid.ts` delegator (a 1:1 passthrough service would be facade theater; the §8.1 HistoryService and the §13 `/api/quota` route compose the facade read when those tasks land). The per-metric decision is forced by the done-condition's own words plus §8.4's sentence — validity being per metric, "the last valid measurements" can only mean each metric's own; the collection-time decision follows from §7.2's "their collection time" (the values' own stamp) and keeps D-070's storage-side answer (latest snapshot's stamp) and this query consistent: both read the §8.4 `collected_at` the D-039 denormalization freezes. The empty-array convention matches `getMetricSeries`/`getLatestSnapshot` (unknown account → empty), keeping every facade read total over its input vocabulary.

**Consequences.** The method is the storage seam the §13 `/api/quota` and §14.3 overview consumers read for "latest values per account"; task 110's `test/integration/polling-persist.spec.ts` keeps its narrow seam proof (failed runs cannot create false snapshots), while `test/integration/repository.spec.ts` owns the generalized done-condition: happy path (each metric's newest valid value with its own time, full-record round-trip), unchanged-after-failures (parse error with its §7.4 payload, network error, auth rejection), invalid-row-does-not-erase with the sibling updating from the same snapshot (values provably from different snapshots), invalid→valid recovery, only-invalid/runless/unknown accounts answering empty, multi-account isolation, the equal-stamp tiebreak, and the index service proof. The exported name and the per-metric/empty-array semantics are contract: changing either requires a successor decision. No new SQL exists outside `src/storage/` (D-058's gates untouched); no schema or migration change — the query is expressible over the landed tables and indexes exactly as §11.2 specified them.

## D-078 — Cycle reset-event detection wiring: the previous valid point is the last valid stored row, pairwise per cycle, with truthful evidence runIds (spec §12.1, §11.1; task 118)

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§12.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#121-quota-reset-events), [§11.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#111-collection-runs-and-snapshots) · **Tasks:** [118](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-021, D-046, D-058, D-060, D-069, D-074
