**Decision.** `src/services/events-cycle.ts` implements the storage-reading half of §12.1 — `detectCycleResetEvents(repository, accountId, snapshot)` — and `createCycleRecorder`'s success write (D-069) carries exactly its output as the cycle's `events` through D-060's §11.1 transaction, superseding D-069's interim empty array. Pinned interpretations: (1) **The "previous valid point" is the last valid stored row of the series** — `getMetricSeries` (the D-058 facade method built for per-account metric series), `collected_at`-ascending, walked from the end past any trailing invalid rows (§12.1's "invalid points do not participate" applies to the comparison base as much as to the new point). Storage order is arrival order and arrival is chronological under the same contract D-074 documents for its producers, so an out-of-order new snapshot (collected before the stored tail) is suppressed by the detector's own chronology guard — a missed event, never a false one; a time-bounded lookup (`to: collectedAt`) was rejected because it would compare such a snapshot against a point the stored timeline already superseded, manufacturing an event from evidence the service has newer readings for. (2) **Detection is pairwise and per-cycle, never a re-fold over history.** Each valid metric of the new snapshot is compared once, against the last valid stored point only: the events of a cycle are a function of its own snapshot and the stored tail alone, so a reset a previous cycle recorded can never be detected again and no backfill over already-persisted history ever runs (test-pinned: a stored p1→p2 reset is attributed to the cycle that detected it, exactly once, and a steady p3 mints nothing). (3) **Reads happen before the write** — outside and before D-060's transaction — so the new snapshot's own points cannot become their own comparison base; the events then ride the same transaction as the snapshot they evidence, which the D-046 composite foreign key makes the only structurally possible home for them. Detection runs on the success branch only: failed cycles have no snapshot (and an event-without-its-snapshot row is unrepresentable anyway), a cancelled cycle persists nothing (D-069), and a provider success failing §8.4 classification never reaches detection. (4) **Invalid metrics of the new snapshot are skipped at the seam**, before the pair API — D-074 deliberately treats an invalid point reaching the pair comparison as a wiring `TypeError`, and the seam is the layer that guarantees the contract rather than the detector that weakens for it. (5) **Evidence runIds are truthful, not symmetric**: `details.previous.runId` passes through from the stored row (which run produced the comparison base); `details.current` carries none — the cycle's run id does not exist until the write assigns it, and the event row's `run_id` is D-060's injection, pointing at the snapshot the event came from. (6) **Duplicate metric keys cannot reach detection**: the §8.4 boundary rejects them, so the snapshot a success write carries has unique keys by construction. (7) **The per-cycle read is a full (indexed, retention-bounded) series scan per valid metric** — `metric_values_series_access` serves it and §11.3 retention bounds it; a latest-point facade variant is a future optimization, not a correctness need.

**Reasons.** §12.1 says "compare each new snapshot with the previous valid point for the same account and metric", and in a persisted world that phrase has exactly one natural referent: the stored tail of the series the repository already serves (`getMetricSeries` exists for §13 history and carries the §8.4 validity flag per row — no new storage surface is needed, keeping the sibling-task boundary of the wave intact). Pairwise-only detection is what makes the wiring idempotent: a fold over the stored series at every cycle would re-mint already-recorded resets (the stored p1→p2 pair fires again when p3 arrives), so the alternative is not "more thorough" but wrong twice over — duplicate events and detection cost growing with history. The invalid-current skip keeps D-074's fail-fast contract meaningful: the pure detector may not grow a tolerance for its own callers, so the layer that knows which points are new enforces the participation rule. The runId asymmetry follows D-046's evidence ethos — the audit trail records what was actually known at detection time, and fabricating a not-yet-assigned run id (or dropping the previous point's provenance) would make the evidence less truthful, not more uniform.

**Consequences.** A successful cycle's persisted events are exactly the detector's output — reason in `details.reason` (D-074's vocabulary, `rolling_window_conservative` suffix included), `event_at` per §12.1's rule — so tasks 119/124 (the EventService and `/api/events` consumers) read §12.1-faithful rows via `listQuotaEvents` from the first cycle after upgrade; existing databases need no migration (events are produced going forward; no backfill, by pin 2). The exported name `detectCycleResetEvents` and the seam's placement (success branch of `createCycleRecorder`, reading only `getMetricSeries`) are contract; moving detection into the storage layer or the scheduler would be a successor decision. The success path now performs one indexed series read per valid metric per cycle — bounded by retention, and the flagged future facade extension (a `getLatestMetricValue`-style method) would be its own D-058-successor decision. `test/integration/events-cycle.spec.ts` is the standing end-to-end proof of the task's done-condition (both event-time branches, evidence round-trips, every silence, the skip-back, the no-refold invariant, per-metric independence); `test/unit/events-cycle.spec.ts` pins the mapping edges.

## D-079 — §9.3's DST policy computed explicitly in a dedicated resolver, and peak-occurrence union clipping replacing D-073's monotonicity assumption (spec §9.3, §17.1; task 115)

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§9.3](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#93-schedule-calculation-and-display), [§9.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#92-configuration-and-validation), [§17.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#171-required-test-coverage), [§17.3](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#173-enforced-quality-thresholds) · **Tasks:** [115](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-021, D-073

**Decision.** `src/services/peak-hours-dst.ts` implements §9.3's two DST rules as the authoritative `LocalInstantResolver`, `resolveLocalInstantDst(time, timeZone)` — now the default of `calculatePeakHoursIntervals` — with these pinned interpretations: (1) **Policy by offset differencing, not delegation.** The wall reading becomes a pseudo-epoch (fields as if UTC); the distinct zone offsets active at one-day probes around it are the candidates; a candidate proves an occurrence by round-trip (the proposed instant reads back as exactly the input calendar date and time); occurrences found → the earliest is the answer (**first occurrence** for ambiguous readings — §9.3), none found → the reading is inside a gap and the answer is the pre-transition (smaller) offset's instant, which lands after the jump reading as wall + gap (**shift forward by the exact gap** — the offset delta, so `Australia/Lord_Howe`'s 30-minute gaps and `Pacific/Chatham`'s 02:45 gaps shift by their own sizes, and `America/Havana`'s midnight gap shifts day-start and `24:00` edges alike). `24:00` normalizes to the next calendar day's 00:00 wall reading before resolution (§9.2's "the midnight that ends the day"). All zone access goes through the canonical D-021 epoch→zone direction (`zonedParts`); the assumptions are the modern tz-database envelope (minute-aligned transitions between two offsets — every zone post-1972, second-level offsets like Monrovia's −00:44:30 are outside the minute-granular `LocalScheduleTime` vocabulary — and never two transitions within 48 hours; probe sufficiency holds through the 24-hour dateline gaps, whose pre-offsets are ≤ −10 hours) and are documented in the module. (2) **Why not Luxon.** Luxon's wall-time resolution converges from an offset guess seeded by the machine's current instant (`fixOffset`/`guessOffsetForZone`); it produces §9.3's answers across the matrix on the pinned runtime (verified), but as a property of its iteration, not a contract — and it demonstrably diverges on `24:00` of a day whose own midnight was gapped (Havana 2026-03-08: shifted-midnight plus a calendar day applies the shift twice, landing an hour late). `resolveLocalInstantLuxon` therefore stays exported as the compat alternative, pinned equal to the authoritative resolver across the §17.1 matrix (every minute of every transition day and its neighbors) with exactly that `24:00` divergence carved out and pinned. (3) **Union clipping supersedes D-073's monotonicity clause.** §9.3's gap shift is provably not monotone in wall order — a nonexistent 02:30 resolves to the instant of 03:30, later than the real 03:00 — so two wall-disjoint §9.2-valid windows (e.g. 02:10–02:50 and 03:10–03:50 on a New York spring-forward day) can resolve to overlapping or identical instants, which the landed sort-and-complement walk would double-cover; the claim "any §9.3-faithful policy satisfies this" (D-073) is false and is corrected here. The calculator now sorts peak candidates by `(start, end)` and clips each start to the still-uncovered stretch (dropping fully covered ones, rendering local times from the finally emitted boundaries), so the timeline is the **union** of the occurrences — the D-073 partition contract (chronological, adjacent, single coverage of `[from, to)`) holds for any resolver, monotone or not; seam implementations are no longer required to be monotone, and windows whose edges meet or invert under the resolver still collapse to off-peak. (4) **Matrix.** §17.1's zones (`America/New_York`, `Europe/London`, `Asia/Shanghai`, `Asia/Kolkata`, `Australia/Lord_Howe`, `Pacific/Chatham`, `UTC`) plus `America/Havana` (midnight-starting gap — the shape task 114's review required) and `Asia/Singapore` (the §9.1 production zone); transition coverage is three-layer: hand-derived pinned epochs at every gap/ambiguity edge, whole-timeline walks (23/25-hour days, windows inside/across gaps and overlaps, `24:00` ends), and an exhaustive every-minute check of every transition day and its neighbors against an independent brute-force scan oracle (first occurrence / gap shift re-derived from a minute-step sweep), with fast-check properties (fixed-offset zones never shift; arbitrary 2024–2028 readings agree with the oracle) and TZ-invariance of the pinned literals verified under six host `TZ` values.

**Reasons.** §9.3 commands "document and test these rules" — a policy the application merely inherits from a library's convergence behavior is neither documented as its own nor testable at its edges; computing it from the canonical offset function makes the rules the code and lets the matrix pin them directly (including the half-hour and quarter-hour shapes the matrix zones exist to cover). The union-clip repair is forced: the non-monotonicity is inherent to the shift rule itself (not an implementation choice), so no §9.3-faithful resolver can buy back D-073's assumption — only the consumer of the seam can restore the partition, and the union of the peak occurrences is the only set the complement (off-peak) can be exact against. Keeping the Luxon resolver exported (rather than deleting it) preserves task 114's landed test surface and gives the parity sweep a second, independent implementation to cross-check the authoritative one against. `Australia/Sydney`'s fall-back is pinned as an extra case because it is the shape that separates policy from convergence: for zones east of UTC the pseudo-epoch sits after the transition instant, exactly where guess-seeded resolution is most at risk of returning the later repetition.

**Consequences.** The Stage 12 `/api/peak-hours` route consumes timelines whose partition no longer depends on resolver monotonicity; injecting a non-monotone resolver (or a future policy change) cannot produce double coverage or non-chronological output — it can only change which instants are peak. The exported names (`resolveLocalInstantDst`, `EPOCH_RANGE_MS` semantics, the error vocabulary) are contract; changing the gap/ambiguity policy or the union-clipping semantics requires a successor decision. Scoped coverage of both peak-hours modules is 100% statements/branches/functions/lines (§17.3's target); the exhaustive minute sweeps and scan-oracle properties are the standing proof for any future zone-rule change (rerun with `FC_SEED` to reproduce fast-check failures). The `src/services/README.md` entry for the new module is owed by the main session's docs pass for this wave (file-set discipline kept it untouched here). D-073's seam documentation in `peak-hours-intervals.ts` carries the corrected contract with a pointer here; D-073's other clauses (partition, half-open bounds, guard day, span cap, output shape) are unchanged.

## D-080 — §12.2 timeline indicators: per-cycle error markers and the record-based stopped-service class (spec §12.2, §13; task 120)

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§12.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#122-collection-gaps-and-errors), [§13](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#13-http-api) · **Tasks:** [120](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-021, D-034, D-048, D-059, D-062, D-066, D-069, D-070, D-075

**Decision.** `buildTimelineIndicators(runs, range)` in `src/services/history-timeline.ts` derives §12.2's two timeline-indicator classes from the run records themselves — the complementary view to D-075's gaps between successful metric points — as one pure function (records plus an explicit `[from, to]` range in, a `kind`-discriminated `TimelineIndicator` union out; no storage, no clock per D-021). Pinned interpretations: (1) **One `collection_error` indicator per failed run, no merging.** §12.2 asks for "distinct symbol/tooltip per error type" and §14.4 renders "failed collection attempts as markers on a lower timeline strip" — cycles are the unit, so merging contiguous failures would erase adjacent distinct failure types and §7.2's per-cycle attempt count. Each indicator is typed by the §11.2 outcome (the D-048/D-034 vocabulary imported from `polling-outcomes.ts`, never redefined), positioned at the cycle's own `[startedAt, endedAt]` span, and carries the run's evidence (HTTP status, sanitized error message, attempts, deferred-429 `retryAfterSeconds`) so the §13 route and §14.4 tooltip need no second lookup. An indicator is emitted only for a failed cycle whose `startedAt` falls inside the range (inclusive both ends — the marker position decides); every supplied record, in range or not, still bounds silence. (2) **The stopped class is record-based and shares D-075's silence threshold.** §11.1 writes a run row for every executed cycle whatever the outcome, so "no collection-run records at all" is exactly "no collection activity"; a `stopped_service` region is a maximal run-less sub-interval of the range whose silence **strictly exceeds three jitter-expanded effective intervals** — `gapThresholdMs` imported from `history-gaps.ts` (one source of truth, D-070's precedent), not redefined. Below that threshold lies the legitimate inter-poll cadence (§7.1 interval + jitter); without a threshold, every inter-poll gap would be hatched as downtime. `Retry-After` deferrals (§7.2, up to one hour) and auth-suspension probe gaps (D-064, hourly) are deliberately **not** subtracted: D-075's own precedent keeps scheduler policy gates out of the §12.2 history view, the class is defined by records, and the deferral/suspension evidence travels on the boundary runs' own fields for §13/§14 consumers to refine tooltips — the accepted cost is that a legitimately deferred 429 at 300 s cadence paints a "no collection activity" area, which is factually true of the records. (3) **Region edges and the judge cadence.** Interior silence spans `[max(previous record's endedAt, from), min(next record's startedAt, to)]` against an aliveness frontier — the maximum `endedAt` walked so far, so overlapping records can never shorten silence, and the frontier owner's own interval stamp is the left anchor; the leading edge is `[from, first.startedAt]`, the trailing `[frontier.endedAt, to]`, each judged by its single bounding record's cadence when the other side has no record. Interior silence is judged by the **more permissive** of the two boundary stamps — D-075's span-widening with the per-run `interval_seconds` (D-069) as the cadence evidence: a mid-silence §6.4 change re-anchors the schedule (D-066), the polls that should have arrived are ambiguous evidence, and the fail-safe direction is no region. All supplied records participate, so a caller that supplies the immediate out-of-range neighbors anchors its edge silences exactly; without them, a lone edge record's cadence judges (documented). (4) **Degenerate inputs.** Empty input answers `[]` — no records means no cadence evidence to judge silence by, and full-range downtime is expressible by supplying the bounding records outside the range; `from === to` is a degenerate range yielding at most the markers starting exactly on that instant, never a region (a region needs positive span past the threshold). (5) **Determinism and validation.** Accounts partition through nested maps in first-appearance order; within an account the single chronological walk emits sorted output by construction (a region starts strictly before the record that closes it); input order is irrelevant and equal `startedAt` keep input order. Fail-fast validation follows the D-059/D-064/D-075 convention with caller-addressed English messages: finite `from ≤ to` range, per run non-blank account, finite non-inverted cycle bounds, integer interval in §7.1's 60–3600 (checked against the scheduler's own constants), `isCollectionOutcome` membership (unknown values — including `'cancelled'` — fail fast), integer `attempts ≥ 1`, optional `httpStatus` in D-034's 100–599, optional `retryAfterSeconds` in `[0, RETRY_AFTER_MAX_SECONDS]` — the same bound the `collection_runs` CHECK enforces, whose `0` boundary is D-062's elapsed-`Retry-After` value the writer persists and the row reader must therefore accept (a code-review finding against the first draft, which demanded ≥ 1 and would have 500ed a future `/api/events` on any account holding such a row), optional string error message.

**Reasons.** §12.2's second paragraph names both classes in record terms, and D-069 pinned the same boundary from the write side — a `stop()` abort is deliberately unpersisted and therefore belongs to the no-records class, not the failed-cycle class; this module reads that boundary back without re-deciding it. The per-cycle granularity is forced by the spec's own per-error-type symbols; the threshold reuse is forced by the reductio of the alternative and by §12.2/§7.3's shared "three intervals" silence vocabulary; the boundary-cadence widening and the refusal to encode deferral/suspension gates both follow D-075's landed reasoning (ambiguous schedule evidence resolves fail-safe; consumption-side simplicity over scheduler-internals leakage — a per-poll chained walk was rejected there and is rejected here for the same reason). The done-condition — "API-ready events distinguish failure types from no collection activity" — is met structurally rather than by convention: the `kind` discriminant carries the distinction into the type system (error indicators have an `outcome`, stopped indicators have no such property), so `GET /api/events` can serialize the union as-is beside resets and gaps.

**Consequences.** The exported names (`buildTimelineIndicators`, `TimelineIndicator`, `CollectionErrorIndicator`, `StoppedServiceIndicator`, `CollectionRunInput`, `TimelineQueryRange`, `FailedOutcome`) are contract; changing any requires a successor decision. The §13 `GET /api/events` route serializes the union directly; the §14.4 chart consumes `kind`/`outcome` for its symbol and tooltip choices; `src/services/README.md` gains its module entry in the next sequential docs pass (main-session-owned in this wave). Verification is executable: `test/unit/history-timeline.spec.ts` pins all six failure types, adjacent distinct types unmerged, the threshold boundary on both sides, an interleaved record splitting an outage, both range edges with clamping and out-of-range anchoring, boundary-cadence widening in both directions, overlapping records against the aliveness frontier, per-account isolation with first-appearance and chronological order, unsorted and duplicate-timestamp input, the degenerate ranges, the full fail-fast table, and the done-condition as a runnable block (runtime property absence plus type-level narrowing); `test/unit/history-timeline.property.spec.ts` proves over generated histories that error indicators are exactly the failed cycles, stopped regions are disjoint/in-range/past-their-threshold/record-free, and the output is invariant under input permutation up to the account-block order, with vacuity tripwires. A legitimately deferred 429 or a suspended account's probe gap paints "no collection activity" by design; a deployment needing deferral-aware downtime must bring a successor decision with the scheduler-resolution evidence.

## D-081 — History downsampling as boundary-separated segments: per-field extrema, first/last point references, slice-width resolution, and the must-not-be-lost precedence (spec §13, §17.1; task 121)

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§13](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#13-http-api), [§17.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#171-required-test-coverage) · **Tasks:** [121](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-010, D-021, D-059, D-068, D-074, D-075

**Decision.** `downsampleHistorySeries(points, maxPoints, boundaries?)` in `src/services/history-downsample.ts` is the pure §13 aggregation rule — points, a point budget, and the critical boundaries (as data: the D-074 `ResetEvent`s' `eventAt` and the D-075 `CollectionGap`s' interval, via structural interfaces both satisfy verbatim, already filtered to the one series being downsampled) in; frozen buckets or a passthrough out. Pinned interpretations: (1) **Per-field extrema, first/last by reference.** §13's "preserving each bucket's minimum, maximum, first, and last points" is undefined for multi-field points read as whole points, so the minima/maxima are per field (`used`, `remaining`, `percentUsed`, `percentRemaining`) over the members that carry each field — a field absent from every member is absent from the extrema — while `first`/`last` are the earliest/latest member point objects themselves, references to the caller's input, so fields beyond the declared vocabulary ride along untouched (§14.4's charts read used/remaining; §8.4/D-010 fixes the vocabulary). (2) **Boundaries are separations between consecutive points, not grid instants.** A reset instant `e` separates the pair with `previous < e ≤ next` — a reset stamped at a point's own collection time (D-074's `current_collected_at` source) groups that point with the **post** side, where it belongs, and a `previous_resets_at` event strictly between points separates naturally. A gap `(from, to)` separates exactly the pair straddling its whole interval (`previous ≤ from ∧ next ≥ to`): both edge points — D-075 guarantees they are adjacent successful points — keep their own side of the silence, and gaps whose edges fall between the points (detection over a wider range than the requested series) split the same pair. Equal-timestamp pairs never separate (both windows are empty). This replaces the natural first reading — boundaries as instants that split uniform grid buckets — because a grid-edge split needs a per-edge tie rule that cannot serve both gap edges (the from-point must stay pre-gap, the to-point post-gap, and a single instant rule sends one of them to the wrong side), while consecutive-pair separations pin both exactly. (3) **Segment-first apportionment, not a global grid.** Separations cut the chronologically (stably) sorted series into segments aggregated independently, so the boundary rule holds by construction — no bucket can span a boundary. Segment `i` with `nᵢ` of `N` points receives `1 + ⌊nᵢ·E/N⌋` buckets, `E = maxPoints − S`: at least one per segment, never more than its own points (`nᵢ·E < nᵢ·N` since `E < N`), and the floors sum to at most `E` — the budget holds by arithmetic, with no capping, remainder passes, or iterative redistribution (all drafted and dropped: cap-and-redistribute largest-remainder apportionment admits states where the exact-budget sum is unsatisfiable under per-segment minimums and needs defensive termination guards, and the house rule rejects defensively unreachable branches in a §17.3 Stryker-critical module). Within a segment, members land in time slice `⌊(t − s)·b/span⌋` — cross-multiplied arithmetic, exact for the integer timestamps epoch milliseconds are, every product below 2⁵³ over any §14.4 range and budget — anchored at the segment's first member; empty slices are not emitted (a cluster may leave interior slices vacant), and a zero-span segment lands entirely in slice 0. Bucket edges are observed member timestamps, never synthetic grid values. (4) **The boundary rule outranks the budget.** §13's "Reset events and gap boundaries must not be lost" is the sentence with _must_; `maxPoints` is a threshold and target. When the boundary structure itself needs more buckets than the budget (more segments than `maxPoints` — unreachable below 100 boundaries, since §13 caps the accepted range at 100–5000), every segment stays exactly one bucket and the count may exceed `maxPoints`; merging across a boundary to satisfy the count is exactly the loss §13 forbids. The count stays bounded regardless: `≤ max(maxPoints, segments)` always, `≤ maxPoints` whenever `segments ≤ maxPoints`. (5) **Passthrough and resolution.** A series with at most `maxPoints` points ("more points" is strict) passes through unaggregated — stably sorted, the caller's objects — with `resolutionMs: null`. The effective resolution §13 wants in the response is the **widest allocated slice width** (`segment span / bucket count`, maximized over segments) — the granularity the aggregation operated at; observed bucket member spans can fall below it (clustered or simultaneous points) and would understate how coarsely values were merged, which is why the first draft's max-observed-span definition was replaced mid-task by its own failing fixture. Constants from §13 verbatim: default 1500, accepted 100–5000, both validated fail-fast.

**Reasons.** §13 states the contract in one sentence with five open questions — what min/max mean for multi-field points, how boundaries survive aggregation, whether buckets are uniform in time or count, what resolution to report, and what happens at exactly `maxPoints`. The consumers are already landed: D-074's and D-075's detectors give the boundaries as data (the task forbids recomputing detection), §8.4/D-010 fixes the value vocabulary, and D-068's rolling ranges fix the spans that get downsampled. The consecutive-pair separation rule is forced by the two detectors' own timestamp conventions; the apportionment closed form is the unique one satisfying `1 ≤ bᵢ ≤ nᵢ` and `Σbᵢ ≤ maxPoints` without iteration; and the precedence (4) resolves the only genuinely contradictory corner — a series with more boundaries than the budget, where "count ≤ budget" and "no bucket spans a boundary" cannot both hold — in the direction of §13's only unconditional verb.

**Consequences.** The exported names (`DEFAULT_MAX_POINTS`, `MIN_MAX_POINTS`, `MAX_MAX_POINTS`, `DownsamplePoint`, `ResetEventBoundary`, `GapBoundary`, `DownsampleBoundaries`, `BucketExtrema`, `MetricBucket`, `DownsamplePassthrough`, `DownsampledSeries`, `DownsampleResult`, `downsampleHistorySeries`) are contract; changing any requires a successor decision. The §13 `GET /api/history` route (Stage 12) composes the service: request `maxPoints` validated/clamped at the HTTP boundary, points from the repository read, reset boundaries from the events table and gap boundaries from `detectCollectionGaps` for exactly this series and range; `resolutionMs` serializes as the response's effective resolution (`null` = raw points), and a chart layer can detect segment breaks between adjacent buckets by consulting the same boundary data. The done-condition (§17.1 "preserve bucket extrema, first/last points, reset markers, and gap boundaries") is verified by `test/unit/history-downsample.spec.ts` (the passthrough boundary at exactly `maxPoints`, a hand-computed 200-point pair layout with exact per-field extrema and first/last reference identity, both boundary kinds in both edge placements — at-point resets going post-side and interior-edge gaps —, out-of-span boundaries, adjacent separations with a one-point segment, one separation for a reset and a gap sharing a pair, simultaneous and clustered series including empty-slice skipping, the carve-out at 102 segments over a 100 budget, allocation never exceeding segment size, determinism/shuffle invariance/freezing, and the fail-fast validation table) and `test/unit/history-downsample.property.spec.ts` (over generated strictly-chronological series with generated D-074/D-075-shaped boundaries: the mode boundary follows `maxPoints` exactly; bucket counts respect the budget and the unconditional carve-out bound; a chronological member walk reproduces every bucket's `first`/`last` references and count — the coverage, no-loss, and no-reorder oracle —; each bucket's per-field extrema equal the true aggregates of exactly the walked members; the whole series' extrema survive in the bucket extrema; no bucket spans any reset or gap; resolution bounds; determinism and input-order invariance — task 124 extends this suite). `src/services/README.md` stays untouched this wave (main-session-owned); the module header carries the consumer contract until the sequential docs pass.

## D-082 — Retention-aware history queries as a storage sibling: the three-outcome bounded-range report, lower-bound-only clamping on the reads' closed intervals, and rejection as data (spec §11.3, §13; task 123)

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§11.3](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#113-retention-and-cleanup), [§13](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#13-http-api) · **Tasks:** [123](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-014, D-021, D-039, D-058, D-060, D-063, D-068, D-073, D-077

**Decision.** `src/storage/history-retention.ts` implements §13's range sentence — "Reject or explicitly truncate requested ranges beyond retention and state that in the response" — as the query-side twin of D-063's cleanup: `boundHistoryRange(requested, window)` computes and reports the effective range, and three wrappers (`getMetricSeriesWithRetention`, `listQuotaEventsWithRetention`, `listCollectionRunsWithRetention` — the storage sources §13's range-bearing endpoints draw from) serve the already-clamped reads beside the report as `RetentionAwareRead<T> { range, rows }`. Pinned interpretations: (1) **A sibling storage module, not facade methods** — the fifth application of the D-060/D-061/D-063/D-067 pattern. D-058's facade is the config-agnostic per-table surface; a retention bound is configuration policy (`app.historyRetentionDays`, D-014/D-022) that would force a window argument onto every `getMetricSeries` caller, including consumers that legitimately read raw series (D-078's reset detection, D-075's gap detection over caller-bounded input). The existing reads stay unclamped (pinned by test); no new SQL exists — the wrappers delegate to facade methods whose index service is already query-plan-proven (D-058/D-077). (2) **The window is caller-supplied and validated before anything is read** (D-021/D-063): `{ now, retentionDays }` arrives from the caller's clock and loaded configuration, and §11.3's 7–3650 bounds are enforced at this boundary too (reusing D-063's exported constants), because a range about a query parameter is policy no schema CHECK can express; malformed requests (non-finite `now`/`from`/`to`, `from > to`) fail the same way — an inverted range is bad input, not a retention outcome. (3) **Three outcomes, `rejected` among them is data, not a throw**: a range entirely older than the horizon returns empty rows with the horizon and the requested bounds, so the §13 layer can state it in the response — whether that becomes an HTTP error or an empty-series notice is the API layer's choice, kept open by the spec's own "reject **or** explicitly truncate"; a partially older range is truncated to `[horizon, to]` with the requested `from` reported; a range at or after the horizon passes through unchanged. (4) **Only the lower bound clamps** — retention is a rule about old data; `to` passes through untouched (§10's rolling ranges legitimately end at `now`, and a future `to` is not retention's concern). (5) **The bounds share the landed reads' closed-interval convention** (`>= from AND <= to`, D-068) — not the half-open intervals of D-073's peak-hours timeline, a different surface. The horizon arithmetic is identical to D-063's `historyCutoff`, and those deletes are strict-before, so `[horizon, ∞)` is exactly the set of timestamps cleanup leaves: the effective range serves precisely what retention retains, down to a row collected exactly at the horizon. Each read bounds its own time column (series `collected_at`, events `event_at`, runs `started_at`); the one shape diverging from the delete side — a run started before the horizon whose snapshot collected at or after it — is served until the cleanup deletes its run, a divergence bounded by one run's duration around the horizon (pinned by test, not papered over with a join the D-039 denormalization exists to avoid). (6) **Enforcement is independent of cleanup timing** — rows older than the horizon are never returned through this seam even while they still sit in the database between daily cleanups; out-of-policy data is not queryable through history reads, merely not yet deleted.

**Reasons.** The placement question had the same answer as the four siblings before it: D-058 designed the facade by walking consumers and this task's policy composes that surface without extension, while clamping inside the reads would smuggle configuration into a layer pinned config-agnostic and break raw-series consumers. The outcome vocabulary is forced by §13's own disjunction: "reject or truncate" cannot be decided at the storage boundary (the wire form is the API layer's), so the seam returns the decision's ingredients — outcome, effective bounds, horizon, requested bounds — as a discriminated union in which nonsense states (a rejected range with effective bounds, an untruncated range echoing its request) are unrepresentable, the D-062 pattern. Lower-bound-only clamping follows retention's direction (§11.3 deletes old rows; nothing ever truncates a range's future end). The closed-interval pin is alignment, not preference: D-068 fixed §13's server-side filter as closed intervals, D-063's deletes are strict-before on the same arithmetic, so closed clamp + strict-before delete describe one retained set — provable by running the cleanup and comparing (pinned), where a half-open clamp would systematically drop or keep the horizon row depending on which end moved. The straddle divergence is recorded rather than engineered away because the alternative is a series-to-runs join at §11.3's ~52,000-snapshots-per-account scale — exactly what the D-039 denormalization eliminated — to recover, at most, one run's duration of accuracy at the horizon edge on data the next cleanup deletes anyway.

**Consequences.** The Stage 12 consumers (the timeline service, the downsampling service, the events endpoint) call these wrappers as their storage seam and receive the §13 truncation/rejection notice as data; `boundHistoryRange` is also exported for range-only consumers (the §14.4 disable-ranges-exceeding-retention rule can decide from it without touching the database). The exported names (`boundHistoryRange`, `getMetricSeriesWithRetention`, `listQuotaEventsWithRetention`, `listCollectionRunsWithRetention`, `RetentionWindow`, `RequestedHistoryRange`, `RetentionBoundedRange`, `RetentionAwareRead`) and the three-outcome semantics are contract: changing any requires a successor decision. `test/integration/history-retention.spec.ts` is the standing proof of the done-condition ("callers can identify the effective history range") and pins both sides of every boundary: ok/truncated/rejected with full reports, the horizon at each range edge (both sides of `from` and `to`, the point range at the horizon), the unclamped upper bound, §11.3's 7/3650 day boundaries accepted and 6/3651/fractional/NaN rejected before anything is read, non-finite and inverted requests, empty databases, a horizon newer than all data, per-account isolation, the pass-through facade filters (metric key, run outcome), out-of-policy rows hidden while undeleted, the raw facade reads staying unclamped (D-058), and the D-063 alignment — after a cleanup with the same window, nothing the clamp served is deleted and nothing it hid survives, with the straddle case pinned separately. No new SQL exists outside `src/storage/` (the D-058 gates untouched); no schema or migration change.

## D-083 — The latest-valid-point read consumed by cycle reset detection: task 122's facade method is the D-058-successor read, and the ordering reconciliation that makes the swap behavior-identical (spec §12.1, §11.2; task U-011)

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§12.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#121-quota-reset-events), [§11.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#112-required-logical-tables) · **Tasks:** [U-011](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-036, D-058, D-074, D-077, D-078

**Decision.** U-011 closes D-078's flagged consequence (its pin 7: the per-cycle read was "a full (indexed, retention-bounded) series scan per valid metric … a latest-point facade variant is a future optimization") by consuming the read task 122 had already landed: `detectCycleResetEvents`'s comparison base is now `getLatestValidMetricValues(accountId)` (D-077) — one account-level read per successful cycle, mapped by metric key, performed lazily so a zero-metric or all-invalid snapshot still reads nothing — replacing the per-metric `getMetricSeries` full-series walk-back (O(series) rows per metric per cycle, ~52 000 rows at §11.3's default retention, per the task-118 review estimate). Pinned interpretations: (1) **Facade taxonomy: no new method.** D-078's consequences anticipated that "a `getLatestMetricValue`-style method would be its own D-058-successor decision"; D-077 **is** that decision — its read is the latest-valid-point read (per metric key, the newest `metric_values` row with `is_valid = 1`, skip-invalid in SQL, `metric_values_series_access`-served with the EXPLAIN-capturing index proof in `test/integration/repository.spec.ts`), so U-011 adds nothing to the facade and `src/storage/repository.ts` is untouched. (2) **The ordering reconciliation: the two reads are the same selection.** D-078's prose described the walk-back as "the last valid stored row **in arrival order**", but the facade's `getMetricSeries` orders by `(collected_at ASC, run_id ASC)` — never arrival/rowid — so the walk-back selected the valid row maximizing `(collected_at, run_id)` lexicographically, which is exactly D-077's `ORDER BY collected_at DESC, run_id DESC` window. Every case therefore resolves identically before and after the swap: trailing invalid rows (skipped by the walk-back's walk and by the `is_valid = 1` filter alike), out-of-order arrivals where a later-arriving run carries an older `collected_at` (both pick the chronologically newest valid row — `repository.spec.ts` pins "a later run with an older stamp never wins" for the facade read, and the walk-back's ordering key was `collected_at`, not arrival), and equal stamps (both break to the later `run_id`, D-036's strictly increasing identity). The swap introduces no time bound, so D-078's rejection of a `to: collectedAt` lookup stands: the base remains the stored tail, and an out-of-order **new** snapshot stays suppressed by D-074's chronology guard — missed, never false (§12.1's conservatism). **Observable behavior is unchanged; the swap is a pure cost change** (one indexed window-function statement per cycle instead of one full-series materialization per valid metric).

**Reasons.** D-078 accepted the full-series scan only because `src/storage/**` belonged to the parallel task 122 in that wave (recorded in D-078's own consequences); task 122 has since landed the exact read D-078 flagged, so consuming it is the flagged follow-up executed, not a new policy. The ordering question was pinned rather than assumed because D-078's "arrival order" wording and D-077's `collected_at DESC` ordering appear to disagree for out-of-order arrivals; reading the facade's actual SQL settles it — the implemented orderings were already the same, and the apparent divergence existed only in D-078's rationale prose (which described why the producers' arrival contract makes chronology the common case, not a second ordering rule). The lazy single read keeps the seam's no-read guarantees (an all-invalid or empty snapshot performs no repository call — pinned by the unit suites) while serving a multi-metric snapshot from one statement, the same account-level shape §13's `/api/quota` consumer will use.

**Consequences.** The seam's read method is contract now: the success branch of `createCycleRecorder` reads only `getLatestValidMetricValues` (moving detection into the storage layer or the scheduler remains a successor decision per D-078). The task-118 suites keep their observable behavior — `test/integration/events-cycle.spec.ts` proves both §12.1 event-time branches end-to-end against a real database through the new read unchanged, and `test/unit/polling-persist.spec.ts`'s D-078 pin 3 proof (read strictly before the transaction) now records one account-level `read:<account>` entry; the fake repositories serve the 122 method with its per-key newest-valid contract. `test/unit/events-cycle.spec.ts` additionally pins the ordering reconciliation at the seam (a later-arriving, older-stamped row never becomes the base). No new SQL exists outside `src/storage/` (D-058's gates untouched); no schema or migration change; existing databases need nothing — detection output is byte-identical. The per-cycle cost of §12.1 detection stops growing with retention.

## D-084 — Task 124's property additions: the §12/§13 cross-module invariants as data-level contract, the gap-explanation bound, and the canonical reason-code order (spec §12, §13, §17.1; task 124)

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§12](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#12-events-reset-detection-and-missing-data), [§13](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#13-http-api), [§17](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#17-automated-testing-and-quality-gates) · **Tasks:** [124](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-021, D-068, D-074, D-075, D-080, D-081

**Decision.** Task 124 extends the five landed property suites additively and adds two new ones (`test/unit/rolling-ranges.property.spec.ts`, `test/unit/history-cross.property.spec.ts`); three interpretations the extensions pin are contract. (1) **The §12/§13 pipeline composes as a data-level invariant, observable as bucket edges.** §13's "must not be lost" for reset markers and gap boundaries is tested end-to-end over shared generated scenarios: a fixed-period series runs through the actual D-074 and D-075 detectors and their outputs feed the D-081 downsampler as boundary data — every D-075 gap's edge points must come back as bucket endpoints (a bucket ending at `fromEpochMs`, a bucket starting at `toEpochMs`), and every D-074 `eventAt` must fall strictly between consecutive buckets (`bᵢ.toEpochMs < eventAt ≤ bᵢ₊₁.fromEpochMs`, the D-081 split semantics: a reset applies through its instant, a gap separates exactly its bracketing pair) — for strictly chronological series, the detector's own caller contract; on equal stamps D-081's never-separate rule deliberately leaves a shared-stamp event inside one bucket, which is why the clustered downsampling suites assert the one-bucket invariant instead. No new API, event, or format exists — the invariant binds modules that already landed, so it is recorded here rather than in a successor to D-074/D-075/D-081. (2) **"Every gap is explained by a visible timeline indicator" holds whenever cycle durations are bounded below the gap-slack margin; the residual skew is deliberate divergence, not a defect.** On a shared run history (metric points at successful run starts, one constant cadence), every `stopped_service` region straddled by observed points on both sides is covered by a `CollectionGap`, and every `CollectionGap` contains a stopped region or at least one `collection_error` marker — §12.2's consumer promise that a chart line never breaks invisibly. The two thresholds share one vocabulary (D-080 imports `gapThresholdMs`) but judge different inputs: snapshot instants (start→start) versus run records (end→start), so a long-running success cycle can compress record silence below the threshold while the snapshot pair exceeds it — a gap with neither indicator inside. That window is the modules' honest semantics, so the property generator bounds it away (durations ≤ 30 s against stretched silences ≥ 90 s past the threshold) and asserts the invariant exactly where it is a promise; nothing pins the skew window itself, and a future consumer relying on gap⇒indicator unconditionally would need a successor decision. (3) **The condition-1 reason codes join in `RESET_SIGNAL_CODES` canonical order** (usage codes before remaining codes, `resets_at_advanced` last, `rolling_window_conservative` appended) — previously an incidental artifact of the detector's field-iteration order, now pinned by the biconditional oracle (an event fires exactly when an independent table oracle fires, with exactly its codes), so reordering the iteration is a contract change.

**Reasons.** The landed suites prove each module against its own oracle; nothing proved the modules compose, which is where §12's semantics actually live (the detectors' outputs are the downsampler's inputs and the events endpoint's payload by construction — both shapes satisfied verbatim, D-081). The observable forms in (1) were chosen because they are what a chart consumes: a broken line needs the silence's edges visible as bucket boundaries, and a reset marker needs its instant between buckets, not inside one. The explanation bound in (2) follows from §11.1's run-per-cycle rule: between two adjacent successful points the runs are exactly the failed cycles or nothing at all — the only escape is the duration skew, which is real (§7.2 retries stretch cycles) and unpromised. The order pin in (3) cost nothing to make explicit: the storage CHECKs and the D-046 writer vocabulary already treat `reason` as data, so its stability is cheaper to promise than to leave undefined.

**Consequences.** `test/unit/events-detection.property.spec.ts` gains the condition-1 biconditional (with tolerance-edge tripwires: a one-point percentage move is neither evidence nor veto, a one-unit absolute move is always decisive), the event-time biconditional over generated declaration placements (both sources stamped for value-only events too — the previously untested §12.1 interaction), and a generator-growth fold oracle (80-point interleavings, equal-timestamp clusters, double-run determinism); `test/unit/history-gaps.property.spec.ts` gains the interval-change-timeline oracle with the D-075 span-widening exercised (tripwired) and gap-record self-consistency; `test/unit/history-downsample.property.spec.ts` gains equal-timestamp clusters under boundaries (every stamp-sharing group lands in one bucket), the degenerate zero-span overfull series (one bucket, `resolutionMs: 0`), and growth to §13's budget ceilings (400-point series against budgets up to 5000); `test/unit/history-cross.property.spec.ts` and `test/unit/rolling-ranges.property.spec.ts` are new (the §10 invariants over generated instants across the whole ECMAScript epoch-millisecond range, including range nesting). Every addition follows the shared `test/helpers/property` convention (100 runs, `FC_SEED` reproduction, no clock reads — D-021); no existing assertion was weakened, and D-074's standing rolling-window property is untouched. No production code changed.

## D-085 — §17.3's critical-module 100% target enforced as per-file coverage thresholds in the Vitest config, with the secret-handling boundary drawn at §15.4's protection mechanisms (spec §17.3; task 125)

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§17.3](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#173-enforced-quality-thresholds), [§15.4](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#154-secret-protection) · **Tasks:** [125](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-004, D-021, D-041, D-045, D-073, D-079

**Decision.** §17.3's sentence "Target 100% for time-zone logic, peak-hours, sanitization, and secret-handling modules" becomes enforced configuration, not a hand-verified claim: `vitest.config.ts`'s `coverage.thresholds` gains per-file glob entries — `{ statements: 100, branches: 100, functions: 100, lines: 100, perFile: true }` each — beside the unchanged global 90% aggregate (which keeps judging every file, critical ones included; a glob entry adds a requirement, never an exemption). Pinned interpretations: (1) **Mechanism: native per-glob thresholds, not a post-coverage script.** The installed Vitest 5 supports glob keys in `thresholds` (verified in `node_modules/vitest/dist/chunks/plugin.d.C8mmycim.d.ts` and the runtime `resolveThresholds`/`checkThresholds`: each glob forms its own judged set over files matching relative to the config root; `perFile` on the glob judges every matching file individually, and globs do not inherit a top-level `perFile`), so a shortfall fails the run naming the exact file and axis. A JSON-summary-checking script was rejected: same guarantee, but a second threshold implementation to maintain, another pipeline hook, and a second place the module list could drift — the config is the single source of truth, and no new tool means the container-uid invariant (env-configured output only) is kept trivially. (2) **Module map.** Time-zone logic → `src/util/clock.ts` (the D-021 epoch↔zone bridge) and `src/util/rolling-ranges.ts` (§10's zone-anchored windows); peak-hours → the family glob `src/services/peak-hours*.ts` (D-073's calculator and D-079's resolver today; a glob rather than exact keys so the still-landing §9.3 service files join enforcement the moment they exist, and a 100% threshold on a multi-file glob is exactly per-file 100% anyway — no file can exceed it, so nothing is maskable); sanitization → `src/providers/sanitize.ts` (D-041); secret-handling → `src/util/logger.ts` (§15.4's "Configure Pino redaction … never log keys" — the only sanctioned path secrets have to logs), `src/config/permissions.ts` ("configuration directory 0700, config file 0600"), and `src/config/write.ts` ("atomic writes" of the secret-bearing config, D-004) — §15.4's three named protection mechanisms, each measured 100/100/100/100 before enforcement. (3) **The boundary is the deliberate exclusion, not a threshold exception.** `src/config/env.ts` (97.67% branches), `src/config/load.ts` (98.27%), and `src/config/reload.ts` (97.22%) — the configuration-loading mechanics of §6 that the U-008 mutation round grouped with the secret-handling set — are **not** given keys: they are not secret-handling modules under §15.4 (their job is loading and overriding configuration generally; the secrets ride through), and their branch coverage sits below 100 today, so including them would mean threshold exceptions that encode current test debt as permanent CI configuration. The same clause covers `src/providers/transport.ts` (95.45% functions today): §15.4's "must never appear in … error messages" is implemented by its error-path scrub, but that is one protection aspect of a §8.1 transport module, not the module's whole job — the whole-job test is what separates the mapped set from everything that merely touches secrets. No exception exists in the config; every configured number is 100, and every configured module measures 100. The sanctioned widening path is: first lift a candidate to 100% on all four axes, then add its key (a successor decision if it is a new category reading of §17.3, a routine config edit if it is another file of an already-mapped family — the `peak-hours*` glob being the standing example). (4) **Wiring: `make check` runs `test-ci`.** CI's `test` job runs `npm run test:ci`; `make check` now runs the same script (coverage + JUnit + thresholds), so the local gate fails exactly where CI fails — including the global 90%, which `make check` never enforced before. The suite cost rises 44.6 s → 57.5 s (~13 s for v8 coverage on 57 files); `make test` remains the fast loop without coverage, and `make check-all` is unchanged (it already ran `test:ci`). No workflow, `package.json`, or `scripts/` change is needed — CI inherits the enforcement through the shared config.

**Reasons.** §17.3's 100% target had already been _reached_ repeatedly (D-021 for clock, D-073/D-079 for the peak-hours pair, D-079's consequences recording 100% scoped coverage) but each proof was a one-time report — nothing failed the next time a suite edit dropped a branch, which is the exact regression §17.3 exists to prevent. Native per-glob thresholds close that gap with zero new moving parts. The secret-handling line follows §15.4's own sentences rather than the mutation round's broader file set because §17.3's coverage categories and §17.3's mutation categories are different lists with different purposes: coverage 100% is asked of the modules whose _whole job_ is a protection mechanism, where an uncovered branch is a potential leak or corruption path; mutation score is asked of logic-dense detectors. Drawing the line at §15.4's mechanisms also makes the map self-maintaining: every module in it is identifiable from the spec text alone. `make check`'s switch to `test-ci` is the CI-parity rule taken literally — a gate that passes locally while CI fails on thresholds (documented in `docs/agents/gotchas.md` as a known trap) is a gate that teaches developers to ignore it; 13 seconds is the price of one source of truth for "green".

**Consequences.** Any drop below 100% on any axis of a critical module — including a brand-new matched file with zero tests, since `coverage.include` brings untested files into the map at 0% — fails `make check`, `make check-all`, `make test-coverage`, `make test-ci`, and CI's `test` matrix with a per-file, per-axis error. Future §17.3-relevant landings join automatically only within the mapped families (`peak-hours*`); new critical modules outside them (e.g. Stage-13 auth/session/hashing secret-handling code) require their own key — and a successor decision if they extend a category's reading. The enforcement was verified in both directions on the landed tree: the real config passes (`make check` green; measured baseline clock/rolling-ranges/peak-hours-intervals/peak-hours-dst/sanitize/logger/permissions/write all 100/100/100/100, overall 99.28/98.11/99.51/99.49), and a scratch run with an injected unmeetable key (`src/storage/maintenance.ts`, measured 83.33/50/50/83.33 — not committed) failed with four `ERROR: Coverage for … does not meet "src/storage/maintenance.ts" threshold (100%)` lines and a non-zero exit. `docs/agents/testing.md` documents the two threshold layers and the boundary; the config comment in `vitest.config.ts` carries the same map for the reader of the file.

## D-086 — The single-instance recovery guard: serializing path-vacating recovery spans against publications, with under-guard aside recovery (spec §5.6, §17.1; task U-017)

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§5.6](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#56-process-lifecycle-backups-and-upgrades), [§17.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#171-required-test-coverage) · **Tasks:** [U-017](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-017

**Decision.** U-017 closes the stranding window the 2026-10-31 kimi review reported as P1 inside D-017's rename-aside protocol: between `removeIfIdentifiedBy`'s `rename(lockPath, aside)` and its restoring `fs.link(aside, lockPath)`, the lock path is vacant, and a third process may publish its own lock into the vacancy — the restore then fails `EEXIST`, the catch swallows it ("best effort: the path is owned by a newer lock"), and the displaced live holder's lock stays stranded in the aside file while both processes run against one data directory (the same hole exists on the release path, which shares the primitive). Pinned interpretations: (1) **Mechanism — a recovery guard file, `.quotameter.lock.guard`, acquired by the same atomic scratch+`link(2)` publication as the lock** (`{"pid":N,"id":<token>}` payload). Every operation that vacates the lock path (stale break, release — both `removeIfIdentifiedBy` callers) holds the guard across the entire rename→read→decide→remove/restore span, and the only operation that occupies the path (publication's `fs.link(scratch, lockPath)`) holds it across its link attempt. Guard acquisition is a single unconditional `link`: there is no check-then-act window on the acquiring side, so no publisher can interleave into a breaker's vacancy and the restoring link always finds the path provably vacant — this is the atomicity argument, and it is what an aside-announcement scheme (publishers polling for `.aside.` files before linking) cannot give: a publisher's readdir→link pair is itself a check-then-act window a capture can land inside. (2) **Crash recovery — stale-guard break plus under-guard aside recovery.** A guard holder that dies mid-span leaves a stale guard and possibly a capture aside; the next guard waiter inspects the guard's pid (dead — or payload that does not parse, since atomic publication means damaged content is never a guard this protocol wrote) and breaks it with the same capture-then-decide primitive applied to the guard path, unguarded — the recursion ends one level down because the guard path's occupancy is decided by a single atomic link, not by a guarded span. Once under the guard no live recovery span can coexist, so any remaining `<lock>.aside.<uuid>` file is an orphan: it is restored to the lock path if the path is vacant (it may be a live holder's only artefact — a live holder's lock now survives even a crash of the process recovering it) or its name is dropped when the path carries byte-identical content (a restore that crashed between link and aside-removal); divergent content — producible only through the accepted residual or an out-of-protocol writer — is kept aside, never destroyed. The normal content-driven loop then re-judges whatever sits at the path. (3) **Bounded waiting, no new refusal vocabulary.** Guard acquisition waits out live holders for `guardTimeoutMs` (default 1000 ms, `guardPollMs` 5 ms polls, both injectable seams) and gives up; a publication that could not acquire the guard counts as a contended attempt, a break that could not counts as a failed one, and both flow into the existing `maxAttempts` refusal; a release that could not acquire the guard is abandoned silently — the lock file stays for the next starter's stale-break, which is the D-017 self-healing property, never a hang. (4) **Unchanged contracts.** The lock payload `{"pid":N,"id":<token>}\n` is byte-compatible (the guard is an additional internal file, like D-016's documented temp residue); D-017's invariants all hold — no false-dead break of a live lock's bytes, damaged/foreign lock content never stomped, token-guarded release, bounded attempts, the existing error messages. (5) **Accepted residual.** The guard's own stale-break can, in principle, capture a _live_ guard installed between the waiter's inspect and its rename, and the guard-path restore can then hit `EEXIST` against a third waiter's acquisition — the same shape one level down. Closing it needs a guard for the guard, ad infinitum; it requires a crash _inside a millisecond-scale span_ plus a multi-party interleave around it, is not producible by any deterministic interleaving of non-crashed processes, and is accepted exactly as D-017 accepts pid recycling. The live-captured guard is never deleted (it is restored or left aside as documented crash residue), the orphan-aside scan drops an aside name only on byte-identity with the occupied path, and divergent asides are kept — so the residual degrades to contention and leftover files, never to the destruction of a live holder's lock. Mixed-version data directories (an old binary that knows no guard) are out of scope for the same reason D-017 scopes single-version locking.

**Reasons.** The vacancy is inherent to capture-then-decide — the rename both captures and vacates in one atomic step — so the only closable design removes the _occupiability_ of the vacancy, not the vacancy: serializing the vacater against the occupier through a second atomically-acquired file does that with primitives the module already has (scratch+link publication, pid liveness, capture-then-decide), adding no dependencies and no new syscalls beyond a handful per startup operation. Restore-by-rename (overwriting the newer lock) was rejected because it merely chooses a different victim; detection-at-release (the holder exits when its lock vanished) was rejected because mutual exclusion is violated for the holder's entire runtime before detection — prevention, not detection, is the requirement; the aside-announcement scheme was rejected on the check-then-act argument in (1). The crash-recovery leg exists because a guard without it trades a stranding window for a deadlock: an orphaned aside would block every future publisher forever, violating D-017's "a crash must not require human intervention".

**Consequences.** `src/server/single-instance.ts` gains `guardFilePath` and the `guardTimeoutMs`/`guardPollMs`/`onCaptured` seams (`onCaptured` pauses the recovery at the captured-file decision point and is deliberately lock-path-only — guard-path captures never fire it; the seam is what the regression tests orchestrate through `test/helpers/singleInstanceRunner.ts`'s new `break-pause` mode with marker files, keeping the real module in real child processes, while the runner's `guard-waiting` marker makes the third process's arrival at its first guard-wait poll causal, not timing-based); `test/integration/single-instance.spec.ts` grows to 58 tests — the two real-process regressions reproduce the reviewer's interleaving (breaker parked after the rename, path vacant, third starter waiting on the guard; resume restores the holder's lock, breaker and third both exit 1 with the actionable refusal, holder keeps the lock) and the crash-mid-recovery case (breaker SIGKILLed with the capture aside; the next starter breaks the stale guard, restores the holder's lock from the aside, and refuses), and eleven in-process tests pin the guard machinery enumerated in the CHANGELOG entry. Operators may occasionally see `.quotameter.lock.guard.aside.*` files after a crash inside a recovery span, and `.quotameter.lock.guard.tmp.*` after a crash inside guard publication — documented crash residue, like D-016's `.config.json.tmp-*`. The mid-break restoration test (task 074) and all 45 pre-existing tests are unchanged and green. Future lock-protocol changes extend this decision, not D-017.

## D-087 — Validate-suite deadlines re-pinned: delivered-response assertions run at §7.2's minimum configured deadline; deadline-expiry assertions keep a load-uninvertible short deadline (spec §7.2, §17.1; task U-012)

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§7.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#72-retry-and-error-behavior), [§17.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#171-required-test-coverage) · **Tasks:** [U-012](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-042, D-085

**Decision.** `test/integration/zai-coding-plan-validate.spec.ts` no longer wires one `TIMEOUT_MS = 120` into every provider it constructs. Pinned interpretations: (1) **Delivered-response assertions use `DELIVERED_RESPONSE_TIMEOUT_MS = 5_000`** — the transport suite's own value for the same loopback mock round-trip (`test/integration/transport.spec.ts` has run its delivered-response cases at 5 s since task 104) and §7.2's minimum _configured_ timeout (5–60 s), so the suite exercises `validateCredentials` at a production-legal deadline. The justification bar is the mock-server round-trip, never CI runner speed: D-042's deadline is one total bound that starts inside `providerFetch` _before_ the request is sent (DNS, connect, headers, and the full body read included), so a 120 ms value silently asserted "the runner finishes the whole exchange within 120 ms" — and v8 coverage instrumentation (permanent in `make check` since task 125, D-085's `test:ci` wiring) plus parallel-suite load violated that once (2026-10-31, t-125 worktree: "resolves on 200 with the /models stand-in body" died on `provider request timed out after 120 ms`; green in isolation and two full re-runs; a task-120 reviewer observed the same suite flake once). The transport classified correctly throughout — the defect was the test's coupling, not the deadline semantics. (2) **The deadline-expiry test keeps the short total deadline (120 ms) against a 10× response delay** — the mock's delay timer starts at request arrival, strictly after the deadline starts, so the response cannot complete before deadline-start + 1200 ms while the deadline fires at deadline-start + 120 ms plus timer lateness; inverting the race requires over a second of timer lateness _while the same load delays everything else_, and load only moves the response further past the deadline. The expiry pin is therefore deterministic under load — the same shape (60 vs 400 ms, 120 vs an 800 ms trickle) that holds the deadline pins in the transport suite. (3) **Deterministic synchronization (the U-001/U-002/U-010 pattern) does not apply**: those fixed phase assumptions — kill-before-handler windows, an abort that must land in a specific endpoint's flight window — gateable on an observable readiness marker. The delivered-response tests have no phase to synchronize: the assertion is the classification of an arrived response and the only racer is the deadline itself; gating on request arrival cannot bound the arrival-to-read window. The fix is to stop racing, not to synchronize the race.

**Reasons.** §7.2 requires the transport to enforce one configurable total deadline (default 15 s); it requires nothing about how fast a test machine executes a loopback exchange, so a deadline value in a delivered-response test can only be justified as "generous against the round-trip it bounds" — 5 s is three-plus orders of magnitude over the sub-10 ms loopback round-trip and matches the landed transport-suite precedent, while a hung mock is still bounded at ~5 s by Vitest's own per-test timer (which starts at test start, marginally before the transport deadline). The expiry test's asymmetry argument (delay starts at arrival, deadline before dispatch) is what makes a _short_ deadline safe exactly where a short deadline is the subject: every load factor increases the gap the assertion depends on. Splitting the constants also makes each test file's intent legible: which deadline a test passes states whether the deadline is the subject or the scenery.

**Consequences.** The validate suite's ten generous-deadline tests (nine delivered-response plus the refused-connection case) no longer share any timing coupling with runner load; the expiry test remains the only short-deadline consumer and its `10 * TIMEOUT_MS` delay coupling keeps the margin self-maintaining. The pattern is the standing rule for future real-socket suites: a short total deadline appears only in tests that assert its expiry, always against a server delay that starts after the deadline and exceeds it by a wide margin; delivered-response assertions use a round-trip-justified generous value (5 s is the house default). A future transport change to phase-split deadlines (D-042 successor) must revisit this entry's margins. No production code changed; the mock server (`test/helpers/mockProviderServer.ts`) was investigated and is not implicated — it responds synchronously unless a behavior sets `delayMs`.

## D-088 — Retryable cleanup after a failed startup rollback: the app records unreleased components and stop() retries exactly those from 'failed' (spec §5.6, §17.1; task U-018)

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§5.6](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#56-process-lifecycle-backups-and-upgrades), [§17.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#171-required-test-coverage) · **Tasks:** [U-018](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-020

**Decision.** `QuotameterApp` (task 060's lifecycle contract) closes the resource-leak dead end the full-project review found: a startup rollback's best-effort stops swallow per-component rejections so the original startup error can propagate, but the state then became `'failed'` and `stop()` was documented as a no-op from there — a component whose rollback `stop` rejected (an open SQLite handle, a listener, a timer) kept its resource with no retry route through the app, contradicting `start()`'s own "startup either fully succeeds or leaves nothing running" and letting a leaked handle keep the process alive after `runServer` had returned its failure code. Pinned semantics: (1) **Recording** — the rollback returns exactly the components whose `stop` rejected, in its reverse-registration visit order; successfully released components are never recorded and therefore never re-stopped, and components that never started are not in the record either. (2) **The retry route** — `stop()` from `'failed'` with a non-empty record retries exactly those components, through the same per-component stop loop as the normal shutdown (one shared helper collecting `{component, error}` pairs, so shutdown reports errors and rollback records components); from `'failed'` with an empty record it stays a no-op with the state unchanged — a clean rollback already released everything, and a `stopping`/`stopped` flip with nothing to do would be event noise. (3) **Terminal states** — a fully successful retry ends at `'stopped'` (every resource released; later `stop()` calls return the settled success); a failed retry rethrows the shutdown vocabulary's `AggregateError` (`'one or more components failed to stop'`, single-sited in one helper) carrying **this round's** errors only, replaces the record with the still-unreleased components, returns the state to `'failed'`, and clears `stopPromise` — exactly what makes the route repeatable: every subsequent `stop()` retries again until every component releases. Historical rollback errors are not re-surfaced after a later success: the actionable set is what the current round failed to release. (4) **Coalescing and events** — the retry sets `stopPromise` like a normal shutdown, so concurrent stop calls (a second signal) join the in-flight retry; it enters `'stopping'` and emits `component-stopped` per released component, keeping the observable event shape (state-change → releases → terminal state). (5) **Unchanged by construction** — the component stop ORDER (D-020's reverse-registration teardown and §5.6 sequencing), the normal `'running'` route (failure leaves `'stopped'` with the settled rejected `stopPromise`, not retriable — pinned by the existing suite), `start()`'s observable behavior (best-effort rollback, original error rethrows), and `main.ts`/`runServer` (which never calls `stop()` after a failed start; the app-side route is additive, so the entry point works unchanged). No new states, event types, or exported names; `AppState` and the `LifecycleEvent` vocabulary are untouched.

**Reasons.** The review's P2 was real: a rejected stop is the one failure mode "leaves nothing running" cannot honestly cover — no framework code can force a component to release — so the honest contract is that a rollback failure stays _addressable_, not that it cannot happen. Recording the failed components (rather than re-stopping all started ones on retry) is forced by the double-stop hazard: a successfully released component's second `stop` is at best a wasted call and at worst undefined behavior against a closed handle. Ending a failed retry at `'failed'` (rather than `'stopped'`, the normal route's failure terminal) encodes retryability in the state itself — the app is not stopped while a resource is held, and `'failed'` plus a non-empty record is precisely the retryable condition; symmetrically, clearing `stopPromise` only on the retry route leaves the landed settled-result semantics of the normal route intact (a caller arriving after a failed _shutdown_ still re-receives that failure; a caller arriving after a failed _retry_ gets a fresh attempt — the two routes promise different things because their components are in different worlds: released-with-errors versus possibly-still-holding). Per-round `AggregateError` contents keep the promise monotone: once `stop()` resolves, everything the rollback leaked is released.

**Consequences.** `stop()`'s state table and `start()`'s docstring now describe the recorded-and-retryable semantics, and the `LifecycleComponent` interface contract changes wording: `start` is called at most once, but `stop` may be re-called after its own rejection — every component implementation must tolerate a retried release after rejecting (documentation of the contract for the construction tasks that follow; `buildComponents()` still assembles no components, and the landed stop implementations are idempotent releases). A flagged follow-up for the main session: `runServer` could call `app.stop()` in its startup-failure branch to attempt the release before returning 1 — today it returns immediately, so a still-leaked handle can outlive the returned failure code; `main.ts` was outside this task's file set and works unchanged. `test/integration/server-app.spec.ts` proves the done-condition with a release-marker component: a rejected rollback stop leaves the marker held and emits nothing, one `stop()` retry releases exactly it (never the successfully rolled-back sibling, never the never-started component) and emits its `component-stopped`, a permanently failing stop surfaces the `AggregateError` with that round's error and stays retryable across rounds until a finite failure count releases, a clean rollback keeps `stop()` a no-op from `'failed'`, and concurrent stop calls coalesce into one retry whose settled success later calls return unchanged; the existing server-app and server-main tests are unmodified and green.

## D-089 — The D-085 widening executed: the four excluded modules join the enforced coverage map at their measured maxima, with three single-branch arms documented as construction-unreachable exceptions (spec §17.3; task U-016)

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§17.3](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#173-enforced-quality-thresholds), [§6.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#62-configuration-load-and-validation), [§7.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#72-retry-and-error-behavior) · **Tasks:** [U-016](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-085, D-018, D-023, D-026, D-042

**Decision.** `src/config/env.ts`, `src/config/load.ts`, `src/config/reload.ts`, and `src/providers/transport.ts` — the modules D-085 left outside the per-file 100% map with "lift to 100 first, then add the key" as the widening path — are now enforced keys in `vitest.config.ts`. The lift was measured first (v8 `coverage-final.json`, arm-exact): two gaps were reachable product surface and closed with tests — the transport's `ignoreReleaseFailure` catch handler (functions 21/22 → 22/22) is executed by a unit test whose injected fetch resolves a non-2xx response whose `body.cancel()` rejects, pinning that the status observation is delivered and the release failure never surfaces; and `parseJson`'s non-Error arm (`String(error)`, load.ts branches 114/116 → 115/116) is executed by a value whose string coercion throws a non-Error class instance, pinning the total-function promise — one readable problem, never a rethrow. Three single-branch arms are **unreachable by construction** and become the map's only threshold exceptions, each key pinned at the measured maximum instead of 100: (1) **`env.ts` branches 97.67** — the unknown-name sort comparator's equal-key arm (`a < b ? -1 : a > b ? 1 : 0` returning `0`): the sorted array holds `Object.entries`-derived key strings, unique by object-key semantics (a Proxy `ownKeys` trap throwing on duplicates is spec-enforced), and string `<`/`>` is a total order over code-unit sequences, so "neither less nor greater" entails identical keys, which cannot occur — the same equivalence the in-code Stryker note records from the U-008 round. (2) **`load.ts` branches 99.13** — the `'must be one of the allowed values'` fallback inside `parseConfig`'s failed-union rendering: every `anyOf` in the landed `ConfigSchema` is a literal union (`WeekDay`, `auth.mode`, `logging.level`), and Ajv (`allErrors: true`) emits one `const` error per branch at the same `instancePath` beside the `anyOf` error, so `allowedValuesIn` is never empty; the arm is the U-009-adopted graceful-degradation path for a future non-literal union. (3) **`reload.ts` branches 97.22** — the `?? CONFIG_DEFAULTS.logging.level` fallback in the reloader's `setLevel` call: `next` comes exclusively from `loadConfigWithEnv` → `parseConfig`, whose `applyConfigDefaults` always materializes `logging.level` (the `Validated<Config>` brand's only sanctioned construction site), and the injected `filesystem`/`env` seams only feed that parser — no route bypasses it. Pinning the threshold at the measured maximum (floored to two decimals) keeps every exception exact rather than slack: one further uncovered arm costs 0.86–2.78 pp (1/116 in `load.ts`, 1/43 in `env.ts`, 1/36 in `reload.ts`), always below the pinned value, so the gate still fails naming the file and axis.

**Reasons.** D-085 drew the secret-handling boundary at §15.4's mechanisms and explicitly deferred these four modules on measured coverage, not on principle; U-016's measurement shows the deferral was 80% repairable (two arms coverable, one function coverable) and 3 arms deep in type-system or schema invariants a test cannot cross without lying about the input contract. Deleting the dead arms (the mutation-testing doc's rule for no-coverage fallbacks) was considered and rejected as out of scope: production code is frozen for this task, the `reload.ts` arm is load.ts-mirroring defensive style the U-008/U-009 rounds deliberately kept, and the `load.ts` arm is forward compatibility for schema growth — removal is a possible follow-up task, flagged in the report, not a coverage-task edit. A per-axis number below 100 was chosen over omitting the key because omission returns the file to the 90% aggregate — a regime where a brand-new uncovered branch (2+ pp) can pass silently; the pinned maximum is stricter than 100-minus-one-arm by construction, as the scratch demonstrations show. The two new tests assert behavior, not coverage: the transport pin documents that a failing body release must not mask a delivered status (the reason the catch exists), and the parseJson pin documents the "never throws, always one problem" boundary contract for inputs whose coercion itself fails.
