**Consequences.** `make check` (and CI's `test` job) now fail naming any of the four files on any new uncovered arm — demonstrated on scratch runs (not committed): `it.skip` on the transport test yields `Coverage for functions (95.45%) does not meet "src/providers/transport.ts" threshold (100%)`, and on the parseJson test `Coverage for branches (98.27%) does not meet "src/config/load.ts" threshold (99.13%)`. If a future schema change introduces a non-literal union, the `load.ts` fallback arm becomes reachable: the correct move is to cover it and raise the key to 100, not to widen the exception. The same applies to `reload.ts` if the parser ever stops materializing `logging`, and to `env.ts` only if unknown-name scanning ever sorts non-key material. `docs/agents/testing.md` and the `vitest.config.ts` comment carry the exception list with reasons; D-085's "no threshold exceptions" sentence is superseded for exactly these three arms by this entry. No production code changed; no Stryker comment was touched (mutation-ignore and coverage axes are independent — an ignored mutant's line can be covered or uncovered).

## D-090 — The epoch-millisecond comparator is single-sited in `src/util/` and fails fast on non-finite input (spec §10; task U-013)

**Date:** 2026-10-31 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§10](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#10-time-and-time-zones) · **Tasks:** [U-013](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-021, D-059, D-064, D-075, D-081

**Decision.** `compareEpochMs(a, b)` lives once in `src/util/compare-epoch-ms.ts` (a new `util` leaf, kebab-case, one family per file — `clock.ts` untouched: ordering timestamps is a clock-adjacent dependency-free concern, not a clock API change) and replaces the three byte-identical private copies the history services each carried (`history-gaps.ts`, `history-downsample.ts`, `history-timeline.ts`; tasks 119–121 — task 121's review P3 recommended exactly this promotion, declined then only on parallel-wave file-set grounds). Pinned contract: (1) **Total order over finite epoch-ms** — exact −1/0/1 sign comparison, no subtraction, so no precision corners anywhere in the finite domain: exact at the ±8.64e15 ECMAScript time-value bounds (the domain task 124's rolling-range properties generate over) where a difference-based comparator starts relying on IEEE-754 rounding for magnitudes ≥ 2⁵³. (2) **Non-finite input fails fast** — `NaN` and `±Infinity` in either argument throw a `TypeError` naming both values. The private copies' sign-only form silently answered "equal" for `NaN` against anything — not a total order (NaN=5 ∧ NaN=7 but 5≠7) and a quiet degenerate sort over corrupt data; the shared module refuses exactly what the discipline forbids.

**Reasons.** D-021 treats timestamps as validated-finite data: `createFixedClock` rejects non-finite readings (`requireFinite`), and every history-service seam rejects non-finite timestamps before any sort (`requirePoints`, `requireRuns`, `requireBoundaries`, `normalizeTimeline` — their suites already pin those rejections), so every migrated call site sorts only values already proven finite and no consumer's observable ordering behavior changes (the reconciliation changes only unreachable-in-practice input handling, from silently degenerate to loud — the D-059/D-064 fail-fast convention for wiring mistakes). The non-subtraction form is kept rather than `a - b` because sign comparison needs no arithmetic at all: it is exact at every finite magnitude, where a difference at ±8.64e15 is already a rounded magnitude (1.728e16 > 2⁵³) that only happens to keep its sign. Single-siting follows the D-021 discipline the original P3 cited: three sibling services cannot import each other's private helpers, so the shared leaf is the only placement that keeps one contract and one test surface.

**Consequences.** Every chronological sort over `EpochMs` data imports the shared comparator (`services` may import `util` per the layout DAG; intra-`util` imports stay within the leaf directory — the `rolling-ranges.ts` → `clock.ts` type-import precedent). The contract is pinned by `test/unit/compare-epoch-ms.spec.ts`: −1/0/1 ordering incl. pre-1970 epochs, exactness at the ±8.64e15 anchors (and adjacent integers there), finiteness-only domain beyond the time-value range, antisymmetry/reflexivity/transitivity-of-sign across the anchors, `Array#sort` use, and the `TypeError` table for NaN/±Infinity in either position. Two structurally similar subtraction-based instant sorts with compound keys exist outside this task's file set and are deliberately not migrated: `peak-hours-intervals.ts` (`start − start || end − end`, D-073/D-079) and `storage/backups.ts` (`byInstant`: `timestampMs, seq`) — both need a two-key variant, not a mechanical swap; both are flagged for the main session. A future second comparator family (e.g. compound-key ordering) gets its own `src/util/` leaf or extends this one by decision, never another private copy.

## D-091 — The §11.3 retention horizon single-sited as `historyCutoff` in the cleanup module, over `util`'s `DAY_MS` (spec §11.3; task U-014)

**Date:** 2026-11-01 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§11.3](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#113-retention-and-cleanup) · **Tasks:** [U-014](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-021, D-058, D-063, D-082, D-090

**Decision.** The horizon arithmetic that existed as twin computations — `retention-cleanup.ts`'s `now − retentionDays · MS_PER_DAY` over a private day-ms constant (D-063) and `history-retention.ts`'s `now − retentionDays · DAY_MS` over `util`'s constant (D-082), behaviorally equal only because the cleanup-alignment tests say so — is now one exported definition: `historyCutoff(now, retentionDays): number` in `src/storage/retention-cleanup.ts`, consumed by the cleanup's own delete cutoffs and by `boundHistoryRange`'s horizon. Pinned interpretations: (1) **Placement is the cleanup module, not a neutral leaf.** The intra-`storage` import edge already exists — D-082 consumes D-063's exported `MIN/MAX_RETENTION_DAYS` and documents that reuse — and the D-058 sibling taxonomy makes `retention-cleanup.ts` the storage-side owner of §11.3 window policy (the bounds constants, the raw-age constant, the meta markers, the cutoffs); D-082's own text already said the horizon "is D-063's `historyCutoff` arithmetic exactly", so D-063 was the named definition owner and this task makes that literal. A `retention-horizon.ts` leaf would split §11.3 policy across two modules or force moving the bounds too — export-surface churn with no consumer benefit; the D-090 `compareEpochMs` precedent promoted a helper to a shared leaf because three _services_ siblings could not import each other's privates, which is not this shape. (2) **The day-ms unit is `util`'s `DAY_MS` end-to-end.** Storage may import `util` (the layout row), the query twin already imported exactly this symbol, and the private `MS_PER_DAY` is deleted: no day-ms literal remains in the retention path (`migrations.ts`'s two §15.2 session constants are a different, individually single-sited family, out of scope). (3) **The helper is pure arithmetic; validation stays at the consuming seams.** Both consumers validate `now` and §11.3's 7–3650 window before calling, with their own context-named, test-pinned errors; a validating helper would add a second error vocabulary and branches unreachable through the sanctioned call paths (which the D-085 coverage gates would then count).

**Reasons.** The alignment tests prove the two sides agree today but cannot keep them agreeing — the equality was two literals that happen to coincide, the exact gap a D-021-style single definition site closes (task 123's review P3 flagged it; the fix was declined then only because the D-063 surface belonged to another wave's file set). The one structural question was who owns the definition — the cleanup that enforces the window, or a neutral site both consume. Enforcement ownership wins: the alignment invariant is "query-side horizon == delete-side cutoff", and defining the value inside the enforcing module with the query twin consuming it makes the invariant true by construction, with the definition sitting where §11.3's other policy constants already live and one import edge already points.

**Consequences.** Both modules' observable behavior is unchanged — the computed value is identical, pinned by the untouched D-063/D-082 alignment suites (green with unmodified assertions) plus new direct pins: the helper's value table at the 7/30/180/3650 windows against the test spec's own independent day-ms literal (guarding against a corrupted shared definition), the day-boundary semantics (a row exactly at the helper's cutoff survives the strict-before deletes, one 1 ms earlier goes), and the clamp's reported horizon equal to the helper at both §11.3 window bounds. `historyCutoff` joins `retention-cleanup.ts`'s exported consumer contract (D-063's list) — changing its semantics or placement requires a successor decision. The export is documented in `src/storage/README.md`. Future day-denominated cutoffs in storage consume `DAY_MS` or this helper, never a new private literal.

## D-092 — Local gates run the full CI type check: `typecheck-all` wired into `make check` and `make check-all` (spec §4.4, §17.3; task U-019)

**Date:** 2026-11-01 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§4.4](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#44-cicd-and-supply-chain-safeguards), [§17.3](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#173-enforced-quality-thresholds) · **Tasks:** [U-019](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-045

**Decision.** The `check` and `check-all` Makefile gate recipes run `typecheck-all` — `npm run typecheck:all`, i.e. server `tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.json` followed by `vue-tsc --noEmit -p ui/tsconfig.json` — instead of the server-only `typecheck`, making them run exactly the command CI's `static` job runs at its "Type-check server and UI" step (the job the required `CI` gate consumes). The standalone `make typecheck` target is kept unchanged as the fast server-only loop; `typecheck-ui` and `typecheck-all` stay available individually. No workflow change: `.github/workflows/ci.yml` already ran `typecheck:all`.

**Reasons.** The 2026-10-31 kimi full-project review (P3, verified) found the parity hole: task 125 had wired the test leg (`make check` → `test-ci`, D-085) to CI's `test` job, but the type leg still ran only server `tsc` — a `vue-tsc` error passed both local gates and failed the required CI job, contradicting the documented parity (D-045's "per-push CI and `make check-all` stay in exact parity", AGENTS.md "Commands", `docs/agents/gotchas.md`, the README gate table). The `typecheck-all` target already existed but was wired into neither gate — a wiring omission, not a deliberate local-omission policy, so the narrowing alternative (documenting what the gates do not check) was rejected. The cost of closing it is the `vue-tsc` run: measured ≈2.2 s wall on the current `ui/` scaffold (`make typecheck` 10.96 s → `make typecheck-all` 13.16 s, warm deps, container under wave load) — trivially cheap for catching at commit time what CI would otherwise reject.

**Consequences.** A UI type error now fails `make check` before committing — demonstrated on a scratch run (not committed): a Prettier- and ESLint-clean `ui/src/__scratch-type-error.ts` carrying only a `TS2322` mismatch failed the gate at the `typecheck-all` leg, `vue-tsc` naming the file and position, where the same state previously passed both gates; the file was deleted afterwards and the tree verified clean. AGENTS.md "Commands", the `docs/agents/gotchas.md` CI-parity bullet (extended from the test leg to the type leg), and the README gate-table `make check` row now state the type leg explicitly. If `vue-tsc` ever grows slow enough to matter as the `ui/` scaffold grows through Stage 13, the response is a faster type-check placement (e.g. incremental/composite builds), not re-splitting the gates; any re-split requires a successor decision updating the same documents. D-045's parity sentence is unchanged — this decision restores its truth for the type leg rather than amending an immutable entry.

## D-093 — The coverage-threshold guard: threshold keys must stay anchored to existing files, with the §17.3 critical-module map enumerated in an executable spec (spec §17.3; task U-015)

**Date:** 2026-11-01 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§17.3](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#173-enforced-quality-thresholds) · **Tasks:** [U-015](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-085, D-089

**Decision.** The orphaning hole in D-085's enforcement — a zero-match key in `coverage.thresholds` passes silently, task 125's review P3-1 — is closed by `test/unit/coverage-thresholds.spec.ts` (the `package-layout.spec.ts`/`storage-sql-gate.spec.ts` structural pattern), which imports `vitest.config.ts` as a module (same-process truth) and pins the config's structural shape: the object form of `thresholds` (a switch to the number or array form fails with instructions), `coverage.include` staying `['src/**/*.ts']` (the universe the guard offers as threshold-key candidates — widening it forces a conscious guard update in the same commit), and the presence of the four global threshold axes (§17.3/D-085's aggregate layer; values stay policy, presence is structure). Pinned interpretations: (1) **Anchor requirement** — every non-global threshold key must match at least one existing `src/**` `.ts` file, judged with the same semantics the installed Vitest applies: verified in `node_modules/vitest/dist/chunks/cli-api.De07GUeT.js` (5.0.5), `resolveThresholds` compiles each non-global key to `picomatch(key)` with default options and matches it against the coverage file's path relative to the config root, skipping `perFile`, `autoUpdate`, `100`, `lines`, `functions`, `statements`, `branches` as global options — the guard mirrors that exact call through the same library over repo-root-relative posix paths, with a positive control pinning the default semantics (prefix globs match no sibling outside the family, `*` never crosses `/`, exact paths are literal). (2) **The map is executable** — the §17.3 critical-module map (D-085 plus D-089/U-016's four) is enumerated in the spec as patterns with reasons; each pattern must match at least one existing file (a stale pattern means a critical module moved or was deleted — the failure says to update map and config key together), and every file a pattern matches must be matched by some threshold key (a dropped or narrowed key — e.g. replacing the `peak-hours*` family glob with one exact file — leaves a §17.3 target unenforced and fails). (3) **Accepted limit** — a single family member renamed out of the `peak-hours*` glob is not caught: no structural signal distinguishes a rename from a removal, the symmetric cost of D-085's glob design accepting new family files automatically; and threshold _values_ (D-089's branch maxima) are coverage policy, not structure, and stay out of the guard's scope.

**Reasons.** The silence was structural, not hypothetical: `checkThresholds` with `perFile` judges exactly `coverageMap.files()` of the key's group — an empty judged set yields zero groups and no error — so a config key is a second place the critical-module list can drift, exactly the drift D-085 rejected a post-coverage threshold script for. The guard avoids D-085's objection because it does not re-implement thresholds (the config stays the single enforcement point) — it checks the config's structural anchoring, and even the matcher is not re-implemented: importing `picomatch` and calling it exactly as `resolveThresholds` does means the mirror cannot drift from the mechanism it mirrors without the installed Vitest itself changing (the chunk filename in the provenance comment dates the verification). Importing the config rather than parsing its text keeps the guard on the same object Vitest loads — a regex over TypeScript is the fragile second implementation the house pattern avoids.

**Consequences.** Renaming or deleting a critical module, or dropping/narrowing its threshold key, now fails `make check` with a message naming the exact key or file; adding a new critical-module key requires extending the spec's map in the same commit (the map is the deliberate second site, co-located so the two change together), while new `peak-hours*` family files continue to join enforcement automatically. Demonstrated live on scratch runs (not committed): with the family key renamed to `peak-windows*.ts`, the exact `npm run test:ci` command `make check` runs exits 0 with the dead key present (2067 tests green, zero threshold errors) and exits non-zero once the guard is in place; `git mv`-renaming both family files fails the targeted guard run the same way; deleting the `clock.ts` key line fails it with the uncovered-module message. No production code changed; `vitest.config.ts` is untouched (the guard reads it as-is).

## D-094 — Compute-bound property tests carry explicit per-test timeouts sized from starvation-rig worst cases (spec §17.1; task U-020)

**Date:** 2026-11-01 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§17.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#171-required-test-coverage) · **Tasks:** [U-020](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-085, D-087, D-090

**Decision.** The four compute-bound property tests of the task-124 suites — `history-downsample.property.spec.ts`'s preservation, equal-timestamp-cluster, and budget-scale properties, and `history-cross.property.spec.ts`'s detector-boundaries property — declare `{ timeout: 20_000 }` through the installed Vitest 5.0.5 options-object form (`TestOptions.timeout`; the `(name, options, fn)` overload verified against the shipped typings), superseding the default 5 s per-test timeout for exactly those tests. Pinned interpretations: (1) **The census is measured, not guessed** — a property test joins the compute-bound census when it measures ≥ ~250 ms clean in isolation or ≥ ~1 s under the starvation rig; under that rule the four tests above carry timeouts (0.43–0.98 s clean, 2.4–6.8 s worst under the rig) while the scanned remainder stays on the default (events-detection's heaviest 0.8 s under the rig, history-gaps 0.37 s, history-timeline 0.62 s, rolling-ranges 18 ms — a timeout on those would be noise, not a statement; `peak-hours-dst.property.spec.ts` already pins its own at 15/30 s since task 115, the landed precedent this entry generalizes). (2) **The mechanism is the per-test options object, not a global `testTimeout`, a `describe`-level option, a fast-check timeout budget, or a smaller `numRuns`** — per-test explicitness is the contract (a suite mixes weights: downsample's first describe holds a 54 ms boundary pin beside the 3.7 s preservation property); the global bump hides which tests are slow and why; fast-check's own `timeout` changes failure semantics (a preemptive generation abort) rather than raising a wall-clock ceiling; and `numRuns: 100` is the shared §17.1 convention (`test/helpers/property.ts`) — shrinking it to fit a timeout would weaken every property in the suite. The legacy trailing-number form (also supported, and `peak-hours-dst`'s landed spelling) was not used because at these test-name lengths Prettier explodes the signature into one-arg-per-line either way, and the object form stays self-describing in that layout. (3) **Sizing is ≈3× the measured worst case under the full rig, and the worst case must be measured on a full `make check`, not an isolated suite run** — six busy-loop hogs pinned across the container's 8 cores (the U-010/U-012 method) starve the isolated suites to 3.8 s worst, but the full 104-file coverage run under the same hogs contends far harder and pushed the same test to 6.8 s (the cross property to 5.9 s, the preservation property to 5.5 s — all three past the 5 s default, reproducing the U-012 ambient flake at host load 11–17 against its observed ~18); 20 s ≈ 3× that 6.8 s tolerates a doubling of the worst observed wave while a genuinely stuck run still fails in 20 s.

**Reasons.** The 5 s default is a runner-speed assertion these tests never meant to make: a property sweeping ~100 generated max-size series through brute-force oracles is compute-bound by design, v8 coverage instrumentation (permanent in `make check` since task 125/D-085) multiplies it ~1.4–1.8×, and parallel-wave load multiplies again — 0.95 s clean became 6.8 s worst observed, past the default at exactly the ambient parallel-worktree load where U-012's matrix flaked it. This is the same load-sensitivity family as D-087 with one structural difference: D-087's delivered-response tests raced a product deadline that could be re-scoped to a production-legal value, while a compute-bound property has no deadline semantics at all — there is nothing to synchronize (no phase assumption to gate, per D-087's own criterion) and nothing to re-scope; the only honest fix is to stop asserting an unstated wall-clock bound by accident. The measured worst cases walk the D-090 comparator paths (the history-services sorts these suites exercise), so the sizing also bounds the worst realistic post-D-090 code path cost.

**Consequences.** The standing rule lives in `docs/agents/gotchas.md` ("Test stability under parallel load"): new compute-bound property tests declare their timeout at authoring time, sized from a rig-measured worst case, and a generator that grows its `size: 'max'` ceilings re-measures. No assertion, `numRuns`, seed, or generator changed — the four suites' properties are byte-identical, only their signatures gained an argument (plus the Prettier-mandated one-arg-per-line layout). Stability matrix (all on the pinned 22.13.0 container): the two named suites 10/10 green under the rig in coverage mode (worst per-test 2.4 s, loadavg 11–14); four full `make check` runs under the rig green (host load 11–17); two full runs at ambient parallel-worktree load green (final run 2071 tests, 0 failures). Flagged for the main session, outside this task's file set: `peak-hours-dst.property.spec.ts`'s scan-oracle property measured 17.2 s against its 30 s under the same rig (1.75× margin — adequate for every observed wave but below this entry's 3× rule), and the remaining sub-second property suites need no action until a generator grows them into the census.

## D-095 — `runServer`'s startup-failure branch performs an awaited best-effort `app.stop()` before returning the failure code (spec §5.6, §17.1; task U-022)

**Date:** 2026-11-01 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§5.6](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#56-process-lifecycle-backups-and-upgrades), [§17.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#171-required-test-coverage) · **Tasks:** [U-022](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-088, D-020

**Decision.** `runServer` (`src/server/main.ts`) closes the caller-side half of D-088's retryable cleanup: the startup-failure branch — which previously printed the startup error and returned `1` without touching the app — now reports the startup error **first**, then performs a best-effort `app.stop()` through a dedicated helper, **awaited before the failure code is returned**. Pinned semantics: (1) **One attempt, not a loop** — the branch calls `stop()` exactly once; after a clean rollback that call is D-088's documented no-op from `'failed'` with an empty record (nothing extra logged, existing tests unaffected), and after a leaked rollback it is exactly one retry round. (2) **Never masks the startup error** — a rejecting retry is reported through the same fatal-diagnostics seam the signal-shutdown path uses (`reportFatal(describeError(...))`: the shutdown vocabulary's `one or more components failed to stop: …`, message-only, English, no stack-spam, `AggregateError` flattened) and swallowed; the startup error stays the process's diagnosis and the exit code stays `1` — the branch never rejects. (3) **Error-first ordering** — the startup error is on stderr before the stop is attempted, so the root cause is printed even if a component's `stop` were to hang, and the stop-failure report reads as the secondary complication it is. (4) **The `undefined` app arm** — the local is typed `QuotameterApp | undefined` because assembly (`buildComponents()`, the constructor call) sits inside the same `try` and may throw before assignment; the helper's early return on `undefined` (nothing exists to stop) has no executable route today — `buildComponents()` assembles nothing and the constructor cannot throw — and is this file's single construction-unreachable branch arm, documented in place rather than restructured away (the D-089 exception class): every restructure that would remove it either leaves an entirely uncovered standalone catch block (splitting the `try`) or changes today's observable contract (hoisting assembly out of the `try` would turn a throwing future `buildComponents()` into a `runServer` rejection instead of the documented exit `1`). (5) **Unchanged** — the runtime-gate branch (no app exists), the signal path, the `onSignalsReady` fail-fast (deliberately leaves started components running), and `QuotameterApp` itself (consumed, not modified: D-088's semantics are already exactly what the branch needs).

**Reasons.** D-088 built the retry route but explicitly flagged that `runServer` "could call `app.stop()` in its startup-failure branch to attempt the release before returning 1" — the entry point is the only caller that knows the startup failed, so without this call the route is unreachable from the process and a leaked handle can outlive the returned failure code (§5.6's construction tasks make it real: the storage connection and HTTP listener own handles). Awaited-before-return is the point of the change: an unawaited fire-and-forget stop could not guarantee the release attempt (or even its diagnostics) happened before the process exits. Swallowing the retry's rejection follows from the branch's own contract — the exit code already reports failure (`1`), and the startup error is the actionable diagnosis; letting the stop error escape would replace the caller's expected `number` resolution with a rejection and mask the original cause. One attempt is deliberate: the entry point owes the process its failure code, a component that still refuses after its retry is unreleasable from here (the app-level route remains repeatable per D-088 for embedders), and a retry loop would trade a bounded shutdown for an unbounded one against a stuck resource. Error-first ordering also preserves the diagnosis under a hung `stop` — the very failure mode the await could otherwise couple it to.

**Consequences.** `runServer`'s docstring describes the branch; the `src/server/main.ts` coverage delta is exactly the documented `undefined`-app arm (the file measured 100/100/92.85/100 statements/branches/functions/lines on the integration baseline before, and stays far above the global 90% gates after — it is not in the D-085 per-file 100% map, so no threshold pin is required; when a §5.6 construction task makes `buildComponents()` able to throw, the arm becomes coverable and should be covered). `test/integration/server-main.spec.ts` pins the done-condition with a release-marker `leakyComponent` (U-018's pattern, local to the suite) registered before a failing-start sibling: with one failing stop the entry point's awaited retry releases the marker (two stop calls, no stop-failure output) — D-088's route proven reachable from `main`; with two, the retry's `AggregateError` is logged after and swallowed beside the still-first startup error while `runServer` resolves `1` with the component still held and addressable. The existing 21 server-main tests are unmodified and green; `src/server/app.ts`, the shutdown coordinator seam (task 075), and the child-process runner are untouched.

## D-096 — The compound-key ordering family extends `compare-epoch-ms.ts`, and both flagged instant sorts migrate to it (spec §10; task U-023)

**Date:** 2026-11-01 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§10](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#10-time-and-time-zones) · **Tasks:** [U-023](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-021, D-059, D-064, D-073, D-079, D-090

**Decision.** `compareByEpochMs(primary, tieBreak)` joins `compareEpochMs` in `src/util/compare-epoch-ms.ts` (the file D-090 created; its consequences sentence offered "its own leaf **or extends this one**" — this decision exercises the second branch): a comparator builder ordering by a primary epoch-ms key and breaking exact ties by a second key, both compared with the shared exact-sign ladder, ascending. Pinned contract: (1) **One family, one file.** The two consumers the U-013 census flagged — `peak-hours-intervals.ts`'s `(start, end)` over epoch pairs (D-073/D-079) and `storage/backups.ts`'s `byInstant` `(timestampMs, seq)` (D-065) — need the identical contract ("order by an instant, break exact ties by a finite number, ascending") and differ only in which fields feed the keys; `EpochMs` is a plain `number` alias, so the shapes are structurally identical at the comparator level and one key-extractor builder serves both without forcing symmetry (each call site names its own keys; a four-argument primitive was rejected because it makes key-pairing mistakes between items representable). The file grows rather than gaining a sibling leaf: its charter already reads "every chronological sort over `EpochMs` data", and one import site for one concern beats a second leaf splitting a single contract family (the layout's "one family per file" rule reads the family as _epoch-ms ordering with D-090 semantics_, single-key and compound-key being two members of it). `tieBreak` is required, not optional: both real consumers tie-break, and a primary-only sort-by-field keeps the established `(a, b) => compareEpochMs(f(a), f(b))` house pattern (three history call sites). (2) **Tie-break domain: any finite `number`, ascending.** Not restricted to integers (the services site's secondary key is an epoch — `end`), not claimed to be an instant (the storage site's is a counter — `seq`); compared with the same exact-sign ladder, so exact at every finite magnitude. Equal primary and equal tie yield `0`, and a stable `Array#sort` keeps input order — the property the peak-hours suite pins ("the earlier-listed window is the one reported"). Deeper key chains are out of scope until a third consumer exists. (3) **Non-finite policy: D-090 verbatim, both roles, eager.** `NaN`/`±Infinity` in either role throw a `TypeError` naming both values of that role (primary first); both keys of both items are validated on every invocation, so rejection never depends on where a sort happens to stop comparing — a lazy tie-break check would make the throw data-dependent on comparison outcomes. (4) **Both migrated seams already guarantee finite keys — no new guards.** The peak-hours edge values come from the D-079 `LocalInstantResolver` contract ("return finite instants", a test-injection seam; the sort now enforces the promise loudly instead of silently collapsing a `NaN` onto the tie-break — the same unreachable-in-practice reconciliation D-090 recorded for the history services). The backups side is sealed by construction: `createAutomaticBackup` validates `now` as a non-negative integer, and the listing path is bounded by the file system itself — a grammar name caps at 255 bytes (`backup-` + digits + `.sqlite`), bounding a digit run at 241 digits, while a run that parses non-finite needs 309 (verified on the pinned runtime: a 323-byte name fails with `ENAMETOOLONG`); the longest name any supported file system can hold parses to ~1e241, finite, and the family orders every finite magnitude exactly. A parse-seam guard rejecting non-finite digit runs was implemented and then withdrawn: its arm is unreachable through the real file system, so it could ship only as a defensively-unreachable branch — the class `docs/agents/testing.md` forbids — and on any hypothetical filesystem that did allow such a name, the comparator's loud `TypeError` is already the D-059/D-064-correct answer for corrupt data.

**Reasons.** D-090's own reconciliation pattern prescribed the whole shape: the history services' seams already validated finiteness, so `compareEpochMs` could afford to throw — and the same audit of the two flagged sites found both seams finite by construction (the resolver contract on the services side; the `now` gate plus the 255-byte name cap on the storage side), so the family can afford the same contract with no consumer's observable ordering behavior changing. Softening the family's non-finite policy instead (ordering `±Infinity`, throwing on `NaN` only) was rejected: it would fork the family's contract away from D-090's for exactly one corrupt-input corner that no supported file system can even materialize. The withdrawn parse guard is recorded above because its unreachability is measured, not assumed: the shortest digit run parsing to `Infinity` (309 nines) makes a 323-byte name, which the pinned runtime's file system refuses outright (`ENAMETOOLONG`) — a guard for it fails the project's own "avoid defensively unreachable branches" rule and would leave an arm no real-file test can cover.

**Consequences.** Both call sites are wiring-only migrations with zero assertion changes in their suites (`test/unit/peak-hours-intervals.spec.ts` and `test/integration/startup-migrations.spec.ts` green unmodified) and zero behavior change at the backups seam (`parseAutomaticBackupName` is untouched — no name leaves the grammar); `compareEpochMs` is behavior- and message-identical (D-090's suite untouched). The family's contract is pinned by new blocks in `test/unit/compare-epoch-ms.spec.ts` mirroring the U-013 structure: ordering by primary at everyday magnitudes, ascending tie-breaks, exactness at the ±8.64e15 anchors for both roles, antisymmetry/reflexivity over an anchor grid, `Array#sort` use incl. the equal-keys stability pin, and the non-finite throw table — primary and tie-break, both items, eager validation with primaries differing, and the primary-before-tie-break message precedence. `src/util/README.md` documents the family; a future third compound-key consumer imports `compareByEpochMs` — never another private subtraction copy, per D-090's single-siting discipline.

## D-097 — The §17.1 time-zone regression matrix as a dedicated CI job over the time/peak-hours subset, with a zone-facts non-vacuity guard and an executable selection contract (spec §17.1, §10; task 126)

**Date:** 2026-11-01 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§17.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#171-required-test-coverage), [§10](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#10-time-and-time-zones) · **Tasks:** [126](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-021, D-073, D-079

**Decision.** Task 126's done-condition ("CI covers DST and non-DST offsets including half/quarter-hour zones") is implemented as a dedicated `timezone` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (behind the `CI` gate) that runs the time/peak-hours suite — `npm run test:time`, a new script selecting the twelve time and peak-hours spec files through Vitest CLI substring filters — once per process `TZ` matrix cell. Pinned interpretations: (1) **A separate job, not a `tz` axis on the main `test` job.** The main matrix's dimension is runtimes (22.13.0 / 22 / 24) and already runs the full suite once per runtime under the runner's default zone; multiplying it by nine zones would re-run ~90% time-agnostic suites 27 times for no additional invariance signal. The suites under test are `TZ`-invariant by construction (D-021's zone-explicit branded API, D-073's pinned-literal epochs), so the matrix's job is to catch construction regressions — a module that silently starts reading the machine zone — which the subset exposes exactly as well as the whole tree. (2) **The zone set: the seven §17.1-required identifiers as process `TZ` values (`UTC`, `America/New_York`, `Europe/London`, `Asia/Shanghai`, `Asia/Kolkata`, `Australia/Lord_Howe`, `Pacific/Chatham`) plus two selected extras** — `Asia/Kathmandu` (+05:45, never-DST quarter-hour: the required list covers quarter hours only through DST Chatham) and `Pacific/Kiritimati` (+14:00 dateline extreme, the task-116 precedent). The grid this covers: DST whole-hour (New York, London), DST with a half-hour offset and 30-minute shift (Lord Howe), DST quarter-hour (Chatham), non-DST whole-hour (Shanghai, UTC), non-DST half-hour (Kolkata), non-DST quarter-hour (Kathmandu), and the +14 edge. (3) **Non-vacuity is a guard, not a hope**: `scripts/verify-tz.mjs` runs in each cell before the suite, in the fresh process (the task-116 discipline — `Intl` resolves the process zone at startup), and verifies that the default zone `Intl` resolves equals the expected canonical name (ICU canonicalizes `Asia/Kolkata` → `Asia/Calcutta`, `Asia/Kathmandu` → `Asia/Katmandu`) and that the zone's `longOffset` at two fixed probes (2026-01-15, 2026-07-15) equals the recorded facts — so a CI wiring bug that leaves every cell in one zone, or a tzdata that lost a zone or its transitions, fails loudly instead of passing vacuously. The facts table was generated from the declared-minimum runtime (Node 22.13.0, full ICU) and the job pins that version so the table is a genuine oracle; the runtime dimension stays with the main `test` job. (4) **The selection is an executable contract**: `test/unit/time-suite-manifest.spec.ts` parses `test:time` from package.json, applies the filters to the real `test/unit` + `test/integration` trees with the same substring-OR rule (verified against the installed Vitest 5.0.5), and requires the selection to equal the pinned twelve-file manifest — a time/peak-hours spec renamed outside the filters (or a dead filter) fails `make check` instead of silently shrinking the matrix. A spec **added** outside the filter vocabulary is not detected: no structural signal says a file is "time/peak-hours" besides its name, and an inventory classifying every future spec would tax unrelated suites — the accepted convention is that these specs are named after their modules (`clock`, `rolling-ranges`, `peak-hours*`, `compare-epoch-ms`), so they join the filters naturally, and a new vocabulary family edits the filters and the manifest in the same change. `test/integration/tz-verify-script.spec.ts` pins the guard's own contract (all nine zones accepted with the zone echoed, unset/empty `TZ` rejected naming the fresh-process rule, a valid non-matrix zone rejected listing the nine) and the zone-membership on both remaining sides: a line scanner compares the workflow's `timezone` job matrix in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` with the same pinned list, so a zone dropped from (or added to) the workflow or the script's table fails the suite. (5) **No coverage in the subset run**: thresholds are judged once by `test:ci` in the main job (D-085); the matrix adds environmental repetition, not coverage.

**Reasons.** §17.1 says the time-zone suites must "run under different `TZ` values", and until this task no CI leg ever set `TZ` at all — every suite ran under the runner's default zone, so the invariance D-021/D-073 built was verified only in local ad-hoc runs (D-073's "verified under four zones" was a manual act). A child-process proof per test file (task 116's shape) would multiply spawns for what is a property of the whole suite-under-environment; one CI job per zone runs the real suites unmodified under the real environment, which is also the honest level for "the app must work consistently under any `TZ` setting" (§10). The zone-facts guard exists because a matrix that silently collapses to one zone passes everything while proving nothing — the exact failure mode `rolling-ranges-tz.spec.ts` guards against with its resolved-zone assertion, lifted here to the job level where vitest cannot see it. The guard compares offsets numerically, parsed from `longOffset`, because ICU spells a zero offset `GMT` on Node 22.13.0 but `GMT+00:00` on Node 24 — and the main test matrix spawns the guard on Node 22.13.0/22/24 through the integration spec (the review-caught P1: a display-string table made the guard fail UTC and London-winter on Node 24). Pinning the `timezone` job to 22.13.0 rather than a floating `22` trades runtime breadth (already the main matrix's dimension) for the guard's canonical-name expectations being an oracle rather than a coincidence across ICU builds. The three-place zone list (CI matrix, script table, integration spec) is guarded on every side: the spec pins the script's table behaviorally and the workflow's matrix structurally (a small line scanner, loud on any shape it cannot read), so drift fails a test rather than a pipeline at 3 a.m.

**Consequences.** `make test-time [ZONE=<zone>]` reproduces any cell locally (the guard runs first under `ZONE`, refusing non-matrix values with the membership list); plain `make test-time` runs the subset under the container's default zone, and `make test-time-matrix` walks all nine cells — wired into `make check-all`, which keeps its documented full CI parity by running the same guard-plus-suite loop per zone that the CI job runs. Adding a time/peak-hours spec file means updating the `test:time` filters and the manifest together (the failure message says so); a spec added outside the filter vocabulary is the documented blind spot above. Extending the matrix means editing the three zone lists together (the integration spec fails until they match). The subset's own tests (the manifest guard) live outside the filter vocabulary, so they run in the main suites only. The property tests inside the subset keep their D-094 timeouts — the matrix does not change per-test budgets, only the environment. A future zone-facts drift (ICU canonicalization or tzdata change) fails the guard with actual-vs-expected and is resolved by regenerating the table deliberately, not by deleting the guard; offset display spellings may keep varying across runtimes — the numeric comparison is the contract, and only a canonical-name change or a real offset change fails.

## D-098 — The runtime version gate: `engines.node` as the single source of truth, prefix-ordered comparison, fail-closed refusal, and an in-repo child-process boundary matrix (spec §5.1, §17.2; task 129)

**Date:** 2026-11-01 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§5.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#51-supported-environment), [§17.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#172-installationpackage-tests) · **Tasks:** [129](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-002, D-044 (launcher mechanics)

**Decision.** Task 129's done-condition ("reject Node.js below 22.13.0 with an actionable message before loading unsupported features; supported and unsupported versions are tested") is implemented with four pinned interpretations. (1) **The declared minimum is derived from `package.json`'s `engines.node`, exactly `>=X.Y.Z`** — `bin/quotameter.mjs` reads the manifest (it already read it for the package version), requires that one shape, and fails closed otherwise: an unreadable/corrupt manifest or an unexpected declaration ("*", a range, a missing field) is a fatal packaging error, because a gate that cannot determine its own minimum must not run. The launcher's hardcoded `[22, 13, 0]` is gone, so the gate and the declaration npm surfaces cannot drift; the manifest-finalization task (184) moves the gate by editing one field. `src/server/main.ts`'s `MINIMUM_NODE_VERSION` constant stays a documented mirror (src/ cannot import package.json — the layout rule) and is pinned equal to `engines` by tests on both sides (`test/unit/smoke.spec.ts`, the gate suite). (2) **Comparison orders by the numeric `major.minor.patch` prefix; a prerelease/build suffix (the first `-` or `+` onward) is ignored**, uniformly in all three implementations (`bin/`'s plain-JS copy — the launcher is build-free by D-044's packaging shape — `src/util/version.ts`, and `scripts/verify-runtime.mjs`): a nightly of a supported line (`22.13.0-nightly…`) passes, a nightly below the line (`22.12.9-nightly…`) rejects. Semver precedence is deliberately not implemented: the gate exists to keep features absent below the numeric release line (`node:sqlite` without a flag, the D-002 minimum's reason) from loading, and suffix ordering carries no information for that purpose. Malformed values (`''`, `v22.13.0`, `22.13.x`, garbage) keep `version.ts`'s loud `Invalid version string` throw on the server path, while the **launcher fails closed** with a dedicated "cannot determine the Node.js version" refusal that echoes the raw value — replacing the old NaN-semantics comparator, which passed `'garbage'` and `'v22.13.0'` by accident (`NaN < 22` is false). (3) **Ordering inside the launcher is fixed: manifest read → engines parse → version gate → the `--version`/`-v` fast path → dynamic-import delegation.** The gate precedes every path that could load `src/**`; `--version` does not bypass it (task 054's CI contract — Node 20 tarball invocation fails naming 22.13.0 — is preserved), and gate exits set `process.exitCode` and let the event loop drain instead of `process.exit()`, extending the file's own pipe-truncation discipline to the one exit that lacked it. `scripts/verify-runtime.mjs` adopts the same declaration-reading and moves its `node:sqlite` import behind its version check via dynamic import — the module is the unsupported feature the gate exists to withhold, so it must not load before the check. `verifyRuntime` (the `quotameter run` defense-in-depth behind the launcher gate) gains the launcher's upgrade hint; its existing partial-regex pins are unaffected. (4) **The test seam is the real launcher in a child process with `process.versions.node` redefined through a data-URL `--import` preload** (`Object.defineProperty` — the property is non-writable but configurable; verified empirically on the pinned 22.13.0 runtime and its CI siblings' family), not an import-time mock and not a test-only production seam. The boundary matrix lives once in `test/helpers/nodeVersionGate.ts` (exactly 22.13.0; 22.13.1; 22.12.9/22.12.0; 21.7.2/20.18.0/18.20.4; 23.0.0/24.14.1; short forms 22.13/22; suffixed nightlies on both sides of the boundary; four malformed values) and is consumed by both gate suites — the unit block pins `satisfiesMinimum`'s verdict per case, `test/integration/cli-bin-version-gate.spec.ts` pins the real gate's exit code, stream routing, message content, and two structural pins: a faked 22.12.9 with a delegating argument stops at exactly the gate line (no ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND fallback — no command-module load attempted), and fixture packages (copied launcher + crafted manifest) prove the gate follows a raised (`>=22.14.0` rejects 22.13.0 naming 22.14.0) and relaxed (`>=20.0.0`) declaration and refuses without a usable one.

**Reasons.** The environment note's constraint — the pinned 22.13.0 container cannot run a genuinely older runtime — makes the boundary evidence the done-condition demands impossible to produce with real old binaries in `make check`; task 054's CI job covers exactly one real old runtime (Node 20, tarball install) per push, but nothing in-repo pinned the boundary at all: the gate's rejection path had zero coverage until CI ran, and the nearest-below case (22.12.x) was never executed anywhere. Redefining `process.versions.node` in a preload runs the real production gate unmodified — no test-only bypass of a lifecycle gate — and the data-URL form needs no committed `.cjs` helper (which the ESLint node-globals config does not cover). Single-sourcing the minimum in `engines` removes a three-place constant (bin array, server constant, dev script) whose drift was already latent: 184 will edit `engines` and would have had to remember the launcher. The prefix comparison fixes two real defects, not style: `verifyRuntime` threw a non-actionable `Invalid version string: "22.13.0-nightly…"` on real nightly builds (a refusal to _run_ a supported runtime), and the old bin comparator's NaN path admitted unparseable values — both exactly the "actionable message" and fail-safe posture the task names. The `exitCode` change closes the one `process.exit()` remaining in the launcher, which sat beside the file's own comment explaining why every other exit avoids it (console.error to a pipe is asynchronous on POSIX; CI captures it through a pipe).

**Consequences.** Every change to the declared minimum is now a manifest edit that moves all three gates at once; the `>=X.Y.Z`-only acceptance means a future compound range in `engines.node` (say `^22.13 || >=24`) is a deliberate decision that must also relax the parse — the failure is loud and names the field, never a silent pass. The launcher keeps its plain-JS comparison twin of `version.ts` (build-free requirement); the shared `nodeVersionGate.ts` list is the equivalence contract — a boundary case added in one place and not the other fails the other suite, and the twin itself stays small enough to review by eye. Nightly/custom runtimes at or above the minimum now run the server instead of being refused; ones below it are rejected with the actionable message, and unparseable version strings never pass anywhere. `test/integration/cli-bin-version-gate.spec.ts` adds ~35 child spawns to the integration suite (well under the existing cli-bin suite's jiti-spawned cost, no jiti here) at the 20 s per-test pin the sibling suites use. The `process.versions.node` configurability the seam relies on is a V8/Node implementation property, not a documented contract — it holds on every runtime the CI matrix runs (22.13.0 verified directly; the descriptor shape matches on 24.x) and the suite fails loudly if a future Node freezes it, at which point the seam moves to a `--require` CJS preload or equivalent, not to a production bypass.

## D-099 — The interactive `init` contract: owned line queue (never `readline.question`), `null`-on-close, empty-answer semantics per question kind, and the system zone as hint-only (spec §5.3; task 130)

**Date:** 2026-11-01 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§5.3](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#53-init-workflow) · **Tasks:** [130](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-044 (exit codes, output seam), D-014 (IANA validation twin reused, not re-derived)

**Decision.** Task 130's interactive question layer pins five interpretations. (1) **The production prompter never calls `readline`'s `question()`; it owns the line queue.** Two verified runtime defects motivate this: piped input delivering several answers in one chunk makes the interface emit every `line` synchronously, and all lines firing while no question callback is pending (the first callback resolves only in a later microtask) are silently dropped — interactive typing works while piped automation loses everything after the first answer; and `question()`'s promise never settles when the input closes without a final line, hanging the process forever. `createReadlinePrompter` keeps the `node:readline` interface for what it is good at (raw-mode line editing, keypress decoding, echo) but feeds a first-in-first-out queue from its `line` events: a question takes a buffered line or registers a waiter; `close` settles every waiter with `null`; a question after close resolves `null` immediately; queued lines are delivered before the closed sentinel (a final partial line still counts, matching readline's own end-of-stream behavior). Cancellation is uniform — EOF, Ctrl-C (the interface's `SIGINT` handler closes it), or a closed pipe all surface as `null`, which the `init` handler renders through the dispatcher's standard failure path (`quotameter init: input closed before the questions were answered — initialization cancelled`, exit 1 per D-044; no separate interrupt code exists in the contract). (2) **Secret entry mutes echo in terminal mode only, and type-ahead never echoes.** `askSecret` writes the prompt itself, mutes the echo gate, reads the line, unmutes, and writes the newline itself. Terminal (raw) mode is enabled exactly when stdin `isTTY` — the only mode in which readline performs echo through the output stream (so muting hides the typed key); with `terminal: false` on a real TTY the kernel line discipline echoes regardless of any output muting, and piped input has no echo to suppress. Because the line queue accepts answers typed before their question, echo muting must cover type-ahead too (a code-review finding on the first version, whose mute engaged only at the secret prompt: pasting the whole answer block at the first prompt would have echoed the key long before the key question): a `data` listener attached **before** the interface counts line endings per chunk and mutes the gate before readline processes any chunk carrying more than one answer, and a line arriving with no question pending latches a silent mode for the rest of the flow — once the user is ahead of the wizard, nothing further echoes (prompts, complaints, and the summary remain the feedback). PTY transcript tests pin both shapes: line-by-line typing echoes normal answers but never the key, and a whole-block paste echoes nothing (the key appears nowhere; the time zone exactly once — in the summary). The one boundary no reader can close, documented here deliberately: a **single line typed into an earlier, non-secret prompt** is echoed before the program can know it will later be classified as a key (and an invalid answer complaint for a non-secret question names the offending value) — the program itself never prints or logs the key anywhere (§15.4 holds for program output); the terminal echoes what the user types into the wrong prompt, as every readline-based wizard does. (3) **Empty-answer semantics are per question kind, not uniform.** Where §5.3 names a default and the prompt shows it (host `127.0.0.1`, port `8787`, interval 300 s), Enter is an informed choice of that default; defaults are read from `CONFIG_DEFAULTS`, never a second copy. Where empty means skip (account label; API key — "add it later in the UI"), blank-but-not-empty input is an error, because blankness cannot mean skip without silently discarding an account the user tried to name. The time zone has **no default of any kind**: empty or blank is the loud "Time zone is required: Quotameter never applies the system time zone automatically" error; the system zone (injectable seam, default `Intl.DateTimeFormat().resolvedOptions().timeZone`, `undefined` on failure) may appear inside the prompt text as a hint, and adopting it still means typing it — §5.3 step 2's "must never be silently adopted" is enforced structurally: there is no code path from the hint to an answer. Time-zone validity reuses `isValidTimeZoneName` from the configuration contract (D-014) — `init` accepts exactly what startup validation accepts, no more (legacy `Intl`-accepted names included); accepted names are canonicalized through `Intl` casing (`utc` → `UTC`; aliases like `Asia/Calcutta` kept). (4) **Validation errors re-ask; closed input aborts; nothing is ever half-collected.** Each invalid answer is one stderr complaint (naming the offending value for non-secret fields, never for the key) and the same question again — the retry loop is bounded by the input itself, which either yields a valid line or ends. (5) **Shared infrastructure is single-sited for tasks 131–133.** The per-value parsers (`parseTimeZone`, `parseHost`, `parsePort`, `parseIntervalSeconds`, `parseAccountLabel`, `parseApiKey`) and `buildInitConfig` (answers → the `server`/`app` config sections) are exported; the `accounts` array is deliberately not assembled (a stable account id and the §6.3 secret-source choice are task 133's safe-account-setup concern), and `auth` stays with its §15.1 defaults until the password question lands with its task. The post-question summary reports the key only as `configured (hidden)`/`skipped` (§6.3, §15.4), warns for non-loopback hosts (§5.3 step 4 — password required before start, `quotameter passwd`), and states "Nothing has been written yet" — exit 0 never implies a configured service until the persistence tasks land.

**Reasons.** The line-queue decision fixes a real defect found by manual verification, not a theoretical one: the first end-to-end run against piped input (answers in one chunk, the way every scripted install and CI invocation behaves) answered exactly one question and then reported input closed — `question()`-based multi-question wizards are broken for piped input by construction. The EOF-hang defect was verified directly on the pinned 22.13.0 runtime (`question()` pending forever after `end()`), and the done-condition explicitly demands known behavior for empty/EOF answers, so both needed a structural fix rather than a workaround at each call site. Terminal-mode-only muting follows from how echo actually works: with `terminal: false` on a TTY the kernel echoes, so hidden key entry would silently not work — pinning the TTY gate to the mode where muting is meaningful is the difference between a masked secret and a decorative one. The type-ahead muting exists because muting only at the secret prompt is decorative in exactly the automation case the queue exists for: a user who pastes the whole answer block (or types ahead) delivers the key while a normal question is active, and readline echoes each character as it decodes — the review round proved this against the first implementation; the chunk-level `data` listener runs before readline's own chunk processing (attachment order), so the mute beats the echo for the entire chunk, and the line-level latch keeps the flow silent afterwards. The residual single-line-into-the-wrong-prompt echo is inherent to terminals — no reader can classify input before reading it — so the decision documents the boundary instead of pretending absoluteness. Reusing `isValidTimeZoneName` keeps `init` and startup validation from drifting apart (a zone accepted by one and rejected by the other would be a §6.2 contradiction); canonicalization only fixes casing and keeps aliases, so nothing the user validated changes meaning. The per-kind empty semantics are the minimal reading of §5.3 that keeps every Enter-press meaningful: a default is only a default when the prompt shows it, skip is only skip on a truly empty line, and the time zone's "explicit" requirement means typing — the hint stays a hint.

**Consequences.** Follow-up tasks extend rather than rework: `init --yes` (131) validates flag values with the same exported parsers and errors identically (a missing `--timezone` is the same loud failure, not an invitation to use the machine's zone); the idempotent flow (132) reuses `buildInitConfig` for keep/change merges; the account setup (133) consumes `InitAnswers.accountLabel`/`accountApiKey` and adds the id/secret-source assembly. Any future interactive command (e.g. `passwd`) should build on the `Prompter` seam rather than readline directly — the queue, the mute, and the type-ahead latch are load-bearing. The prompt text and complaint wording are not pinned as a public contract beyond what the suites assert (values, masking, and the no-default rules are pinned; exact phrasing may evolve). The PTY tests write each answer only after its prompt appears (the D-087 readiness-marker pattern, not fixed sleeps) and cover both typing and a whole-block paste; if `script` is ever unavailable the cases degrade to an environment failure, not a silent pass, because the transcript assertions require them to have run.

## D-100 — The `init --yes` contract: parser reuse with absent-flag-as-empty-input, `--api-key-env` as the only key channel (name-only, checked at the input boundary), and collect-all problems (spec §5.3; task 131)

**Date:** 2026-11-01 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§5.3](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#53-init-workflow) · **Tasks:** [131](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-099 (the parser contract reused), D-011 (empty counts as unset), D-023 (no `QUOTAMETER_*` secret channel), D-044 (exit codes)

**Decision.** Task 131's non-interactive layer pins five interpretations. (1) **Validation is the interactive flow's, reused verbatim**: `src/cli/init-yes.ts` feeds every flag value through the task-130 exported parsers, and an absent optional flag is fed as the parser's empty input — so "flag omitted" inherits exactly the "pressed Enter" semantics D-099 pinned (`127.0.0.1`/`8787`/`300` from `CONFIG_DEFAULTS`, no account), one set of range/shape/canonicalization rules for both modes with no second validator to drift. `--timezone` absent or blank is one dedicated handler failure naming the flag and the reason (`--timezone is required with --yes: Quotameter never applies the system time zone automatically…`, exit 1 per D-044's command-failure code — a mode-conditional requirement is command semantics, not a parser-detectable usage error); a present-but-invalid value goes through `parseTimeZone` and fails identically to the typed answer. A set `QUOTAMETER_APP_TIMEZONE` does not satisfy the missing flag: init writes explicit values, and the service-load override layer (D-023) plays no role at collection time. (2) **The API key enters only through the environment, by name.** There is deliberately no `--api-key <value>` option — a value flag puts the secret in the process listing and shell history (§15.4), which is the hazard the environment channel exists to avoid; a key-carrying unknown flag fails as a usage error without echoing the value (strict `parseArgs` names the option, not its argument — verified on the pinned runtime). `--api-key-env <variable>` is §6.3's `apiKeyEnv` mechanism at the input boundary: the name must match the account schema's variable pattern (now single-sited as the exported `API_KEY_ENV_NAME_PATTERN`, referenced by both the TypeBox schema and the CLI so the input and the persisted form cannot drift), must not use the reserved `QUOTAMETER_` prefix (the service's strict unknown-name scan rejects such a variable once it is set, so that name is a guaranteed-broken setup — failing here, with the remedy, is strictly earlier), and the variable must be set as an own property with a non-empty value (empty counts as unset, D-011's uniform rule; inherited prototype names do not count — `Object.hasOwn` keeps a `toString`-shaped argument from passing as a set variable, verified necessary on the pinned runtime where `process.env.toString` resolves through the prototype). Only the **name** is recorded — the new `InitAnswers.accountApiKeyEnv`, mutually exclusive with `accountApiKey` by construction (the interactive flow asks for the value, `--yes` records only a name) — and the value is consulted exactly once, for the non-empty check, never retained, echoed, or logged; no `--api-key-env` problem contains the supplied argument either: the argument may be a mistyped key (the value pasted where the name belongs — an underscore-only key is a syntactically valid variable name), and §15.4 forbids keys in error messages (a review-round finding on the first version, which echoed the argument); task 133 consumes the name for the connection test and the secret-source decision. (3) **A key source requires an account**: `--api-key-env` without `--account-label` is a problem (the label is what creates the account in the interactive flow; a floating key belongs to nothing), while `--account-label` alone keeps §5.3's "skip the key, add it later in the UI" semantics. (4) **All value problems are reported in one pass** — `buildYesAnswers` collects every problem and the handler prints each as its own `quotameter init: …` stderr line before a single exit 1; the interactive flow complains per question because it can re-ask, but a script deserves the complete diagnosis in one run. (5) **Value options require `--yes`**: any of the six without it is a clear failure (`--<name> requires --yes (non-interactive mode)`), not a silently ignored flag and not a half-prefilled wizard — §5.3 defines no middle mode, and the task-130 interactive path runs unchanged otherwise. The `--yes` branch sits before prompter construction in the handler, so no prompter is ever built in non-interactive mode (pinned by a `createPrompter` seam that throws) and `init --yes` works with stdin closed.

**Reasons.** The spec sentence "API keys may be supplied through an environment variable" had two readable mechanisms, and the landed architecture decides: §6.3 makes `apiKeyEnv` the account-level secret source with "exactly one of `apiKey`/`apiKeyEnv`", and the configuration layer deliberately exposes no `QUOTAMETER_*` secret channel (D-023; `src/config/README.md`) — a fixed `QUOTAMETER_API_KEY` value channel would additionally be rejected by the service's strict unknown-name environment scan the moment it stayed exported, so it is not merely stylistically worse, it composes into a broken `run`. Reading only the variable's set-ness — one own-property existence check plus one non-empty check, nothing retained — is the strongest §15.4 posture available at collection time: the one fact init needs (the key exists) is checkable without keeping the value, and the no-echo rule for the argument closes the one path where the value could still reach a terminal (a mistyped `--api-key-env "$KEY"` invocation). Reusing the parsers with absent-flag-as-empty-input is what keeps D-099's "errors identically" promise load-bearing instead of aspirational — a second CLI-side validator would have re-derived ranges, canonicalization, and blank-vs-empty rules that the interactive suites already pin. The missing-`--timezone` wording is new (the parser's empty-case message is prompt-register "Enter…"), but the rule is the same loud no-default failure, and one message for "absent" and "empty" avoids two wordings for one fact. Collect-all reporting follows from non-interactivity: there is no re-ask loop to justify first-failure-only, and the task's own done-condition ("a valid invocation is reproducible") is served by `buildYesAnswers` being pure over flags plus an injected environment snapshot — the summary carries no timestamps, hints, or randomness, which the integration suite pins by running the real launcher twice and comparing stdout bytes.

**Consequences.** The `init` option surface is now declared (`-y, --yes` plus the six value options, rendered in `init --help`), and follow-up tasks extend rather than rework: the idempotent flow (132) reuses `buildYesAnswers` for explicit-value re-runs exactly as it reuses `buildInitConfig`; the account setup (133) consumes `accountApiKeyEnv` (connection test reads the variable; persistence maps it to the account's `apiKeyEnv` field, whose pattern the input already guaranteed) and gains the id/secret-source assembly. `API_KEY_ENV_NAME_PATTERN` is the single site for the env-name shape — a future relaxation is one edit that moves both the schema and the CLI check. The flag names beyond the spec's three (`--polling-interval`, `--account-label`, `--api-key-env`) are this decision's vocabulary; they are CLI-facing only, and help wording derives from the same table, so renames stay one-row edits. The reserved-prefix rejection means a hypothetical future first-class `QUOTAMETER_*` secret variable would first have to relax the config-layer scan this rule leans on — a deliberate decision, not drift. Reproducibility is a property of the collection+rendering path only; tasks 132–133 add environment-dependent steps (existing config, connection test) whose outputs will legitimately differ between runs.

## D-101 — The idempotent `init` contract: three detection outcomes, retain-on-empty in both modes, change-only writes, the §15.1 password-pending tolerance, and the §5.3 step-5 split (spec §5.3; task 132)

**Date:** 2026-11-01 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§5.3](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#53-init-workflow), [§6.1–§6.3](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#6-configuration-and-secrets), [§15.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#151-network-and-authentication-modes) · **Tasks:** [132](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-099 (the parser contract and informed-Enter semantics), D-100 (the `--yes` contract extended), D-022 (`validateSettings` and the placeholder technique), D-018 (canonical completion), D-016/D-019 (atomic write, permission enforcement)

**Decision.** Task 132 implements §5.3's sentence — "`init` must be idempotent: on subsequent runs, display current settings and let the user keep or change them" — with six pinned interpretations. (1) **Three detection outcomes at the resolved configuration path** (`configFilePath(resolveConfigDir(env))`): absent (the fresh task-130/131 flows unchanged, and the run writes the configuration for the first time), a valid configuration (the subsequent-run flow below), or present-but-unusable — and the third is a hard refusal (exit 1, the loader's own secret-free problems, the file left byte-identical): overwriting a configuration whose contents cannot be read and validated is never consented to, because the user cannot know what they are consenting to lose (§6.2's "refuse and explain" applied to the writer's side). (2) **Consent is per setting, and absence retains.** Interactive re-runs ask exactly the four settings questions, each prompt naming the current value (`IANA time zone (Enter to keep Europe/Berlin): `) with the empty answer keeping it — `retainOnEmpty` wraps the shared task-130 parsers, so retain is the same informed-Enter semantics D-099 gave shown defaults, and the timezone's anti-default rule is not weakened: it targets the _system_ zone silently adopted, while retaining a previously explicit, validated choice is precisely the "keep" §5.3 offers. In `--yes` re-runs an absent optional flag keeps the current value — not D-100's fresh-install revert to the spec default, which would silently overwrite a customized setting, exactly what the done-condition forbids — and an explicit flag is the explicit consent to change that setting; a blank flag value (`--port ''`) retains, matching blank-means-not-supplied (D-022). `--timezone` stays mandatory against an existing configuration (§5.3's "absence is an error" is unconditional, and re-stating the zone keeps init from ever persisting a timezone the user did not type in the current invocation); `--account-label`/`--api-key-env` against an existing configuration are one clear failure — the optional initial account is a first-run step, D-100 promised these flags are never silently ignored, and collecting a label no write would persist (account assembly is task 133's, D-099) would break that promise. Existing accounts and every setting init does not ask about (retention, logging, providers, auth) are preserved verbatim through `validateSettings`' §5.3 merge (D-022), and the account questions are not asked on re-runs at all: §5.3 step 3's own escape ("add it later in the UI") is the answer. (3) **Writes happen only on change.** A first run always writes (creating the configuration is the consented act the questions or flags collected); a re-run compares the four owned settings and, when none changed, prints `No changes — the existing configuration is kept` and writes nothing (the file stays byte-identical); otherwise it writes the merged canonical configuration. Every writing run also re-reads the file immediately before the write and refuses (exit 1, nothing written) when the state is no longer what the run displayed — a fresh run requires the file to still be absent (a file created after the initial `none` result is never replaced: the no-clobber half of the guard), a re-run requires the same configuration it displayed (compared structurally, `config/reload.ts`'s `jsonEquals`, so a reformatted-but-unchanged file is not a change), and a file that became invalid after detection refuses the same way. The short re-read-to-rename window that remains is an accepted residual: a per-config lock would serialize only cooperating init processes, not the hand edits and foreign writers the guard exists for, and exclusive-creation (`wx`-style) semantics would fork the landed atomic write (D-016) to protect the fresh case only — one revalidation through the landed read path covers both cases instead. (4) **The §15.1 password-pending state is tolerated on both sides of the pipeline** — a non-loopback bind or `auth.mode: required` without a password hash is probed structurally with a placeholder hash/password (D-022's technique, never by matching problem wording) both when reading an existing file and when assembling a write, and the probe applies only where the password is absent — `auth` missing or a plain object without `passwordHash` — so a present-but-malformed hash (empty, non-string) or a non-object `auth` section is a defect the tolerance never masks: such a file stays invalid, is refused, and is never rewritten; if that is the only defect the configuration counts as existing/pending and is persisted hash-less with the `quotameter passwd` remedy, and any further defect still refuses loudly. The spec's own text decides this: §15.1 says "If remote binding is configured without a password, **refuse to start**" — the constraint binds starting, not existing — §6.2 anticipates invalid-on-disk configurations by defining the startup refusal, §15.2 names `passwd` (and `init`) as password setters, and task 130's pinned note already promised "set one with quotameter passwd", a journey that requires the intermediate file to exist (passwd needs a config to edit; failing the write would strand remote-binding setups until password support lands, with no way back through init). Password collection inside init lands with the scrypt tasks (task 153; §15.2), at which point the pending state simply stops being produced. (5) **§5.3 step 5 splits along the artifact**: the configuration half (directory `0700` via `enforceConfigPermissions`, file `0600` via `writeConfigFile`'s atomic temp+fsync+rename — the landed task-066/065 layers, no new filesystem code) is task 132's, because the configuration file is the artifact init is idempotent about and the done-condition's double-init sequence needs it on disk; the database half lands with the storage-consuming init steps (task 133+), because creating a database nothing in init consumes yet would couple the CLI to the storage composition (connection + migrations, D-030) ahead of its task. (6) **A type-only canonical view** (`CanonicalConfig` on `src/config/load.ts`) describes what `parseConfig` actually emits — sections materialized with concrete `server.host`/`port` and defaulted `app` numbers, `auth.passwordHash` deliberately still optional — so the CLI reads validated configurations without re-deriving optionality; it adds no runtime code, leaving the module's D-089-pinned coverage keys untouched.

**Reasons.** Every ambiguity was resolved from the spec text. "Keep or change them" reads per setting (the display names each setting; a single keep-everything gate would force re-entry of everything on any change and could not express "change only the port"); the interactive and non-interactive modes then deserve one rule — absent input retains — expressed through one shared parser wrapper, or `--yes` would silently revert what Enter keeps, the exact asymmetry the done-condition exists to prevent. The invalid-existing refusal follows from consent semantics rather than charity: the display §5.3 mandates ("display current settings") is impossible for a file that cannot be validated, so proceeding would mean offering keep-or-change over unknown contents with the write as a trap. The pending tolerance was the one place the landed contract (findConfigProblems' §15.1 rule) and the landed UX (task 130's exit-0 note with the passwd remedy) genuinely conflicted if init wrote only fully-valid configurations; §15.1's own sentence ("refuse to start") and §15.2's password-setter list resolve the conflict in favor of the intermediate state, and D-022's placeholder device implements it without coupling to problem wording the module does not own. The step-5 split keeps task 132 inside its scope boundary (detection and consent) while still landing everything the done-condition's evidence requires: the config file must exist after the first run for "the second run does not overwrite it" to be a meaningful claim, but nothing in that claim needs a database. The seams (`InitDeps.readExisting`/`persistConfig`) keep the unit suites filesystem-free while the integration suite exercises the real wiring — the established `YesEnv`/`systemTimeZone` pattern extended, not a new injection style.

**Consequences.** Task 133 extends without rework: it consumes the pending-account answers on fresh runs, adds the id/secret-source assembly (making the collected account real), and gains the connection test; the password step (with task 153's scrypt) replaces the pending state by supplying `auth.password` through `validateSettings`' existing `pendingPassword` channel — D-022's design already anticipated exactly that hand-off. A password-pending configuration makes `quotameter run` refuse to start with the §15.1 problem until `passwd` completes it — intended, and the refusal message is the spec's own remedy path; `doctor` (145) will report the same state. The retain semantics are now part of the CLI contract: future init options (a `--history-retention` flag, say) must decide absent-flag behavior per mode — retain against an existing configuration, default on a fresh one — or the no-silent-overwrite invariant fails. `CanonicalConfig` is the shared vocabulary for "a validated configuration's guaranteed shape"; consumers reading optional-by-type sections should use it rather than scattering casts. The double-init done-condition is pinned executably in two layers (in-process real-filesystem handler runs and real-launcher child processes), so a regression in either the semantics or the plumbing fails `make check`.

## D-102 — The initial-account contract of `init`: deterministic id slug, exactly-one assembly over the collected answers, the §5.3 step-6 failure offer, structural outcome classification, and a shared-core provider factory (spec §5.3 step 6; task 133)

**Date:** 2026-11-01 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§5.3](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#53-init-workflow), [§6.2, §6.3](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#6-configuration-and-secrets), [§7.2, §8.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#8-provider-architecture-and-zai-adapter), [§15.4](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#154-secret-protection) · **Tasks:** [133](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-004 (secrets in config), D-099/D-100 (the collection layers consumed), D-101 (the write path extended), D-052 (the credential check's own vocabulary)

**Decision.** Task 133 makes the optional initial account real, with six pinned interpretations. (1) **A label without a secret source stores no account.** §6.3's "exactly one of `apiKey`/`apiKeyEnv`" is a validated configuration invariant (`findConfigProblems`), so the keyless label tasks 130/131 legitimately collect cannot be persisted as an account; the run keeps §5.3 step 3's own escape — the summary states the account is added later in the web UI — instead of writing invalid configuration. (2) **The account id is a deterministic slug of the label** (`initialAccountId`: lowercased, disallowed runs collapsed to `-`, separator-only heads/tails removed — underscores included, since the id charset's first character must be alphanumeric (review round: the first version trimmed hyphens only, and `_work` produced a schema-invalid id that surfaced as a post-test assembly failure); capped at the schema/SQL id length of 64, fallback `account`), written once and stable thereafter; the provider id is the injected provider's own `id`, so the CLI hardcodes no adapter identifier. Deterministic keeps `--yes` reproducible (D-100) and the id human-readable in API paths; on a fresh run there is exactly one account, so slug collisions are impossible by construction.
