**Reasons.** §5.2's table row fixes the object ("Control an installed service through systemd") and its next sentence the failure mode ("If service control is requested before installation, display a helpful next step instead of failing cryptically") — together they make the installed-unit discovery load-bearing and the not-installed branch a designed outcome, not an error report. Reusing 139's exists-seam (instead of asking the managers, say via `systemctl cat`) keeps the discovery pure and testable on the systemd-less container and CI images, faithful to the same file the install command itself wrote. The both-installed rule is D-108's recorded delegation, not a fresh choice; the sudo-prefixed steps and the never-root note are D-108/D-106 review findings applied to the new surface; and the exit-code contract mirrors the D-108 asymmetry already argued for install (whose whole job is the service) rather than init (whose configuration is already written when its service step falls back). Skipping a polkit-style unprivileged system-verb attempt follows D-105's frozen vocabulary: system-manager operations are privileged operations, and whether a given machine's polkit would authorize them is a distribution variable the v1.0 contract does not depend on.

**Consequences.** Tasks 141–143 (`reload`/`status`/`logs`) operate on the same installed-unit discovery and should import it rather than fork a second probe; task 145's `doctor` may surface the cross-unit state through the same facts. The exported surface (`runServiceControlCommand`, the renderers, `ServiceControlDeps`/`ServiceControlVerb`) is internal API under `src/cli/`, not package surface; `service-install.ts` gained exactly one additive export (`resolveOwnerForCommand`, its deps parameter widened to any seam set carrying `resolveOwner` — both 139 call sites unchanged), following D-108's own additive-sharing precedent (`failureLine`/`thrownMessage`). The done-condition ("commands use the correct service scope") is pinned executably: `test/unit/cli-service-control.spec.ts` drives the full matrix seam-by-seam — every verb × every installed-kind × privilege × manager-availability combination, asserting the exact command arrays (`['systemctl', verb, 'quotameter.service']` / `['systemctl', '--user', verb, 'quotameter.service']`), the both-installed selection with its warning, the unusable-home edges, owner-problem and broken-database gates, and every renderer byte-for-byte — while `test/integration/cli-service-control.spec.ts` pins the one route the systemd-less container really produces (nothing installed → exit 1 with the guidance naming the install command, no files written) through the real launcher. Changing any rendered sentence is a coordinated renderer+test change; reordering the privilege check before the systemd-absent check on the system kind (or the held check after the capability probes on the user kind) would change which guidance a doubly-broken machine sees and is therefore a decision-requiring change.

## D-111 — The public health-response contract of task 147: the literal body enforced at serialization (closed TypeBox response schema in `src/schemas/api/`), route-scoped `no-store` pending 158, the authenticated-diagnostics half deferred, and the endpoint public in every auth mode (spec §13, §15.1, §15.5; task 147)

**Date:** 2026-11-01 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§13](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#13-http-api), [§15.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#151-network-and-authentication-modes), [§15.5](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#155-headers-and-limits) · **Tasks:** [147](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-109 (the task-146 server construction and `/api` route seam this endpoint joins), D-085 (the coverage gate the new modules sit under), D-025 (the redacting logger whose §16 gate the endpoint rides)

**Decision.** Task 147 ships the first Stage-12 endpoint — unauthenticated `GET /api/health` — and pins five interpretations. (Correction trail: the task's review round — kimi, one round — disproved the first draft's claim that a wrong `status` value fails serialization loudly with a `500`; on the pinned runtime (fastify 5.12.7, fast-json-stringify 7.2.0) the compiled `const` serializer emits the literal `'ok'` whatever the handler returns. The correction is folded into interpretation (1) below; this entry had not landed when corrected — the D-109 correction precedent. Decisions are immutable once landed.) (1) **The literal response is enforced at the serialization layer, not by handler discipline.** §13's row says the unauthenticated response "contains only `{ "status": "ok" }`", and §13's opening sentence says every request and response is "defined through TypeBox/JSON Schema" — so the route carries a response schema from day one: `HealthResponseSchema` in the new `src/schemas/api/health.ts` (the API-contract home the server README already documented), a `Type.Object` closed with `additionalProperties: false` over `Type.Literal('ok')`. Fastify compiles that schema into the route's serializer, which emits exactly the declared key and structurally drops every other — a future handler edit returning diagnostics cannot leak them through this route; a wrong `status` value serializes as the literal anyway (the compiled `const` serializer emits `'ok'` regardless of the input), so the wire output is invariant under any handler result — which serves the leak condition even better than a loud failure would, and is pinned on the wire by the serializer regression block of the integration suite rather than only at Ajv validation (different engines — the review round's point). The done-condition ("no extra system diagnostics leak before authentication") therefore holds by construction, and task 163's OpenAPI generation inherits a definition that cannot describe a second field. (2) **`Cache-Control: no-store` applies route-scoped now.** §15.5 prescribes `no-store` "for API responses", and this response is one — withholding it until task 158 would ship a cacheable health endpoint in the interim. The handler sets the header on this route only; task 158's global security-header pass (CSP, `nosniff`, `no-referrer`, `no-store`) generalizes it later, additively — no conflict, no pre-emption of the headers that remain 158's deliverable. The content type stays the framework's default `application/json; charset=utf-8` (§13/§15.5 prescribe no exact value), pinned by test so a Fastify default change is seen rather than drifted past. (3) **The authenticated-diagnostics half of §13's row is deliberately unimplemented.** "Authenticated response may include process/database diagnostics" is a permission ("may"), not a requirement, and the task is the _minimal public_ response; the response is byte-identical for every caller today (there is no authentication to branch on — tasks 152–155), and extending `/api/health` with diagnostics is a future task's own decision, not something this task's contract forecloses or pre-builds. What the endpoint must never contain is named in the schema module's contract: versions, uptime, memory/pid, storage or database state, account data, errors, timestamps. (4) **The endpoint is public in every auth mode.** Nothing on the route consults credentials, and §13's "except the public health response" binds tasks 149–152: Origin/Fetch-Metadata checks and Host validation protect state-changing requests (§15.3), and the auth-mode selection must keep `GET /api/health` reachable unauthenticated in `auto` and `required` alike (§15.1) — a `required`-mode deployment still needs an unauthenticated liveness answer. (5) **Routing is GET-only and slash-exact.** Other methods find no route and keep task 146's pre-148 default 404 shape until task 148 replaces the error surface with the §13 envelope; Fastify's default `exposeHeadRoute` derives a HEAD twin that answers with the same headers and no body — nothing can leak through it; `/api/health/` is a 404 (the path is exact); query strings are ignored — no diagnostic mode hides behind parameters.

**Reasons.** Every choice follows the smallest surface that keeps the done-condition structural. The response schema is forced by §13's own first sentence ("Define every request and response through TypeBox/JSON Schema") read together with its health row ("contains only"): a closed schema is the only mechanism that makes "only" a property of the route rather than a habit of its handlers, and it costs nothing the spec does not already require. Route-scoped `no-store` resolves the one genuine overlap with task 158 in the direction that never violates §15.5 in the interim — 158 generalizes, it does not re-decide. Deferring the diagnostics half keeps the task inside its title and avoids minting an authenticated health surface with no consumer (the §14 UI reads `/api/status`, and no §13 consumer is specified for authenticated health diagnostics); "may" is the spec's own word for that latitude. The public-in-every-mode pin is recorded because it is the one property later tasks could accidentally break: a naive "all endpoints require authentication when authentication is enabled" reading of §13's opening sentence would take the service's liveness answer away from exactly the deployments (`auth.mode: required`, behind a reverse proxy) where an unauthenticated health check matters most for monitoring and §5.3's install-verification step.

**Consequences.** Tasks 148–163 register inside the same `/api` scope and follow the same pattern — endpoint contracts in `src/schemas/api/`, route plugins in `src/server/api/` — so task 163's OpenAPI generation reads one canonical home; task 148 replaces the 404 shape the method-routing tests pin (they pin the pre-148 shape deliberately, as 146's suite did, and update with 148); task 158 generalizes `no-store` and may drop this route's local header without changing any pinned observable; tasks 149–152 must leave the route unauthenticated (a change requiring a superseding decision); extending health with authenticated diagnostics is a future task's coordinated schema + route + decision change (`additionalProperties: false` makes any such edit loud, not silent). The endpoint is pinned by `test/integration/api-health.spec.ts` (byte-exact body, single-key parsed shape, headers, query and credential invariance, the method-routing table with the pre-148 404 shape, the HEAD twin, trailing-slash exactness, one real ephemeral loopback socket through the `http-listener` component, and zero request-log lines at `warn`) and `test/unit/api-health-schema.spec.ts` (the closed-object contract: the literal accepted, every diagnostic-carrying, wrong-valued, and non-object shape rejected) plus the integration suite's serializer block — a test-only route carrying the same schema, driven with diagnostic-carrying, wrong-valued, and hostile-keyed handler results, every one serializing to the byte-exact literal (the structural leak guard pinned on the wire, not just at validation). The exported surface (`HealthResponseSchema`, `HealthResponse`, `healthRoutes`, `HEALTH_RESPONSE`) is internal API under `src/`, not package surface.

## D-112 — The `reload` command contract: running-service discovery through the §5.6 lock (run-mode-independent, single-sited), the accepted/rejected feedback answered by re-running the load pipeline in-process (no signal for a rejected file), and the §6.4 restart advisory without a fabricated classification (spec §5.2, §6.4, §6.2; task 141)

**Date:** 2026-11-01 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§5.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#52-cli-commands), [§6.4](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#64-configuration-mutation-and-reload), [§6.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#62-configuration-contract), [§5.6](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#56-process-lifecycle-backups-and-upgrades), [§6.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#61-paths) · **Tasks:** [141](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-110 (the service-control contract whose consequences sentence this task resolves — reload deliberately does **not** take its installed-unit route; the shared additive-export precedent), D-026/D-023 (the reload result vocabulary and the env-snapshot discipline of the pipeline this command re-runs), D-025 (the reloader whose log line is the authoritative service-side record), D-017/D-086 (the single-instance lock whose file and recycled-pid residual this command consumes), D-105/D-108 (the owner resolution and owner-scoped §6.1 path discipline reused through `resolveOwnerForCommand` and the now-exported `ownerUnitDirectories`)

**Decision.** Task 141 ships `src/cli/service-reload.ts` — `runReloadCommand(deps)`, plugged into the top-level `reload` row of the dispatch table (§5.2's table names the command unprefixed, beside `start`/`stop`/`restart`) — and pins five interpretations. (1) **Running-service discovery is the §5.6 single-instance lock, not a manager-scoped command.** The handler reads `lockFilePath(<owner's data directory>)` — the exported helper of `src/server/single-instance.ts`, imported read-only (task 141 must not modify `src/server/**`; the `cli → server` import is the sanctioned `init.ts` → `providers` direction) — and the payload parse (`{ pid: <positive integer>, id: <token> }`) mirrors the lock module's private `parseHolderPid`, whose contract that module's own tests pin. The lock is the one fact that exists for **every run mode**: a systemd unit and a foreground `quotameter run` alike hold it while running, so one read answers both "is a service running on this data directory?" and "at which pid?", where D-110's installed-unit discovery would answer only "is a unit installed?" and `systemctl kill` could neither reach a foreground run nor distinguish installed-but-stopped. The recorded pid is liveness-probed with the lock module's exported `isProcessAlive` (its `EPERM`-means-alive conservatism routes an other-user holder to the signal's own permission arm), and the four read states map to outcomes: absent → not-running guidance (§5.2's helpful next step: `quotameter start` / `quotameter run`); dead pid → the same guidance with the stale-lock explanation (a crash leftover §5.6's next start clears automatically, plus the lock module's recycled-pid remedy sentence); unreadable or invalid payload → a loud failure carrying the lock module's own refusal wording — none of them signals anything. (2) **The accepted/rejected feedback is a pre-flight validation, not an observation.** The command re-runs `loadConfigWithEnv` — the exact pipeline function `createConfigReloader.reload()` executes on SIGHUP (D-026/D-023) — over `configFilePath(<owner's config directory>)` in its own process; validation is deterministic, so the answer is immediate, and it needs no observation channel because v1.0 has none to use: the health API is task 147 (in flight in parallel — a dependency this task must not take), and reading the service's log record is task 143's `journalctl` machinery. A file with problems is **rejected**: every pipeline problem prints verbatim (one `quotameter reload:` stderr line each — D-018 field-addressed, value-free), the stdout outcome states §6.2's guarantee (the service keeps the last valid configuration), and **no SIGHUP is sent**, because §6.2 pins the service-side consequence of signalling anyway as a guaranteed no-op — reporting a rejection and then asking the service to confirm it would be incoherent UX for zero effect. A valid file is signalled (`process.kill(pid, 'SIGHUP')`), and the success report names the mechanism honestly ("Validated with the same checks the service applies on SIGHUP"). (3) **The §6.4 advisory is stated, the §6.4 classification is not fabricated.** The success output lists the live settings and the restart-requiring trio with the `quotameter restart` hint, but does not claim `applied` vs `pending-restart`: that classification diffs against the service's in-memory configuration, which only the service's reloader can see (D-026), and the authoritative record is its `configuration reloaded` log line — the output directs to `quotameter logs` (task 143). The `src/config/reload.ts` docstring sentence that anticipated a three-way CLI report is corrected with this commit. (4) **Owner scoping reuses the D-108 path discipline**: `resolveOwnerForCommand` (D-105 problems, broken-database throw, exit 1) and the now-additively-exported `ownerUnitDirectories` — `HOME` forced to the owner's passwd home with `QUOTAMETER_*` overrides honored — so a `sudo quotameter reload` finds the owner's data directory and lock, never root's, and the same environment snapshot feeds the validation (its only read is the `QUOTAMETER_*` scan; `HOME` is irrelevant there). (5) **Exit codes and signal failures**: 0 exactly when the configuration validated and SIGHUP was delivered; every other outcome exits 1. `process.kill` failures classify through a pure errno classifier (`ESRCH` → the service exited meanwhile, with the start-again guidance; `EPERM` → permission denied, with the `sudo quotameter reload` and owner-account steps; anything else → the standard failure line) — pure so every arm is a table test, because a real `EPERM` cannot be produced deterministically under the container uid (signalling pid 1 to provoke it is environment-dependent and dangerous — the landed single-instance suite's own reasoning).

**Reasons.** §5.2 defines reload by the signal ("Reload configuration on SIGHUP"), not by the manager — the row beside start/stop/restart says "through systemd", this one does not — so the mechanism must work wherever a service runs, and the lock is the only landed layer that knows. The task's done-condition ("reload feedback reflects whether the config was accepted or rejected") forced the one open interpretation — how the outcome is observed — and the honest answer is that v1.0 has no channel: an HTTP status surface does not exist yet (147 runs in parallel; depending on it would make independent tasks dependent), and the journald reader is 143's. Re-running the identical pure pipeline is not a heuristic: with no `QUOTAMETER_*` overrides in the service's unit environment (the default — `init` and `service install` write no override `Environment=` lines, D-103/D-104's no-secrets rule keeps it that way), the CLI's answer and the service's are the same function of the same file. The residual is recorded: an operator-pinned override set in the unit but not this shell (or vice versa) can diverge the two verdicts, in which case the service's own log line is the authority and the output says where to find it. Skipping the signal on a predicted rejection is the coherent half of the same choice: §6.2 makes the signal a no-op exactly when the pre-flight says rejected, so sending it would add a warn line to the service log and nothing else. The recycled-pid residual of signalling a lock's pid (a crashed holder whose pid was reused before the lock was broken) is accepted with the lock protocol's own stance (D-017's remedy text names it); the exposure is the crash-plus-no-restart-plus-full-pid-wrap window, and adding a `/proc` identity check would invent a mechanism no landed layer provides (rejected as scope creep the spec does not ask for).

**Consequences.** The composition task that wires SIGHUP into `src/server/main.ts` and registers the single-instance lock in `buildComponents()` completes the production path this command targets — until it lands, a real running `quotameter run` holds no lock and `quotameter reload` reports not-running (the CLI layer's contract is with the §5.6 mechanism, not with the server's current assembly state). Tasks 142/143 (`status`/`logs`) may reuse the lock read for their own running-service facts (the exported `readServiceLock`/`parseServiceLockPid`) or D-110's installed-unit discovery for installed-service facts — running vs installed is now an explicit choice both suites can name; 143's `logs` output is where this command's accepted outcome directs users for the authoritative `applied`/`pending-restart` record. A future reload-outcome observation channel (a health-endpoint field, say) supersedes interpretation (2) via a new decision. The exported surface (`runReloadCommand`, `readServiceLock`/`ServiceLockRead`, `parseServiceLockPid`, `classifySignalFailure`/`sendSighup`/`SignalDelivery`, the renderers, `ServiceReloadDeps`/`ConfigValidation`) is internal API under `src/cli/`, not package surface; `service-install.ts` gained exactly one additive export (`ownerUnitDirectories`, doc-noted for the shared use — D-110's `resolveOwnerForCommand` precedent) and `src/config/reload.ts` a docstring-only correction. The done-condition is pinned executably: `test/unit/cli-service-reload.spec.ts` drives the full handler matrix seam-by-seam (owner problems and throw, unusable home, all four lock states with the discovery-before-validation ordering pinned by uncalled seams, the rejected route's no-signal contract, the accepted route, all three signal-failure arms, byte-exact renderer output) beside the payload-parse table, the real-filesystem lock reader (absent/held/invalid, and a kernel-genuine `EACCES` through a 000-mode directory), the pure errno classifier, and the real signal sender against real child processes; `test/integration/cli-service-reload.spec.ts` pins the three real-launcher routes — not-running guidance, rejected (problems on stderr, and the live signal-holding child receives no SIGHUP, asserted by its marker's absence), and accepted (exit 0 and the child's SIGHUP marker appears; U-001 readiness handshake before any signal, D-087-generous marker wait). Changing any rendered sentence is a coordinated renderer+test change; replacing the pre-flight oracle with an observed outcome is a superseding decision.

## D-113 — The common error-envelope contract of task 148: the code registry as the single vocabulary (§13's codes resolved), strict unknown→INTERNAL classification, root-scope normalization of every native fastify error shape verified on the pinned runtime, and the INTERNAL class's generic-wire/logged-cause split (spec §13, §15.4, §15.5, §16; task 148)

**Date:** 2026-11-01 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§13](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#13-http-api), [§15.4](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#154-secret-protection), [§15.5](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#155-headers-and-limits), [§16](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#16-logging-and-diagnostics), [§6.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#62-configuration-contract) · **Tasks:** [148](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-109 (the task-146 construction whose not-found API branch this task replaces with the envelope, exactly as its consequences scheduled), D-111 (the `src/schemas/api/` contract home and the test-only-route/byte-pinning precedents this task follows), D-025 (the redacting logger whose Layer-A `err` serializer carries the INTERNAL class's server-side cause), D-085 (the coverage gate the new modules sit under)

**Decision.** Task 148 ships the §13 error machinery as two modules — the registry `src/schemas/api/error.ts` (code → `{statusCode, message}` plus the closed TypeBox envelope schema, the schemas-layer leaf D-111 established) and the behavior `src/server/api/error.ts` (`ApiError`, the pure `classifyApiError`, `sendApiError`, `apiErrorHandler`, `notFoundClassification`) — and pins six interpretations. (1) **The registry is §13's resolved code table.** §13 prescribes the envelope and demands "`code` is stable and machine-readable" but names no codes, so the registry is the contract: `VALIDATION` 400, `UNAUTHENTICATED` 401, `FORBIDDEN` 403, `NOT_FOUND` 404, `PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE` 413, `URI_TOO_LONG` 414 (any single decoded path segment past the router's parameter bound — a segment that long can never fill a route parameter, so the request is un-routable; see (4) for why the class is re-derived from the path itself), `UNSUPPORTED_MEDIA_TYPE` 415, `INTERNAL` 500, each with a default message that is English, actionable, and leak-free by construction. The envelope schema's `code` field is a hand-written literal union; a unit test pins the literals against the registry keys (membership and count), so neither table can drift. Adding a class (rate limiting's 429 in task 156, say) is a coordinated registry entry + schema literal + tests change — the sanctioned path, never a thrown error with a private status. (2) **Classification is strict: unrecognized means INTERNAL.** `classifyApiError` is total over `unknown` (a route can throw a non-Error; fastify hands it to the handler verbatim) and resolves everything it does not recognize — unknown errors, foreign `statusCode`s (a thrown 409 becomes the generic 500, pinned), non-Error throwables — to `INTERNAL` with the generic message. The unknown-provenance rule is the §13/§15.4 message discipline made structural: no classifier can forward a message it cannot vouch for, so a path or secret embedded in an error message never reaches the wire; the cost is that a legitimately-shaped future 4xx producer must register its class, which is exactly the extension-point discipline this task exists to establish. (3) **The native fastify shapes were verified before being mapped** (pinned runtime, fastify 5.12.7, probed in-container): schema-validation errors carry `error.validation` (Ajv error objects) and `validationContext` (`body`/`querystring`/`params`/`headers`) → `VALIDATION` with `details.validation` entries `{ where, path, message }` — a projection of client- and schema-derived text only; the transport codes `FST_ERR_CTP_BODY_TOO_LARGE` → `PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE`, `FST_ERR_CTP_INVALID_MEDIA_TYPE` → `UNSUPPORTED_MEDIA_TYPE`, and `FST_ERR_CTP_INVALID_JSON_BODY`/`FST_ERR_CTP_EMPTY_JSON_BODY`/`FST_ERR_CTP_INVALID_CONTENT_LENGTH` → `VALIDATION` (a body that cannot be parsed is a validation failure of the request; `details: null` — the class message suffices), plus the two router-level bounds `FST_ERR_BAD_URL` (a malformed percent-escape in the path) → `VALIDATION` and `FST_ERR_MAX_PARAM_LENGTH` → `URI_TOO_LONG`. Two precision points the review probes added: the 413 and body-parse classes reach `setErrorHandler` even for unmatched routes (body parsing precedes routing), but the 415 class needs a matched route — an unmatched one answers the 404 envelope first, because no parser ever runs for it; and the two router-level codes never reach `setErrorHandler` at all — fastify's router rejects them before routing and, with no `frameworkErrors` callback configured, writes a hardcoded framework body (the unstable native code on the wire, no envelope, no `no-store`) straight to the socket, which is why the construction wires the same handler as the `frameworkErrors` callback. Validation errors are recognized by code and shape together — `FST_ERR_VALIDATION` plus a non-empty `validation` array — so a foreign throwable that merely carries a `validation` property of its own is not projected. `text/plain` is a registered fastify parser and produces no error — §15.3/150's content-type requirements are that task's to add on top. (4) **The envelope is the server's one error shape, registered at root scope.** §13 calls it the _common_ error envelope; a second, framework-default error body for non-API paths (the API-only mode's non-API 404s, static-serving failures) would split the contract the UI client (169) builds against, and root registration also catches errors thrown inside the not-found handler. That registration alone, however, does not make the claim true on the wire — three error paths bypass a root `setErrorHandler`, and the construction closes each (the review round's central finding): the router's own rejections travel through the `frameworkErrors` callback wired to the same handler; the static layer's `send` client rejections (a `%00` byte or traversal shape in the path — foreign 403/404s with no framework code, which the strict rule would answer as a false 500 INTERNAL plus one error-level log record per request) are contained inside the static-serving child scope, whose local handler maps them onto `FORBIDDEN`/`NOT_FOUND` envelopes with generic messages — never `err.message`; and the SPA fallback requires `index.html` itself to exist, so a partial build (assets, no index) degrades to the envelope 404 instead of `sendFile`'s ENOENT inside the 404 handler, which fastify answers with a plain-text basic 404 plus a warn line. A fourth bypass surfaced in post-landing verification (`make check-all` on a tree with a built `ui/dist`): find-my-way reports an over-long parameter (`FST_ERR_MAX_PARAM_LENGTH`, the 414 class) only when the failed match leaves the router no other candidate — any registered catch-all rescues the request first, so with static serving active the SPA wildcard swallowed the over-long parameter into a plain 404 and the 414 class existed only in API-only mode, while production always ships the UI. The `/api` scope therefore carries its own catch-all route (`unmatchedApiClassification`): registered for every method inside the scope, it outranks the static wildcard for `/api` paths and answers unmatched ones with the NOT_FOUND envelope — or URI_TOO_LONG when any decoded path segment exceeds the router bound (`API_MAX_PARAM_LENGTH`, single-sited with the construction's `maxParamLength` option and measured on the decoded segment, the same yardstick find-my-way applies to parameters). The native-code mapping stays as the dead-end mechanism for param routes outside the scope; the bad-percent-escape class is mode-independent by construction (URL sanitation precedes the tree walk, pinned in both modes). An unmatched route is not an error in fastify, so the 404 arm lives in route/not-found handlers: task 146's interim verbatim fastify-default body (D-109's documented placeholder) is replaced by the envelope with `details: { method, path }` — the client's own routing facts, query string stripped, nothing internal — and a fixed "Not found" message instead of the old route echo. Every envelope response carries §15.5 `Cache-Control: no-store` (the D-111 route-scoped precedent generalized to error responses until 158's global pass) and `details` is always present (`null` when empty) so the body is byte-stable. (5) **`ApiError` is the throw-side extension point** for 149/150/152/156/159+: constructed from a registry code (unknown codes throw `TypeError` at construction — D-013's fail-fast registry style), it carries the registry's status and default message with `message`/`details` overridable (§15.1's "403 with instructions" shape); thrown from a handler or a pre-handler hook (where the auth checks will run), it is already its own classification. (6) **The INTERNAL class splits wire from log**: the response is the generic envelope (no message, no stack, no `details`) — generic by construction rather than handler discipline, because `ApiError` refuses `message`/`details` overrides for the INTERNAL code at the throw site and `classifyApiError` re-forces the registry shape for the class, so even a mutated instance cannot carry its own words to the wire — while the real cause goes to exactly one `request.log.error({ err }, 'request failed with an internal error')` record — through the construction's redacting logger (D-025 Layer A), whose `err` serializer normalizes type/message/stack and sanitizes them; the 4xx classes log nothing, because §16's "at `info`, log only lifecycle events" forbids request-outcome chatter above `debug`.

**Reasons.** Every interpretation closes a hole the interim surface left open. The registry resolves §13's own gap (stable codes, none named) in the one place both sides of the wire read: the schemas layer, where task 163's OpenAPI generation and the future UI client consume the same literals the server sends — a codes table living only in server code would leave OpenAPI and client typing to drift from the wire. Strict classification exists because the alternative (trusting any thrown `statusCode`/message) is precisely how internals reach the wire: fastify's own default handler forwards error messages verbatim, and an `ENOENT` path or a provider secret interpolated into a message would leak with it — the projection boundary has to refuse what it cannot vouch for, and the foreign-409 pin makes the refusal's cost visible and deliberate rather than accidental. Verifying the native shapes before mapping them follows the D-109/D-111 correction-trail lesson (both entries record first-draft claims the runtime disproved): every mapped code was produced by a real probe on the pinned fastify, not read from docs that may describe a different version. Root-scope registration and the not-found-arm placement follow fastify's actual control flow — 404s never reach the error handler, the router's rejections never reach `setErrorHandler`, and the static layer's `send` errors arrive with foreign statuses the strict rule cannot trust — so the envelope's "common" claim is enforced where each class actually travels: root handler + `frameworkErrors` callback + the static scope's containment, each pinned on the wire. The one-record logging contract keeps §16's level discipline intact at the default `warn`: an internal failure is a lifecycle-grade event the operator needs (the response deliberately says nothing actionable), while 4xx classes are client behavior the spec explicitly keeps out of non-debug logs.

**Consequences.** Tasks 149/150/152 reject through `ApiError` (`FORBIDDEN` carries their instruction messages; `UNAUTHENTICATED` the 152 modes) — a divergent second envelope or a thrown raw status is a decision-requiring deviation. Task 156 adds `RATE_LIMITED` (or its chosen code) to the registry + schema literal + tests and maps `@fastify/rate-limit`'s error onto it; task 158's global header pass generalizes `no-store` (already present on every envelope and the health route) without changing any pinned observable. Route tasks 159–162 throw `ApiError` for domain failures (`NOT_FOUND` with a resource message is the pinned pattern) and declare request schemas whose validation failures the handler normalizes with no per-route work; task 163 consumes `ApiErrorBodySchema` alongside the route schemas, and the UI client (169) types its error surface from the same literals. `src/server/http.ts` never changes shape again for errors (the handler registration is construction, like the not-found handler). The exported surface (`API_ERROR_DEFINITIONS`, `ApiErrorCode`, `isApiErrorCode`, `ApiErrorBodySchema`, `ApiErrorBody`, `ApiError`, `ApiErrorClassification`, `classifyApiError`, `sendApiError`, `notFoundClassification`, `apiErrorHandler`, `staticServingErrorHandler`, `unmatchedApiClassification`, `API_MAX_PARAM_LENGTH`) is internal API under `src/`, not package surface. The done-condition ("validation, auth, not-found, and internal errors have tested stable codes") is pinned executably: `test/integration/api-errors.spec.ts` byte-pins the envelope on the wire through the full construction — the 404 arm (unknown paths, method mismatches, query forms, bare `/api`, the `/apiary` boundary with the SPA fallback intact, API-only non-API 404s, HEAD headers), schema-validation `details.validation`, the 413/415/parse transports, the router-level `frameworkErrors` arms (`%zz` and a malformed-UTF-8 path → `VALIDATION` in both API-only and static-fixture modes, and the over-long-segment → `URI_TOO_LONG` **mode matrix**: API-only and static-fixture, GET and POST/DELETE, param-route and no-param paths, with the decoded-segment yardstick edge), the static-serving containment arms (`%00` → `FORBIDDEN` and a partial build → the envelope 404, both with zero log records), an error thrown inside a registered plugin scope reaching the root handler through inheritance, `ApiError`-thrown 401/403/404 (the auth classes representable before 152), and the generic 500 whose body provably carries none of a path-and-secret-bearing thrown message while the sink holds exactly the one error-level record with the full cause — plus the foreign-statusCode 500 and the 4xx-log-nothing §16 pin; `test/unit/api-error.spec.ts` pins the pure matrix (ApiError defaults/overrides/guard, validation projection incl. malformed items, every native code, unknown/foreign/non-Error arms) and `test/unit/api-error-schema.spec.ts` the closed-object Ajv contract with the literals≡registry drift guard and the registry table itself. Changing any envelope byte, code, status, or default message is a coordinated registry+schema+suite change; reclassifying a mapped native code or softening the unknown→INTERNAL rule needs a superseding decision. The review round (deepseek, P0–P3: 0/1/3/5) produced nine findings; all nine were accepted and fixed in this task's commit — the `frameworkErrors` bypass (a malformed percent-escape path answered a hardcoded framework body), the static layer's `%00` false-500/log-amplification containment, the partial-build fallback, the INTERNAL-override guard, the schema-typed payload, the scope-inheritance and 413/415 log pins, and the doc-precision corrections (unmatched-route 415 behavior, code-gated validation recognition, and the universality claims made true on the wire). A post-verification fix followed the first landing (cycle step 5, no new review round): `make check-all` against a built UI exposed that the 414 class was mode-dependent — the static wildcard rescued the router's over-long-parameter error into a plain 404 — and the `/api` scope's catch-all route plus the mode-matrix pins landed with this correction.

## D-114 — The `status` command contract: three independent service facts (disk-discovered scope, lock-discovered running, unprivileged manager view), the answered-question exit code, §7.3 through the landed derivation with separate-process proxies, and §7.2's two most-recents as bounded outcome probes (spec §5.2, §7.3, §7.2, §10, §15.4; task 142)

**Date:** 2026-11-01 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§5.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#52-cli-commands), [§7.3](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#73-account-status-precedence), [§7.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#72-retry-and-error-behavior), [§10](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#10-time-and-time-zones), [§15.4](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#154-secret-protection), [§11.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#112-required-logical-tables) · **Tasks:** [142](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-110 (the installed-unit disk discovery reused; the manager-scope vocabulary), D-112 (the lock read, the shared `readServiceLock`, and the CLI-cannot-see-the-service's-environment residual this task inherits for `configured`), D-070 (the §7.3 derivation, its `INITIAL_SUSPENSION_STATE` status-view stance and caller-resolved `configured`), D-105 (the unprivileged-query vocabulary and the never-reach-into-root's-user-manager rule), D-021 (the clock seam), D-048 (the sanitized-by-construction stored messages), D-041 (§7.4's exact-occurrence redaction rule mirrored for error lines)

**Decision.** Task 142 ships `src/cli/service-status.ts` — `runStatusCommand(deps)`, plugged into the top-level `status` row of the dispatch table (§5.2 defines no options for it) — and pins six interpretations. (Correction trail: the task's review round — deepseek, one round, APPROVE with 3 P2 / 7 P3 — sharpened interpretations (1), (2), (4), and (5); the corrections are folded into this entry, which had not landed when corrected — the D-109/D-111 precedent. Six findings were accepted and fixed in the same commit; four were declined with reasons recorded in the commit body.) (1) **The report carries three independent service facts, each from the layer that owns it**: the _installed scope_ from D-110's disk probe (system / user / both — rendered as the mistake task 139 warns about, in the report's own Installed line, stdout not stderr, because status reports where 139/140 act; privileges select only in the both-installed case, D-108's rule); the _running state_ from D-112's lock read — run-mode independent, so a foreground `quotameter run` reports running exactly like an installed unit, which a manager-scoped query cannot do; and the _manager view_ as `systemctl [-–user] is-active quotameter.service` through task 137's command seam, only for an installed unit and only as an **unprivileged query** (D-105's vocabulary names status/journalctl queries service-owner operations) — a privileged run never asks a `--user` manager (it would be root's, not the owner's; the regular-account step is printed instead), and systemd-less or session-less machines get honest `unknown (<reason>)` lines rather than a spawn failure. The binary exit status is the contract (`active`/`not active`) **only for a command that ran and answered**: a non-zero exit carrying a stderr diagnostic (the spawn seam's error arm, or a manager that cannot reach its bus) is a probe that did not answer — it renders `unknown (<diagnostic>)` and makes the exit 1, never the negative fact "not active" (a clean non-zero exit with an empty stderr is how `is-active` answers "inactive"/"failed"); the unit kind disambiguates the line only when both are installed. (2) **The exit code answers "did every probe answer?", not "is everything okay?"**: 0 exactly when every probe produced a fact — stopped, not installed, no accounts configured, and no database are _states_ rendered in a full report (a bare machine exits 0 with the init hint); 1 when a probe could not answer (D-105 owner problems or broken-database throw, an unusable owner home, an unreadable or invalid lock file, an invalid configuration, a storage open/read failure, or a manager command that could not answer) — the report still renders everything the other probes established, with one prefixed stderr failure line per unanswerable probe. This is the deliberate contrast with D-108/D-110's action-command asymmetry (install/control exit 1 when there is nothing to act on): status is a question, and an answered question succeeds; only an unanswerable one fails. A configuration _file that does not exist_ is the answered "not configured yet" (the pipeline's pinned not-found message is the sanctioned absence detection, the 141 technique), not a failure — and §6.3's env-only mode (an absent file plus `QUOTAMETER_*` overrides) reports its provenance as `valid — from environment overrides, no configuration file`, never implying a file exists. (3) **Account facts compose the landed §7.3 machinery with two separate-process proxies**: the account list is the live configuration (the service's own `loadConfigWithEnv` pipeline, D-112's precedent); each status is task 111's `deriveAccountStatus` over `readPollingRunEvidence`, with the D-064 suspension state passed as `INITIAL_SUSPENSION_STATE` — the stance D-070 recorded for exactly this consumer (a status view that cannot see the scheduler's in-memory state; the `auth_error`-run branch keeps `Auth rejected` truthful for it) — and `configured` resolved against **this invocation's** environment (§6.3's usable-secret rule, the D-011 empty-is-unset rule): the CLI cannot see the service's environment, so an env-sourced key missing in this shell reports `Not configured` — D-112's recorded residual stance for CLI-side mirrors of service-side reads, with the same authority note (the service's own view is the truth; here it is unreachable). (4) **§7.2's "most recent successful collection and most recent error" are two independent facts**: the last collection is the evidence object's `lastSuccessAt` (the latest snapshot's §8.4 stamp, D-058's designed lookup), and the last error is the newest **non-success** run — `success` excluded by construction, `rate_limited` included (a 429 cycle is a §11.2 outcome that was not a success) — found by six bounded, indexed `getLatestCollectionRun(accountId, outcome)` probes (the `collection_runs_account_outcome_start` index; newest by `(started_at, id)`, the repository's own ordering). The stored `error_message` renders verbatim — sanitized by construction (D-048) — after a belt-and-suspenders exact-occurrence redaction of **every §6.3 secret source** (file-stored `apiKey` values, environment-supplied key values, and `auth.passwordHash` → `[REDACTED]`): §7.4's rule mirrored in a private helper because the public `sanitizeRawResponse` is payload-shaped (JSON walk + 64 KiB cap) — the wrong tool for a one-line error; the redaction is defense in depth against a write-side bug, pinned by markers seeded into stored errors for both secret sources. (5) **An absent database file is empty evidence, not a failure, and an existing one opens read-only**: a data directory no service ever opened has no runs by construction, the §7.3 derivation's no-run paths answer (`Collecting`, or `Not configured`/`Disabled`), and the command **never creates a database** — the existence probe runs before any storage module loads (a database-less machine imports nothing: `node:sqlite`'s ExperimentalWarning belongs to invocations that open a database, not to every launcher invocation through the dispatch table — the raw-diagnostics.ts discipline, without which the landed suites' byte-exact stderr pins regress), and the open goes through the new additive storage sibling `openReadOnlyStorageConnection` (`src/storage/connection.ts` — the read-only knowledge single-sited where `node:sqlite` lives, the layout's own rule): a read-only handle cannot create the file (closing the probe-then-open window), cannot write pages (no hot-journal recovery as another user under `sudo`), and still passes the §11.1 pragma verification because a quotameter database is already WAL (verified on the pinned runtime). The accepted residual: a database needing WAL recovery (a crashed writer's hot journal) refuses a read-only open — an honest `failed` read; a writer must open it first. Every open/read failure is the `failed` state the handler renders with the accounts section marked unavailable, and only the repository reads sit inside that failure's try — the renders beside them cannot throw on these inputs. (6) **§10 time discipline**: every rendered timestamp is `formatZonedDate` + `formatZonedTime` in the configured display zone with the zone's name (`2025-11-01 13:26 (Europe/Berlin)`) — never a machine-local reading, the D-021 discipline carried into CLI output — and `now` enters through the injectable clock seam whose production default is `createSystemClock().now` (the clock module keeps the only sanctioned `Date.now` call site).

**Reasons.** §5.2's row asks for four things at once (service status, latest collection, account status, last error), and the done-condition ("output is useful for both system and user units") forces the discovery choices: the manager knows an installed unit's state but not whether a foreground run holds the data directory, and the lock knows the holder pid but not what systemd thinks — three facts, three owners, no synthesis. The exit-code interpretation follows from the same sentence read as a monitoring contract: `quotameter status` in a cron or an alert needs a non-zero exit to mean "the _observation_ failed", because the observed states (stopped) must reach the operator as report content, not as indistinguishable failures. The §7.3 composition is D-070's own forward reference (`quotameter status` is a named consumer of `deriveAccountStatus`); forking a second status derivation for the CLI would duplicate the precedence table the spec pins once. The two most-recents stay independent because §7.2's sentence names them side by side ("Retain and display the latest valid values and their collection time after an error") — a report that shows only the latest _run_ would hide a succeeded-after-failure account's error history, and one that shows only the latest _error_ would hide recovery; the six-probe shape follows from the repository's outcome-filtered latest read being the designed primitive (a `listCollectionRuns` scan would read an unbounded history, the §11.3-scale table). The lazy import is not cosmetic: the landed launcher suites pin stderr byte-exactly, and a static `node:sqlite` edge in the dispatch graph regresses all of them — the same lesson `raw-diagnostics.ts` already encodes structurally.

**Consequences.** Task 143 (`logs`) reports the installed scope through the same D-110 probe and the running state through the same D-112 lock read if it needs them; task 145 (`doctor`) inherits the lazy-import discipline for its own database checks and may reuse `openStatusStore`'s absent/open/failed shape; the future composition task that registers the single-instance lock and the storage connection in `buildComponents()` completes the production path the lock reads describe. The future §13 `/api/status` route consumes `deriveAccountStatus` with the service-side inputs (its own scheduler's suspension state and its own environment) — the CLI's proxies are not its contract. The exported surface (`runStatusCommand`, `openStatusStore`/`StatusStoreRead` (beside the one additive `src/storage/connection.ts` export `openReadOnlyStorageConnection`, pinned by a read-only/no-write/seam-precedence block in `test/integration/connection.spec.ts`), `planManagerProbe`/`ManagerProbePlan`, `describeManagerState`, `findLatestErrorRun`, `resolveAccountConfigured`, `RUN_OUTCOME_LABELS`, `formatStatusTimestamp`, `redactSecrets`, `renderStatusReport`/`StatusReport`/`AccountReportLine`/`AccountsSection`, `ServiceStatusDeps`) is internal API under `src/cli/`, not package surface. The done-condition is pinned executably: `test/unit/cli-service-status.spec.ts` drives the full matrix seam-by-seam — every installed scope × manager outcome × reason, all five lock states, valid/absent/invalid configuration, absent/open/failed/throwing storage, one §7.3 status per derivation arm, the last-error selection (newest failure over an older one, HTTP-status fallback, `none`), §10 rendering with Asia/Kolkata against the UTC container, and the §17.1 marker scenario (configured key and hash absent from every output line; a marker inside a stored error rendering as `[REDACTED]`) — beside the pure-helper tables and the production opener against real directories (a kernel-genuine absent file and a corrupt database refused by the §11.1 settings); `test/integration/cli-service-status.spec.ts` pins the real-launcher routes (the bare machine exit 0, the full report over a real migrated SQLite database with deterministic CET timestamps, the invalid configuration exit 1 with service facts kept, a real lock naming a live pid) and the in-process opener-over-seeded-database read. Changing any rendered sentence is a coordinated renderer+test change; changing the exit-code contract or the three-fact discovery split is a superseding decision.

## D-115 — The §15.3 Origin/Fetch-Metadata verdict table of task 149: fail-closed validation over three request signals, same-site rejected beside cross-site, scheme deliberately un-compared (TLS-terminating proxy), both-headers-absent allowed (the non-browser client), and the FORBIDDEN envelope with a closed reason vocabulary (spec §13, §15.1, §15.3; task 149)

**Date:** 2026-11-01 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§15.3](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#153-csrf-dns-rebinding-and-host-validation), [§13](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#13-http-api), [§15.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#151-network-and-authentication-modes), [§15.4](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#154-secret-protection), [§16](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#16-logging-and-diagnostics) · **Tasks:** [149](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-113 (the error envelope the guard rejects through — `FORBIDDEN` was registered as the CSRF class, and the mode-independence hardening this guard inherits as a structural rule), D-109 (the task-146 construction and `/api` route seam the guard registers into), D-111 (the byte-pinning and test-only-route precedents the suites follow)

**Decision.** Task 149 ships the §15.3 Origin/Fetch-Metadata check as `src/server/api/security.ts` — a pure `classifyOriginRequest` over `{method, origin?, secFetchSite?, authority?}` plus the `originGuard` Fastify `onRequest` hook the `/api` scope registers in `src/server/api/index.ts` — and pins six interpretations of the spec's one-line "validate `Origin`/`Sec-Fetch-Site`". (1) **The verdict table is fail-closed over every present signal.** Safe methods (everything outside §13's state-changing set `POST`/`PUT`/`PATCH`/`DELETE`, single-sited as `STATE_CHANGING_METHODS`) pass untouched. A present `Origin` must be parseable (else `malformed-origin`), must be an http/https tuple origin — `file:`/`data:`/`mailto:` URLs parse but carry no origin authority, so they reject as `malformed-origin` (a review-round fix; the empty-host corner needs no separate arm: the WHATWG parser fails every empty-host http/https form, so only non-http schemes could carry one) — must not be the literal `null` (else `opaque-origin` — a sandboxed iframe or cross-scheme redirect, never the UI's own fetch), and its URL authority must equal the request's own `Host` authority after `normalizeAuthority` — case-normalized, with **only the Origin scheme's own default port** (`:80` for http, `:443` for https) stripped from the authority side, so the browser's never-serialized default port and a proxy's explicitly written one compare equal while the opposite scheme's default stays identity (`http://a.example:443` does not collapse onto a port-80 authority — the P2-2 review fix; the scheme-less form strips both and is the yardstick task 151 refines); a mismatch, or no `Host` to compare against, is `origin-mismatch`. A present `Sec-Fetch-Site` (trimmed, lowercased) must be `same-origin` or `none`; **`same-site` is rejected beside `cross-site`** (`cross-site-fetch`) because same-site ≠ same-origin — a sibling subdomain or another port on the same host is still a cross-origin mutation, which is exactly what the done-condition binds — and any malformed token fails closed the same way. Both signals present must independently pass; a browser never lets them disagree, so disagreement is a forged client. (2) **The Origin scheme is deliberately not compared.** Behind §15.6's documented TLS-terminating reverse proxy the browser's Origin is `https://…` while the internal hop is plain HTTP, so scheme equality would reject the legitimate proxied UI; the `host:port` authority is the CSRF-relevant boundary, and the check composes with 151 (whose Host allowlist then bounds which authorities are acceptable at all). (3) **Both headers absent passes** — only browsers emit `Origin`/`Sec-Fetch-Site` on mutations, so their joint absence is the curl/CLI client, not a CSRF vector; the residual gap (an old browser omitting `Origin` on a cross-site form post) is closed by §15.3's own second layer, task 150's mandatory custom header, which no HTML form can set while CORS stays disabled (§13). (4) **Rejection is the §13 envelope's `FORBIDDEN`** — the registry's registered CSRF class, no new code — thrown from the hook as `ApiError('FORBIDDEN', { message: 'Cross-origin request rejected', details: { reason } })` with a closed four-value reason vocabulary (`opaque-origin`, `malformed-origin`, `origin-mismatch`, `cross-site-fetch`); the reason names the failed check and never echoes the attacker-controlled header value (§15.4). (5) **Mode-independence is structural**, per D-113's hardening rule: the verdict consults exactly three headers and the method — never static-serving state, configuration, or the auth mode — and the hook lives in the `/api` scope, so it runs identically in API-only and static-serving modes (pinned with the static-fixture matrix) and in every auth mode (152's selection is a separate layer the guard precedes); the guard also runs for the scope's catch-all route, so unmatched and method-mismatched mutations are screened before routing's 404. The bare `/api` (no trailing segment) is the documented boundary: no route exists there, so routing itself rejects the mutation through the root not-found arm — the guard owns routed `/api` mutations. (6) **The hook is async by runtime necessity**: fastify's hook runner advances on the returned promise, and a synchronous hook that never calls `done` stalls the request forever (verified on the pinned fastify 5.12.7 — the first draft's sync hook hung every injection; likewise verified: a throw from a scoped `onRequest` hook reaches the root-scope error handler, and the hook applies to the scope's catch-all route).

**Reasons.** §15.3 prescribes the check in one sentence and names no pass set, so every row of the table is an interpretation the tests pin. Fail-closed is the only defensible default for a security verdict that cannot establish sameness — an unparseable Origin, an opaque origin, or a missing authority cannot be validated, and §13's mutation set is small enough that over-rejection costs a clear 403 while under-rejection costs a forged mutation. Rejecting `same-site` follows the done-condition's own wording ("cross-origin mutation attempts are rejected"): Fetch Metadata's `same-site` token explicitly permits cross-origin initiators (the browser asserts a shared registrable domain, not a shared origin), and the service is single-user with no sibling-subdomain deployment to serve. Skipping the scheme comparison follows §15.6's deployment story — `auth.mode: required` behind nginx/Caddy with TLS is the documented remote-access path, and a scheme-strict check would break its legitimate UI fetches on every mutation; the layered §15.3 defenses (150's custom header, 151's Host allowlist) cover what scheme equality would have added. Skipping it carries an operational prerequisite recorded here (a review-round finding): the proxy must forward the client-visible authority as the `Host` header — nginx's default `proxy_set_header Host $proxy_host` rewrites it to the upstream and every mutation would answer `origin-mismatch` (use `Host $host`; Caddy preserves it by default) — and whether `X-Forwarded-Host` should be consulted is task 151's own decision, not smuggled into this guard. Allowing the both-absent case keeps every non-browser client working (the CLI's future API use, curl, health checks) — CSRF is a browser mechanism, and the browsers that could omit `Origin` on mutations are exactly the ones 150's unforgeable header answers; the spec's own structure (two independent requirements in one sentence) reads as the layered defense, not alternatives. The reason vocabulary stays closed because `details` is client-visible surface: a fixed set keeps the envelope stable for the UI client (169) and gives security tests a discriminative assertion without turning the response into an echo of hostile input.

**Consequences.** Tasks 150/151 build on the same module: 150's custom-header/JSON-content-type guard registers as a sibling `onRequest` hook in the same scope over the same `STATE_CHANGING_METHODS`, and 151's Host allowlist reuses `normalizeAuthority` as its yardstick (it registers root-scope for frontend routes — a different hook, the same comparison base; the module is the §15.3 seam by design). Task 152 must keep the auth hooks ordered after the guard so a cross-origin mutation is rejected without consulting credentials (the order is observable in the error class). Task 164's contract suite inherits the matrix; task 163 documents `FORBIDDEN`'s mutation-time semantics from the same registry entry. The rejection message and the four reason values are stable, test-pinned vocabulary on the wire — but deliberately not schema-typed here: the envelope's `details` stays `Type.Unknown()` per D-113, and whether task 163 models per-code details (typing the reasons for OpenAPI and the UI client) is that task's call; changing either value is a decision-requiring deviation. The exported surface (`STATE_CHANGING_METHODS`, `OriginGuardReason`, `OriginDecision`, `OriginRequestSignal`, `normalizeAuthority`, `classifyOriginRequest`, `originGuard`) is internal API under `src/`, not package surface. The done-condition ("cross-origin mutation attempts are rejected in security tests") is pinned executably: `test/unit/api-origin-guard.spec.ts` holds the pure table (every `Sec-Fetch-Site` token × all four mutation methods, authority normalization incl. the scheme-aware default ports/IPv6/case with the opposite-scheme non-collapse pins, the non-http/empty-host Origin rejections, opaque/malformed/incomparable Origins, disagreement precedence, safe-method immunity, the joined-split-header arm) and `test/integration/api-origin.spec.ts` pins the wire through the full construction — byte-pinned 403 envelopes per reason with `no-store` and JSON content type, pass-through evidence via the scope catch-all's 404 (a class the guard can never produce), the disagreeing-headers matrix, the guard-before-body-parsing ordering (a cross-origin mutation with malformed or over-limit body answers 403, a same-origin control answers the 400/413 transport classes), mode-independence with the static fixture (SPA deep links still serve), the bare-`/api` boundary, the inject-default-host (`localhost:80`) same-origin pass, and §16's zero-records discipline for rejections. Review round (one round, deepseek, 0 P0 / 0 P1 / 2 P2 / 5 P3): all seven findings accepted and fixed in the same commit — the scheme-aware default-port strip with its non-collapse pins (P2-2), the full token × method unit matrix matching the recorded coverage claim (P2-1), the non-http/empty-host fail-closed rejections (P3-1), the guard-before-body-parsing wire pins (P3-2), the `src/server/http.ts` docblock refresh (P3-3), the `details.reason` "wire contract" wording corrected to stable-but-untyped (P3-4), and the proxy Host-preservation prerequisite recorded in the Reasons (P3-5).

## D-116 — The `logs` command contract: installed-unit scoping with unprivileged reads, D-112's lock as the foreground-run honesty check, the convenience default set (`--no-pager`, `--lines=100`, `-o short-precise`, opt-in `-f`), and raw stdout passthrough where a forwarded interrupt is a success (spec §5.2, §16; task 143)

**Date:** 2026-11-01 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§5.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#52-cli-commands), [§16](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#16-logging-and-diagnostics), [§5.4](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#54-systemd-unit-requirements) · **Tasks:** [143](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-110 (the installed-unit disk discovery and the D-108 privileges-select rule this task reuses, plus the 140 handler shape), D-112 (the §5.6 lock read whose run-mode independence this task turns into the foreground-run honesty check, through the shared `readServiceLock`), D-114 (the capability-gate and unprivileged-query precedents of `status`), D-105 (the vocabulary that names journalctl queries service-owner operations and forbids a privileged run's `--user` reach), D-044 (the dispatch-table extension point and the exit-code grammar)

**Decision.** Task 143 ships `src/cli/service-logs.ts` — `runLogsCommand(deps)`, plugged into the top-level `logs` row of the dispatch table (§5.2's table names the command unprefixed) with the option surface `-f/--follow`, `-n/--lines`, `-o/--output` — and pins six interpretations. (Correction trail: the task's review round — deepseek, one round, REQUEST_CHANGES with 1 P1 / 2 P2 / 6 P3 — sharpened interpretations (4) and (6); the corrections are folded into this entry, which had not landed when corrected — the D-109/D-111/D-114 precedent. Seven findings were accepted and fixed in the same commit; one P3 was declined with reasons recorded in the commit body — a rejecting injected `runViewer` seam propagates to the dispatcher's exit-1 failure arm, exactly the landed 140/141/142 shape.) (1) **The journalctl scope follows the installed unit, and reading is unprivileged.** The handler reuses D-110's disk probe exactly as the 140 verbs do (system unit → `journalctl … -u quotameter.service`; user unit → `journalctl --user … -u quotameter.service`; both → D-108's privileges-select rule with 139's cross-unit note, now exported from `service-control.ts`, printed on stderr **before** the stream because a post-follow stderr line is lost under the entries). D-105's vocabulary names status/journalctl queries service-owner operations, so the system journal is read in-process whatever this invocation's privileges are — an OS-level refusal (exit non-zero, journalctl's first stderr line as the detail) renders the exact `sudo journalctl --no-pager --output=short-precise -u quotameter.service` remedy and the `systemd-journal`/`adm` group hint instead of a refusal, and a privileged run facing a user unit is refused to the regular account (root's `--user` query filters root's own user units, never the owner's — the D-105 never-reach-into-the-user-manager rule). The capability gates mirror 140/142: `systemd` absent means no journal at all (journald is part of systemd — the gate fires before the user-manager questions because a regular-account re-run on a systemd-less machine still finds no journal), and an unreachable user manager gets the exact next-login-session command `journalctl --user -u quotameter.service`. (2) **Foreground-run honesty through the D-112 lock, on the nothing-installed path only.** A foreground `quotameter run` has no journal — its messages are on the terminal it was started from — so when neither unit is installed the handler reads `lockFilePath(<owner's data directory>)` through the shared `readServiceLock` and liveness-probes the holder: a live pid renders the honest "nothing for this wrapper to show" guidance naming it, a dead pid (the stale lock) is 142's report rather than a journal question (the plain install steps answer completely), and an unreadable or invalid lock costs one stderr line beside the same steps — the lock read is best-effort because it cannot change the primary answer (nothing installed means no journal either way), and the directories resolution needs no defensive guard (the handler's own ordering validated the owner's home at `userUnitInstallPath` first, which precludes `resolvePaths`' only throwing arm). An installed unit's journal is read regardless of running state (journals persist across stops), so the lock is not consulted on the installed paths. (3) **The convenience default set is pinned here because §5.2/§16 name none.** `--no-pager` always — a wrapper must not nest a pager under the user's own scrollback; `--lines=100` default — journalctl's own 10 is too short for §16's Pino JSON lines (`-n/--lines` accepts a whole count ≥ 1 in the safe-integer range or `all`, the `--restart-sec` grammar, so no flag value confuses journalctl); `--output=short-precise` default — wall-clock timestamps with µs precision around the JSON message, with `-o/--output` validated against a closed enum of journalctl's stable human-facing formats (`cat` for the raw JSON line, `json`/`json-pretty` for the full journal record, …) so a typo is an immediate self-explaining exit 1 rather than journalctl's own error from deep inside a run; `-f/--follow` opt-in. The vector is deterministic (scope flag, defaults, `-f`, unit match) and byte-pinned by tests — `buildJournalctlCommand` is pure data-in/vector-out. (4) **Streaming is a raw passthrough with a forwarded-interrupt-is-success contract.** The new `runJournalctlPassthrough` seam exists because `spawnServiceCommand` ignores stdout by design; it spawns the built command with piped stdio, forwards every stdout chunk to `process.stdout` as it arrives (no line reassembly — follow mode is a live stream, and the stream is the product: a clean run prints no wrapper chatter on either stream; the raw byte path is the one documented exception to the `CliOutput` line contract, recorded in `output.ts`'s docblock and the README's output-contract section), captures stderr bounded to the house cap (`STDERR_CAPTURE_CAP`, now exported additively from `service-setup.ts` beside `firstDiagnosticLine` — the `resolveOwnerForCommand` additive-export precedent; the capture is sliced chunk-exactly through the pure `appendCappedStderrChunk`, so the bound is real, not cap-plus-one-chunk) for the one-line failure detail, and installs SIGINT/SIGTERM forwarders that signal the child and wait for its close: a Ctrl-C ends a follow as **exit 0** (the `docker logs -f` convention — an interrupted follow is the user's "stop", not a failure), a **second** forwarded signal escalates to SIGKILL (a wedged child cannot hold the terminal hostage), the forwarders are removed on close (restoring the process's default dispositions), and a resolved promise keeping its first value makes the spawn-error/close arms race-free without a settled guard. The consumer's pipe closing (`quotameter logs | head`, EPIPE on `process.stdout`) gets the same stop-early semantics: run-time stream-error listeners catch it, terminate the child, and resolve as an interrupted success instead of an unhandled stream error crashing the CLI (a non-EPIPE stream error becomes the failure detail and kills the child; an EPIPE on stderr — `2>&1 | head` — is swallowed, with nowhere left to report). When `write` reports backpressure the child's stdout is paused until the sink drains, so `--lines=all` over a slow pipe cannot queue the whole journal in memory — one pending drain listener at a time, removed by the run's cleanup, with an `exit`-time resume guaranteeing `close` even on a paused stream. journalctl's own stderr is part of its product: a non-empty capture is flushed to `process.stderr` on a successful exit (warnings must not vanish), while a failed exit quotes the first captured line in the detail. A child killed by an unrelated signal (exit code null, nothing forwarded) is a failure carrying `the command was terminated` — the house phrase. (5) **journalctl availability is the spawn error arm, not a probe.** ENOENT (or EACCES) on spawn resolves as a `spawnFailed` outcome that renders `journalctl is not available` with the ships-with-systemd explanation — no `which`/PATH heuristics, the same reasoning that made 137 probe only well-known marker paths for capabilities, never binaries. (6) **Exit codes (the D-044 grammar)**: 0 exactly when journalctl ran and exited 0, or was interrupted through a forwarded signal; 1 for every honest failure — owner problems (D-105's problems and the broken-system throw, both through `resolveOwnerForCommand`), an unusable owner home with no system unit (the 140 shape), nothing installed (foreground or not), a privileged run facing a user unit, an unavailable manager, a missing journalctl, or a failed journalctl (the exact command in the failure line, and the scope's direct journalctl remedy rebuilt from the vector that ran — the user's own `-f`/`-n`/`-o` flags carry over, prefixed `sudo` only for the system scope — beside `quotameter status` on stdout). The handler's own logic never throws; a rejecting injected seam propagates to the dispatcher's exit-1 failure arm, exactly the landed 140/141/142 shape.

**Reasons.** §16's single sentence about the command ("wraps `journalctl` conveniently") plus §5.2's row ("for system or user service") make the wrapper's two obligations the correct scope and convenience, and force exactly two interpretations the spec does not pin: what the defaults are, and what happens when the service is not what the journal question assumes. The scope question was settled by D-110/D-114 for control and status — the disk probe, never a re-derived install route — and logs follows it verbatim because the same user (a regular account facing an installed system unit, a sudo run facing a user unit) asks all three questions; the unprivileged-read half follows D-105's own vocabulary (journalctl queries are owner operations), with the sudo remedy rendered on failure rather than pre-checked because the OS, not the CLI, owns journal-access policy (a user in `systemd-journal` reads the system journal without sudo, and predicting that would duplicate policy). The foreground-run check is D-112's recorded forward reference made concrete: the lock is the only landed fact that distinguishes "installed but stopped" from "a foreground run holds the data directory", and the task's done-condition — logs work for the supported installation modes, honestly otherwise — makes the nothing-installed-+-running state exactly the state a user hits after following the manual-run instructions 137/139 print; showing an empty journal there would be a silent lie, so the wrapper says what a foreground run's messages are and where they live. The defaults are engineering choices recorded as the contract because the spec's "conveniently" must mean something testable: no pager (nesting one subverts the terminal), a 100-line tail (§16's default `warn` level means the interesting history is short; 10 hides it), µs-precision wall-clock (correlating §16's lifecycle events across a restart boundary), and a closed format enum (the help stays honest and failures immediate). The interrupt-is-success rule follows the stream-is-the-product premise: an interrupted `journalctl -f` is how every follow ends in practice, and exiting non-zero for it would make the wrapper unusable in scripts (`docker logs -f`, `kubectl logs -f` set the convention). Capturing stderr rather than passing it through keeps the failure envelope in the house shape (one bounded diagnostic in the failure line) without flooding the terminal — journalctl's own complaint is its first stderr line, quoted verbatim.

**Consequences.** Task 145 (`doctor`) may reuse the capability gates and the `--user`-under-sudo refusal shape for its service checks, and the systemd-less arm of its unit-freshness check; the §17.2 installation tests (a systemd-capable environment) exercise the real journalctl paths this task's container tests cannot reach. The exported surface (`runLogsCommand`, `ServiceLogsDeps`, `buildJournalctlCommand`/`JournalctlCommandInput`, `parseLogLines`/`LogLinesParse`, `parseLogOutputFormat`/`LogOutputParse`/`LOG_OUTPUT_FORMATS`, `LOGS_DEFAULT_LINES`, `LOGS_DEFAULT_OUTPUT`, `runJournalctlPassthrough`/`LogViewerOutcome`/`LogViewerRunner`, the renderers) is internal API under `src/cli/`, not package surface; `service-setup.ts` gained two additive exports (`STDERR_CAPTURE_CAP`, `firstDiagnosticLine`) and `service-control.ts` one (`otherUnitWarning`), each doc-noted for the shared use — the D-112 `ownerUnitDirectories` precedent. A future `logs --since`/`--until` or a `--directory` debugging flag extends the option surface and the vector builder without touching the handler's routing; a per-user journal layout (journald's `SplitMode=user`, non-default) would revisit the `--user` query shape via a new decision. The done-condition is pinned executably: `test/unit/cli-service-logs.spec.ts` drives the full matrix seam-by-seam (owner problems and throw, unusable home, nothing installed × five lock states with the foreground pid named and the stale holder's pid absent, system/user/both × manager gates and viewer outcomes, flags into byte-pinned vectors, the interrupted-success contract with empty output streams) beside the parser tables, the bounded-capture helper table, and the real-child passthrough tests (stdout forwarding order and split-line content exactness, exit-status and first-stderr-line details, the stderr cap and the success-exit stderr flush, the SIGKILL arm, the missing-binary arm, the EPIPE-as-interrupted and stream-error arms, the backpressure gate with its drain replacement, the second-signal SIGKILL escalation, forwarder and stream-listener removal restoring counts); `test/integration/cli-service-logs.spec.ts` pins the real-launcher routes (nothing installed, a real lock naming a live U-001 child, `--help`) and the follow-mode interrupt through a driver child running the real runner — SIGINT to the CLI-like process, forwarded to the grandchild whose readiness was awaited first, marker written, `{"ok":true,"interrupted":true}` printed, exit 0; `cli-dispatch.spec.ts` drops `logs` from the still-stubbed list.

## D-117 — The §15.3 custom-header/JSON-content-type guard of task 150: the resolved `X-Quotameter-Request` name (presence required, value uninterpreted), the body-bound application/json leg, the FORBIDDEN/415 envelope split with the native-identical media-type body, and the second-onRequest layering after the Origin guard (spec §15.3, §13; task 150)

**Date:** 2026-11-01 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§15.3](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#153-csrf-dns-rebinding-and-host-validation), [§13](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#13-http-api), [§15.4](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#154-secret-protection), [§16](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#16-logging-and-diagnostics) · **Tasks:** [150](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-115 (the §15.3 seam this guard joins — the shared `STATE_CHANGING_METHODS`, the fixed layering rule the second hook inherits, and the closed reason-vocabulary discipline), D-113 (the error envelope the guard rejects through, and the one-vocabulary rule the media-type body follows), D-109 (the `/api` scope the hook registers into)

**Decision.** Task 150 ships §15.3's second leg in the task-149 seam `src/server/api/security.ts` — a pure, fail-closed `classifyCustomHeaderRequest` over `{method, customHeader?, contentType?, contentLength?, transferEncoding?}` plus the `customHeaderGuard` Fastify `onRequest` hook the `/api` scope registers in `src/server/api/index.ts` **strictly after `originGuard`** — and pins six interpretations of the spec's "require a dedicated nonstandard header. Accept only `application/json`." (1) **The header's name is `X-Quotameter-Request`**, single-sited as the exported `API_MUTATION_HEADER_NAME`: the spec names no header, and the resolution takes a project-namespaced, purpose-specific name outside the CORS-safelisted set (`Accept`/`Accept-Language`/`Content-Language`/`Content-Type`-with-limited-values), so no browser sends it implicitly, no proxy strips or adds it by convention, and no HTML form can send it at all while CORS stays disabled (§13) — a cross-origin page would need a successful CORS preflight to set any non-safelisted header, and there is none. (2) **Presence with a non-empty (trimmed) value is the whole requirement; the value is deliberately uninterpreted.** The CSRF property is exactly "a browser cannot have set this cross-origin"; a fixed literal or a token exchange would add no security (a client that can set the header at all is already not a form or a cross-origin page) and a version handshake is not §15.3's business. An absent or whitespace-empty header answers `403 FORBIDDEN` as `ApiError('FORBIDDEN', { message: 'The X-Quotameter-Request header is required', details: { reason: 'missing-custom-header' } })` — the message names the header per §15.1's "403 with instructions" precedent (the name is public client-bundle knowledge the moment the UI ships, never a secret), the reason is a one-value closed vocabulary, and nothing the client sent is echoed (§15.4). (3) **The JSON content-type leg binds body-carrying requests only.** "Carries a body" is derived in the hook from the wire signals an `onRequest` hook sees: an exact `Content-Length: 0` or the absence of both `Content-Length` and `Transfer-Encoding` is bodiless; any `Transfer-Encoding`, any non-zero length, and any value that is not the canonical zero — leading zeros like `00` included, verified live: fastify treats `00` as a body present and demands a content type, so the guard must not read it as bodiless either — count as carrying a body (fail closed and transport-aligned; the transport's own content-length class answers genuinely malformed values further down the lifecycle). A body-carrying mutation must send a `Content-Type` whose base media type (the segment before the first `;`, trimmed, lowercased) is exactly `application/json`: charset parameters are allowed (fastify's JSON parser ignores them), `+json` suffixes, `text/json`, the three HTML form enctype values, an empty value, Node's joined duplicates, and an absent Content-Type all reject.
