A bodiless mutation — `DELETE /api/accounts/:id` (§13), logout — carries no payload to type, so the leg does not apply: **verified live on the pinned runtime (fastify 5.12.7), a bodiless request that claims `application/json` is answered by fastify's own empty-body `400` (`FST_ERR_CTP_EMPTY_JSON_BODY` → the VALIDATION class)**, so requiring the header unconditionally would make a legal bodiless mutation inexpressible (any choice of Content-Type fails: present → the parser's 400, absent → the guard's 415). A bodiless request that still carries a stray Content-Type is answered by the transport from its own parser registry — verified live: an empty `application/json` body → the empty-body 400, an unregistered type (e.g. `application/xml`) → fastify's native 415 (which D-113's handler answers as the same envelope the guard's 415 produces), and fastify's default `text/plain` parser accepts the empty body and passes — an asymmetry the guard deliberately does not adjudicate: on a bodiless request there is no payload whose type could matter. The layering stays safe because the two legs are asymmetric by design: the dedicated header is the unforgeable CSRF leg and applies to every mutation regardless of body; the content type is the JSON-contract leg (§13 speaks JSON) and binds exactly where there is content to type. (4) **The media-type rejection keeps the registry's default 415 body** — `UNSUPPORTED_MEDIA_TYPE`, `Content-Type is not supported`, `details: null` — deliberately byte-identical to fastify's native `FST_ERR_CTP_INVALID_MEDIA_TYPE` mapping (D-113), so the 415 class has exactly one wire body regardless of which layer rejected — the guard preempts the parser for every body-carrying routed mutation, and the native mapping stays live behind it for the bodiless requests that still carry a stray unregistered type (verified live: `Content-Length: 0` with `application/xml` reaches fastify's own 415, which the byte-identity turns into the same envelope; the "dead-end mechanism" phrasing of D-113's 414 precedent does not carry over); the classifier's `non-json-content-type` reason exists for the hook's error mapping and the unit table, and is deliberately not serialized. (5) **The layering order is pinned: Origin first, headers second** — the hook registers after `originGuard`, so a cross-origin mutation always answers the Origin verdict (`origin-mismatch` et al.) even when it also lacks the custom header, and only an Origin-passing mutation answers the header/content-type classes; inside the guard the header check precedes the content-type check, so a request failing both answers `missing-custom-header`. (6) **Mode-independence is inherited structurally**: the verdict consults exactly the five wire signals and never server state (auth mode, static serving, configuration), runs for every route in the `/api` scope including the catch-all and method mismatches, ahead of any body parsing (a rejected mutation is never read), and the bare `/api` stays the root not-found boundary D-115 documented.

**Reasons.** §15.3 names no header, so the name is this task's resolution: "dedicated" reads as purpose-specific (not a borrowed convention like `X-Requested-With`, which some frameworks and proxies emit on the client's behalf and which therefore is neither dedicated nor reliably attacker-absent), and "nonstandard" reads as outside the browser's safelist — the two properties that make presence a CSRF proof. Requiring only presence (not a value) is the standard custom-header CSRF construction (the defense is the preflight, not a secret) and keeps the guard total over its two signals without consulting server state — a token check would drag session/credential state into a layer D-115 deliberately kept stateless. The body-bound content-type leg follows from the runtime fact recorded in (3): the unconditional reading — the first draft's — broke on the wire within the task's own test matrix, and HTTP semantics agree with the runtime (Content-Type describes the request's representation; a request with no payload has none to describe). The form-CSRF story survives the relaxation twice over: a form-built POST that carries any body must type it one of the three form enctype values (all rejected), and even a bodiless form post cannot carry the dedicated header — the leg that applies always. Keeping the native-identical 415 body (instead of a guard-specific message) follows D-113's one-vocabulary rule: two wire bodies per status class differing by which layer rejected is client surface for no diagnostic gain — the class already says everything client-actionable ("send application/json"), and the reachability difference (the guard also answers unmatched routes) is invisible to a legitimate client and useless to a hostile one.

**Consequences.** Every §13 mutation consumer now carries the contract: the UI client sets `API_MUTATION_HEADER_NAME` on each mutation and `Content-Type: application/json` exactly when it sends a body (setting it without a body is answered by the transport's empty-JSON 400 — an operational note for the endpoint tasks 159–162 and the UI tasks, and for any CLI API use); task 164's contract suite inherits the matrix; task 163 documents the mutation-time semantics of `FORBIDDEN` and `UNSUPPORTED_MEDIA_TYPE` from the same registry entries (whether to model the FORBIDDEN `details.reason` literals in OpenAPI remains task 163's call per D-115's stance). Task 152 keeps its hooks ordered after both guards (a cross-origin or header-less mutation is rejected without consulting credentials — the order stays observable in the error class). The exported surface added to the D-115 seam (`API_MUTATION_HEADER_NAME`, `HeaderGuardReason`, `HeaderDecision`, `HeaderRequestSignal`, `classifyCustomHeaderRequest`, `customHeaderGuard`) is internal API under `src/`, not package surface. The done-condition ("missing header or wrong content type is rejected") is pinned executably: `test/unit/api-custom-header-guard.spec.ts` holds the pure table (safe-method immunity, absent/empty/whitespace header × the four methods bodied and bodiless, the uninterpreted-value arms, the body-carrying derivation incl. the fail-closed non-canonical-zero (`00`) / unparsable / duplicate-joined lengths and the chunked-with-zero-length case, the delimiter-only joined header value (`, ` — Node's duplicate-join shape) accepted as present beside the uninterpreted-value arms, charset/case/padding accepts, the form-enctype and suffix and joined-duplicate rejections, the fixed header-then-content-type order, and the hook's byte-shaped ApiError throws incl. the registry-default 415 and the joined-split-header arms) and `test/integration/api-custom-header.spec.ts` pins the wire through the full task-146 construction — byte-pinned 403 and 415 envelopes with `no-store` and the JSON content type, the wrong-name lookalike rejections (`X-Quotameter-Requests`, `X-Quotameter`, `X-Requested-With`, `X-CSRF-Token`), the content-type rejections pinned on all four methods, pass-through evidence via the scope catch-all's 404 on all four methods bodied and bodiless, the bodiless stray-type transport pins (`text/plain` passes, `application/xml` answers the native 415's envelope), the Origin-guard precedence pins (both-hostile → `origin-mismatch`; same-origin without the header → `missing-custom-header`), the guard-before-body-parsing ordering (a `text/plain` body answers the guard's 415 before the parser or the body limit; the same malformed body under `application/json` reaches the parser's 400), the empty-JSON-body transport fact as the bodiless boundary's proof, the static-fixture mode twin, the bare-`/api` boundary, and §15.4/§16 discipline (no echoed values, zero log records) — while the landed suites' mutation arms (`api-origin`, `api-errors`, `api-health`, `server-http`) now carry the dedicated header (bodiless) or header + JSON content type (bodied) exactly as the future §13 clients will, so every later endpoint test inherits the shape by example.

## D-118 — The `passwd` command contract: interactive-only password pair, the self-describing scrypt encoding owned by `src/services/password-hash.ts`, fail-secure revocation before the write, and the never-privileged write of the owner's configuration (spec §5.2, §15.2, §6.3; task 144)

**Date:** 2026-11-02 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§5.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#52-cli-commands), [§15.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#152-passwords-and-sessions), [§6.3](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#63-secret-storage-and-writes), [§11.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#112-required-logical-tables) · **Tasks:** [144](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-022 (the settings boundary whose `MIN_PASSWORD_LENGTH` and placeholder-hash technique this task consumes, and whose `pendingPassword` half stays task 153's), D-101 (the detection/staleness layer `passwd` reuses verbatim), D-105/D-108 (the owner resolution and owner-scoped directories), D-112 (the §5.6 lock read behind the reload advisory), D-099 (the muted `askSecret` prompt seam), D-030/D-056 (the storage connection and the `deleteAllSessions` primitive), D-085 (the coverage-gate discipline the new secret-handling module meets through full test coverage, without joining the pinned critical-module keys)

**Decision.** Task 144 ships the §5.2 `quotameter passwd` row as the new `src/cli/passwd.ts` (`runPasswdCommand(deps)`, no options — §5.2 declares none) plus the new hash encoding `src/services/password-hash.ts`, and pins five interpretations. (Correction trail: the task's review round — deepseek-v4.1-flash, one round, APPROVE with 3 P2 / 6 P3 — corrected the revocation probe (fail closed, below), the no-leak and base-survival test coverage, and the reload citation (D-026, not §6.4); six findings were accepted and fixed in the same commit, two P3 ideas declined with reasons in the commit body.) (1) **The hash encoding is self-describing and travels with the hash**: `scrypt$N=65536,r=8,p=1,keylen=64$<salt base64>$<hash base64>`, derived through `node:crypto`'s async scrypt with a 16-byte random salt per hash, a 64-byte key, and an explicit 128 MiB `maxmem` (Node's 32 MiB default refuses this `N × r`); the constants are frozen and exported as `SCRYPT_PARAMETERS` so tests pin the encoding against `node:crypto` itself. The schema's `auth.passwordHash` stays an opaque non-empty string (its docblock already assigns the encoding to the auth service); task 153's verifier parses the parameters from the stored string, so a future cost raise never invalidates stored hashes. Hashing is this task's half — verification (constant-time comparison, invalid-password paths) is task 153's, whose `Done when` names it. (2) **The command is interactive-only**: the password is asked twice through the prompter's muted `askSecret` (`New password (at least 12 characters): ` / `Confirm password: `), a blank or too-short first answer and a mismatching confirmation each draw one secret-free stderr complaint and restart the pair, up to three attempts; the length rule is the D-022 boundary's own exported `MIN_PASSWORD_LENGTH` (12), validated on the raw untrimmed value (secrets are never trimmed). There is deliberately no `--password` value flag (the §15.4 process-listing rule — the same reasoning that kept `--api-key` out of init, D-100) and no env-var channel yet: §5.2/§15.2 name none, and the option table makes adding one a small additive change if automation ever demands it. (3) **The write is composed of landed layers, and never privileged**: D-101's `readExistingConfig` classifies the file (absent → refusal pointing at `quotameter init` — there is no configuration to hang the hash on, and a stub would violate the mandatory-timezone contract; invalid → problems verbatim, nothing changed; existing → the D-022 `validateSettings` boundary merges `{auth: {passwordHash: <hash>}}` over the canonical base and re-validates, so what is written is exactly what the loader accepts), D-101's `sameDetectionState` re-read guard runs before any effect, and `writeInitConfig` (permissions `0700`/`0600` + the atomic temp-fsync-rename) persists. A run with privileges held (`sudo quotameter passwd`) is refused to the owner's regular account before anything is asked: the atomic write replaces the inode, so a root write would leave the owner's configuration root-owned `0600` — unusable for the regular account §5.1 requires the service to run as — and the password needs no privileges; D-105's vocabulary has no privileged variant of "write the owner's configuration", so none is invented (the deferred ownership machinery of D-106/D-108 stays out of scope). (4) **Fail-secure ordering: the stale guard runs, sessions are revoked, then the file is written.** §15.2's "changing the password revokes all sessions" is executed through the repository's `deleteAllSessions` over a read-write connection of the owner's data directory, behind an existence probe that **fails closed**: only `ENOENT` reads as absence, and every other probe failure (an unsearchable data directory, an I/O error) is a loud failure that aborts with the password unchanged — the probe gates a §15.2 control, so an unreadable directory must never read as "no sessions" while sessions stay valid behind the error (review round P2; the D-114 `status` probe may treat the same states as absence because it is diagnostic, not gating). A data directory without a database file reads as "no stored sessions", and so does an empty sessions table (a zero count renders like absence, never "0 sessions revoked" — review round P3). A failed revocation aborts with the configuration untouched (the password is unchanged — the reverse order would leave old sessions valid under a password the user believes changed); the residual failure — revocation succeeded, the write then failed — is the safe direction and is reported exactly: sessions revoked, password unchanged, run passwd again. (5) **The reload advisory is conditional on a live lock holder, advisory-only, and never fabricates service state** (the D-112 stance): after a successful write, D-112's `readServiceLock` + `isProcessAlive` decide whether a running service still authenticates with the old password (`auth.passwordHash` is live-on-reload by D-026's classification — one of the two settings §6.4's own list does not name, the citation corrected in review); only `held` + alive renders the `quotameter reload` line naming the pid — every other lock state changes nothing about the completed write and neither fails nor decorates the command.

**Reasons.** The spec fixes the mechanics (scrypt, random salt, documented parameters, the `0600` file, minimum 12, revocation-on-change) but leaves the encoding, the input surface, and the ordering open. The encoding choice makes the parameters data rather than convention — the only future-proof shape for a stored credential whose cost needs raising over the package's lifetime; the OWASP-class interactive parameters (~64 MiB, tens of milliseconds) price a set/change operation, not a per-request verification, and the async API keeps the module reusable by task 153's login path under request load. The interactive-only surface follows the spec's own list of where passwords come from (init, passwd, the UI — task 153+/Stage 12 owns the UI half) and the repo's established secret-channel discipline; the three-attempt bound is passwd(1)'s, and the pair-restart after a rejected first answer keeps the confirmation honest (confirming a value the user cannot see after a complaint would be ceremony). The privileged-write refusal is forced by §6.3's permission model interacting with the atomic write's inode replacement — the same interaction task 137 documented for init's manual route — and refusing is smaller and safer than shipping chown machinery this task does not otherwise need. The revocation ordering is the security-relevant half of "changing the password revokes all sessions": the two effects are only atomic in one order that is safe to fail in, and the report says which state the machine is in for both failure arms (the house rule — honest partial outcomes, never silent ones).

**Consequences.** Task 153 lands verification against this encoding (`parse` the string, re-derive, constant-time compare) and the UI password-set path (task 159+'s settings endpoints) reuses `hashPassword` unchanged; a future non-interactive channel (e.g. a `--password-env` flag named like `--api-key-env`) is an additive option-table change that must keep the §15.4 no-value-flag rule. The §15.1 password-pending state init writes (D-101) now has its completer: a pending configuration plus `passwd` produces a file `loadConfigWithEnv` accepts — pinned end-to-end in integration. The exported surface (`hashPassword`, `SCRYPT_PARAMETERS` in services; `runPasswdCommand`, `PasswdDeps`, `askNewPassword`, `PasswordPromptOutcome`, `revokeAllSessions`, `SessionRevocation`, the renderers and prompt constants in cli) is internal API under `src/`, not package surface. The done-condition ("no raw password is written to config/logs or shown after input") is pinned executably: `test/unit/password-hash.spec.ts` pins the encoding (format contract, salt randomness, the known-answer recomputation from the exported constants, determinism), `test/unit/cli-passwd.spec.ts` drives the full handler matrix seam-by-seam with a marker password asserted absent from every output line in every scenario (set/change/pending completion, owner problems and throw, privileged refusal, unusable home, no/invalid config, closed/interrupted input at both questions, exhausted attempts, hash failure, boundary drift alarm, stale-guard refusal, revocation failure, write-after-revocation failure, the lock-advisory matrix) beside the real-filesystem revocation arms, and `test/integration/cli-passwd.spec.ts` runs the real launcher — real piped prompter, real scrypt, real migrated SQLite database with seeded sessions — asserting the marker absent from stdout, stderr, and the written file, the stored hash `scrypt$`-shaped, the sessions table emptied, and the no-config/closed-stdin/--help routes. `password-hash.ts` measures 100% on all four axes under the unit project; `passwd.ts` carries the init.ts-style residual (the production-default `??` right arms of its seams and the process-stream `defaultPrompter`, all exercised by the real-launcher integration suite, which does not feed the coverage report) under the global §17.3 gate, without joining D-085's pinned critical-module keys — a threshold-key change would be its own decision.

## D-119 — The `doctor` command contract: the four-status check-result vocabulary with attention-flagging exit semantics (fail = act on it; unavailable/skip never fail), the eleven §5.5 checks each composed from the owning layer, and `--raw <account>` as an informational appendix over the 103 read path (spec §5.5; task 145)

**Date:** 2026-11-02 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§5.5](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#55-doctor), [§5.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#52-cli-commands), [§5.4](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#54-systemd-unit-requirements), [§7.4](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#74-sanitized-raw-responses), [§15.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#151-network-and-authentication-modes), [§15.4](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#154-secret-protection) · **Tasks:** [145](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-114 (the `status` contract this command's exit semantics deliberately diverge from, and the exported manager-probe pair, read-only storage stance, and lock-fact reuse), D-067 (the §7.4 CLI-only read path `--raw` composes), D-101 (the placeholder-hash probe technique, its helper now additively exported), D-112 (the service pipeline precedent and the env-key residual), D-116 (the lazy-import discipline the new module follows), D-110/D-108 (the installed-scope disk discovery and owner-scoped directories), D-105 (owner resolution; queries unprivileged), D-044 (the dispatch-table extension point and exit-code grammar)

**Decision.** Task 145 ships the §5.5 `quotameter doctor` row as the new `src/cli/doctor.ts` (`runDoctorCommand(deps)`, the already-declared `--raw <account>` option, every collaborator injectable with a production default) and pins five interpretations. (Correction trail: the task's review round — deepseek-v4.1-flash, one round, REQUEST_CHANGES with 1 P1 / 2 P2 / 6 P3, every finding reproduced against the real launcher — is folded into this entry, which had not landed when corrected — the D-109/D-111/D-114/D-116 precedent. Eight findings were accepted and fixed in the same commit: the `--raw` read became exception-safe with the handle released in a `finally` on every path (the P1 — an appendix must not be able to lose the report), the account rows gained totality guards (a schema-valid whitespace label or key is a fail row, not a thrown `AccountContext` TypeError aborting the report — init-account's own precedent; an account naming a provider this build does not carry is never probed with the bundled adapter, so a key cannot travel to a provider its configuration never named), the `ExecStart` comparison became token-exact (a spacing-only hand edit is not staleness) quoting only the compared tokens, the timedatectl spawn gained a kill-timeout so a wedged D-Bus cannot hang the diagnostic, the bind classifier gained the unbindable address errors and the privileged-port-under-sudo caveat, the version remedies interpolate the derived minimum instead of hard-coding it, and two weak test assertions were made real. Two P3 ideas were declined with reasons in the commit body: threading the pipeline's parsed input out to the §15.1 probe (a signature change to a landed module out of proportion to the millisecond TOCTOU window, accepted-with-bound in a docblock instead) and checking the recorded schema version inside the Database row (the row states exactly what `PRAGMA quick_check` verified; a database that predates the `raw_responses` table surfaces through the guarded `--raw` section instead). (1) **The check-result contract is the product.** Every check yields one report row `{status, summary, detail?}` over a closed vocabulary: `pass` states the fact it established (a version, a path, a verdict); `fail` names a problem needing operator attention with the next step as indented detail lines (a quotameter command or a system remedy); `unavailable` states honestly that the check could not run and **never fails the exit code** (a non-diagnosis is not a diagnosis — D-114's `unknown` stance applied to exit semantics); `skip` states the unmet precondition (an invalid configuration skips the zone, port, auth, and account checks; the failing row carries the remedy). The renderer is deterministic and byte-pinned (tags padded to `[unavailable]`, details indented to the summary column, a closing count line). (2) **Exit semantics are attention-flagging: 1 exactly when at least one check is `fail`** (or the pre-flight — owner/directory resolution, or the blank `--raw` account id — failed, which renders the standard failure lines and no report); otherwise 0. This is the deliberate divergence from `status` (D-114: states never fail a question): doctor is the flutter/brew-doctor-style command whose non-zero exit must mean "something here needs you", so a stopped service, an occupied port, or an absent configuration are `fail` rows with their next steps (`quotameter start`, free the port / change `server.port`, `quotameter init`) — exactly the states a user runs doctor for. (3) **Each check composes the layer that owns its fact, never re-derived**: the runtime minimum from `src/server/main.ts`'s `MINIMUM_NODE_VERSION` (lazily imported, D-098's mirror of `engines.node`) with a fail-closed unparseable-version arm; `node:sqlite` availability through the new `src/storage/sqlite-availability.ts` probe (the layout gate confines every `node:sqlite` import form to `src/storage/`, and doctor reaches it dynamically so the CLI dispatch graph loads storage only where SQLite is genuinely touched — D-116; the probe's ExperimentalWarning on every doctor run is intrinsic to a check that can only answer availability by importing the built-in); the configuration from the service's own `loadConfigWithEnv` (absence included — a machine doctor runs on should be configured, so absence fails with the init step, and env-only success states its provenance); the §6.3 permissions **diagnostically** (lstat only, never chmod — a diagnostic that mutates its subject lies about what it found; the fail rows render the `chmod`/`chown` remedies and compare owner uid against the resolved service owner, so a `sudo doctor` still judges the owner's objects correctly); the display zone through the clock module's IANA gate (total but defense-in-depth: the parser pre-validates); the database through `openReadOnlyStorageConnection` plus `PRAGMA quick_check` (absent = skip "not created yet"; a refused open fails with D-114's hot-journal hint; problems quote the first rows) with the existence probe before any storage import (the restated `DATABASE_FILENAME` discipline); per-account connectivity through the §8.1 `validateCredentials` contract (`createInitialAccountProvider` default) classified by init-account's secret-scrubbing `classifyTestFailure` — rejected fails with the replacement remedy, inconclusive is **unavailable** (D-052: unavailability is not a verdict on the key), disabled skips, an `apiKeyEnv` unset in this shell is the D-112 residual (unavailable, the service's environment may hold it); the service as two rows — installed scope from D-110's disk probe (both units is the 139 mistake; the unit's content through the §5.4 `parseUnitFile` with `ExecStart` compared token-exactly against `serviceExecPaths()` — §5.4's own "detect stale Node/CLI paths" with `service install` named as the regeneration remedy, sudo-prefixed for a system unit — beside `validateSystemUnit(content, ownerDirs)`/`validateUserUnit`, so a hand-edited unit's drift is caught, and an unreadable unit is unavailable) and state from the exported D-114 `planManagerProbe`/`describeManagerState` for installed units (not active fails with `quotameter start`, sudo-prefixed for a regular user facing a system unit; a non-zero exit carrying stderr renders unknown-unavailable, never a false not-active) with D-112's lock read answering the unit-less machine (a live holder passes as the foreground run naming its pid — run-mode independence; absent or stale fails with the install/run steps; unreadable/invalid is unavailable); port occupancy from a real ephemeral `net` bind of the configured `host:port` (no `ss`/`lsof` subprocess — availability and output format are distribution properties, D-107's well-known-path reasoning; `EADDRINUSE` passes only when the lock fact says the running service holds it, `EACCES` fails with the unprivileged-port advice, everything else is unavailable); §15.1 consistency as a rendered classification for valid configurations (the parser already refuses the inconsistent ones — `findConfigProblems`' own rule) and, for invalid ones, the **D-101 placeholder-hash probe** re-run through `parseConfigWithEnv` (via the additively exported `withPlaceholderHash`, absent-hash-only by D-101's rule) so the password-pending state fails with its precise `quotameter passwd` remedy while any further defect stays the Configuration row's problem list; and the clock from `timedatectl show --property=NTPSynchronized --property=NTP` parsed as `Key=value` — never the human table, whose wording is locale-dependent — through a local bounded-capture spawn (`spawnServiceCommand` ignores stdout by design and stdout is this check's product): unsynchronized, or synchronized with the NTP service inactive (drift risk), fails with `sudo timedatectl set-ntp true`; a failed command (the systemd-less container) is unavailable. (4) **`--raw <account>` is an informational appendix, never a gate**: after the checks, the report appends the account's retained §7.4 payloads through the task-103 read path verbatim (`readRawDiagnostics` + `renderRawDiagnostics`) over the same read-only handle the Database check opened — one open answers both consumers, §7.4's CLI-only exposure stays enforced by the raw-response gate, the section never changes the exit code, a blank account id is a handler failure (exit 1) naming the correct spelling, and a missing database or an unknown account renders its honest sentence (the database is the source — payloads may outlive a removed account's config entry). (5) **The report is the only success output** (stdout, one deterministic string; stderr carries only the pre-flight failure lines), composed of paths, versions, labels, pids, and the landed layers' already-secret-free problem strings; the per-account secret is scrubbed from every detail line by the reused classifier (defense in depth, §15.4), and the handler never throws (a rejecting injected seam propagates to the dispatcher's exit-1 arm, the landed 140–144 shape).

**Reasons.** §5.5 is one sentence listing eleven checks plus the `--raw` clause, so the contract — what a check reports and what the process exits — is this task's design freedom, and the done-condition names exactly that ("actionable messages and a stable exit status"). The four-status vocabulary splits the two honest non-verdicts (unavailable, skip) from the two verdicts, because conflating them produces the two classic doctor-command defects: a machine without systemd failing every doctor run (noise that trains users to ignore the exit code), or an inconclusive network check reported as a bad key (D-052's distinction at the CLI surface). The attention-flagging exit semantics follow from what doctor is for: `status` answers "what state is it in?" (states are facts), doctor answers "what needs fixing?" (a stopped service is the answer, not context) — the divergence is deliberate and recorded against D-114 so the two contracts cannot drift together. Composing the owning layer everywhere (pipeline, parser, lock, disk probe, manager-probe pair, generators' own validators, the D-101 probe) keeps doctor a pure orchestrator: no second validator to drift, and every rendered sentence inherits its layer's secret discipline for free. The timedatectl `show` form over the human table is machine-readability; the bind probe over `ss` is portability; the diagnostic-only permission check is honesty (the enforcement half exists and runs at startup — doctor's value is naming what drifted and the command that fixes it). The permissions check compares against the resolved service owner's uid rather than the invoking uid so a `sudo doctor` judges the owner's objects by the owner's rule (D-105's vocabulary: diagnostics are owner operations; privileges change nothing about the verdict).

**Consequences.** Only `run` remains stubbed in the dispatch table (its suite's stub list updated); `cli-raw-diagnostics.spec.ts`'s dispatch pin now reaches the real handler. `src/cli/init-persist.ts` gains one additive export (`withPlaceholderHash`, doc-noted — the `ownerUnitDirectories` precedent) and `src/storage/` one new module (`sqlite-availability.ts`); a future check joins `doctor.ts`'s list without touching the contract, and changing the vocabulary, the exit semantics, or a rendered sentence is a coordinated renderer+test change recorded here. The ExperimentalWarning on every doctor invocation (the availability probe) is accepted collateral of §5.5's own check and documented in both READMEs. The exported surface (`runDoctorCommand`, `DoctorDeps`, `DoctorCheck`/`CheckStatus`, `renderDoctorReport`/`anyCheckFailed`, `parseTimedatectlShow`/`ClockSyncFacts`/`TimedatectlRead`/`runTimedatectlShow`/`clockCheck`, `classifyQuickCheck`/`databaseCheck`/`DoctorDatabaseRead`/`openDoctorDatabase`, `classifyBindError`/`portCheck`/`PortProbeOutcome`/`probePortBinding`, `runtimeCheck`/`sqliteCheck`/`probeNodeSqliteDefault`, `statConfigEntry`/`EntryStat`/`permissionsCheck`, `timezoneCheck`, `authConsistencyCheck`/`authPendingProbeCheck`, `unitFreshnessCheck`) is internal API under `src/`, not package surface. The done-condition is pinned executably: `test/unit/cli-doctor.spec.ts` drives the full matrix seam-by-seam — every check × every D-119 status, the renderer byte-pinned, the timedatectl/quick-check/bind-error/classifier tables, the production opener against real directories (kernel-genuine absent, real migrated quick_check pass, corrupt refusal), the real-socket bind probe, and §15.4's marker discipline (the configured key and hash never rendered; a key a contract-violating provider echoes back scrubbed to `[REDACTED]`) — while `test/integration/cli-doctor.spec.ts` pins the real-launcher routes (the bare machine exit 1 with the init and install/run next steps, the healthy machine over a real migrated database with a real §5.6 lock naming a live child exiting 0, the env-key residual, the seeded `--raw` payload, the invalid configuration with its passwd remedy, `--help`); `doctor.ts` carries the init.ts-style residual (the production-default `??` arms of its seams, exercised by the real-launcher integration suite, which does not feed the coverage report) under the global §17.3 gate, without joining D-085's pinned critical-module keys.

## D-120 — The §15.3 Host allowlist of task 151: name-only comparison (ports unpinned for §15.6's tunnels), construction-time configured-host injection over the existing `HttpServerOptions.host`, root-scope registration binding API and frontend routes, and the absolute-form/duplicate/missing-Host runtime closes (spec §15.3, §15.6, §6.4; task 151)

**Date:** 2026-11-02 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§15.3](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#153-csrf-dns-rebinding-and-host-validation), [§13](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#13-http-api), [§15.6](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#156-operational-security), [§15.4](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#154-secret-protection), [§16](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#16-logging-and-diagnostics) · **Tasks:** [151](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-115 (the §15.3 seam the guard joins and the fail-closed/reason-vocabulary discipline it inherits), D-117 (the fixed §15.3 layering this guard extends outward), D-113 (the one-envelope rule its rejections answer through, and the mode-independence lesson), D-109 (the task-146 construction the root registration lives in)

**Decision.** Task 151 ships §15.3's third leg — "Validate the `Host` header against `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `[::1]`, and the configured host; reject any other host" — as a new layer of the task-149 seam `src/server/api/security.ts`: `createHostAllowlist(configuredHost)` builds the frozen comparison set (the spec's three literal names, exactly those — not the `127.0.0.0/8` range `isLoopbackHost` admits for bind addresses, because the spec spells three names and the Host header carries the name the client used, never a sibling loopback address), `classifyHostRequest({host?, url?}, allowlist)` is the pure, fail-closed verdict with `parseAuthorityName` as its strict RFC 9112 authority-name parser, and `createHostGuard(allowlist)` is the factory `onRequest` hook (a factory, unlike the two scope guards, because the verdict needs construction-time configuration). Five interpretations are pinned. (Correction trail: the task's review round — deepseek-v4.1-flash, one round, REQUEST_CHANGES with 2 P1 / 2 P3, every finding verified against the code — is folded into this entry, which had not landed when corrected, the D-119 precedent. All four findings were accepted in substance: the configured IPv6 host is normalized into its bracketed wire form with zone ids percent-encoded (`fd00::5` → `[fd00::5]`, `fe80::1%eth0` → `[fe80::1%25eth0]` — the first draft's verbatim pass-through made a non-loopback IPv6 bind reject every request, the P1); the authority parser is structure-first (a trailing default port no longer collapses multi-colon garbage like `localhost:8080:80` onto a real name — the P3); the wildcard bind consequence is now audible as one construction-time `warn` line naming the reachable shapes (the P3); and the reverse-proxy consequence paragraph was rewritten because the first draft's `proxy_set_header Host localhost:8787` recipe was internally inconsistent with D-115 — see (3) below.) (1) **Registration is at root scope in the construction** (`src/server/http.ts`), not the `/api` scope of tasks 149/150 — the done-condition binds "both API and frontend routes", and only the construction registers what every route shares: the guard runs for `/api` endpoints, static assets, the SPA fallback, and the API-only not-found arm alike, in both static-serving states and every auth mode (D-113's lesson, structural again). Root registration also makes it the outermost §15.3 layer by fastify's own hook chain — root-scope `onRequest` hooks run ahead of scoped ones (verified on the pinned runtime 5.12.7) — so a hostile-Host request answers the Host verdict before the Origin/custom-header guards, with no wiring ordering to maintain. (2) **The comparison is over authority NAMES; ports are unpinned.** The allowlist entries are names, every port shape reduces to its name before the lookup (the parser validates structure first, and the port never reaches the verdict — so `localhost` ≡ `localhost:80` ≡ `localhost:443` ≡ `localhost:8787` ≡ `localhost:9999` all reduce to the one name), while the listening port is never a criterion: §15.6 recommends SSH tunneling as the access method, and a tunnel remaps ports freely (`ssh -L 9999:127.0.0.1:8787` sends `Host: localhost:9999` — pinning the port would break the spec's own recommended access shape), while the DNS-rebinding threat the check exists for is a name confusion (the attacker's DNS name rides the Host header), which name comparison fully defeats; the origin guard (D-115) already compares complete authorities for mutations, so ports add nothing there either. (3) **The configured host is injected at construction time through the existing `HttpServerOptions.host`** — no new option, no request-time config lookup: §6.4 pins `server.host` as restart-requiring (`RestartRequiredField` in the config layer), so the value cannot change under a running listener and capturing it where the listener is built is the value's own lifecycle. Recorded consequences, sharpened by the review round: a wildcard bind (`0.0.0.0`, `::`) admits only its literal name — direct access through any concrete interface address is rejected, the construction logs one `warn` naming the reachable shapes, and operators bind the concrete address they serve (IPv6 binds work in both spellings, normalized to the bracketed wire name); and **the loopback-bound reverse proxy forwarding the public name (`proxy_set_header Host $host`) is not expressible under today's single-host config surface** — the public name must be allowlisted, and D-115's Origin comparison simultaneously requires the Host to carry it, so the working recipes under this surface are the hosts-file pin (configure the public name as `server.host` and pin it to the loopback in `/etc/hosts`, so the listener binds loopback by name and both guards see the public name — the `api-origin.spec.ts` proxied arm pins the shape) or a tunnel; a dedicated public-name/public-URL setting that decouples the bind address from the allowed name is **deferred to task 157's §15.2 public-URL configuration** (the `Secure`-cookie decision needs the same field), recorded here as the explicit gap-closing move rather than a config-surface change smuggled into a security task. (4) **Absolute-form request targets are adjudicated as a second authority.** Verified live over a real socket: the router (find-my-way) matches an absolute-form target by its extracted path while `request.url` keeps the full attacker-controlled URL — an unguarded, routable authority; the classifier therefore requires an absolute-form target (`^https?:\/\//i`) to parse, carry an allowlisted name, and carry the SAME name as the Host header (RFC 9112 §3.2.2: with an authority in the target the client must send an identical Host — both-allowlisted-but-different is the smuggling shape and rejects as `target-mismatch`). `fastify.inject` cannot express the shape (light-my-request normalizes the URL to `pathname + search`), so these verdicts pin over real loopback sockets. (5) **The runtime's Host gaps close beside the spec text, all fail closed over a closed five-value reason vocabulary** (`missing-host`, `duplicate-host`, `disallowed-host`, `disallowed-target`, `target-mismatch`): an HTTP/1.0 request without a Host is accepted by the parser and rejected here as `missing-host` (the Host-less HTTP/1.1 shape is answered 400 by llhttp before fastify — the documented transport boundary, also pinned); duplicate Host entries, which Node folds onto the first value while every wire entry survives in `rawHeaders`, are rejected as `duplicate-host` by a hook-side scan (the RFC's MUST-reject; the folded first value being allowlisted must not smuggle the pair); unbracketed IPv6 (`::1`), invalid ports (`:abc`, `:99999`), unterminated brackets, the empty literal, multi-colon shapes, and Node's duplicate-join forms are not names the grammar can establish and reject as `disallowed-host`. Rejections throw `ApiError('FORBIDDEN', { message: 'Request host rejected', details: { reason } })` — the registry's §15.3 family, answered by the root error handler on every path (D-113's one-envelope rule), echoing nothing the client sent (§15.4) and logging nothing at `warn` (§16).

**Reasons.** §15.3's one sentence names four hosts and a rejection duty; the design freedom is where the check runs, how the configured host reaches it, and what "the Host header value" means when the wire offers ports, IPv6 literals, absolute-form targets, and duplicate or missing headers. Root-scope registration follows the done-condition's own words ("both API and frontend routes") — the rebinding page reads the frontend through GET as surely as it posts to the API, so the guard is deliberately method-blind (the one §15.3 check with no method dimension; 149/150 bind §13's four methods because CSRF is a mutation attack, while rebinding is a routing/name attack). Name-only comparison follows the threat model: the port on a Host header never routes anything inside this service (no vhosts, no Host-derived links or redirects, no cache), so rejecting `localhost:9999` would gate nothing but the tunnel shapes §15.6 recommends. Construction-time injection follows §6.4's restart-requiring pin — a request-time lookup would consult a value the config model itself forbids from changing, and the wildcard-bind consequence is the spec-literal fail-closed reading recorded rather than silently widened (admitting "whatever the wildcard covers" would enumerate interfaces the service has no way to know it serves). The absolute-form and duplicate/missing closes follow three runtime probes on the pinned fastify 5.12.7/Node 22.13.0: routing matches absolute-form targets with the URL intact on the real wire, Node folds duplicate Hosts instead of rejecting them, and HTTP/1.0-without-Host reaches handlers unchallenged — each a live path the RFC names and the runtime leaves open, which is exactly the §15.3 seam's job to close.

**Consequences.** Every client of the server must now reach it under an allowlisted name: browsers on the loopback bind (`localhost`/`127.0.0.1`/`[::1]` in every port spelling), LAN clients under the bound concrete address (IPv4 or IPv6 — both configured spellings normalize to the bracketed wire name), proxied deployments under the hosts-file-pinned public name, tunnels under `localhost` — while `127.0.0.2`, sibling subdomains, and foreign names answer 403 on every route (the done-condition's fail side). The review round's central consequence: **the loopback-bound proxy forwarding the public Host is the one legitimate shape this surface cannot express** — it needs the public-name setting task 157's §15.2 public-URL work introduces (the same field the `Secure`-cookie decision reads), and task 187's reverse-proxy documentation must carry the hosts-file-pin recipe until then (never `proxy_set_header Host localhost:8787`, which D-115's Origin comparison would reject on every mutation). Task 152's auth-mode hook keeps its place after the two `/api` scope guards, which now sit under the Host guard structurally (the observable order is pinned: a request failing Host and Origin answers `disallowed-host`). The exported surface added to the seam (`createHostAllowlist`, `HostGuardReason`, `HostDecision`, `HostRequestSignal`, `classifyHostRequest`, `createHostGuard`) is internal API under `src/`, not package surface. The done-condition ("invalid Host values fail for both API and frontend routes") is pinned executably: `test/unit/api-host-guard.spec.ts` holds the pure table (the allowlist builder's normalization arms — case, padding, both IPv6 spellings with zone-id encoding, unterminated bracket; the configured IPv6 bind under its wire spelling; every accepted shape — bare, default-port, non-default-port incl. the SSH-tunnel port, case, padded; the full rejection table — foreign names and lookalikes, `127.0.0.2`, wildcard and foreign IPv6, unbracketed IPv6, invalid ports, multi-colon shapes, joined duplicates, missing/empty/whitespace; the absolute-form verdicts incl. unparseable and uppercase-scheme targets; the fixed Host-then-target order; and the hook's throws incl. the rawHeaders duplicate scan and the array-joined header shape) and `test/integration/api-host.spec.ts` pins the wire through the full task-146 construction — byte-pinned FORBIDDEN envelopes with `no-store` on API routes, the frontend static/SPA twin and the API-only not-found arm (both serving modes), the method-blind loop, the precedence pins over the landed guards (Host outermost; Origin intact beneath), rejection-before-body-parsing, the configured-host arms (`192.168.1.5` + ports, foreign address rejected, base names still admitted), the wildcard-bind warning arm (one `warn` record, literal name passes, concrete address rejects, tunnel stays reachable), §15.4 no-echo and §16 zero-log, and the raw-socket arms inject cannot express: HTTP/1.0 missing Host (with an allowlisted control), the HTTP/1.1 no-Host parser-400 boundary, duplicate Host, and the three absolute-form verdicts; `api-origin.spec.ts`'s proxied arm now builds the server with the public name configured (the hosts-file-pin shape, exercising the configured-host allowlist arm) — the other landed suites keep their allowlisted Hosts unchanged.

## D-121 — The §15.1 auth-mode selection of task 152: the mode/password facts split by §6.4 lifecycle (mode and bind captured at construction, password presence read per request), presence-only proxy indicators over header names, the fail-closed full matrix with §15.1's own 403-with-instructions cell, the public health opt-out as route config, and the `RequestAuthenticator` seam that keeps credential verification (153–156) out of the mode layer (spec §15.1, §13, §15.4, §16, §6.4; task 152)

**Date:** 2026-11-02 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§15.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#151-network-and-authentication-modes), [§13](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#13-http-api), [§15.4](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#154-secret-protection), [§16](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#16-logging-and-diagnostics), [§6.4](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#64-configuration-changes) · **Tasks:** [152](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-120 (the guard family the layer joins and the placement pin it recorded), D-115/D-117 (the §15.3 scope guards it registers after), D-113 (the one-envelope rule its rejections answer through), D-026 (the §6.4 live/restart split the facts follow), D-118 (the `passwd` command the 403 instructions name), D-111 (the public health route whose opt-out becomes route config)

**Decision.** Task 152 ships §15.1's mode selection as a new module beside the §15.3 seam — `src/server/api/auth.ts`, not `security.ts`, because the two layers answer different spec sections with different inputs: the §15.3 guards decide over request signals alone (mode-independent by construction, D-115's rule), while the §15.1 layer deliberately decides over server state (mode, bind, password presence) beside one request signal (the proxy indication). Five interpretations are pinned. (1) **The verdict is a pure function over four facts, split by the config model's own §6.4 lifecycle.** `classifyAuthMode({mode, bindIsLoopback, passwordConfigured, proxyIndicated})` answers `'not-required'` (exactly `auto` + loopback bind + no proxy indication — a configured password does not tighten the cell: §15.1's own words are "direct loopback requests do not require a password"), `'required'` (`required` mode unconditionally; `auto` on a non-loopback bind; `auto` behind a proxy indication — in each case with a password configured), or `'proxy-without-password'` (the proxied request against a passwordless server: §15.1's explicit `403`-with-instructions cell, reachable only as `auto` + loopback because `required`-without-password and non-loopback-without-password refuse to start in `findConfigProblems`, task 073's leg — those two cells are still answered fail-closed `'required'` so a construction fed inconsistent facts stays shut, unit-pinned and wire-pinned as 401-forever, never open). The two construction-time facts (`auth.mode`, the bind) are §6.4 restart-requiring, so the guard factory captures them once — the D-120 precedent for `server.host`, applied to its §6.4 table-mate `auth.mode`; the password fact is §6.4-live (D-026: "a password hash is checked per authentication attempt, not wired into a listener"), so it enters as a **thunk read on every request** and a `passwd` run against a live server flips the proxied answer from the 403 instructions to the demanding 401 on the next request, no restart. The bind fact is the listener's own `host` passed through `HttpServerOptions.auth`-adjacent derivation in the construction; its loopback-ness comes from `isLoopbackHost` (`src/schemas/config.ts`), the single owner of that semantics (`127.0.0.0/8` and both `::1` spellings), never re-derived. (2) **Proxy indication is presence-only over header names.** `proxyIndicatorPresent(headerNames)` fires on the trimmed, lowercased exact names `forwarded` and `x-real-ip` and the `x-forwarded-` prefix family — §15.1 spells exactly that family, so lookalikes (`x-forwarded`, `x-forward`, `forwarded-by`, `xx-forwarded-for`) do not fire, and over-matching ordinary headers would lock every local client out. The value is deliberately never read: an empty forwarded value still proves the hop, and — the inverse of D-120's duplicate-Host lesson — any single occurrence suffices here, so Node's duplicate fold (which preserves the key) cannot hide an indicator and the folded `headers` view is enough; no `rawHeaders` scan is needed. (3) **The credential check is an injected seam, absent by default.** `RequestAuthenticator = (request) => boolean | Promise<boolean>` is the whole contract tasks 153–156 implement (scrypt verification against `auth.passwordHash`, the session-cookie lookup and expiry rules, and — composed inside their authenticator — the login rate limiter): the guard consults it only on `'required'` verdicts, awaits it, and rejects with `ApiError('UNAUTHENTICATED', { details: { reason: 'authentication-required' } })` (the registry's 401) when it answers false. Until those tasks land the default is `() => false` — fail closed: a mode demanding credentials and a seam that cannot verify any keeps every protected route shut (401), which is also today's honest wire behavior, since no endpoint beyond health exists to serve. The 403-instructions rejection (`'proxy-without-password'`) never consults the seam — there is no password to check against. (4) **Registration is the `/api` scope's third `onRequest` hook**, exactly where D-120 pinned it ("task 152's auth-mode hook keeps its place after the two `/api` scope guards"): Host outermost at root, then Origin, then the custom-header/JSON guard, then this layer — the observable order is wire-pinned (a hostile-Host proxied request answers `disallowed-host`; a cross-origin proxied mutation answers `origin-mismatch`; a header-less one `missing-custom-header`; only a request the §15.3 layers passed answers the auth verdict). The hook is method-blind — §15.1 protects the web interface's reads as much as its writes — and runs for the scope's catch-all route too, so an unmatched `/api` path under a demanding verdict answers 401 instead of enumerating the route table's shape by 404ing; the bare `/api` boundary (root not-found, D-115/D-117's documented edge) keeps its mode-independent 404. **The frontend (static assets, SPA shell) stays outside the layer entirely**: the login page §14.6 requires must load before any credential can be presented, and no protected surface exists there — the API is the data boundary, and it is the one §15.1 speaks about ("the web interface demands the password" is enforced where the interface's data lives). (5) **The public health route opts out through route config, not registration order.** `GET /api/health` (§13's public exception, D-111) carries `config: PUBLIC_AUTH_ROUTE_CONFIG` (`{ auth: 'public' }`, declaration-merged into fastify's `FastifyContextConfig` for typing); the guard reads `request.routeOptions.config` (available to `onRequest` hooks on the pinned runtime 5.12.7, verified by probe and by the wire pin) and skips the verdict — explicit, method-scoped (the auto-generated HEAD twin inherits the route options, wire-pinned), immune to hook-order accidents, and the same contract the future login endpoint (153) uses to stay reachable for the client that has no session yet; the health route answers 200 in every mode, address, and proxy state (a proxied health probe against the passwordless misconfiguration still answers `{"status":"ok"}` — it leaks nothing, and 403ing it would break every properly-configured proxied deployment's health monitor at the one moment the operator is looking).

**Reasons.** §15.1 names three sentences of behavior — the `auto` loopback exemption with its proxy-indicator trigger, `required`'s unconditional demand, and the refuse-at-start/403-with-instructions pair — and leaves open where the decision runs, how its inputs reach it, and what "the request contains reverse-proxy indicators" means on a wire that folds, joins, and cases headers. The fact split follows the config model rather than inventing a lifecycle: §6.4 already classifies `auth.mode` as restart-requiring and `auth.passwordHash` as live, so construction-time capture for the first and a per-request thunk for the second are the values' own semantics, not an implementation convenience (a captured password boolean would silently keep the 403-misconfiguration answer after a `passwd` run, contradicting D-026's recorded classification). Presence-only name matching follows the threat: the header's job is to witness a proxy hop, which existence witnesses as strongly as any value, while reading values would import parsing rules (RFC 7239 lists, comma joins) whose only failure mode is a false negative on a malformed proxy — the one direction §15.1 forbids. The fail-closed reading of the startup-refused cells follows the same D-115/D-120 discipline every guard in the family carries: the classifier is total, and no cell answers "open". The scope decision follows the seam D-120 already recorded plus §14.6's own dependency (a login page cannot demand a login), and the route-config opt-out follows the runtime fact the probe verified — registration-order exemptions would work only until someone reorders hooks, while `routeOptions.config` is the route's own declaration.

**Consequences.** The §17.1 "matrix of bind address × proxy headers × password presence" is pinned executably end to end: `test/unit/api-auth-mode-guard.spec.ts` holds the pure tables (the indicator family with lookalikes and casing, the full 16-cell classifier matrix, the hook's byte-shaped throws, the public-config skip, the seam's consult-only-when-required and awaited-promise arms, and the live-password-thunk flip) and `test/integration/api-auth-mode.spec.ts` pins the wire through the task-146 construction (byte-pinned 403-instructions and 401 envelopes with `no-store`, each §15.1 indicator alone against the default surface, the passwordless pass-through with and without a password set, the non-loopback and `required` arms, the fail-closed startup-refused wire answers, the health pin under every mode/address/proxy state including the HEAD twin, the login-shell/SPA arms that must stay reachable under `required`, the catch-all 401 and bare-`/api` boundary, the four guard-order pins, and §15.4/§16 no-echo/zero-log). Task 153 inherits a ready contract: the login endpoint declares `PUBLIC_AUTH_ROUTE_CONFIG`, the verification lands inside a `RequestAuthenticator`, and the mode layer needs no change; task 156's limiter composes inside the same authenticator (or ahead of it inside the login route), never here; task 157's cookie flags and §15.2 public-URL work are untouched by this layer, whose proxy semantics stay header-based per §15.1's own text. The composition root that will one day build the listener from configuration maps `auth.mode` and `auth.passwordHash` presence onto `HttpServerOptions.auth` 1:1 (the projection is documented in the interface); until then the construction defaults are the config layer's own (`auto`, no password), which is exactly the loopback-private default §15.1 prescribes. The exported surface (`proxyIndicatorPresent`, `AuthModeFacts`, `AuthModeVerdict`, `AuthGuardReason`, `classifyAuthMode`, `RequestAuthenticator`, `PUBLIC_AUTH_ROUTE_CONFIG`, `AuthModeGuardOptions`, `createAuthModeGuard`) is internal API under `src/`, not package surface.

## D-122 — The §15.2 password verification of task 153: parameters parsed from the stored string (never the module constants), strict structural parsing with `node:crypto` as the sole parameter authority, constant-time comparison of derived keys with lengths settled before any secret is touched, and no §15.1 seam wiring (the password meets the verifier at the login endpoint, not on requests) (spec §15.2, §15.1, §15.4; task 153)

**Date:** 2026-11-02 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§15.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#152-passwords-and-sessions), [§15.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#151-network-and-authentication-modes), [§15.4](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#154-secret-protection) · **Tasks:** [153](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-118 (the encoding this verifier parses, the forward-compatibility rule it executes, and the review-correction precedent this entry follows), D-121 (the §15.1 seam this task deliberately does not wire, and whose docblock now says so), D-085 (the coverage discipline the extended suite meets at full branch coverage without joining the pinned critical-module keys), D-022 (the settings boundary whose `MIN_PASSWORD_LENGTH` stays the length rule's owner and whose `pendingPassword` half stays with its settings-endpoint consumer)

**Decision.** Task 153 lands §15.2's verification half — "Store only a password hash made with `scrypt` from `node:crypto` … and constant-time comparison" — as `verifyPassword(stored: string | undefined, candidate): Promise<boolean>` beside `hashPassword` in `src/services/password-hash.ts` (one module owns the credential format end to end; D-118 named it the owner and left verification to this task), and pins five interpretations. (Correction trail: the task's review round — deepseek-v4.1-flash, one round, APPROVE with 1 P2 / 4 P3 — folded five fixes into this entry and the same commit: the entry guard making the function total over an absent or non-string stored hash (the P2 — `auth.passwordHash` is optional in the configuration schema, so a `string`-typed parameter turned a pass-through caller into a 500; the signature now mirrors the field and runtime junk answers `false`), the `VERIFICATION_MAX_PARALLELIZATION` CPU ceiling (a P3 — `maxmem` does not bound `p`'s compute, measured `p=4000` ≈ 21 s on the pinned runtime; see (1)), a non-quantum-base64 test row, two wording corrections in (2) and below, and the stale task-153 promise in `src/cli/README.md` (see Consequences).) (1) **The stored string is the only source of derivation parameters.** The verifier parses `N`, `r`, `p`, and `keylen` from the encoding and never reads `SCRYPT_PARAMETERS`: D-118's forward-compatibility rule ("a future cost raise never invalidates stored hashes") is executable behavior here, pinned by a test that builds a valid encoding under `N=16384, keylen=32` — values the constants disagree with — recomputes the derivation itself, and asserts the verify. The derivation runs under two exported budgets of the module's own: `VERIFICATION_MAXMEM_BYTES` (1 GiB of memory — sixteen times today's 64 MiB requirement, so any plausible future raise (`N` up to `2^19` at `r=8`) verifies unchanged, while a corrupt or hostile stored string can never talk the verifier into unbounded allocation: `node:crypto` refuses a derivation beyond `maxmem` and the refusal classifies as a mismatch) and `VERIFICATION_MAX_PARALLELIZATION` (1024 — the CPU twin `maxmem` cannot provide: `p` multiplies compute without touching memory and Node offers no `p` knob, so an unbounded `p` in a corrupt string could pin a libuv thread for hours; the producer writes `p=1` and every realistic raise goes through `N`, so 1024 is a generous bound whose worst case is seconds). (2) **Parsing is structural and strict; parameter semantics belong to `node:crypto`.** The parse accepts the producer's grammar — and, deliberately, any self-consistent parameter set inside the module's two budgets (parameters are data, D-118): four `$`-fields, the one `scrypt` algorithm id, the canonical parameter grammar (canonical key order, plain decimal, no leading zeros — this module is the encoding's only producer, so anything the grammar rejects is by definition not one of its hashes), canonical padded base64 for salt and hash (alphabet + quantum-length + re-encode round-trip, which also rejects quanta with non-zero trailing bits — `AB==` decodes to one zero-valued byte but re-encodes as `AA==`), and internal consistency (the decoded hash length equals the claimed `keylen`). It deliberately does NOT re-validate power-of-two `N`, ranges, or memory: `node:crypto` owns those rules, the derivation's `catch` answers `false` when it refuses them, and one authority replaces a mirrored table that can drift. (3) **The comparison is constant-time over derived keys, with lengths settled before any secret is touched.** `timingSafeEqual` compares the freshly derived key bytes against the stored hash bytes — never strings — and its equal-length precondition is guaranteed by the parse's consistency check ahead of any derivation; the encoding's length facts are public (whoever can read them already has the `0600` config file). There is no early exit on candidate content: every candidate under a parseable stored hash costs exactly one full derivation, wrong passwords included. (4) **The function fails closed and never throws.** An absent stored hash (in-contract, not a caller duty: the optional `auth.passwordHash` passes straight through the `string | undefined` signature, and non-string junk at the JS boundary answers `false` through the same entry guard), an empty or malformed one, and any parameter set `node:crypto` refuses all answer `false`: an unverifiable credential is a wrong password to this function, never an error and never an accept. The boolean is the whole surface — the login path (154+) needs nothing else, and the operator-facing diagnosis of a corrupt configuration belongs to the config layer; the §15.1 mode layer's absent-password cells stay the caller's own concern, but the primitive itself can be handed the field directly. (5) **No §15.1 seam wiring, by design.** The `RequestAuthenticator` seam (D-121) authenticates _requests_, which present session cookies (154/155) — a password travels only in the login endpoint's body, and that endpoint stays reachable through `PUBLIC_AUTH_ROUTE_CONFIG` and consumes this primitive directly; wiring verification into the request guard would have required building 154+ surface (the endpoint, the session store) inside this task. The seam's docblock, the module docblock, and both READMEs were updated to state where the verifier is consumed, so the recorded expectation ("the verification lands inside a `RequestAuthenticator`", D-121's consequences) is corrected in place: it lands inside the login endpoint's verify-then-establish flow instead.

**Reasons.** §15.2 fixes the mechanics (scrypt, the stored-hash-only rule, constant-time comparison) and D-118 already fixed the encoding; this task's design freedom is the verification contract — what parses, what refuses, what the caller sees, and where the check runs. Parse-from-string is forced by D-118's own recorded rationale (parameters as data, not convention); the memory ceiling bounds the one dimension a corrupt string could otherwise inflate without adding a second parameter-authority (Node's `maxmem` refusal does the classification). The structural/semantic split keeps the parser honest about what it can know — grammar and self-consistency are format facts this module owns; power-of-two and memory are scrypt facts Node owns — and leaves every parse arm deterministically testable without a derivation. The strict base64 round-trip exists because Node's decoder is deliberately permissive and a verifier must not best-effort-guess a credential format. The fail-closed boolean follows the §15.1 family's discipline (D-115/D-120/D-121: total, fail-closed, never open) and the D-114/D-119 honesty split: a boolean cannot misreport, and the corrupt-config diagnosis is a different layer's sentence. The no-wiring scope is the seam's own type: `(request) => boolean` has no password to verify — only sessions answer it — so the smallest correct scope is the primitive plus the documented consumption point.

**Consequences.** Task 154+ consumes `verifyPassword` at the login endpoint (verify, then establish the session) and task 156's limiter composes around that endpoint, never inside the verifier; a future non-interactive password channel or UI password-set path reuses `hashPassword` and this verifier unchanged. A cost raise is now a three-constant change with explicit blast radius: raise `SCRYPT_PARAMETERS` (new hashes), keep `VERIFICATION_MAXMEM_BYTES` at or above the new `128·N·r` and `VERIFICATION_MAX_PARALLELIZATION` at or above the new `p` (old hashes keep verifying), and the suites pin both relationships executably from the exported bounds. The exported surface added to the module (`verifyPassword`, `VERIFICATION_MAXMEM_BYTES`, `VERIFICATION_MAX_PARALLELIZATION`; the parser and grammar patterns stay private) is internal API under `src/`, not package surface. The done-condition ("password verification and invalid-password paths are tested") is pinned executably: `test/unit/password-hash.spec.ts` grows from 5 to 29 cases — the `hashPassword` round-trip accept/reject, unicode accept/reject, the string-parameters pin, a seventeen-row malformed-encoding table (empty, unknown and miscased algorithm ids, missing/trailing fields, swapped order, unknown key, non-numeric, leading-zero and zero values, non-canonical / non-quantum / non-zero-trailing-bits / empty base64 fields, `keylen` disagreement, `p` beyond the CPU ceiling), the absent (`undefined`) and JS-boundary (`null`, number) stored-hash rows, and both `node:crypto` refusal arms (`N=1`; a set beyond the memory ceiling, derived from the exported bound so the pin follows it) — each invalid path asserted through `resolves` (fail closed is also never-throws), deterministic (no clocks; fixed salts where determinism matters), and the module holds 100% on all four coverage axes without joining the D-085 critical-module keys (the D-118 precedent). `src/server/api/auth.ts` changes comments only (the seam docblock, the guard-options default note, and two task-number references); `src/cli/README.md`'s review-corrected sentence records that init-side password collection has not landed — task 153 delivered the §15.2 primitives and `quotameter passwd` completes the pending state, and no task in `plan/tasks.md` currently owns the init-side prompt (a plan gap left to the main session); `src/services/README.md`/`src/server/README.md` and `CHANGELOG.md` carry the behavior, and no public API, format, or event changes: the stored encoding is exactly D-118's, unchanged.

## D-123 — The §15.2 session creation of task 154: base64url wire tokens fulfilling D-056's never-hex precondition, SHA-256 over the wire string, the effective-expiry formula single-sited on the schema's exported constants, the raw token disclosed exactly once through a logger-free synchronous primitive, and no HTTP wiring (creation belongs to 155's login endpoint, lookup to its authenticator) (spec §15.2, §11.2, §15.4, §16; task 154)

**Date:** 2026-11-02 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§15.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#152-passwords-and-sessions), [§11.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#112-required-logical-tables), [§15.4](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#154-secret-protection), [§16](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#16-logging-and-diagnostics) · **Tasks:** [154](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-056 (the `sessions` schema this writer feeds: the hex-shape CHECK whose never-hex precondition this encoding fulfills, the two expiry CHECKs, the exported window constants, and `last_seen_at` born at creation), D-058 (the repository facade whose sync contract and CHECKs-are-the-write-gate rule the primitive inherits), D-118/D-122 (the sibling credential module and the land-the-primitive-not-the-endpoint precedent), D-121 (the `RequestAuthenticator` seam 155 composes over this module), D-021 (the explicit-`now` clock seam), D-090 (the fail-fast finiteness discipline of the comparator family the timestamp guards follow)

**Decision.** Task 154 lands §15.2's creation sentence — "Use a random 256-bit session token in a cookie … Store only SHA-256 of the token in SQLite" — as `src/services/sessions.ts`, the session twin of `password-hash.ts` inside the future `AuthService`, and pins five interpretations. (Correction trail: the task's review round — deepseek-v4.1-flash, one round, APPROVE with 3 P3, zero P0–P2 — folded three fixes into this entry and the same commit, which had not landed when corrected (the D-119/D-122 precedent): the per-pair collision probability corrected to 2^-256 (the first draft wrote the birthday-bound figure ~2^-128 as though it were the per-pair probability), the "never hex" test pin restructured to the deterministic shape-identity guarantee (a base64url token of only hex-alphabet characters is still 43, never the digest's 64 — the first draft's regex demanded a non-hex character and would have failed a legitimate all-`A` mint), and the timestamp guard strengthened from finite to safe-integer, per the integrality reading below.) (1) **The wire form is base64url**: `randomBytes(32).toString('base64url')` — exactly 43 unpadded URL-safe characters. D-056 recorded the precondition when it built the schema: the `sessions_token_hash_hex` CHECK pins `token_hash` to 64 lowercase hex precisely so the raw token's wire forms cannot fit, with one honest exception no SQL constraint can close — a lowercase-hex cookie encoding would be shape-identical to the digest. Choosing base64url closes that gap from the writer's side: the raw token is structurally distinguishable from everything the table can store (pinned executably — a minted token can never match the digest's shape: 43 characters against the CHECK's 64), it is cookie-safe without escaping (RFC 6265 cookie-octets, no `+`/`/`/`=` that quoting rules would mangle), and it is the shortest standard padding-free encoding of 256 bits. (2) **The digest is taken over the wire string, never over re-decoded bytes**: `hashSessionToken(token)` is `createHash('sha256').update(token, 'utf8').digest('hex')` — the cookie value exactly as a request presents it. The consequence lands in 155's lookup path: `hashSessionToken(cookieValue) → getSession` is the whole cookie→row key transform, with no base64url decode step and therefore no decode-failure arm to adjudicate, and the digest equals the `sha256(<string>)` shape task 087's schema tests already pinned (`BASE_TOKEN_HASH` over a fixture string). (3) **The effective expiry is single-sited**: `effectiveSessionExpiry(createdAtMs, lastSeenAtMs)` is the one home of D-056's formula `min(lastSeen + 7 d, created + 30 d)`, computed from `SESSION_INACTIVITY_TIMEOUT_MS`/`SESSION_MAX_AGE_MS` — the constants migration 0007 exported "so the session layer (tasks 154/155) computes expiries from the same numbers the shipped schema enforces" — so the writer's arithmetic and the CHECKs' bounds cannot drift apart short of a successor migration. Creation passes `lastSeen = created` (the login that mints a session is its first sighting, D-056's own rule), so a fresh row expires at the tighter 7-day inactivity bound; task 155's sighting refresh calls the same helper after `touchSession`, keeping one formula across creation and refresh. Non-integer inputs — fractional or non-finite — throw a `TypeError` naming the field (the D-090 comparator-family fail-fast, extended to integrality: §11.1 timestamps are integer epoch milliseconds and the STRICT INTEGER columns would otherwise answer a fractional value with SQLite's own opaque `cannot store REAL value in INTEGER column` instead of this diagnosis). (4) **The raw token is disclosed exactly once, through a logger-free synchronous primitive**: `createSession({ repository, now })` returns `{ token, session }` — the token's only existence outside the cookie, handed to the caller that sets it (157 owns the flags), with the drop-it-after-setting contract in the docblock; the module persists only the digest row and holds no logger at all, so §15.4's "never in logs" and §16's secret discipline hold by construction (pinned executably: zero console calls during creation). It is synchronous because the repository it writes through is (D-058: `node:sqlite` sync — a promise here would wrap nothing), takes its clock as an explicit `now` argument (the D-021 `deriveAccountStatus(input, nowEpochMs)` house pattern — 155's fake-clock tests pass readings directly), propagates repository failures unchanged (the named CHECKs are the write gate; the repository re-validates nothing, and neither does the service), and **retries no mint**: the digest is the table's primary key, so a collision with a stored session surfaces as the repository's constraint failure — the per-pair collision probability of two independent 256-bit tokens is 2^-256 (the birthday bound sits near 2^128 mints for a ~50% risk), whose retry loop would be untestable dead code dressed as robustness. (5) **No HTTP wiring, by scope**: the `RequestAuthenticator` seam (D-121) authenticates requests, which present cookies — its half is a lookup over this module's rows and is task 155's, alongside the login endpoint that consumes `verifyPassword` (D-122) and then this `createSession` (verify → mint → set cookie), and 156's limiter composes around that endpoint. `src/server/api/auth.ts` changes comments only, naming the landed primitive — the D-122 precedent for landing a §15.2 half without building endpoint surface.

**Reasons.** §15.2 fixes the mechanics (256 bits, cookie, SHA-256-only storage, the two expiry bounds) and D-056 already fixed the row's storage shape (digest identity, the three times, the CHECKs) — this task's design freedom is the token's wire encoding, what exactly the digest is taken over, where the expiry arithmetic lives, and how the primitive discloses the token. Base64url is forced by D-056's own recorded precondition plus the cookie grammar (the hex exception is the one encoding that would break the schema's structural guarantee; padded standard base64 would carry `=` into a cookie value and need quoting); hashing the wire string follows the lookup path's shape (the request hands the server a string — hashing what arrived, rather than a re-decode of it, leaves the 155 path total with one authority for the encoding); single-siting the formula follows the constants' own export rationale (two homes for `min(…)` would be a new drift pair the schema tests cannot catch); and the logger-free construction is the strongest form of the §15.4 rule available — a module that cannot log cannot be misconfigured into logging the token, and the test keeps it honest against future edits.

**Consequences.** Task 155 composes this module twice — the login endpoint (verify with D-122's primitive, then `createSession`, then set the cookie with 157's flags) and the request authenticator (`hashSessionToken(cookieValue)`, `getSession`, the expiry verdict against `expires_at`, the sighting refresh through `touchSession` + `effectiveSessionExpiry`, revocation through the already-landed `deleteSession`/`deleteAllSessions`) — without touching `src/storage/` or this module's contract; a future cookie-encoding change (say raw-cookie binary forms) is a D-123 successor decision, because it moves the digest's preimage and the never-hex guarantee together. The exported surface (`SESSION_TOKEN_BYTES`, `generateSessionToken`, `hashSessionToken`, `effectiveSessionExpiry`, `SessionCreation`, `CreateSessionOptions`, `createSession`) is internal API under `src/`, not package surface. The done-condition ("raw tokens are not present in the DB") is pinned executably in `test/integration/sessions-creation.spec.ts`: after a real creation over a migrated disposable database, **every cell of every table** from `sqlite_master` is stringified and asserted to contain neither the minted token nor its base64/hex/latin1 byte forms, while the one `sessions` row positively stores `sha256(token)` with the §15.2 creation timestamps (the insert itself proving the 087 CHECKs accept the writer's shape — acceptance and marker discipline in one row), plus the §15.2 lookup round-trip with the unknown-digest miss and the two-session independence with the marker scan repeated; `test/unit/sessions.spec.ts` (17 tests) holds the pure tables — wire shape over hundreds of mints incl. the deterministic never-digest-shape pin, the digest's known answer against `node:crypto` itself, the D-056 expiry table incl. the absolute-bound clamp and the safe-integer throws, and the creation contract over a capturing stub (field-exact inserted row, mirrored record, distinct tokens, clock-seam stamps, failure propagation with no partial row, zero-console pin). `sessions.ts` measures 100% coverage on all four axes without joining the D-085 pinned critical-module keys (the D-118/D-122 precedent); `src/services/README.md`, `src/storage/README.md`, and `CHANGELOG.md` carry the boundary; no public API, format, or event changes.

## D-124 — The §15.2 session expiry and revocation of task 155: half-open validity `[created_at, expires_at)`, the sighting refresh through the single-sited formula, a verdict that never deletes, `unknown` as revocation's only aftermath, and no service-level revoke-all wrapper (spec §15.2, §11.2, §11.3, §17.1; task 155)
