Tests: the new `test/component/chart-sync.spec.ts` (the state machine: both event shapes, the epsilon, report/reset, late-joiner, empty-group forgets, the survives-while-one-live cell), `chart-series.spec.ts`'s builder cells, `metric-history-chart.spec.ts`'s mounted cells (the recording runtime grows `on`/`off`/`dispatchAction`/`emitDataZoom` and the sync-group record), `overview-view.spec.ts`'s page cells (the points-bearing history arm and the injected recording runtime), and the new `test/e2e/chart-sync.spec.ts` — the real relay in a real browser over route-intercepted data, asserted through the DOM alone (the affordance appears on shift+wheel over one canvas and retires on the click). Hand-offs: a future sub-hour zoom precision adds D-150's sub-hour rungs and relaxes `MIN_ZOOM_SPAN_MS` in the same change; a future brush/select zoom joins the same dataZoom id; the D-133 rule extends to any future cursor/zoom chrome. Known residuals, recorded: ECharts' own relay behavior and painting stay outside the test stack (D-148's boundary — the wiring, the option, and the DOM state are asserted; the canvas is the library's), and the connect cursor path degrades to a hidden pointer where the receiving chart's series 0 lacks a datum at the source's sample index (a cross-metric collection mismatch — `findPointFromSeries` returns no point, the receiver hides; value alignment itself stays exact, and the degradation self-heals on the next shared sample) — upstream's own connect contract, accepted rather than re-implemented.

## D-154 — Task U-031's no-network guard hardening: the exhaustive fetch input-shape taxonomy with fail-closed rejection of unknown shapes, the prototype-level agent interception, and the tripwire-not-sandbox scope ruling (spec §17; task U-031)

**Date:** 2026-11-04 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§17](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#17-automated-testing-and-quality-gates) · **Tasks:** [U-031](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-085/D-089 (the coverage-gate decisions that made the hermetic suite's integrity load-bearing — the guard is what makes "no internet access" a verified property rather than a habit), D-087/D-094 (the test-stability disciplines the guard's own suite follows), D-113 (error-vocabulary discipline mirrored in the guard's two distinct, actionable messages)

**Decision.** Task U-031 closes the `fetch(new Request(...))` hole three reviewers found and pins three interpretations. (Correction trail: the task's review round — deepseek-v4.1-flash, one round, APPROVE with 0 P0 / 0 P1 / 1 P2 / 3 P3, every finding reproduced live by the reviewer — was folded in before landing, the D-148/D-149/D-150 precedent. All four findings accepted and fixed in the same commit: **fetch redirect following joined the documented-out scope** (the P2 — undici follows a `3xx Location` after the initial input is inspected, so a loopback mock answer can redirect a test fetch off-host; the guard never fires on the hop, reproduced against a loopback 302 — documented in the docblock and gotchas with the `redirect: 'error'` rule the provider transport already pins, rather than "fixed": a wrapper cannot portably downgrade redirect handling without changing fetch semantics for every test); **the instance branches now read what fetch reads** (the P3 — the guard had kept reading the public `URL#hostname` accessor and the `Request#url` property, both shadowable, so a tampered instance could hand the guard a decoy loopback host while fetch connected elsewhere; extraction is now `new URL(String(input)).hostname` for URLs — `ToString` is exactly fetch's own boundary conversion — and `new URL(String(Reflect.get(Request.prototype, 'url', input))).hostname` for Requests — the internal-slot-backed prototype getter fetch itself reads — pinned lethal by the reviewer's two probe shapes); **the blocked-host pins moved from the live public IP to TEST-NET** (the P3 — `192.0.2.1` instead of `93.184.216.34`, so a guard regression fails an assertion instead of causing real egress from the suite); and **the advertised-but-unpinned behaviors got pins** (the P3 — reinstall idempotency via the marker, `agent: false` interception, and the this-bound https loopback delegation).) (1) **The input-shape taxonomy is exhaustive and closed over fetch's actual call grammar.** WHATWG fetch accepts `string | URL | Request` and webidl-coerces anything else via `ToString` at the call boundary; the guarded `fetch` now extracts the host for each named shape — `string` against the `http://localhost` base (relative URLs stay allowed for component tests), `URL` via `hostname`, `Request` via `new URL(input.url).hostname` parsed **without a base** (the `Request#url` getter is spec-guaranteed to return an absolute, normalized URL string, so base-less parsing cannot mis-resolve a legitimate Request, while a spec-violating relative value becomes a loud parse failure rather than a silent pass-through) — and every other shape is **rejected** with a distinct "unrecognized input" error naming `typeof input`. The unknown-shape policy is reject-never-inspect, and the reason is structural, not stylistic: inspecting a coerced object means trusting one of its properties for the host while the real fetch derives its URL from `ToString` of the whole object, so any inspection strategy is a decoy — `{ url: 'http://localhost/', toString: () => 'https://evil.example/' }` is exactly the bypass duck-typing would open, and even `String(input)` followed by parsing inherits the same fail-open shape the fix removes (a `toString` that throws, or yields an unparseable string, would have to be caught and then… rejected — collapsing inspection into rejection anyway, with more moving parts). `assertAllowedHost` tightens to a `string` parameter, so the `undefined`-host path that was the hole can no longer be reached from fetch at all; `isLoopback` keeps its `string | undefined` signature for the agent layer, where an absent host is the relative/default case, not an inspection failure. Cross-realm `instanceof` mismatches (a `Request` or `URL` from a different realm than the guard's identifiers) land in the reject arm — fail-closed by construction; in this suite that cannot arise, because Vitest's `populateGlobal` gives the tests and the setup file one realm per project. (2) **The `node:http`/`node:https` interception moves from the two global agents to `Agent.prototype.createConnection`.** The old code patched `globalAgent.createConnection` as an own property on each of the two global agents; the patch now sits on the prototypes (marker-idempotent via the same `__quotameterGuarded` flag the fetch wrapper uses, with `http.Agent` patched before `https.Agent` so that if `https.Agent.prototype` ever inherits rather than owns its `createConnection`, the already-guarded http function is skipped by the marker instead of double-wrapped). Coverage strictly grows: the global agents (by inheritance), custom `new http.Agent()` / `new https.Agent()` instances, `agent: false` per-request default agents, and third-party `Agent` subclasses that do not carry their own `createConnection` are all intercepted now; host extraction and the error message are unchanged. (3) **The scope ruling: the guard is a tripwire, not a sandbox — the residual gaps are documented, not closed.** Deliberately outside the guard: a `createConnection` passed as a request or agent option (per Node's own precedence, an explicit option beats the agent method), direct `node:net`/`node:tls` sockets, direct `undici` module imports (`undici.fetch`, `undici.request`, `setGlobalDispatcher`), and `node:dns`. Closing them means intercepting `net.connect`/`tls.connect` process-wide — invasive to every library that runs in the worker (reporters, tooling, the framework itself), far beyond what §17 asks ("Tests must not require a real API key or internet access"), and no suite code uses those paths today (grepped). The honest scope is stated in the guard's own docblock (the canonical statement) and in a new `docs/agents/gotchas.md` section addressed to test authors: use the loopback mock server, and know that deliberate raw-socket use is covered by review attention, not the guard.

**Reasons.** The hole was a pass-through by omission, and its fix had to close the _class_, not the instance: patching only the Request arm would leave the next exotic shape (a coercible object, a subclass, a cross-realm value) uninspected again, so the taxonomy had to be exhaustive with a fail-closed default — the same closed-vocabulary discipline D-113 applies to wire errors. Rejecting unknown shapes beat inspecting them because inspection cannot be sound: the guard's host and fetch's URL would come from different operations on the same object, and any divergence is a bypass; rejection makes divergence impossible. The base-less Request parse is the same principle one level down — a guarantee the spec gives (absolute `Request#url`) is relied on exactly, and its violation fails loudly. The prototype-level agent patch is strictly wider coverage for the same interception point and the same code shape (the old own-property patches were its special case), with the marker check making the move idempotent; the http-before-https ordering removes the one double-wrap window the move would otherwise open. Documenting the socket-level gaps beat closing them because §17's requirement is about test behavior (no credentials, no internet), which the fetch and agent layers fully cover for code a test writes in the ordinary way; a process-wide socket firewall protects against a hostile test author — a threat model the suite does not have — at the cost of breaking legitimate tooling in-process.

**Consequences.** Test-infrastructure side: `test/helpers/network-guard.ts` (the taxonomy helper `hostnameOfFetchInput` with fetch-aligned instance reads, the tightened `assertAllowedHost`, the prototype-level agent loop, the two-scope docblock) and `test/unit/network-guard.spec.ts` grown from 4 to 15 tests — the Request-refusal pin (external host refused through a Request input), the allowed-host Request pin (loopback Request reaches `ECONNREFUSED`, the guard not the failure), the unrecognized-shape pins (a coercible object and a number both refused), the accessor-alignment pins (a URL with a shadowed `hostname` and a Request with a shadowed own `url` both refused by reading what fetch reads), the agent pins (external http and https through fresh agents blocked, `agent: false` blocked, loopback through fresh http and https agents still connects), and the reinstall-idempotency pin (identity of `globalThis.fetch` and both prototype `createConnection`s unchanged by a second `installNetworkGuard()`), beside the four pre-existing pins unchanged. Docs: the gotchas scope note (including the redirect gap) and this entry. Behavioral changes are confined to the test harness: a fetch with an object input that previously slipped through now throws immediately (no suite code did this — verified by grep before the change), and custom agents to external hosts now fail at socket creation where they previously connected (same verification). Hand-off for future test authors: any new need for real sockets in tests goes through `test/helpers/mockProviderServer.ts` on loopback or an explicit, reviewed exception — the gotchas entry is the contract; a test fetch that follows redirects must pin `redirect: 'error'` or stay on loopback targets only. The unit suite measures green with the new pins in place.

## D-155 — The license gate's self-exclusion matches by package NAME read from package.json at runtime, not by a version-qualified key (spec §4.3, §4.4; task U-032)

**Date:** 2026-11-04 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§4.3](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#43-license-and-attribution), [§4.4](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#44-cicd-and-supply-chain-safeguards) · **Tasks:** [U-032](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-007 (the MIT allowlist this gate enforces), D-152 (the release pipeline whose first version tag would have tripped the stale pin), D-093 (the mirror discipline the pinning spec follows)

**Decision.** U-032 retires the version-qualified self-exclusion in `scripts/check-licenses.mjs` (once `const SELF = new Set(['quotameter@0.0.0'])`) and replaces it with a **name-only** match whose name is read from `package.json` at runtime (`new URL('../package.json', import.meta.url)` — anchored to the script's own location, not the working directory). Each license-checker key is reduced to its package name — everything before the LAST `@`, so scoped keys (`@scope/pkg@1.2.3`) keep their leading `@`, and version-less keys are returned unchanged — before the exclusion set's membership test. Verified live before the fix: scratch-bumping `package.json` to `999.9.9` made the real gate fail with `UNAPPROVED quotameter@999.9.9: UNLICENSED` (the development scope's checked count rising 479→480 — the stale pin let the own package into the checked set); after the fix the same bump keeps `make licenses` green. The defect was found independently by two reviewers (mimo-v2.6-pro P3, minimax-m3 P2) and would have broken the license leg of CI's `static` job and of `make check-all` at the first release version bump — exactly when D-152's publish pipeline first runs. (Correction trail: the task's review round — deepseek-v4.1-flash, one round, REQUEST_CHANGES with 0 P0 / 0 P1 / 2 P2 / 2 P3, every finding verified by the reviewer with a live harness — was folded in before landing, the D-150/D-154 precedent. The production fix was confirmed sound (the split, the approval flow, and the manifest anchor all re-verified on the extracted real code); all four findings concerned the guard and the docs, and all four were accepted: the pinning spec's text-only regexes were shown evadable — a runtime-interpolated version entry passed all five pins while re-breaking the gate — and its scratch-bump pin evaluated a spec-local mirror rather than the script, so the spec now extracts and executes the script's own code with every demonstrated evasion proven lethal live; and the recorded npm-behavior claim ("npm forbids a dependency sharing the root name") was unverified and is replaced below by the verified lockfile fact.)

**Reasons.** §4.3 (MIT license and attribution) and §4.4 (dependency-license checks in CI) prescribe the gate but are silent on the self-exclusion's mechanics, so the match policy is a decision, not a spec reading. Name-only over the alternative considered (keep the `name@version` key shape, read the version from `package.json` at runtime): version-independence then holds **by construction** — no version input exists — instead of by two version strings agreeing (license-checker's reported key vs. the manifest), and the exclusion additionally survives a package rename. The over-match risk of a name-only rule was assessed against the tree, not assumed: no package in `package-lock.json` shares the root name today (verified), so the exclusion swallows no real dependency's verdict; the theoretical residual — a same-named package entering the dependency graph later — is accepted and recorded rather than guarded, because distinguishing the root from a same-named dependency requires comparing versions, the exact coupling this decision removes.

**Consequences.** `scripts/check-licenses.mjs` gains the `readFileSync` import, the `packageNameOf` helper (last-`@` split), the membership test on the name part, and the runtime-manifest `SELF` with a comment citing this entry; the approval flow (ALLOWED, `atomicLicenses`, scopes, reports, exit codes) is unchanged. The policy is pinned executably by `test/unit/check-licenses.spec.ts`, which extracts and executes the script's own code (the script has top-level side effects, so it cannot be imported): the real `packageNameOf` is cut out of the source, compiled, and run over the key table (positive control on the REAL function — no spec-local mirror to drift), and the real `SELF` initializer is evaluated with the manifest read stubbed (`import.meta.url` rewritten to the script's URL — `new Function` bodies are scripts, not modules) against both the current manifest and one bumped to `999.9.9-scratch-bump.0`, asserting the entry array is exactly `[manifest.name]` in both cases — the task's done-condition, and lethal against every version-coupled construction (literal or interpolated). Text pins remain only where execution cannot reach: the `SELF` construction's shape (a runtime `package.json` `.name` read anchored at `import.meta.url`, with no `@` and no `.version` reference in the construction), the skip wiring (`excludeNames.has(packageNameOf(name))` on a `lastIndexOf('@')` split), and the whole-script ban on quoted `name@x.y` string literals (backtick prose in comments stays legal). Lethality was proven live on four mutations: the pre-fix script fails 6/6 (the scanner throws on the missing construction), the runtime-interpolated version entry fails three tests, a one-character helper drift (`slice(0, at + 1)`) fails two, an extra hardcoded entry in `SELF` fails one — the four evasions the review round demonstrated or implied, all restored afterwards. Editing the `SELF` construction, `packageNameOf`, or the skip expression requires updating the spec in the same change. The scratch-bump experiments on the real gate (RED on the original script, GREEN on the fix, `package.json` restored both times) are recorded in the task's commit body, not committed.
