(2) **`createPollingEngine` owns the wiring, and the account selection is a filter, not an error.** Per configured account: `enabled === false` skips (debug log; §7.3's `Disabled` owns the display), an unresolvable secret skips (debug log; §7.3's `Not configured` — the D-140 keyless path; a trim-blank `apiKey` or `apiKeyEnv` value resolves nothing too — the schema's `minLength: 1` admits whitespace-only strings the registry's context gate rejects, and the never-throw selection must skip them rather than abort startup), a trim-blank label skips the same way, an unregistered `providerId` skips (warn log; a schema-valid configuration may name an adapter this build lacks, the D-119 doctor class — §7.2's isolation means one foreign account stops neither the others nor the startup). Survivors get a branded `AccountContext` (the resolved secret non-enumerable, never logged, D-013) and a `createCycleRecorder` over the lazy repository facade (settle time is post-start by construction), spread into `PollingAccount` with `keyIdentity = keyIdentityOfSecret(secret)` — the holder's vocabulary, so the configuration observation and the wiring identity compare like with like. The component's `start` installs the wiring BEFORE `scheduler.start()` (the fresh entries' immediate dues carry into the first dispatch pass, §7.1); `stop` awaits `scheduler.stop()` and propagates a retained loop error (the app aggregates, but storage and the lock still stop — §5.6's checkpoint never depends on the engine). A contained settle failure (D-066 deferred its diagnostics to "the server logger wiring") is logged here: the settle wrapper catches, emits one `warn` per failed settlement (account id and message; load-safe — the engine reschedules regardless), and rethrows into the engine's containment. (3) **The dual D-064 machine runs in lockstep, fed — not unified.** The scheduler's internal machine gates dispatch (D-066's structural design; unifying would mean rewriting a landed, property-tested module); the composition's holder (`AccountSuspensions`) stays the seam `/api/status` and the manual-test flow read (D-140's recorded plan). The bridge that keeps them honest is one feed: the engine's wiring wraps each recorder's `settleCycle` so every settled classification ALSO reaches `suspensions.polledCycleOutcome(accountId, outcome, keyIdentity)` — with the engine's own stale-outcome rule mirrored exactly: the wiring tracks per-account continuity (an epoch that survives mere rebuilds — a label change keeps a kept account's feed — but bumps when the account left the polled set or changed key), so an outcome from a removed, re-keyed, or removed-and-re-added-same-key wiring is skipped, precisely the engine's mid-flight entry-identity discard; an account that LEAVES the polled set (removed, disabled, secret lost) additionally drops its holder episode (`dropAccount`) beside the engine's dropped entry — suspension is process memory (D-064's restart consequence), so a disable/re-enable or remove/re-add cycle starts both machines fresh and D-070's run-evidence arm covers the §7.3 display for the first post-return cycle. Because D-064 is a pure function of `(state, event, now)` and both machines now see the same classified outcomes, the same key-identity reports (`applyReload` already reports them), and the same manual-test events (below), their states cannot disagree in any reachable flow — the property D-070's rank-1 disjunction needed: without the feed, a polled 401 followed by an inconclusive hourly probe would downgrade the display to `Unreachable`, the exact drift D-064's no-op pin exists to prevent. The manual-test half rides two new optional callbacks on `observingManualTests`: `onManualTestRequested` (called right after the holder's release, before the attempt — both §7.2 release events at one site), wired to `scheduler.requestManualTest` — the engine's machine releases too and owes the account one attempt through the dispatch loop, so the sequential and overlap rules of D-066 hold for the recovery cycle — and `onManualTestRejected` (beside the holder's re-entry on a D-052 `credentials-rejected`), wired to the scheduler's new additive `manualTestRejected(accountId)` (this entry is its D-066 successor note): the engine's own machine re-enters suspension with a fresh 60-minute window under the current wiring's key identity and drops any still-owed attempt, so §7.2's pause holds on BOTH sides of a refused manual test — the first draft recorded a one-cycle divergence residual here, which the review round disproved (an inconclusive owed cycle heals neither machine) and this seam closes. (4) **§6.4 rides the D-128 pre-sync seam.** The composition's `applyReload` — the wrapper every store mutation and reload already flows through — now also calls `pollingEngine.applyReloadChanges(result)` after the config-sync and the key-identity reports: `applied` including `accounts` rebuilds the wiring and calls `setAccounts` (the engine's own diff decides the consequences: added accounts poll immediately, removed/disabled ones drop out with their in-flight outcomes going stale, re-keyed ones release and are immediately due), `applied` including `app.pollingIntervalSeconds` calls `setIntervalMs` (re-anchoring every not-suspended account, §7.1's floor re-validated by the engine). A no-op before the component starts (start reads the current configuration itself; no reload can precede the listener). The recorder's `intervalSeconds` reader stays live (D-069's settle-time reading), so a run row always names the interval in effect at its cycle. (5) **The test seam is `ComposeApplicationOptions.pollingSleep`** — the composition's third documented test seam beside `port` and `staticRoot`: §7.1's 60-second interval floor makes a real-time "scheduled subsequent poll" observation unfit for the test gate, so the integration suite injects a clock whose BOTH readings scale ×20 (dues, gates, suspension windows, and the adapter's `collectedAt` stay consistent — the §7.3 freshness arithmetic compares like with like) plus a sleep dividing by the same factor: 60 s elapses in 3 real seconds. Production ignores the option (the scheduler's real abortable timer). (6) **The acceptance worlds stay still by doubling `fetchSnapshot` off, not by a kill switch.** Since the engine now polls every keyed account immediately, the e2e acceptance harness (real adapter + mock, worlds with exact seeded marker/status counts) would persist uninvited runs; a production "polling disabled" option was rejected (a test-only kill switch in the composition), and scripting the mock healthy just changes the corruption's shape — so `test/e2e/helpers/acceptance.ts` keeps the real adapter's `validateCredentials` (the `/models` credential check its scenarios exercise) and delegates-off `fetchSnapshot` with a plain-`Error` rejection: the recorder's fail-fast shape (neither TransportError nor parse failure), contained by the engine, persisting nothing — one contained, warn-logged cycle per keyed account per short-lived lifecycle (the worlds stop long before the real 300 s cadence could re-fire). The in-tree integration suites' existing throwing `fetchSnapshot` doubles take the same path unchanged.

**Reasons.** The order question was settled by `shutdown.ts`'s own docblock (task 075 drew the list this task completes) and by D-069's cancelled-unpersisted rule: the drain must sit between the engine and storage so an aborted cycle's settlement cannot race the close it might have written against. The lockstep-over-unification choice follows from what each machine is FOR: the engine's is structural (its dispatch gates read it in the tight loop), the holder's is a seam (landed route contracts read it per request) — and D-064's purity makes duplication cheap in a way stateful duplication never is: two deterministic machines on identical event streams are one machine observed twice, and the stale-outfeed rule mirrors the engine's own so an old key's 401 can suspend neither. Feeding the holder through the settle wrapper (not a scheduler hook) keeps the observation at the composition layer, where the holder lives, and adds zero scheduler surface. The skip-don't-throw account selection follows §7.2's isolation sentence read against §6.2: an unknown provider id is schema-valid, so refusing startup would let one hand-edit brick the service the spec says must keep serving the healthy accounts — the doctor already owns reporting it. The reload feed rides the existing wrapper because that is the one channel every configuration mutation already flows through (D-140's "the composition never hands the stores a bare reloader.reload()"); adding a second feed point would let storage rows, suspension state, and the polling schedule diverge about one configuration. The acceptance-stillness choice was forced by the acceptance worlds' own design: their marker arithmetic is exact, so ANY persisted run corrupts them, and the harness — not the composition — is the layer that owns the worlds' fixtures.

**Consequences.** A real deployment now collects: §7.1's immediate first poll and scheduled subsequent polls land in `collection_runs`/`snapshots`, `/api/status` can show `Fresh`, the §7.2 retry/`Retry-After`/suspension machinery (tasks 104–111) is production-live, and §19's MVP criteria 4 (five-minute default interval, runtime interval changes, immediate post-restart collection) and 9 (collection without an open browser) are met by the composed service — the deepseek full-project review finding is discharged. The exported surface (`createPollingEngine`, `PollingEngineOptions`, `PollingEngine` in `src/server/polling.ts`; `AccountSuspensions.polledCycleOutcome` in `src/services/account-suspensions.ts`; `ManualTestObservationOptions.onManualTestRequested` in `src/server/providers.ts`; `ComposeApplicationOptions.pollingSleep`) is internal API under `src/`, not package surface. The done-condition is pinned by `test/integration/composition-polling.spec.ts` — the production composition over temp config + SQLite with the REAL Z.ai adapter on the loopback mock: the immediate first poll (run + snapshot + the dossier trio carrying the configured Bearer key + `/api/status` `fresh` + `/api/quota` metrics), scheduled subsequent polls with no external kick (monotonic gaps ≥ the interval), the §6.4 feeds (an interval PUT reflected in the next run's `intervalSeconds`, an added account's immediate first poll, disable-freeze with a live differential, re-enable resumption), the §7.2 rows live (a 429's un-retried single attempt, persisted `retry_after_seconds`, and the gate holding then opening; a polled 401's `auth-rejected` status and the manual-test bridge's recovery to `fresh`), §5.6's mid-cycle shutdown (the stop resolves, the aborted attempt persists nothing, the checkpointed database reopens readable), and the §15.4 marker discipline — beside `test/unit/server-polling.spec.ts` (the wiring filters, the context identity, the delegation and feeds, the holder feed with the stale rule, the contained-failure log, secrets never logged), the `server-providers.spec.ts` bridge pins, the `account-suspensions.spec.ts` outcome-feed pins, and every pre-existing suite green under the now-live engine (the throwing doubles' cycles are contained and unpersisted — the sweep, composition, and acceptance suites assert unchanged). Known residuals, recorded: the engine's per-account suspension state is process memory (a restart forgets it — D-070's run-evidence arm covers the display, D-064's admission floor keeps a restored-stale state fail-safe, and persisting it stays a successor decision if a spec revision asks); and `setIntervalMs`'s re-anchoring means an interval change resets (never shortens below) the pending wait — D-066's own recorded semantics, unchanged here. (Correction trail: the task's review round — kimi/k3.1-pro, one round, REQUEST_CHANGES with 3 P1 / 1 P2, after the deepseek primary timed out at the 1200 s bound with no findings text — folded four findings into this entry and the same commit, which had not landed when corrected, the D-124/D-127/D-140 precedent: the whitespace-only `apiKey`/`apiKeyEnv`/label startup abort (P1 — the schema's `minLength: 1` admits trim-blank strings the context gate rejects; interpretation (2)'s skip now covers them, value-free), the same-key disable/re-enable and remove/re-add lockstep breaks (P1 — the holder kept its episode while the engine dropped the entry, and a same-key re-add fed a stale in-flight outcome; interpretation (3)'s `dropAccount` and the epoch continuity rule close both), the unbounded manual-test-rejection divergence (P1 — the first draft's one-cycle residual was wrong: an inconclusive owed cycle heals neither machine; the scheduler's additive `manualTestRejected` seam closes it, and the engine keeps §7.2's pause on refused keys), and the "one quiet cycle" acceptance wording (P2 — the contained failure logs a `warn`; the wording now says contained and warn-logged).

## D-177 — Task U-052's SIGHUP wiring: the conditional install semantics, the composition-owned signal face, and the deliberate terminal-disconnect consequence (spec §6.4, §5.2, §5.6, §16; task U-052)

**Date:** 2026-11-06 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§6.4](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#64-change-application), [§5.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#52-cli-commands), [§5.6](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#56-process-lifecycle-backups-and-upgrades), [§16](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#16-logging-and-diagnostics) · **Tasks:** [U-052](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-024 (the readiness seam whose handshake covers the new handler), D-026 (the reloader whose §16 records remain the outcome log), D-140 (the composition-root deferral this entry discharges), D-176 (the wrapper the signal routes through), D-175 (the answered-request readiness equivalence the real-launcher test rides)

**Decision.** Task U-052 makes `quotameter reload`'s documented target real: the server runtime catches SIGHUP and performs §6.4's reload instead of dying to Linux's default disposition (the verified defect — the CLI printed "reload accepted" while the signal killed the service, masked by systemd's `Restart=on-failure`). Four interpretations are pinned. (1) **Installation semantics: the handler exists exactly when a reload operation exists.** `runServer` resolves the operation before `app.start()` — the default assembly (`buildApplication`, the renamed `buildComponents`, now returning the whole composed result) provides `composed.reloadOnSighup`; injected `components` provide nothing unless the caller passes the new `RunServerOptions.reload` seam. The handler (`installReloadSignal`, a disposer-returning sibling of `installShutdownSignals`) is installed only when that resolution yielded an operation, immediately after the shutdown pair, before `onSignalsReady` fires — so the D-024 handshake covers SIGHUP too and D-175's answered-request equivalence extends to it structurally (the installation is synchronous in the post-`await app.start()` microtask continuation). Disposal is LIFO in the same `finally`, restoring the OS default exactly as for SIGTERM/SIGINT; a signal during startup keeps the default (D-024's recorded window, unchanged). A bare-components embedder that never passes `reload` therefore keeps the terminal-disconnect default — a handler with nothing to reload would only swallow the signal. (2) **The signal face lives in the composition, not the runtime.** `ComposedApplication` publishes `applyReload` — the D-176 wrapper every store mutation flows through (bare reloader + D-128 config-sync + D-064 key-identity reports + polling feeds; the CLI's reload, a UI mutation, and SIGHUP are one operation, with `applyReloadFollowUps` the single shared definition of the follow-up steps) — and `reloadOnSighup`: one fire-and-forget call that logs a `debug` arrival note and contains every fault at `error` through the shared §16 redacting logger, **distinguishing the two fault worlds by their opposite consequences**: a fault before the reloader adopts (an injected dependency inside the load pipeline — structurally reachable only through a contract-violating logger, D-025's never-throw rule making the arm defensive) keeps the last valid configuration effective and records `'configuration reload failed; keeping the last valid configuration'`; a fault in the follow-up application (the config-sync's repository write racing a shutdown, a stopped scheduler refusing the wiring rebuild — its `setAccounts` throws on a stopped engine) happens AFTER the adoption — the new configuration is already effective while storage rows and polling wiring may lag — and records exactly that (`'configuration reload applied but its follow-up application failed; storage and polling may lag the effective configuration'`), never the contradictory "kept the old one" (the review round's P2-1: the reloader sets `current = next` and logs its success record before the follow-ups run, so one message for both worlds would misreport the partial application; recovery for a lagged sync is honest but narrow — a restart re-syncs from the current effective configuration at storage's start, and a subsequent accounts-CHANGING reload re-runs the sync, while an unchanged-file re-SIGHUP reports `applied: []` and does not retry it, D-176's own semantics, unchanged here). The placement is forced by §16/D-025: post-logger diagnostics travel only through the redacting logger, which `main.ts` does not own (its `reportFatal` is the pre-logger plain-text channel). The wrapper guarantees what a signal handler owes: no synchronous throw, no unhandled rejection. (3) **The terminal-disconnect consequence is deliberate.** Task 060's header deferred SIGHUP because "silently swallowing SIGHUP before that would change terminal-disconnect behavior"; with a reloader in place the trade is decided the other way: a foreground `quotameter run` whose terminal disconnects SURVIVES the TTY's SIGHUP (it triggers a usually no-op, §16-logged reload). Reasons: §5.2/§6.4 designate SIGHUP as THE reload channel and `quotameter reload` must not kill the service; the documented deployment is systemd, where the manager never sends SIGHUP on stop and only `quotameter reload`/`kill -HUP` do; SIGINT/SIGTERM remain the operator's stop channels; and the alternative (ignore-or-terminate) either kills the service on its documented control path or makes the CLI's success report a lie. (4) **Reloads are fire-and-forget process events.** A SIGHUP never resolves the shutdown promise and never touches the exit code; bursts serialize inside the reloader (D-026 §5); a reload still in flight when shutdown completes dies with the process (no shutdown-skip guard — the tiny window's fault, e.g. a config-sync racing storage close, is contained by interpretation 2's arm and honestly logged).

**Reasons.** (1) Conditional install is the only semantics under which both caller classes keep honest behavior: production always has something to reload (the composition exists precisely to own the reload operation), while an embedder's bare component list has none — an unconditional handler would either no-op silently (the finding's "silently no-ops while the CLI claims success" branch) or require `main.ts` to grow a reload dependency it cannot satisfy. The seam (`RunServerOptions.reload`) mirrors the existing `components`/`runtime` injection pattern of `RunServerOptions` and keeps the in-process tests able to pin routing without real signals. (2) The composition is where the logger, the reloader, and the wrapper's other feeds already live; duplicating the wrapper in `main.ts` would fork the reload operation the stores use (the exact divergence D-140/D-176 closed), and routing SIGHUP at the bare `reloader.reload()` would skip the config-sync and polling feeds — the finding explicitly demands the wrapped path. §16 names configuration reload an `info` lifecycle event, and the reloader already emits exactly those records, so the signal face adds only the containment arm and the `debug` note — no new vocabulary. (3) Recording the disposition decision resolves the last "deliberately unwired" note of D-140 with the reasoning on file, replacing a stale deferral comment with the chosen semantics and its foreground consequence. (4) A signal handler that could block shutdown or move the exit code would make a stray SIGHUP a availability event — the opposite of §6.4's intent.

**Consequences.** `quotameter reload` is honest end-to-end: the delivered signal reloads through the same wrapped operation as a settings PUT (account sync, suspension observations, and polling feeds included), the §16 outcome record is the authoritative applied/pending-restart/rejected answer the CLI's D-112 wording already points at, and an invalid file leaves the service serving the last valid configuration. The exported surface (`installReloadSignal`, `buildApplication`, `RunServerOptions.reload` in `src/server/main.ts`; `ComposedApplication.applyReload`/`reloadOnSighup` in `src/server/composition.ts`) is internal API under `src/`, not package surface; `buildComponents` is renamed with only in-tree consumers (its spec, two helper comments, the package-layout doc). The done-condition is pinned at three levels: `test/integration/cli-run.spec.ts` (the real launcher — a health-ready child takes a real SIGHUP after a valid change and stays alive with `/api/status` reporting the new interval and the `configuration reloaded` info line on stdout; a second SIGHUP over an invalid file keeps the last valid interval with the `warn` line; SIGTERM then exits 0 with the §5.6 lock released; defect-pinning verified by mutation — with the handler not installed, the same test dies at the first SIGHUP with `ECONNREFUSED`), `test/integration/composition-sighup.spec.ts` (the published surface: `applyReload`'s effective change through `/api/status`, the arrival note, §6.2's keep-last-valid through the signal face, and the follow-up fault arm over a post-stop config-sync — the lazy facade's wiring error being the deterministic fault shape, with the record sequence asserted honest: the reloader's success record first, the follow-up fault second, never the contradictory keep message), and `server-main.spec.ts` (`installReloadSignal`'s wiring/disposal, the in-process SIGHUP routing with the run still pending, the no-reload arm's absent registration, and the default assembly's registration). One recorded subtlety the tests had to respect: D-026 pins `setLevel` BEFORE the reloader's success record, so a reload that drops `logging.level` from the file resets it to the default `warn` and filters its own `info` line — observability of the success record requires the file to carry a level that admits it. Known residuals: the rejection `warn` record is visible at the default `warn` level and any level that admits `warn` — a configured `logging.level: error` filters rejection records by §16's level design, and the signal face deliberately adds no duplicate outcome record (the review round's P3-2 correction of this entry's first draft); and SIGHUP arriving during startup — after the §5.6 lock exists (naming the pid `quotameter reload` discovers) but before the handler installs past `app.start()` — or in the post-dispose shutdown tail hits the OS default and terminates the starting/stopping service (systemd's `Restart=on-failure` recovers; the review round's P2-2). The proposed code fixes were declined with reasons: installing the handler before `app.start()` with queued reloads would break D-024's install-after-start readiness semantics for shutdown signals and introduce coalescing D-026 §5 explicitly rejected (queueing beats it), and CLI-side readiness verification would change D-112's recorded no-observation-channel design — a successor task owns the window if experience demands it. The pre-adoption fault arm is defensive against a contract-violating logger (D-025's never-throw rule makes it unreachable through this construction — the D-028 findings-not-suppressions discipline). (Correction trail: the task's review round — deepseek-v4.1-flash, one round, REQUEST_CHANGES with 0 P0 / 0 P1 / 2 P2 / 4 P3 — folded in before landing: the two-world fault messages and their honest record sequence (P2-1), the startup/shutdown-window documentation and the CLI README's "always" overclaim corrected to "once the application is running" plus the residual recorded here (P2-2, doc-only discharge with the code options declined above), five stale rename/reference spots (P3-1), the rejection-visibility wording (P3-2), the debug arrival note moved inside the contained phase (P3-3), and the launcher children's ambient `QUOTAMETER_*` overrides stripped so environment overrides cannot silently flip the suite's file-based assertions (P3-4).)

## D-178 — Task U-053's retention schedule: the composition component between storage and the drain, a duration-cadence daily timer over the shared clock, read-at-run-time reload awareness, contained cleanup faults, and the §11.3 applied-days warning surfaced through the settings contract (spec §11.3, §5.6, §6.4, §14.5, §16; task U-053)

**Date:** 2026-11-06 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§11.3](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#113-retention-and-cleanup), [§5.6](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#56-process-lifecycle-backups-and-upgrades), [§6.4](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#64-change-application), [§14.5](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#145-settings), [§16](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#16-logging-and-diagnostics) · **Tasks:** [U-053](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-063 (the cleanup operation whose "the call is the operation, never the schedule" boundary this entry completes), D-176 (the polling composition whose lifecycle-component shape is the model), D-021 (the shared clock), D-130 (the settings contract the applied window joins), D-082 (the query-side twin), D-020 (the drain whose order the new component slots into), D-177 (the wrapped reload the settings PUT rides)

**Decision.** Task U-053 gives `runRetentionCleanup` its production schedule — the deepseek full-project review's verified P2: the operation was implemented and tested but had no caller, so §11.3's startup-and-daily cleanup never ran while U-051's composed polling kept accumulating runs/snapshots/metrics/events/sessions/raw payloads, and the §11.3 reduce-retention warning's data (`retention:applied-days`) had no reader. Five interpretations are pinned. (1) **The schedule is a new composition-root lifecycle component, `src/server/retention.ts`, registered directly after storage**: `[lock, storage, retention, graceful-drain, polling, http-listener]`. Startup ordering is by registration order — storage opens, migrates (§11.4's backup-protected sequence), and completes its config-sync before `retention.start()` runs the first cleanup, so the startup run meets the final schema and the final cascade graph; teardown (reverse order: `http → polling → drain → retention → storage → lock`) cancels the daily wait BEFORE the database closes, and since `runRetentionCleanup` is one synchronous call (no await between its transaction and its maintenance step), a run can never interleave with the close — single-threaded containment that needs no in-flight-tracker entry (the component registers nothing in D-020's tracker by design). The alternative — folding the schedule into the storage component — was rejected: it would couple §11.4's migration orchestration to §11.3's cadence and give the storage component a timer its own `stop` contract never anticipated; D-063's own record ("the server lifecycle owns when") names the layer, and D-176 supplied the shape. (2) **The daily timer is one fixed-duration `DAY_MS` abortable wait, re-armed after each completed run** — the scheduler's `defaultSleep` shape (plain abortable `setTimeout`, no unref, the D-066 convention). "Daily" is 24 hours after the previous RUN, not zone-aligned midnight: §11.3 names no alignment, and a duration cadence is the one reading with no zone, no DST case, and no drift question to answer; the Node timer is monotonic by construction, so a wall-clock step can neither stall the cadence into never firing nor double-fire it, and wall time enters only as each run's cleanup `now`, read once from the shared clock (D-021 — `clock.monotonicMs()` is deliberately unused: there is no elapsed-time measurement to make). `stop()` aborts the controller; the loop treats ANY wait rejection after an abort as its designed exit (an injected seam may report the abort however it likes), so `stop` is prompt and a second `stop` stays a no-op. (3) **§6.4 reload-awareness is read-at-run-time, not a reload feed**: each run reads the live effective configuration's `app.historyRetentionDays ?? CONFIG_DEFAULTS.app.historyRetentionDays` — the value in force at run time. §11.3's own reduce-retention sentence ("older records will be removed at the NEXT cleanup") fixes the application point at the next scheduled run, so there is nothing for `applyReloadFollowUps` to feed: a change between runs lands at the next run, by the spec's own semantics, and the schedule is window-independent (no re-anchoring on reload). (4) **Faults are contained per §16, the polling-settlement precedent**: a failed run — startup or daily — is one `warn` record ("the failure is contained, the next scheduled run retries") and never rejects `start`, never kills the schedule, never touches another component; the daily re-arm happens regardless, and D-063's repeat-safety makes the retry the same cleanup over the same rows. A successful run is one `info` record with the retention window and removal counts (a §16 lifecycle-class event beside migrations and reloads); a run finding storage not open (a wiring bug — teardown order kills the schedule before storage stops) skips with a `warn` and touches nothing; a broken sleep seam is `error` + the loop's death (the next process's startup run is the retry). (5) **The §11.3 warning surfaces through the existing settings contract, not a new endpoint**: `GET /api/settings` gains a top-level `appliedRetentionDays: integer | null` (null before any completed cleanup — the fresh-database arm and the failed-startup-cleanup arm; the annotated view itself stays pure, the paths-block precedent). The production `SettingsStore.read()` reads the `retention:applied-days` marker through the repository — D-063's recorded hook — with a fail-soft parse (absent, non-integer, negative, or beyond-safe-integer markers read `null`: a corrupted marker must not 500 the settings page, and the next cleanup's write is the repair). The UI warns live under the retention field whenever a draft the §11.3 range would accept is below the applied window — deliberately including an UNCHANGED draft that is already below it (a previous reduction whose cleanup has not run is the same pending deletion), so the warning is about the state, self-clears after the next cleanup rewrites the marker, and never blocks the save (reducing retention is legal; §11.3 demands the warning, not a confirmation). The PUT is untouched.

**Reasons.** The component-vs-storage-extension choice followed D-063's layer naming plus D-176's precedent, and the ordering question answered itself twice over: startup placement after storage is forced by the dependency (the cleanup needs the migrated schema), and teardown placement before storage is forced by the hazard (a cleanup must never meet a closing database) — with the synchronous-cleanup observation removing any need for tracker registration, the placement has no timing requirement at all, only the order. The duration-cadence reading of "daily" was chosen over midnight alignment because §11.3's sentence carries no zone and the §10 discipline (no machine-local time) would otherwise force a zone CHOICE the spec never made; 24 h after the previous run is also self-stabilizing after downtime. Read-at-run-time reload awareness was forced by §11.3's own "next cleanup" wording — a feed that re-anchored or ran the cleanup eagerly on a retention PUT would apply the reduction SOONER than the spec's warning promises, breaking the very contract the warning states. The null-vs-fail-soft marker parse rests on the marker being a display annotation: no consumer decision is worse for reading null (the warning simply does not render) than a settings page that 500s would be. The warning's show-on-unchanged-draft rule was chosen over show-only-on-edit because the operator reloading the page a day after reducing retention faces the same pending deletion — the honest surface states the state, and the cleanup's marker rewrite is the natural clearing event. The log levels follow §16's own classes: cleanup completion is a lifecycle event (`info`), a contained-and-retried fault is `warn` (visible at the default level), a dead schedule is `error`.

**Consequences.** A composed deployment now bounds its history: §11.3's startup cleanup and its daily cadence run against the real database, the expired rows go, WAL is checkpointed and `incremental_vacuum` runs after each pass (D-063's maintenance half, previously unreachable in production), and the settings page tells the operator exactly what the next cleanup will delete when they reduce the window. The exported surface (`createRetentionSchedule`, `RetentionScheduleOptions`, `RetentionSchedule`, `RetentionSleep` in `src/server/retention.ts`; `ComposeApplicationOptions.retentionSleep` in `src/server/composition.ts`; `SettingsSnapshot.appliedRetentionDays` and the `SettingsResponseSchema.appliedRetentionDays` field; `appliedRetentionDaysOf` in `src/server/config-stores.ts`) is internal API under `src/`, not package surface. The done-condition is pinned at three levels: `test/unit/server-retention.spec.ts` (the schedule's own matrix — startup input from the shared clock and the live window, the lazy storage resolution, the default-window fallback, the daily re-arm over the real default sleep under fake timers, read-at-run-time reload between runs, stop's cancellation incl. the double-stop no-op, both contained-fault arms with the schedule surviving, the storage-not-open skip, the broken-sleep-seam death), `test/integration/composition-retention.spec.ts` (the production composition over a pre-seeded temporary database with a ×20 000 scaled clock anchored at a fixed §11.1-scale base — multiplying `Date.now()` directly would overflow SQLite's safe-integer epoch range — and the `retentionSleep` compression seam: the startup run's deletions and markers plus `GET /api/settings`'s `appliedRetentionDays: 180`; the first scaled day's cleanup deleting a run that crossed the window with no external kick; a REAL settings PUT to 30 whose reduced window lands at the NEXT daily run — the 100-day run deleted, the 20-day run kept, the marker flipping 180→30 through the GET; §5.6 stop with an absence wait strictly inside the half-day gate, read from a fresh post-stop connection), and the contract/component updates (`server-main.spec.ts`'s order pin gains `retention`; the settings double, the GET envelope rows, and the schema's integer-or-null rejection arms; `config-stores.spec.ts`'s marker read incl. the fail-soft rows; `settings-view.spec.ts`'s warning lifecycle — live on a reduced draft, on-load for an already-reduced configuration, self-clearing when the served marker catches up, absent for null and for out-of-range drafts where the range error stands alone). One testing lesson recorded: the composition suite's config file carries `logging.level: 'debug'` because D-023's reload applies the file's level — a mid-test PUT over a file without it resets the logger to `warn` and every later `info` assertion silently loses its records. The `en` catalog gains `settings.general.retentionReduceWarning`; `docs/openapi.json` is regenerated from the widened response schema; the storage README's "scheduling is not here" pointer now names `src/server/retention.ts`.

## D-179 — Task U-054's production adapter construction: a live-reader factory at the composition root, the shared clock and logger injected, and the CLI's pre-configuration paths deliberately left on the D-052 default (spec §6.2, §6.4, §7.2, §8.3, §10; task U-054)

**Date:** 2026-11-06 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§6.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#62-configuration-contract), [§6.4](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#64-runtime-settings-changes), [§7.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#72-retry-and-error-behavior), [§8.3](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#83-zai-coding-plan-integration-contract), [§10](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#10-time-and-time-zones) · **Tasks:** [U-054](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-026 (the §6.4 classification that already names `requestTimeoutSeconds` live — "governs the next request"), D-021 (the single shared clock), D-052 (the credential-check contract whose 15 s default the CLI paths keep), D-140/D-176 (the composition and polling wiring the factory must not disturb)

**Decision.** Task U-054 closes the verified review finding that the composition's registry default — `createInitialAccountProvider()`, a bare `new ZaiCodingPlanProvider()` — never received the validated `providers.zai-coding-plan.requestTimeoutSeconds` (the adapter kept its 15 s default) and constructed its own system clock, violating D-021 for `collectedAt`. Three interpretations are pinned. (1) **The production default is a live-reader factory, `createConfiguredZaiProvider({ config, clock, logger })` in `src/server/providers.ts`.** Every `validateCredentials`/`fetchSnapshot` call derives `timeoutMs` from the effective configuration (`providers['zai-coding-plan']?.requestTimeoutSeconds ?? CONFIG_DEFAULTS.provider.requestTimeoutSeconds`, ×1000) and delegates to a `ZaiCodingPlanProvider` constructed with `{ timeoutMs, clock, logger }` — the shared clock (D-021: `collectedAt`'s one source) and the shared redacting logger (§16: the adapter's skip reports and endpoints-2/3 soft-failure warnings become visible in production logs instead of silently dropped). The inner adapter is memoized by the effective deadline value: an unchanged configuration reuses one instance, a changed one constructs the replacement on the next request. (2) **Reload propagation is the reader, not a feed.** D-026 already classifies `providers` §6.4-live with the words "governs the next request", and `RESTART_REQUIRED_FIELDS` is the closed trio — so the timeout change had to stay restart-free, and the lazy per-request re-derive satisfies exactly that wording. The chosen shape keeps the registry entry's identity stable: `observingManualTests` keeps wrapping the same object, and the polling recorders — which capture `registry.get(...)` once per wiring build — hold the live wrapper and can never pin a stale deadline; no engine, registry, or re-registration change was needed (D-176's module untouched). The rejected alternative — an eager rebuild on a `providers`-applied reload feed — would have required re-registering the adapter and rebuilding the wiring for a timeout-only change, a larger change to U-051's engine with no behavioral gain. This is the house pattern for §6.4-live values consumed on the request path (the `pollingIntervalSeconds` and peak-hours `schedules()` readers, the retention window's read-at-run-time). The factory also carries optional `codingBaseUrl`/`apiBaseUrl` pass-throughs — the adapter's own loopback-mock test seams; production and the composition pass neither. The seconds value is trusted, not re-validated: the 5–60 s range is enforced where configuration enters (the schema and the load pipeline), D-042's stance for `timeoutMs`. (3) **The CLI's pre-configuration paths deliberately keep `createInitialAccountProvider()`'s D-052 defaults (the dossier base URLs, 15 s).** `init`'s connection test (§5.3 step 6) runs before the configuration write — D-102's ordering; the write is step 5's configuration half, deferred to the run's end, so a FRESH run has no file yet and a re-run keeps the same answer-driven factory rather than reading the file's provider section. `doctor`'s per-account probes are a diagnostic whose probe budget deliberately stays the spec's own §7.2 default — independent of the configuration under test (doctor does load the file, and a pathological 5 s setting must not shrink the diagnostic's own budget; the deliberate residual is that doctor may report reachable where a tightly configured service would time out — the connectivity row is a diagnostic observation, not a simulation of the service's deadline). The running service's manual connection tests (`POST /api/accounts/:id/test`) DO use the configured deadline — they flow through the registry's observed live wrapper. (Correction trail: the review round's two P2s folded in before landing — the §5.3 step-citation fix (step 5 creates the file, step 7 installs the service; the first draft wrongly wrote "the step-7 configuration write") and the composition-wiring textual pin, `test/unit/composition-provider-wiring.spec.ts`, because every behavioral suite injects `providers` and the default adapter's production base URLs are unreachable under the no-network guard.)

**Reasons.** The live-reader choice follows from the landed contracts rather than preference: D-026's classification and the settings surface's closed restart trio leave no restart-required option, and the polling engine's instance-capture design (recorder per wiring build) makes registry-identity stability the difference between "the recorders are always current" and "every providers-only reload must also rebuild the wiring". The memoization exists because per-request construction would re-parse the base URLs every cycle for zero variance — the deadline is the only option that varies, so it is the whole cache key. The CLI split is honest about what each path can know: a fresh init's test predates the file it will create (D-102's before-write ordering), the re-run flow keeps the same answer-driven factory rather than reading the file's provider section, and a diagnostic that inherits its budget from the artifact under test stops being an independent observation. Keeping `validateCredentials` on the same configured deadline inside the running service follows the setting's own scope — §7.2 names one provider HTTP timeout, not one per operation.

**Consequences.** A composed deployment now honors `requestTimeoutSeconds` end to end: polling cycles, the manual connection test, and every future registry consumer derive the §7.2 deadline from the live configuration (a reload changes it on the next request), `collectedAt` comes from the composition's shared clock (D-021 restored at the last unserviced seam), and the adapter's soft-failure degradation is observable in the §16 log stream. The exported surface (`createConfiguredZaiProvider`, `ConfiguredZaiProviderOptions` in `src/server/providers.ts`) is internal API under `src/`, not package surface; `createInitialAccountProvider` keeps its D-052 contract for `init`/`doctor`. The done-condition is pinned at three levels: the new `test/unit/composition-provider-wiring.spec.ts` (the composition's default-arm textual pin — reverting the wiring to the D-052 defaults factory, the original finding, fails it; behaviorally unobservable in the test environment since every composition suite injects `providers` and the default adapter's production base URLs are unreachable under the no-network guard), `test/integration/zai-coding-plan-configured-provider.spec.ts` (the factory over the loopback mock through its base-URL seams: the configured deadline expiring the collection cycle and the credential check — 120 ms injected through the reader with a 10× mock delay per D-087, the range's enforcement living at configuration entry; a schema-legal 5 s deadline delivering; `collectedAt` from an injected fixed clock; a reloaded deadline applying on the very next request through the SAME wrapper — an adapter pinned at construction would deliver; both default-fallback arms; the manual-test observation intact over the live wrapper in the composition's nesting; the shared logger capturing a soft-failure warning with the §15.4 marker absent), and the `server-providers.spec.ts` identity/construction pins. `src/server/README.md`, `src/cli/README.md`, and the provider dossier document the two-factory split.

## D-180 — SPECIFICATION 1.1's FSM-track alignment: archived-status dominance over §7.3, authenticated health diagnostics naming the polling engine, and the live restart-pending settings view (spec §7.3, §13, §14.5; the FSM track, [plan/TZ-fsm.md](plan/TZ-fsm.md))

**Date:** 2026-11-06 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§7.3](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#73-account-status-precedence), [§13](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#13-http-api), [§14.5](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#145-settings) · **Tasks:** [FSM-2](plan/tasks.md), [FSM-4](plan/tasks.md), [FSM-5](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-061 (archiving is terminal — the foundation the dominance rule reads), D-070 (the §7.3 derivation whose input set this extends), D-026 (the restart-requiring trio whose live diff surfaces), D-121 (the health route's public contract), D-179 (numbering neighbor only — U-054's provider split, unrelated content)

**Decision.** The 2026-11 implicit-FSM audit ([plan/TZ-fsm.md](plan/TZ-fsm.md), tasks FSM-1…FSM-5 in [plan/tasks.md](plan/tasks.md)) surfaced three places where a planned correction needed the specification to speak first; the document moves to 1.1 with three amendments, recorded in its header. (1) **§7.3 gains an archived-dominance rule**: an account whose storage row is archived (§8.2) never displays a runtime status (`Auth rejected`, `Format changed`, `Unreachable`, `Stale`, `Collecting`, `Fresh`) — the archived lifecycle fact outranks the entire precedence list, and the accounts surface keeps the archived state and the archive time visible. This closes the audit's reproducible contradiction (a hand-re-added archived id deriving `collecting`/`fresh` on the status surface while the accounts surface shows `archived`, reachable because `syncAccountsFromConfig` skips archived rows per D-061); the concrete wire shape — a rank-0 `archived` input to `deriveAccountStatus` or a route-level merge — stays the implementing task's design choice (FSM-2). (2) **§13's health row now names the polling engine** among the diagnostics an authenticated response may carry: the audit's dead-state finding (a scheduler killed by a broken seam with `running=false` consumed by nobody, `/api/health` answering the literal `{"status":"ok"}` in every state) becomes observable without widening the unauthenticated response, which stays byte-exact `{"status":"ok"}` (FSM-4). (3) **§13's settings row and §14.5 distinguish class from state**: GET `/api/settings` exposes the live restart-pending diff against the startup configuration beside the static §6.4 class markings, and the settings UI labels both (FSM-5) — closing the audit's finding that a hand-edited file plus `quotameter reload`/SIGHUP left the actual pending state invisible everywhere but the PUT response and the reload log.

**Reasons.** The three amendments are the audit's only spec-level findings: each planned rework either implements a rule the spec never stated (archived display), commits an explicit "may" into a concrete surface (health diagnostics), or extends a contract the spec describes only as a class marking (restart-required). Amending the specification before the tasks keeps the source-of-truth discipline (AGENTS.md): tasks implement spec text, never the reverse. The dominance rule is stated as an invariant, not a wire format, so the implementing task retains its design freedom while losing the freedom to contradict the projection.

**Consequences.** No behavior ships with this entry: it changes plan documents only — the implementing tasks (FSM-2, FSM-4, FSM-5) carry their own successor decisions, contract artifacts (`docs/api.md`, `docs/openapi.json`), and CHANGELOG entries, and TZ-fsm's task entries reference this entry as their normative basis. FSM-1 and FSM-3 (the dispatcher phase model and the single D-064 holder) are internal refactors with no spec footprint; their parity invariants live in TZ-fsm §3.3 alone. The spec's version line reads "1.1 (supersedes 1.0)" with the amendment list linked here; §19's MVP criteria are untouched (none of the amendments relaxes a criterion).

## D-181 — The development container runs as the host user: uid/gid build args remap the image's `node` user, ending the host-owned-file EACCES class (one-off dev-environment fix; no plan task)

**Date:** 2026-11-07 · **Status:** Accepted · **References:** the "Container / host boundaries" gotchas (incident at commit `67b75c1`, 2026-11-06), [docs/agents/environment.md](docs/agents/environment.md) ("Matching the host user"), the CI non-root execution note in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (unchanged by this decision), D-015 and D-144 (their uid-1000 output-routing rationale is superseded here; their committed-artifact recipes and freshness guards stand unchanged)

**Decision.** The development image's `node` user is remapped at build time to the host user's uid/gid: the Makefile exports `DEV_UID`/`DEV_GID` (`id -u`/`id -g`) for every recipe, `compose.yaml` passes them as build args (`${DEV_UID:-1000}`/`${DEV_GID:-1000}`), and the Dockerfile applies them by `usermod`/`groupmod` on the existing `node` user followed by the same `chown -R node:node /app /home/node /var/lib/quotameter` the image already performed. Three interpretations are pinned. (1) **The remap edits the user, never a numeric `USER`**: a passwd entry must survive (`HOME=/home/node` is resolved through it by the runtime, and npm/Playwright cache paths hang off `HOME`), and the `docktree exec` surface keeps resolving the same named user. (2) **The `1000:1000` defaults are the compatibility contract**: with matching ids the two remap steps are skipped by an explicit guard and the resulting image state is equivalent to the pre-D-181 image — `1000:1000` hosts, CI (which never builds this image), and any build without the variables see no change; the guard also keeps the expensive layers (apt, global npm) cache-stable across uid changes, since the `ARG`s sit below them, and a target id another image account or group already holds (root, `nobody`, the `users` group, …) fails the build with a named error instead of a raw `usermod`/`groupmod` crash. (3) **The write surface the fix targets is rewrites of tracked files, not generated output**: `prettier --write` (`make format`), `eslint --fix` (`make lint-fix`), and codegen acting on repository files created host-side — the class that failed with EACCES because the image user was uid 1000 while this host's user is uid 1001 and tracked files are mode 664. Generated output (coverage, reports, dist, schema scratch) keeps flowing to the data volume through the `compose.yaml` environment variables; the rule survives on cleanliness and one-convention grounds (artifacts out of `git status` and out of the package on every runner), no longer on the local uid mismatch.

**Reasons.** The documented workaround (gotchas entry of 2026-11-05: stdout-mode prettier plus host-side copy-back) predated the 2026-11-06 incident by a day and did not prevent it — the incident reached for a temporary `chmod 666` instead — so a documentation-only path was already falsified as a control. The trap was also structural, not incidental: format/lint-fix tools write exactly the files that need changing, i.e. the host-owned ones, so the everyday `make format` surface was broken precisely when it had work to do, and a per-file stdout recipe cannot back a whole-tree target. Among durable mechanisms, the runtime `user:` override was rejected: it leaves no passwd entry (HOME and cache paths break) and it cannot fix fresh named-volume seeding, whose root ownership comes from the image directories — only a build-time remap aligns the image user, `/home/node`, and the volume seed ownership in one step. The root-then-drop entrypoint pattern was rejected as disproportionate for a one-off dev-environment fix (an extra init layer, an exec-user split for `docktree exec`, and chown-at-start cost on every boot) when the per-worktree image model docktree already provides makes host-specific builds free. The known cost — one-time migration of pre-D-181 volumes (owned by uid 1000, unwritable by the remapped user) — is paid once per environment with two documented recipes (disposable `make clean` rebuild; data-preserving volume chown in environment.md) instead of per-write forever.

**Consequences.** Container-side rewrites of host-owned tracked files now succeed (`prettier --write` on a host-created `1001:1001 664` file verified live in both directions: EACCES before the fix, clean rewrite with unchanged host ownership after). `make check` is green in the rebuilt environment, proving the toolchain (npm ci into the fresh volume, Vitest, Playwright over the read-only host browser cache) is uid-agnostic under the remap. Environments predating the fix must migrate their volumes once — the failure mode if skipped is EACCES on the first container write inside the volumes (a coverage/reports/build write, or `npm ci` when the lockfile changed; `make deps` alone can pass untouched with a fresh stamp), documented with both migration recipes in `docs/agents/gotchas.md` and environment.md. A direct `docktree build` outside `make` rebuilds at the defaults and flips the trap back, so hosts building that way pin `DEV_UID`/`DEV_GID` in `.env` (`.env.example` documents the pair). The wiring is pinned executably by `test/unit/dev-container-uid.spec.ts` (the release-workflow guard's line-scanner pattern): a dropped `ARG`, a missing guard, or a compose/Makefile edit that stops exporting the ids fails `make check`. The CI non-root scheme (workspace chown + `setpriv --reuid=node`) is untouched — CI never builds this image, and the generated-output routing it shares with the container keeps its independent justification. No `src/` surface, package contract, or event format changes; the public npm package is unaffected. (Correction trail: the review round — deepseek-v4.1-flash, one round, APPROVE with 0 P0 / 0 P1 / 4 P2 / 6 P3, every finding verified live by the reviewer — is folded in: the stale pre-D-181 uid-1000 claims across the living docs and helper docblocks, the Makefile override comment's make-semantics correction, the migration failure-mode correction above with the stop-before-chown step, the collision guard, the executable pin, and the wording of this entry's compatibility claim; nothing was declined.)

## D-182 — Task U-055's `GET /api/auth/session`: the public session reader reporting the per-request §15.1 verdict and the collapsed cookie verdict, with the §15.1 facts scope-injected from the guard's own options, and D-159's UI cache reconciled as probe-free over the now-existing route (spec §13, §15.1, §15.2, §14.6; task U-055)

**Date:** 2026-11-07 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§13](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#13-http-api), [§15.1](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#151-network-and-authentication-modes), [§15.2](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#152-passwords-and-sessions), [§14.6](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#146-statuses-and-authentication-screens) · **Tasks:** [U-055](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-121 (the §15.1 classifier, its verdict vocabulary and facts lifecycle, and the `PUBLIC_AUTH_ROUTE_CONFIG` opt-out the reader joins), D-146 (the auth-routes plugin the reader registers into, the no-re-issue resolution it inherits, and the "this module's registration seam is where it joins" hand-off), D-159 (the UI tri-state whose no-probe rationale this entry reconciles — its consequences named this landing), D-124 (the session verdict the reader composes verbatim and the indistinguishable-absence rule the boolean collapses to), D-123 (the disclose-exactly-once discipline the reader keeps), D-134/D-142 (the epoch-millisecond family rule `expiresAt` follows), D-144 (the OpenAPI drift guard mechanically forced to the third operation), D-113 (the frozen error registry — the reader documents health's public error set)

**Decision.** Task U-055 lands §13's third auth row — "current session and auth-mode information" — as `GET /api/auth/session` inside the auth-routes plugin (D-146's recorded registration seam), with the contract in `src/schemas/api/auth.ts` (`SessionResponseSchema`: `{ mode, authenticated, session? }`, closed at every level), and pins four interpretations. (Correction trail: the task's review round — cursor-agent/grok-4.7-high, the maintainer-designated reviewer, one round, APPROVE with 0 P0 / 0 P1 / 0 P2 / 4 P3 — was folded in before landing (the D-119/D-122 precedent): the published document's sessionCookie scheme description now names the reader among the public operations (`scripts/openapi-document.mjs`, `docs/openapi.json` regenerated), `src/server/README.md`'s U-041 section states three routes again with the reader's section moved below the tests paragraph it had bisected, the injection type was renamed `AuthModeSource` so the classifier's own `AuthModeFacts` (D-121's four-fact input in `./auth`) keeps the unique use of its identifier, and the Unreleased task-180 bullet's "stays unwired" sentence now points at this entry instead of contradicting the endpoint that ships beside it.) (1) **The reader is public, and its mode report is the per-request §15.1 verdict, not the configured mode.** The route declares `PUBLIC_AUTH_ROUTE_CONFIG` exactly as health and login do: its client is the client that may hold no session yet (D-159's chicken-and-egg — every mode-fact surface being itself protected in the mode where the answer matters is WHY the row exists), and public is the only answer that can serve it. The `mode` field carries D-121's own three-value vocabulary from `classifyAuthMode` over the same four facts the guard reads (mode, bind loopback-ness, the live password thunk, the request's proxy indication): the raw config value would mislead (`auto` on a non-loopback bind or behind a proxy indicator still demands a password for the request at hand), while the verdict is the honest answer. The leak question is settled by the guard's own wire behavior: every verdict cell is already observable by probing any protected route (`not-required` answers 200, `required` answers 401, `proxy-without-password` answers §15.1's 403-with-instructions), so the reader states what a probe would force — and `not-required` never reveals whether a password is configured (D-121: a configured password does not tighten the loopback cell). The `proxy-without-password` cell answers 200 with the verdict string rather than re-throwing the 403: the endpoint's whole job is to tell the client the mode, the instructions text is operator-facing and already delivered by every protected route's 403, and a client that wants it can read it there. (2) **`authenticated` is the §15.2 verdict collapsed to a boolean, composed through `authenticateSession` verbatim.** A missing or empty cookie answers `false` without touching storage (the `createSessionAuthenticator` early-return pattern, inline); any other value is digested and judged half-open by the primitive itself; and every rejection — garbage, expired, logout-revoked, password-change-revoked — collapses into `false` per D-124's rule that storage-indistinguishable absence must stay indistinguishable on the wire. On the valid arm the sighting REFRESHES the row exactly as every authenticated request does (the reader is a sighting, not an exempt probe — forking a non-refreshing lookup here would create a check-expiry-without-consequence side channel and a second §15.2 discipline), and `session.expiresAt` reports the refreshed effective expiry in epoch milliseconds (the D-139/D-142 family rule), mirroring `LoginResponse.session.expiresAt`. No session is minted, no cookie is written (D-146's no-re-issue resolution binds the reader too). (3) **The §15.1 facts are scope-injected from the guard's own options — one source of truth.** `AuthRouteOptions` declares its true dependency (`authMode: AuthModeSource` — D-121's guard inputs minus the credential seam, deliberately not named `AuthModeFacts`, which stays the classifier's four-fact input), while `ApiRoutesOptions.authRoutes` is `Omit<AuthRouteOptions, 'authMode'>` and the `/api` scope injects the facts from its own REQUIRED `auth` member at registration: no construction site (the composition root, the drift guard's boot, the integration harnesses) can drift facts between the guard and the reader, and none needed changing. (4) **D-159's UI session cache stays probe-free — the reconciliation D-159's consequences invited.** The tri-state's design reasons survive the endpoint's existence: no boot round trip in the common `auto`-loopback world (where the probe would tax every SPA load for a fact the first protected load reveals for free), the wire's own answers as the flip authority, and the zero-fetch login page property. Consuming the endpoint later (exact sign-out visibility, deep-link pre-seed) stays a future UI task; the stale "stays unwired" texts in the READMEs and the schema header are reconciled to the new state.

**Reasons.** §13's row names the surface and its purpose; every open point had a landed constraint that made one answer the composition of record. Publicness follows the health/login precedent at the layer's own contract level (the opt-out is a route's declaration, D-121), and the alternative — a session-bound reader — is self-defeating: under `required` an unauthenticated client would get the guard's 401 and never a body, so the endpoint could not serve exactly the client its row exists for. Reporting the verdict rather than the config follows D-121's own fact split (the guard's per-request question IS the client's question); reporting nothing new before authentication follows from the guard already publishing every cell through its rejections. Reusing `authenticateSession` rather than a peek-only lookup follows D-124's sighting semantics (the primitive's refresh is not a side effect to avoid but the §15.2 inactivity window's own mechanism), and the collapsed boolean follows D-124's indistinguishable-absence rule verbatim. The scope-injection wiring answers the one structural risk the reader creates — two consumers of the §15.1 facts inside one scope drifting apart — by making the scope's existing required `auth` options the single source, with the plugin-level required member keeping the dependency honest (a scope that somehow wired authRoutes without auth facts would fail to typecheck, not silently misreport). The probe-free reconciliation takes D-159's own recorded baseline ("a served session/mode fact COULD, for instance, …" — permission, not mandate) and answers it with the tri-state's still-valid reasons rather than a UI behavior change, keeping this task's scope the published contract the review finding named (any non-UI client following the document got a 404).

**Consequences.** The published contract now carries §13's full auth row set: the third operation in `scripts/openapi-document.mjs` (public, GET, health's error-code set — `VALIDATION`, `FORBIDDEN`, `INTERNAL`; `UNAUTHENTICATED` deliberately absent since the handler cannot throw it), `docs/openapi.json` regenerated (the sessionCookie scheme description included), `docs/api.md`'s public set and reading guide updated, and the drift guard (`test/unit/openapi-published.spec.ts`) passes unchanged — its public-set and schema comparisons are derived, so the route's declaration keeps them honest in both directions. The exported surface (`SessionResponseSchema`, `SessionResponse`, `SESSION_AUTH_MODES`, `SessionAuthMode` in `src/schemas/api/auth.ts`; `AuthModeSource` and the widened `AuthRouteOptions` in `src/server/api/auth-routes.ts`) is internal API under `src/`; changing the mode vocabulary, the boolean's collapse, the refreshed-expiry semantics, or the scope-injection rule is a successor decision. A future UI consumption of the endpoint (exact sign-out visibility, deep-link pre-seed) changes no server surface — the contract here is final for that consumer. The done-condition is pinned executably: `test/integration/auth-routes.spec.ts` grows the reader's suite (the exact closed bodies per §15.1 mode including the fail-closed passwordless cells, the refreshed-expiry arm with the row's slide pinned in storage, the collapsed invalid-cookie arms — garbage, empty, revoked, expired-at-the-half-open-boundary — and the public-yet-Host-guarded construction proof through `buildHttpServer`: a hostile authority answers the root-scope FORBIDDEN envelope before the opt-out can matter, public is not unguarded), and `test/integration/api-sweep-contract.spec.ts`'s session probe flips from the 404 pin to the production composition's honest `{ mode: 'not-required', authenticated: false }`.

## D-183 — The API timestamp representation reconciled with §10: epoch-millisecond response integers recorded as the deliberate API form, the ISO 8601 UTC clause scoped to the §13 range request parameters, and the spec amended accordingly (spec §10, §13; task U-056)

**Date:** 2026-11-07 · **Status:** Accepted · **Spec:** [§10](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#10-time-and-time-zones), [§13](plan/SPECIFICATION.md#13-http-api) · **Tasks:** [U-056](plan/tasks.md) · **References:** D-139 (the recorded split this entry succeeds — its interpretation (1) becomes the spec's own text), D-128/D-130/D-142/D-182 (the epoch-ms response family: accounts, status/quota, peak-hours, expiresAt), D-073/D-068 (the interim `toUtcIso`-serialization statements this entry supersedes — D-073's consequences note, already superseded by D-142; D-068's consequences note AND its reasons clause; the D-142 precedent), D-021 (the clock discipline whose `toUtcIso`/`epochMsFromIso` pair keeps both directions canonical — its interpretation (4) cites the retired §10 sentence for `toUtcIso`'s output form, and this entry supersedes that citation while the emission contract itself, millisecond precision with `Z`, stands unchanged), D-180 (the spec-amendment precedent this entry follows), D-148 (the ECharts value-axis pin — the decisive consumer evidence)

**Decision.** Task U-056 resolves the verified review finding (deepseek-v4.1-flash, 2026-11-06 full-project review: §10's original sentence said "API timestamps use ISO 8601 UTC ending in `Z`" while every landed response contract carries epoch-millisecond integers) by executing the task's path (b): SPECIFICATION 1.2 amends §10 so the wire rule matches the landed family, and this entry records the representation as deliberate. The amended sentence states both directions: API **responses** carry timestamps as epoch-millisecond integers, while the ISO 8601 UTC form with an explicit offset or `Z` applies to the §13 range **request** parameters (`from`/`to` for history, events, and peak-hours). The choice was argued from a full consumer census, not from inertia: (1) **The API's sole consumer is numeric-native.** §13's first sentence declares the API "internal to the web interface", and the UI's rendering stack consumes epoch milliseconds by pinned design — ECharts' x-axis is a VALUE axis over epoch milliseconds precisely because ECharts' own time axis is local-or-UTC only (D-148), the §12.2 annotations compare timestamps numerically (`event.eventAt < window.from`), tick placement delivers epoch-ms `customValues`, and §10's own client-side rule (`Intl.DateTimeFormat`, relative times) takes numbers; an ISO wire would force a designed ISO→number conversion boundary into the chart adapters — a per-point `Date.parse` at up to §13's 1500-point budget across several fields per payload — serving a human-readable-JSON reader that does not exist (no external API consumer in v1 scope; the package is unreleased). (2) **The landed family staked the same direction five times.** D-128 (`createdAt`/`archivedAt`), D-130 (status/quota), D-139 (history/events, the recorded reconciliation reading §13's ISO sentence as request-side only — "one format per direction, never a mixed clock inside one body"), D-142 (peak-hours), D-182 (`expiresAt`): flipping the response half now would rewrite ~30 schema fields (including the `fromEpochMs`/`toEpochMs` names that encode the representation), every route emission site, ~25 wire-level test suites, and the regenerated OpenAPI — pure churn with zero functional gain, in the worst window (release tasks 184–200 pending, e2e acceptance worlds seeded with epoch-ms). (3) **The spec's own structure supported the split all along**: §10's ISO clause sat in the storage/time-zone section beside the SQLite sentence, while §13 — the section that governs the wire — names ISO only for the `from`/`to` request parameters; D-139 read the two sections that way, D-142 inherited it, D-182 applied it, and the amendment makes the reading the spec's text instead of a decision-trail archaeology. `toUtcIso` is not dead code: its one production consumer is `quotameter doctor --raw`'s stdout rendering (a human-facing CLI display choice), and it remains the canonical epoch→ISO direction beside `epochMsFromIso` (D-021) for any future surface that genuinely needs the string form.

**Reasons.** Both paths were executable; the evidence weighed against rewiring. Path (a)'s only structural argument was the literal §10 sentence — the very sentence under reconciliation — plus JSON human-readability and REST conventionality; but readability serves an audience §13 explicitly disclaims ("internal to the web interface", the reader being the bundled UI that immediately re-parses to numbers), conventionality serves external consumers v1 does not have, and the literal-sentence argument is resolved by the D-180 precedent: the specification yields to a verified audit finding through an amendment with its trail recorded, never the reverse. Path (b)'s cost is one sentence of spec text plus correcting the artifacts that repeated the ISO-response claim — a bounded, zero-risk edit — while path (a)'s cost is a cross-cutting wire migration landing against 25+ suites in the release homestretch. The tie-breaker is that the "contradiction" was never behavioral: every consumer, test, and generated document already agrees with the epoch-ms family; only §10's sentence and four doc-level echoes disagreed. A spec amendment that makes the majority representation lawful is smaller and more honest than a migration that makes the code agree with one ambiguous sentence.

**Consequences.** SPECIFICATION moves to 1.2 (supersedes 1.1) with the amendment listed in its header (the D-180 shape); §13's request-parameter sentence needed no change (it was always request-side). The artifacts that claimed ISO API responses are corrected in the same commit: `src/util/clock.ts`'s `toUtcIso` docblock (it cited "spec §10: API timestamps use ISO 8601 UTC ending in Z" — it now names its real consumer, the CLI stdout rendering, and this entry), `src/util/README.md`'s two stale claims (the `toUtcIso` bullet's "the API timestamp format of spec §10", and the rolling-ranges Consumers bullet that named the §13 endpoints as `toUtcIso` serializers — they only ever PARSE request boundaries through `epochMsFromIso`; the bounds themselves are computed client-side by the UI twin, D-147), `src/util/rolling-ranges.ts`'s docblock ("ready to serialize with `toUtcIso` for the §13 endpoints"), and `src/cli/raw-diagnostics.ts`'s rendering note (it cited "§10's ISO 8601 UTC `Z` form" for `doctor --raw`'s stamps — a CLI display choice, now cited as one). D-068's consequences note and reasons clause ("Stage 12's history/events/peak-hours routes serialize these bounds with `toUtcIso`"), D-073's consequences note ("serializes the timeline (epoch milliseconds → ISO 8601 `Z` via `toUtcIso` at its boundary)" — already superseded by D-142), and D-021 interpretation (4)'s parenthetical (citing the retired §10 sentence for `toUtcIso`'s form) stay untouched per immutability; this entry is their supersession of record — the emission contracts those entries pin (`toUtcIso` emits millisecond precision with `Z`; the strict explicit-offset parse gate) stand unchanged. `docs/api.md` and `src/server/README.md` cite this entry at their timestamp-rule statements; the OpenAPI prose and `docs/openapi.json` needed no change (they already state epoch-ms truthfully). The amendment is pinned executably by `test/unit/spec-timestamp-rule.spec.ts`: the amended §10 sentence, the version/amendment header, this entry's heading and its D-139 successor reference, `docs/api.md`'s response-rule statement, and the absence of the retired sentence from every normative artifact that carried it (the spec, `clock.ts`, `src/util/README.md`, `src/util/rolling-ranges.ts`, `raw-diagnostics.ts`) — the drift class this task found (a docblock or spec sentence quietly contradicting the wire) cannot silently return. Changing the API timestamp representation again — either direction — is a successor decision to this entry.
